title: Blue Planet III review – David Attenborough makes another absolute corker | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s funny, tense, stunningly forceful – the excellence of this franchise’s return is a bright flash of hopeful defiance
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: It’s funny, tense, stunningly forceful – the excellence of this franchise’s return is a bright flash of hopeful defiance
Content: What a fluke … Blue Planet III team film a southern right whale.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jo HaleyView image in fullscreenWhat a fluke … Blue Planet III team film a southern right whale.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jo HaleyTV reviewTelevisionReviewBlue Planet III review – David Attenborough makes another absolute corkerIt’s funny, tense, stunningly forceful – the excellence of this franchise’s return is a bright flash of hopeful defianceJack SealeSun 1 Nov 2026 16.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.23 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe settle down in front of a fresh Blue Planet, trying to escape a weary sadness that stalks us from several angles. It is a new natural history show narrated by the 100-year-old David Attenborough, so there cannot be many more of those to enjoy. It is a Sunday-night showcase on BBC One, which is nothing like as significant a shared cultural event as it once was. The film-making can’t possibly be as revelatory as the original Blue Planet in 2001, and even the impactBlue Planet IIhad on conservation in 2017 feels unrepeatable: the attention it brought to plastic pollution in the ocean turned out to be a minor blow struck in a battle against environmental catastrophe that we have, since then, continued to lose.But if we stop requiring it to be another landmark and appreciate it as just another wildlife series, Blue Planet III is a corker. Its excellence is a bright flash of hopeful defiance, and if it often falls into familiar patterns, that familiarity is a comfort.View image in fullscreenComedy act … harlequin shrimp.Photograph: BBC StudiosThere are, too, still wonders left to find. Episode one lands a scoop on the sandy sea floor in Shark Bay, Western Australia, where the Blue Planet team solve the mystery of why dolphins can be seen clutching sea sponges in their mouths. Stick around for the making-of featurette at the end, which reveals that solving the puzzle required the skilful use of the latest remote cameras, a careful courting of the dolphin in question, and the real risk of Alex, the cameraman, being eaten by a tiger shark.Around the corner in northern Australia, tawny sharks are doing something new, or at least new to us: not just hunting in packs, but pulling off a grand deception as a team by pretending to be asleep so as not to spook the herring, before working together to drive those tasty minnows shorewards, trap them, and feast.Every big new Attenborough show has to have a tense death chase, and for that we travel to Brazil, where it’s shark v turtle. The turtle loves to munch on seaweed at the bottom of the deeper waters away from the beach, but eventually it has to break the surface to grab some air, and by doing so it alerts the shark to its presence. A drone in the air above, and a camera fixed to a turtle’s back show us every play in the game as the turtle flees to the shallows and, when that doesn’t work, pulls off a sharp-turn manoeuvre that leaves the shark’s teeth glancing off hard shell.We must, also, have some comic relief, to the sound of jauntier music and a playful mischief in Attenborough’s tone. So off we go to Indonesia, to marvel at a pair of harlequin shrimp in their ridiculous two-tone livery, tumbling around adorably as they try to snack on a starfish. Their every movement is funny, although it’s less amusing for the starfish, which suffers the indignity of having one of its arms pulled off by two prawns in jester costumes.There’s more hilarity in the Brazilian mangroves, which brings us the obligatory report from the unnervingly relatable animal dating scene. In the sloppy mud of low tide, a fiddler crab is proud of his one big claw and waves it expectantly at the local females, only for the camera to pan back and reveal he is but one of hundreds of filthy loners, waggling their precious appendages and craving attention. We’ve all been there, son. The fiddler crab females, eyes on unbelievably cartoonish stalks that pop wryly up and fold dismissively back down, observe pitilessly as our friend is embroiled in a pincer-measuring contest with a rival, becomes fatally distracted, and is eaten by a passing scarlet ibis.Still, it’s not all fun, and when Blue Planet III turns serious, it does so with stunning force. A lovely clownfish busily attends to the anemone it relies on for shelter, cleaning the tips of its tendrils and bringing it oxygenated water with a vigorous flapping of fins – but it’s doing that because a heatwave is killing the anemone, and the coral reef they both live on. As the destruction brought about by climate breakdown is illustrated with a horrific before/after edit – the sumptuous colours of the reef melting into dead blackish brown, in two shots filmed months apart – Attenborough makes the same plea he has delivered umpteen times before.The delights we have been privileged to see are enough for us to wish, again, that this time he will be heard. “These tiny fish helped to protect their home,” the great man says, his voice these days weathered almost to a whisper. “Imagine what we could achieve if we all worked together to protect ours.”Blue Planet III is available on BBC iPlayer in the UK with an Australian airdate yet to be announcedExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDavid AttenboroughreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The truth about testicles: are we facing spermageddon? | Health | The Guardian
description: When it comes to fertility, testosterone and reproductive fitness, manosphere misinformation is rife - which can lead to a lot of heartache. Meet the man who wants to change all that
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: When it comes to fertility, testosterone and reproductive fitness, manosphere misinformation is rife - which can lead to a lot of heartache. Meet the man who wants to change all that
Content: Are we heading for species-icide?Photograph: Gian Kristiano Costeniero/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAre we heading for species-icide?Photograph: Gian Kristiano Costeniero/Getty ImagesHealthInterviewThe truth about testicles: are we facing spermageddon?Zoe WilliamsWhen it comes to fertility, testosterone and reproductive fitness, manosphere misinformation is rife - which can lead to a lot of heartache. Meet the man who wants to change all thatSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Ithink you can tell it’s for a lay audience,” says Michael Carroll, holding up his book, Your Nuts, its cover illustrated with two walnuts in a string bag. The book has arrived in tandem with worldwide concerns about falling birth rates. “Spermaggedon” is a chunky piece of this puzzle, part of a wider debate about whether and why we’re heading for species-icide. Are people deciding not to have kids because of climate anxiety and economic precarity? Or is this an unchosen fertility cliff edge, created by forever chemicals and our lifestyles? This is not a drill, says Carroll, a biologist and reproductive scientist at Manchester Metropolitan University. “There’s compelling evidence to support a historical decline in sperm count and sperm concentration over the last number of decades.” However, it’s just not that simple.First, it’s not a uniform picture and in some populations sperm counts are going up. The Danish YoungMenStudy, for instance, showed no drop between 1996 and 2022. In Ireland, a study of 15,000 men between 2008 and 2023 showed a 23% increase in sperm concentration.Second, it’s not a direct read-across from sperm count or concentration to fertility – those statistics don’t tell you anything about functionality. “If you deposit 300m sperm at the cervix, only a couple of dozen might actually reach the egg,” Carroll explains, and we still don’t know really basic things, like “how the sperm find an egg in the female reproductive tract. We can extrapolate from animal experiments and conduct in vitro experiments, but biologically, we don’t really know.”View image in fullscreenNo single issue causes infertility.Photograph: AleksandarNakic/Getty ImagesThird, “reproductive biology is a very complicated, multi-stepped, timed process requiring two individuals,” and even while we all understand that, any focus on a single issue, whether it’s sperm count or maternal age or generational anxiety, drives us away from an appreciation of that complexity and towards narratives so simplistic as to be basically superstitious. Back in the day, that woo-hoo was all “selfish women are leaving it too late”; now, thanks in part to an overheated manosphere, testicles are centre stage, freighted with notions of masculine destiny being threatened by an effeminate modernity. These aren’t ideal conditions for understanding what is going on.Carroll grew up in Ireland, the youngest of 12; his unimaginably large family seems salient to his career choices. He brushes off any attempt to psychotherapise him, though, saying this is just how Ireland was in the 60s and 70s (he was born in 1974). “It was very much a theocracy then, and the Catholic church wasn’t in favour of contraception.”He did his PhD in Newcastle, looking at how sperm fertilise eggs in marine animals. Then, after a postdoc at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in Dallas, Texas, looking at stem cells, he trained as a clinical embryologist, working in IVF, before returning to academia to teach reproductive science and reproductive biology, while researching the impact of lifestyle and environmental exposure.Although Carroll, who is married, has three children from a previous relationship and a stepdaughter, he is familiar with the pain of infertility, from his experience working in IVF.“It’s a great job, being an embryologist. You’re working at the very beginnings of life, patients really put their trust into you to handle their gametes, the sperm and eggs, and to culture their embryos and get them to a stage where you can give them a family. It comes with great joy. But you also have to be prepared sometimes to break devastating news.”View image in fullscreenCarroll’s book on the role of sperm in declining birth rates.Illustration: Fiach PressSome types of azoospermia – where no sperm is produced in the ejaculate – have no cure or treatment. It can be caused by anabolic steroid use, which is sometimes reparable when you stop taking them, but sometimes not. “Don’t take health advice from social media!” Carroll says, and writes, often.The global fertility picture, though, can’t just be blamed on TikTok. The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman will have in her lifetime. In 1963, it was 5.3; by 2024, it was 2.2. Most European nations are well below replacement rate (UK, 1.6; Spain, 1.1) and the only reason the world population isn’t falling is that people are living longer and infant mortality rates have dropped. Carroll keeps the economics front of mind: “some estimates put the total cost of raising a child at $280,000 [£209,000]. I don’t know anybody now who could afford to have 12 children.” Plus there are other social factors, including climate change anxiety. Older maternal age is plainly a factor, though paternal age should be considered more than it is. From 40 to 45 is considered advanced paternal age, and “older men tend to have higher levels of DNA damage or mutations, so there’s a higher prevalence of neuropsychiatric disorders in their offspring – bipolar will be one, schizophrenia will be another”.But what researchers are starting to call the “disappointment gap” – between the size of family people want and the one they have – is often driven by brute biological realities for both men and women, and where sperm is concerned, individual choices don’t cover it. In 2005, the epidemiologist Christopher Wild coined the expression “exposome”: the combination of environmental and lifestyle factors an individual would be exposed to throughout their life. Pollution, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, plastics, sunshine, processed foods, “everything matters,” says Carroll. “The best way to examine a drop in any biological marker would be prospective surveillance studies, where you follow populations over time.” The Danish data came from military recruits; the Irish sperm research, which was a retrospective study, took place in a fertility clinic.View image in fullscreenCarroll wants to broach the isolation of infertility.Photograph: Florence Law/The GuardianIf longitudinal research yields a frustratingly mixed picture, the understanding of sperm itself is maddeningly partial. We can measure numbers, but that doesn’t tell us anything about function.For sheer talismanic potency, though, sperm and testosterone are in a class of their own, drawing in social constructs of masculinity and meaning, which collide with these unexplained or only partially understood declines to produce narratives that are unscientific and often work directly against the science. In tandem with that, unwanted childlessness is rising sharply; infertility in broad terms is about 30% down to the woman, 30% down to the man and 30% unexplained. And for men, conventionally the silent partner in this discourse, a diagnosis of low fertility or infertility engenders “feelings of shame, demasculinisation, questioning their own identity and self-worth,” says Carroll. Whether as an embryologist or academic, he just wants people, with or without testicles, to understand what’s going on.Seeing sperm as magic, and its absence a curse, isn’t a new thing. In 1889, Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard, a professor of experimental medicine, mashed up the testicles of dogs and guinea pigs, extracted the juice, injected himself with it and reported “a radical change … I had regained at least all the strength I possessed a good many years ago” (he was 72 at the time). This unleashed an industry of quacks, flogging “Brown-Séquard Elixir” or, more commonly in the US, the “Elixir of life”. To be fair to Brown-Séquard, the literature at the time on what testicles may or may not be capable of was very undeveloped, and he was like the Withnail of medical research, gamely experimenting on himself throughout his life, once covering himself in varnish to discover the properties of skin (he was found unconscious and had to be cleaned with alcohol), another time giving himself cholera by eating the vomit of a patient, to see if he could cure it with opium (he was found unconscious again and had to be resuscitated).View image in fullscreenThe Withnail of medical research … Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard.Photograph: HUM Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesWhat concerns Carroll is the revival of that quackery, this time attached to testosterone. “What’s being promoted, especially by podcasters and social media influencers, is that testosterone is a quick hack to make you feel better and more invigorated, it’s a new elixir.” There is an ambient association of testosterone with “masculinity, aggression and competition, but behaviour is complex and it is too simple to put it down to the level of a hormone released from an endocrine gland”. A lack of vigour is more likely to be down to poor sleep or diet, and testosterone replacement therapy won’t put a dent in that, but it will along the way do the exact opposite of what you took it for. “It’s a very sensitive pathway of signals, the brain telling the testicles to produce testosterone. It’s called the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Some testosterone will be released to do its thing around the body; more is produced in the testicles. And that’s important for spermatogenesis” – or sperm production and development. If you take supplementary testosterone, he says, “it’s telling the brain to shut down your factory downstairs because we have enough testosterone now, thank you. It’s a negative feedback loop, spermatogenesis is affected, and then there’s poor sperm or no sperm output because of that”.It’s so pronounced with bodybuilders, who use testosterone replacement therapy to build muscle, that they get testicular atrophy, where their testicles shrink from underuse. It even has a name: “The Mossman-Pacey paradox,” Carroll writes, “whereby men enhance their visual cues of reproductive fitness while reducing their actual ability to reproduce.” Finasteride, a medicine that arrests and sometimes reverses male-pattern baldness by blocking the hormone DHT, has the top-line impact of boosting testosterone (because testosterone converts into DHT so, unconverted, it stays in the bloodstream). But libido, erectile function and mood track the androgen environment in general – so blocking DHT, like taking synthetic testosterone, is another signal to the brain to shut down the factory.View image in fullscreenPaternal age should be considered more than it currently is in the global fertility picture.Photograph: Posed by models; AleksandarNakic/Getty ImagesAlmost more from a geopolitical than a spermatozoic point of view, it’s sobering to see testosterone make it into US defence policy, with Pete Hegsethannouncing over the summerthe “High-T Department of War”, mandating that all servicemen over 30 have their testosterone tested, to maximise mental and physical readiness, strength and warrior ethos. It’s not even the stupidest thing to come out of the Department of War recently, but it’s a stark illustration of manosphere misinformation working its way up to policy, flooding the knowledge environment.And the problem with that is, it causes a lot of heartache. “A lot of men think that if they’re producing semen and they can get an erection, their bits are working,” Carroll says. “They don’t realise what’s going on within the testes, what can affect the quality of the sperm, what can reduce their capacity to reproduce. They don’t even start to look for the information until they’re trying to start a family and there’s a problem.”Smoking is strongly associated with lower semen volume, lower sperm count, and increased DNA damage. Obesity has been linked to reduced testosterone levels and lower sperm count, but not all studies concur on this, and most obese men are fertile (Carroll is careful to stress this in his book, possibly to ward off anyone thinking they can rely on BMI as a contraceptive). The most solid correlation is between obesity and infertility rather than low sperm count, which also has the most obvious mechanical causation – fat cells produce an enzyme, aromatase, which can convert testosterone to oestrogen. This can directly impair the function of testicular cells. Human bodies are amazing, though sometimes in annoying ways.View image in fullscreenManosphere misinformation working its way up to policy … Hegseth addressing the troops.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesMore broadly, it’d be good for everyone to “know how it works”, Carroll says. “Plenty of lads go to the gym and they’ll know a lot about muscle physiology and contraction and nutrition, and they’ll be able to use that knowledge to make informed decisions to get the physique or fitness level they want. It should be the same with reproductive health. If you know your testicles need to be two to four degrees lower than body temperature, and prolonged high temperatures can damage sperm production; if you know the risks of STIs, which can cause infertility not just in males but in females as well; if you know that taking Finasteride or TRT can have an impact; this will all help you make informed decisions and ask the right questions.”Fundamentally, Carroll wrote Your Nuts to broach the isolation of infertility. WorldHealthOrganization estimates that around 17.5% of the global adult population will experience infertility at some stage. People (like me) rail against the asymmetry of the discourse, that women’s health and choices are endlessly analysed and policed while men and their nuts slip under the radar, but it’s a painful and alienating experience, being the one that nobody talks about. “We’re in an infodemic era,” says Carroll, “and a lot of that information is not correct. I just want to tell people what we know, and more importantly, what we don’t know.”Your Nuts: The Science of How They Work and What it Means for Your Fertility by Michael Carroll is published by FiachPress (£22.99)Explore more on these topicsHealthFertility problemsMenMen's healthinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: What does Olivia Colman’s hot sex with a basket tell us about heteropessimism? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: In Wicker, the love interest is a man made of plaited twigs. In romantasy, women are getting it on with goblins, elves, minotaurs and mothmen. Is this bad news for heterosexual men?, asks Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: In Wicker, the love interest is a man made of plaited twigs. In romantasy, women are getting it on with goblins, elves, minotaurs and mothmen. Is this bad news for heterosexual men?, asks Emma Beddington
Content: Beware of splinters … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.View image in fullscreenBeware of splinters … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.OpinionWomenWhat does Olivia Colman’s hot sex with a basket tell us about heteropessimism?Emma BeddingtonIn Wicker, the love interest is a man made of plaited twigs. In romantasy, women are getting it on with goblins, elves, minotaurs and mothmen. Is this bad news for heterosexual men?Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 14.09 ESTShareApologies if this is too personal, but is there anything in your home that turns you on? A sleek standard lamp, say, or a sexy piece of kitchen kit? I’m casting an eye around here and wondering. I used to have the hots for my furry heated throw when it was sleek and glossy, but it’s so matted and grubby now, it gives me the ick. I still fancy the big kitchen cupboard, though. It is steely blue and so capacious, and its generous spice rack gives me a frisson every time I look inside.I’m prompted to ask by the release ofWicker, the loopy erotic fable in which Olivia Colman’s fisherwoman enjoys a mutually supportive, sexually satisfying partnership with Alexander Skarsgård, whom the basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) has woven from wicker. I haven’t seen it yet, but the trailer is joyful and the premise is sending people – mostly women – wild.The internet is full ofhorny commentsabout Skarsgård who, the fisherwoman’s neighbours gossip, is “strong as a tree and just as hard” (he’s certainly very pleasingly woven; a real statement piece). I also enjoyed an article in New York magazine, entitledWhat Would Happen If You Had Sex With a Wicker Dick?, in which an exceptionally game gynaecologist addresses this question with utmost seriousness, tackling splinters, lubrication and condom advisability, while also declaring, disarmingly: “But what do I know about wicker? Nothing.”Unfortunately, I feel obliged to spoil everyone’s fun by wondering: what does it mean? Why has a film whose romantic (erotic) hero is plaited twigs sparked such enthusiasm? Have we all become basket cases? Because this wicker husband is no outlier: non-human romantic heroes have been wildly popular for a while.At the more human-shaped end of things,romantasyhas exploded (there’s wild excitement for romantasy queenSarah J Maas’s latest), revealing a seemingly infinite appetite for stories about humans getting it on with goblins, elves,minotaursand mothmen. Sentient object smut gets even wilder: I took anonline quiz, guessing which objects of desire came from a real cultural product and which were made up, and completely flunked. There’s real erotica, I learned, about a front door, coronavirus, a garden rake, a coffee mug and Clippy the Microsoft Word paperclip (which does have very come-hither eyes).‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie WickerRead moreSo are humans sick of each other – and are women in particular sick of men? Depressing cautionary tales about everything from men’s reluctance to commit, to manosphere-enabled and excused misogyny have fuelled a climate of reportedheterofatalism: exhausted disillusionment with the unequal burdens and trials of heterosexual relationships. Wicker features some pretty on-the-nose heteropessimism: married women have to wear giant thunking collars and the men mostly seem to be boorish lumps. So why not choose wicker? You don’t need tomankeepa woven spouse and they won’t add much to the domestic load – at most they need a quick wipe with a damp cloth and some furniture polish.But hang on. Skarsgård may be part 70s coffee table, sure, but he’s all man: he’s man-shaped, fixes stuff, wears tweedy trousers and, of course, has a penis. Even the more out-there object erotica novels “overwhelmingly pair human women with male creatures and objects”, according to New York magazine. Unsurprising, maybe, when the latestONS dataindicates 93.7% of UK women identify as heterosexual. Reports of heterofatality may be exaggerated.If anything, I see Wicker-mania and its ilk as indicative of ayearning escapism, a desire for life to be lighter, sexier and sillier. When everything is horrible, why not imagine, and enjoy, a world where – unlike this one – anything’s possible, including mutually satisfying relationships, gender equality and sex with macaroni cheese (alsoreal, yes)?Speaking of escapism, back to cheerier matters. If nothing at home is igniting your loins, what would you make a sexual partner out of other than flesh and blood? Wicker seems way too scratchy. I came up with a shortlist of cashmere and cake, but neither seem sufficiently sturdy.Hmm, maybe Christmas cake, specifically, would work? It’s extremely durable and delicious, and if your fruity lover starts getting difficult, you could always keep them in check by biting a warning chunk off their edge. Yes, this could give Stir-up Sunday a whole new meaning.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds? | Autism | The Guardian
description: There has been a steep rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years. Is that down to greater understanding – or overdiagnosis?
Author: John Harris
Headline: There has been a steep rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years. Is that down to greater understanding – or overdiagnosis?
Content: Illustration: Brian Rea/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Brian Rea/The GuardianAutism‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?There has been a steep rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years. Is that down to greater understanding – or overdiagnosis?John HarrisSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe home of 85-year-old Uta Frith does not exactly look like the latest front in the culture wars. Located in a serenely quiet corner of north-west London, it suggests a life still well lived, a set of deep interests and an idyllic kind of retirement. There are so many books that some are reachable only using a very tall ladder. The four hours I spend talking to her – and her husband Chris, an expert in schizophrenia – are an absolute pleasure. There is no sense of outrage or upset: even when I ask her about the stream of hostile and abusive emails she has recently received, she is relaxed and phlegmatic. “I tend to cope by just deleting them,” she says. “I don’t dwell on it.”“It” is a reference to the controversy kicked up by her recently expressed views on a subject that sits at the heart of Frith’s academic career: what it is to be autistic, and who should or shouldn’t qualify for a diagnosis. Back in March, Dame Uta Frith – she was honoured with the title seven years ago – gave an interview to TES magazine (formerly the Times Educational Supplement) scattered with stark pronouncements. Among them was a claim that the so-called autistic spectrum has “gone on being more and more accommodating”, to the point that it “has come to its collapse”. Then, in August, shepublished a piecein the academic journal Psychological Medicine claiming autism was in dire danger of being turned from a “precise, clinical” term into a “vague, culturally amplified identity category”.What she said has inevitably added to the cacophony of political and media noise about rising autism diagnoses. In the UK, there was a787% increasebetween 1998 and 2018, with the rise greater for women than men, and the single biggest jump among adults; credible American stats have shown an increase across the whole population of 175% between 2011 and 2022, with the largest rise occurring among 26- to 34 year-olds (in both countries, childhood rates have also leapt up). Once, Frith agreed with the idea of a broad autistic spectrum; now, she has come to the conclusion that many people diagnosed as adults are so different from the autistic people whose condition becomes obvious in their early years and have learning disabilities that most of the former group do not merit the label “autistic” at all.“Some of them, I think, are being wrongly influenced by social media to believe that they’re autistic, because it’s a possible way to explain your difficulties,” she tells me. “And then we have a subgroup of people who used to be called neurotic, who have all sorts of mental issues, including anxiety. And a kind of hypersensitivity.”Over the summer, Frithdid an interviewwith the Times’s Andrew Billen, in which she expressed opinions about the TV presenter and autism activist Chris Packham – who was diagnosed with what was then known as Asperger’s syndromewhen he was 44– which she says she did not expect to make it into print. “He cannot be autistic in my opinion,” Frith said. “It is just absolutely absurd to me that somebody who can communicate as brilliantly as he does – that is what I call a blatant contraindication.” The day after we meet, Packham is scheduled to pay Frith a visit with a BBC camera crew: as with just about everything she talks about, her feelings on this prospect are characteristically relaxed (I subsequently learn that they got on very well).I have a 20-year-old autistic son, James, who also has learning disabilities – as well as an amazing talent for music – and now goes to a specialist further education college. When he was diagnosed 17 years ago, understanding and awareness of autism seemed to be moving in roughly the right direction. I could never have anticipated the way it has ballooned into a subject of such controversy, which puts me and millions of others in a worldwide community of people who now follow the news with a mixture of bafflement and dread.On and on it goes. The word “overdiagnosis” is now common currency, partly because of the bestselling bookThe Age of Diagnosisby the neurologist Suzanne O’Sullivan, which claims that autistic people “with the greatest need are becoming invisible” and that there are questions to be asked about diagnoses that cause “more harm than good”. Donald Trump and his health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr look ahead to the absurd prospectof an autism “cure”. The rightwing press and its favoured politicians – whose loathing of any kind of diversity inevitably triggers a mistrust of neurodiversity – rage about how many neurodivergent young people are on disability benefits. Celebrities constantly lay claim to being on the spectrum. Meanwhile, there are real-world tragedies: Jason Arday, for instance, was not only a black Cambridge professor who ended his own life after relentless coverage of his allegedly specious claims about his life story andachievements.He was also autistic – which statistics show put him at a hugely increased risk of suicide.double quotation markThe extension of the spectrum has gone too far. There are too many cases that were not anticipated to appearView image in fullscreenAutism expert Uta Frith, who fears the term has become a ‘vague, culturally amplified identity category’.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianIn December last year, the then health secretary Wes Streeting commissioned three eminent academics to carry out what the government called an “independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism”. The result,published a few weeks ago, traced the increase in autism diagnoses to “socio-cultural changes in awareness [and] recognition”, and the fact that “diagnostic concepts have also broadened”. But in some people’s eyes, its authors had tried to have their cake and eat it. “If present trends continue we are clearly entering a phase in which the balance of risks is changing … towards an increased risk of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis,” they said. The review recommended much closer monitoring of privately run clinics that diagnose autism and ADHD. But it also said “we cannot conclude that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale”.Frith is at pains to stand well away from all this political and cultural hurly-burly, telling the story of her change of mind as a matter of careful thought and worry that, as so-called high-functioning people cast the popular understanding of autism in their image, the needs of more intensely autistic children and adults are in danger of being forgotten. A few minutes after we have talked about the common idea that autism can be a “superpower”, she says, “I have had emails from parents who say, ‘I no longer call my child autistic. When somebody asks, I say he’s intellectually impaired, and they will say, ‘Oh, all right.’ But if I say he’s autistic, they will expect things that are just …not likely.’”Frith is one of the tiny cluster of people who came up with the understanding of autism now accepted across most of the world. In 1964, she came to London from Germany, and found her niche at the Institute of Psychiatry, connected to the famous Maudsley hospital. She had planned to study obsessive-compulsive disorder, but her head was turned by new research into what were then known as “psychotic” children.She vividly remembers her first encounters with such kids, at the UK’s first dedicated school for autistic children, in Ealing, west London. “I was fascinated,” she tells me. “The astounding thing was that they could do things I would not expect children who were then called mentally retarded to do.” Like what? “Jigsaw puzzles, tests that would be given to very young children to measure their intelligence. They did pretty well, sometimes in a way that was completely unconventional – like completing the jigsaw with the picture on the underside.”Frith ran experiments that showed the autistic minds tended to be more responsive to visual cues than words. In 1989, she also came up with the so-called theory of Weak Central Coherence: the idea that autistic people tend to fixate on detail rather than big, over-arching things such as stories and themes.While all this was going on, she was also keeping the company of the psychiatristLorna Wing (who had an autistic daughter)and the psychologist Judith Gould – who would spend four years in the 1970s transforming the understanding of autism. Focusing on the London borough of Camberwell, they interviewed more than 900 teachers of children under 15 who, at one point or another, had needed either psychiatric treatment or attention from social care services. They then visited and closely observed every one of the 132 children those interviews suggested might be autistic, which eventually led to the conclusion that autism was a much more widespread and complex phenomenon than had been previously thought, best considered a “continuum” – or, as they were to later term it, a “spectrum”, a word intended to conjure up images of how light works, combining different colours into a single beam.Autism, Wing said, ran “from the most profoundly physically and mentally retarded person … to the most able, highly intelligent person with social impairment in its subtlest form”. But what unified everyone on the spectrum was what she and Gould called the “Triad of Impairments”: problems with social skills, reciprocal (ie give-and-take) language and “social imagination”, most obviously evident in children not understanding the concept of pretending while they play. Though subsequent diagnostic criteria have changed – it is now accepted, for instance, that autism usually involves sensory issues including heightened or lowered sensitivity to sound, light, texture, heat and cold – these ideas are still at the heart of what most people think autism is, along with a tendency to deep obsessions, or what the autism vernacular calls “special interests”.Frith says when the idea of a spectrum arrived, “I was more than happy. I was always worried about the sort of marginal cases, so that was one good thing. And the other was that we had more people to work with.”‘He nails it on the first take’: how the Beatles helped my autistic son find his voiceRead moreThe subsequent story of autism included Wing’s creation (in 1981) of the category known as Asperger syndrome: a term named after the work with a group of “little professors” of the Austrian psychologist Hans Asperger, now understood as a collaborator in the Nazi extermination of disabled children. Wing used the term to describe autistic people without language issues or learning disabilities. In 1994, it was included in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association and now on its fifth edition. But it was taken out in 2013, leaving “autistic spectrum disorder” as a single broad category, now broken down into three levels: “requiring support”, “requiring substantial support” and “requiring very substantial support”.By then, Wing – who died in 2014 – and her colleagues’ work had led on to the idea of neurodiversity, and the activism of so-called autistic self-advocates. And as all this happened, Frith says she began to feel increasingly uneasy. “I suddenly realised, maybe 15, 20 years ago,” she says, “that I had talked completely differently about autistic people in the past compared with people who didn’t have learning disabilities and had been diagnosed more recently. I’d used completely different language and completely different arguments. And that seemed to me to be a sign of something not being quite right.”She is sceptical about some concepts that are now taken for granted by many autistic people and autism specialists. A good example is “masking”: people – particularly women and girls – trying to cover up autistic traits through a painstaking process of copying which, in most accounts, after a day at work or school, leaves them feeling exhausted. “It’s a non-scientific concept, if ever there was one,” she says. “It’s completely unfalsifiable: if you could use the idea that you’re masking – ie you don’t have any symptoms to show … ”But, I counter, people who mask say, “I have got symptoms to show. And I show them when I get home from school or work or when I’m on my own.”“But that’s entirely subjective. It’s true that they have fatigue and exhaustion. These are the really important things to notice. But why believe that they are caused by masking?”Because it’s such an effort, I reply.“We all do that,” she says. “It’s acting, whichisexhausting. But what does that have to do with autism?”Well, I say, the deficits and impairments they’re concealing are stereotypically autistic. But what Frith craves, on this subject and many others, is scientific certainty. “The studies I’ve seen measure masking on a test with items on it like ‘I copy body language’. And I dismiss that as non-scientific because subjective experience isnot reliable.” She is keen to emphasise there is usually a tentative element to what she thinks and says. “I’m not certain. I may be wrong. But I think we’re at a point where it’s useful to have a debate.”Disagreement with Frith’s opinions has inevitably been led by some of those aforementioned self-advocates. Among them is Mary Doherty, an Irish anaesthetist who was diagnosed at 45 and has a son and daughter who are both also on the spectrum. She has memories from her schooldays of trying desperately to mask her differences, and failing. Now she is one of the founders of Autistic Doctors International, which promotes the idea that medics who are on the spectrum “bring a variety of strengths to healthcare, including an array of benefits for autistic patients”.We spend 90 minutes talking on an outdoor cafe terrace near London’s Victoria station. Throughout the conversation, Doherty constantly stretches and loosens an elasticated hairband: an example, she says, of the “stimming”, or self-stimulatory behaviour, many autistic people use as a way to calm themselves. Frith and others, she says, are effectively averting their eyes from “the harm that’s done by invalidating people’s life experience. If you are autistic, understanding your autistic nature is life-changing. It’s so damaging to deny that to people, particularly people who are already at risk of mental health problems.”Think your parent is neurodivergent? Here’s what you need to knowRead moreEven if they have a blurry intersection, I suggest, there is a pretty obvious distinction between her kind of autism and more intense, “classic” varieties, which is part of what people are now arguing about. “It’snota clear division, she retorts. “If you see me on a bad day … ” So does she feel a strong instinctive affinity with, say, an autistic person who is non-verbal and has learning disabilities? “Yes. And that was probably one of the biggest shocks to me in the earliest days of my advocacy journey.”One big current argument, as she knows, is that when it comes to public services and healthcare, more confident, articulate autistic people will somehow get to the front of the relevant queues much more quickly than more intensely affected people (or their parents and carers). And as a consequence, people with more complex needs will get neglected. Maybe, in fact, that has been happening already.In thousands of people’s everyday lives, the debate about supposed “overdiagnosis” – and whether certain people are now prioritised over others – is very real, not least at the proverbial school gates. One mother I speak to, who asks to remain anonymous, lives in the south-east with her partner and two children, one of whom is a girl with an intense kind of autism that seems to defy cliched categories: she is bright and intellectually curious, but also has profound sensory issues and difficulty navigating through the world that means she requires constant support at school.She has recently heard that one in five of the children in her daughter’s year are reckoned to be autistic. “From day one, I just felt my child’s needs were lost and misunderstood because that word now applies to so many children.” A lot of kids, she says, “find modern school life very difficult. And people are seeking a diagnosis so their child is treated as an individual. I don’t blame them for that. But it isn’t helpful to the children who have a classically autistic inability to cope with those environments.”She has one other concern. “When my daughter got her diagnosis, I would have described her as high-functioning because she was verbal and she could read and write. But that term has shifted very far, even from my child. It now seems to mean children who can do every sort of activity; it’s becoming unrecognisable. And you wonder: how wide can the spectrum be?”Is there any way out of what feels like a polarised stalemate? One possible solution is offered by Frith’s one-time protege Simon Baron-Cohen, another autism expert who has felt the heat of cultural controversy, thanks to his theory that autism might be a byword for what he used to call “the extreme male brain”, low on empathising, but good at understanding systems and patterns (earlier this year, he said such language was no longer useful).Baron-Cohen’s working life has been defined by autism since he began working at a trailblazing autism school called Family Tree in north London in the early 1980s. And he has seen plenty of past conflict about who should and shouldn’t be considered for particular diagnostic categories, not least when Asperger syndrome was first talked about.He now thinks the catch-all term “autistic spectrum disorder” – or “autistic spectrum condition” – is proving to be increasingly problematic. “By removing the diagnosis of Asperger syndrome [from the diagnostic manual] and lumping all forms of autism together,” Baron-Cohen recently wrote, “we have ended up with individuals like Elon Musk calling himself autistic, and a child being called autistic who will never leave home or live independently and who has significant learning and language disabilities … So, in 2013, overnight, the prevalence of autism massively increased, as now both major subgroups of autism were folded together.”I speak to Baron-Cohen – who is in his rooms at Trinity College, Cambridge – via Zoom. “The term ‘autism’ is too much of a sledgehammer,” he says. “It’s being used to cover too many things. So … I want to see subgroups.We can call them type one, type two, type three, and we can decide. You know, type one is autism with an intellectual disability and a language delay. Type two is autism without an intellectual disability. But the reason why I’d be happy to see a proliferation of subgroups is the research that now shows most autistic people have at least six diagnoses: autism with ADHD, autism with dyslexia, autism with dyspraxia, autism with anxiety, autism with gastrointestinal pain, autism with or without epilepsy. I just think we need to start being more precise.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI have one possible objection to that, to do with my son James. Most people who are familiar with the politics of autism will know there is often an awkward tension between articulate self-advocates and parents – like me – who have no choice but to speak on their children’s behalf. And woven through it, for me at least, is a nagging ambivalence. I sometimes worry that ideas of autism being a difference rather than a disability overlook James’s lived experience. On the other hand, because of the broad definition of autism, it’s really helpful for me to be able to say, “You know that thing Chris Packham’s got? This is my son’s version of that.” If we move to subtypes and he’s given the label type one – which is understood as lower functioning – that’s going to other him, and I don’t want that to happen.double quotation markThe term autism is too much of a sledgehammer. We need to start being more preciseView image in fullscreenClinical psychologist Simon Baron-Cohen, who agrees talk of a spectrum is proving increasingly problematic.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian“Nobody wants to be othered,” Baron-Cohen replies. “We want to make sure all subgroups are equal in terms of access to resources and cultural esteem. And we must never prejudge what someone is capable of.”Two days after my chat with him, I go back to where the modern understanding of autism all started: the clump of buildings around the Maudsley, where I meet Francesca Happé, another Frith protege and professor of cognitive neuroscience at King’s College London, who is now pioneering research into how the condition is experienced by older people.“Uta’s right that the most important things to know, to the extent that you can know anybody’s life trajectory, are about levels of language and speech and general intellectual functioning,” Happé says. “Within autism, they’re the most determinate things.”But she clearly worries about categorisation and her sense that it may well not reflect people’s psychological complexity.“We tried it with Asperger’s: we had a go at, on the one hand, high-functioning, lots of language and no intellectual impairment, that type of autism – and then all the rest of autism. And it didn’t work – because everything blurs, and because people change.“I’ve met people where, at first sight, I wouldn’t pick up anything. I meet them on another occasion when they’re more tired, and I can begin to see the mask almost literally slip. There’s a particular woman who came to stay with us, and my children could have diagnosed her within about half an hour when she was out of her comfort zone. You know, if she had a bad day, it was adisastrousday.”Happé has a tentative solution to the overdiagnosis wars. “I would say there’s an argument for autism spectrum disorder as a medical diagnosis, and it must require support. If you don’t require support, then by all means you can say you have an autistic identity, but you don’t have autism spectrumdisorder, because it’s not impairing you. What you need at the ground floor, before you get to the disorder level, is understanding: self-understanding, understanding from other people, reasonable accommodations. That’s level zero.”Which brings us to perhaps the most important question of all: right now, amid all the hue and cry, what is it like to be autistic, particularly if some people might place you – rightly or wrongly – on the borderline? When I contact the National Autistic Society, they put me in touch with two women who roughly fit that description.Hina Shaikh’s story is so fascinating, it probably deserves a book. She lives in Bradford and was diagnosed with autism four years ago, when she was 42. She was working in a car dealership, and made a successful sale to a man who turned out to be a social worker. “He just said, ‘I think you might be an undiagnosed autistic adult’, just like that. And I was taken aback: you thought of special needs children who weren’t living normal lives. But he started pointing out everything he had noticed: I didn’t make eye contact, I didn’t shake his hand, I didn’t do small talk. And he noticed how I had organised my desk, how all my pens were lined up.”double quotation markIn the Asian-Muslim community, if a child is autistic, you take them to an Imam and an amulet is going to cure themView image in fullscreenHina Shaikh, who was diagnosed four years ago, aged 42.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianAs she read up on autism, all this seemed to chime with her past history, and her profound unease about everyday social rituals. After her GP instigated a spell of form-filling, she found the average local wait for an NHS diagnosis was 18 months, and went instead to a private clinic in Shropshire. There, a consultant said, “If I had diagnosed you 15 or 20 years ago we would have called it Asperger’s. Now it’s all under one umbrella called autism. But yes, you are autistic.”She still receives no support for her autism, but has since changed jobs and is now employed by a neurodiversity-friendly company that allows her to work from home. The big issue she spends her spare time on is the lack of autism awareness in her own community. “After I was diagnosed, I went on YouTube, trying to find something in Urdu that would explain autism to my mum. And there was nothing. In the Asian-Muslim community, with a lot of people, if a child is autistic, you take him or her to an Imam and an amulet or something is going to cure them.”Her dad, she tells me, left the family home in his 50s (“He was one of those people who should have never got married – he couldn’t deal with family life”) and moved to Manchester. He died of Covid-19 in 2021, and she and her sister were given the keys to his flat, where they found apparent proof that Shaikh’s autism had genetic roots. “That’s when we realised he had special interests: there were 13 bikes there, and toolboxes, and collections of albums we couldn’t even have imagined.” They also found a pile of medical paperwork. “I realised they were his autism diagnosis. He’d been diagnosed in his late 50s, after he left.”Shaikh likes Baron-Cohen’s idea of new autistic subtypes. “I think maybe they could have changed the name of Asperger’s because of its connotations, but they still needed to keep different criteria and different diagnoses. I’m gonna be very blunt now, but I am not like an autistic child who is having severe meltdowns, and who is really struggling socially and academically.”double quotation markPeople saying, ‘Oh, I’m a little bit autistic’ or, ‘I’m neuro-spicy,  I’ve got a touch  of the tism’ makes me cringeView image in fullscreenAbigail Stow, who was diagnosed in April.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianAbigail Stow is 28. She was diagnosed in April and lives in Stevenage, where she works in the NHS, “booking, doing counselling appointments, answering emails, stuff like that”. As she grew up, she tells me, “I was very horrendously bullied, and it caused a lot of anxiety and depression, and at one point self-harm.” Even if she displayed some signs of autism, she got no extra help or support at school. Then, when she was 19, her stepdad heard a podcast about girls and autism. When she listened, she heard loud echoes of her own experience. “So I went to my GP, got booked in for an assessment, and they turned around to me and said, ‘You can’t possibly be autistic or ADHD because you’re giving me eye contact and you have a boyfriend, and you’re able to work.’ So I was like, I must just be weird.”Nonetheless, she carried on reading about autism and became increasingly convinced she had autistic traits. “I was really struggling to hold down work. If places were busy, that really stressed me out. I’d wear noise-cancelling headphones if stuff was too noisy. And I really struggled to make friends and keep them.”She has an autistic brother who got his diagnosis two years earlier (“School just thought he was an angry kid”) and two special interests: dogs and heavy metal. “When I’m obsessed with something,” she says, “it becomes my whole personality.”She also freely talks about masking. “Work is very masky. I think people at work would probably describe me as outgoing and bubbly and chatty. And then I come home and I’m like, don’t even talk to me.”When she was diagnosed – by a private company paid by the NHS – it was an epiphanic experience. “I cried. I could breathe again. It just felt so good, knowing I wasn’t crazy and I wasn’t wasting anyone’s time.”I wonder how she feels if she sees people on, say, TikTok, laying claim to autism when they seem to show none of the signs? “It really depends. I don’t know … I feel like they’re almost trying to, like,cutifyautism – like, ‘Oh, I’m a little bit autistic’ or, ‘I’m neuro-spicy, and I’ve got a touch of thetism.’ It just makes me cringe. But I also appreciate [that there are] some people like that who are autistic as well. It’s complicated.”Back in north-west London, I ask Uta Frith what she thinks will happen next. “Things come in waves,” she says. “There are sometimes subgroups, then sometimes they’re put together again, and then it splits back up. You always have the splitters and the lumpers, don’t you?”And we’re still in a lump phase, I suggest. “Yes. And the next one will be a split. It’s the pendulum swing.”And why does she think that will happen?“Just because the extension of the spectrum has gone too far. There are too many cases that were not anticipated to appear.”Mary Doherty stands on the opposite side: she insists that what some people see as overdiagnosis is really just the birth pangs of a proper understanding of how many people are autistic. “Without the self-advocacy movement, when [autism] was just people who were obviously disabled, that picture was incomplete. I think we’re moving towards a much more holistic and complete version of what it means to be autistic.”Is there a way through this ever more intense conflict? Simon Baron-Cohen has a different belief again: in accepting an extended spectrum, but moving into what he calls “precision diagnosis” and “support for whichever group you’re in. Because I see them as equally needy; it’s just that the needs are different.”And all the time, yet another quintessentially 21st-century battle rumbles on. “I’d like the polarisation of views to change into a discussion where all sides start with the assumption of goodwill and we can actually talk about things without being afraid,” Francesca Happé says, somewhat optimistically. “But I would like that in all aspects of life.”Explore more on these topicsAutismNeurodiversityNeuroscienceMental healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US elections | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: From the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculous
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: From the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculous
Content: ‘I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionUS midterm elections 2026A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US electionsDave SchillingFrom the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculousSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 15.41 ESTShareChances are, as you’re reading this, your bunker is fully stocked, your doors are locked, and you’re peeking at your computer screen through gaps between your fingers.After all, it’s election day on Tuesday. Once again, democracy will be tested – like Beavis & Butthead taking the SATs. I’m not looking forward to it, and I’m sure you aren’t either.I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.Now, it feels like anything can and will happen this week – from delayed results and slow counts to Donald Trump sending in theDC Comics Suicide Squadto your local polling place. That’s all we need,John Cenachecking your ID before you vote.It’s enough to make you crawl up into a ball and beg for mommy. But fear is a passive emotion, one that leaves a person paralyzed and incapable of action.My preference is for the fully formed anger of the middle-aged curmudgeon. A shaken fist and a choice expletive is healthier than babbling for hours in your panic room. So, in lieu of a voter guide telling you how to fill out your ballot, here’s a list of all the most irritating, confounding and downright stupid things to scream about on Tuesday.The Cheesecake Factory discourseDuring a recent campaign stop, the former president Barack Obama compared the aesthetics of the recentTrump-led White House renovations with a Cheesecake Factory. Not only am I annoyed that this is even a talking point during a crucial campaign, I also resent the comparison being made. I’d rather eat at a Cheesecake Factory than the White House, any day of the week. I have to assume Bill Maheragrees with me.The continued importance of Spencer PrattHere in California, the race everyone is talking about is a contest for Los Angeles mayor, a famous stepping stone to jobs as prestigious as “Ambassador to Country Chosen by Random Lottery Draw” or “Special Adviser to Herbalife”. It’s neck-and-neck between incumbent Karen Bass and the city councilperson Nithya Raman. The unfortunate twist in this daytime soap opera is that the reality show star they combined to defeat in the first round of voting this summer, Spencer Pratt, isstill popular enoughthat his supporters could tip the scales toward one candidate or the other. The only thing I can think of that’s worse than Spencer Pratt as mayor of LA is Spencer Pratt deciding the next mayor of LA.The curious case of the two Dan SullivansAccording to the New York Times, some Democrats figured out that the best way to unseat the senator Dan Sullivan was to force him to run against himself. Retired teacher Dan Sullivan was allegedly recruited to run for US Senate by the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola, in the hopes of unseating … Dan Sullivan. (The Peltola campaign has denied any involvement in his candidacy.)Mary Peltola made a mistake. But her Republican opponent would be a disaster for Alaska | Kim HeacoxRead moreThe Sullivan v Sullivan smackdown has the Republican party so worried that the justice department issuing to invalidatethe results of the election if Sullivan (the senator) narrowly loses to Sullivan (the not-senator) or Peltola (the not-Sullivan).I’m no fan of Dan Sullivan, but I’m not sure how I feel about Dan Sullivan either! This is the kind of goofy dirty trick that makes people hate politics. Who are you really fooling here? Old people? People who are too busy to read the fine print about which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent Alaskan senator? People with an acute case of Sullivantitis (a crippling disease that causes blindness to the name “Dan Sullivan”)? Can’t this country ever be normal?Please don’t message me. I realize the answer is no. I just hope this election is more entertaining than The Undertaker v The Undertaker at WWF SummerSlam 1994. Unlike that match, this face-off of doppelgangerswon’t involve Leslie Nielsen.The continued push to close polling placesIn an attempt to depress turnout amongst Democratic-leaning voters, red state election boards in states such as North Carolina areshutting polling placesin blue areas. In North Carolina in particular, voting sites were shut on numerous college campuses, but that didn’t stop a group of predominantly students from organizing marches in excess of two hours so that they could maintain the franchise.When I was a young man, the main tool crooked politicians had to keep people from voting was good, old-fashioned apathy. We should have changed the motto on the quarter from “E pluribus unum” to “They’re all bums, anyway.” In 2026, politicians have infuriated people to such a degree that they’ll walk miles just to vote.It’s inspiring to see young people exercising their rights in the face of an actively hostile state government, but I find the notion of our nation’s leaders blatantly making it more onerous for citizens to vote absolutely abhorrent. I mean, the peer pressure is bad enough.‘I voted’ stickers and selfiesI get why the stickers exist. An elaborate campaign of shame and embarrassment for those that didn’t bother to vote. I can’t think of two more powerful forces in my life than shame and embarrassment. They’re really the only two reasons I get out of bed these days, but I don’t have to like it.Like a lollipop at the end of a haircut, the “I voted” sticker is the little treat at the end of a long period of interminable waiting. The only difference is, I don’t need to take a picture with myroot beer-flavored Dum Dum. And I hate to be cynical here, but anyone who hasn’t planned on or even considered voting will not be swayed by a sticker.As much as I despise people shirking their responsibility to democracy, I hate internet trends even more. Instead of wearing an “I voted” sticker on Tuesday, just slap it on your laptop. That way, anyone in your general vicinity will have to stop and double-check that there isn’t an election that day.Donald Trump’s Mr America beauty pageantThis is Donald Trump’s last campaign of his risible political career. He has been a cancerous influence on our discourse since 2011, breaking traditions, norms, rules, and some priceless artifacts along the way.I’m sure he’s getting nostalgic for the rush of election fervor – the ups and downs, the thrill of victory and the agony of not admitting defeat. These are some of the last campaign rallies he’ll ever lead, some of the final moments of political combat he’ll engage in in his lifetime.Most of us would get wistful, maybe a tad somber. These days will never come again. Instead, the president is pondering the strength and power that emanates fromvarious Republican buttocks.Nothing, and I mean nothing, makes me bang my head against a wall this election cycle than my social media feed being littered with clips of Donald Trump sexualizing his colleagues.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS politicsDonald TrumpDemocratsRepublicansUS SenatecommentShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley’s November style essentials: fancy flats, sexy knits and a Christmassy pigeon | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Whether it’s a two-in-one coat or a truly delicious handbag, add some fun to getting dressed during the cold, dark months with our expert’s favourites
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Whether it’s a two-in-one coat or a truly delicious handbag, add some fun to getting dressed during the cold, dark months with our expert’s favourites
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley‘s editFashionJess Cartner-Morley’s November style essentials: fancy flats, sexy knits and a Christmassy pigeonWhether it’s a two-in-one coat or a truly delicious handbag, add some fun to getting dressed during the cold, dark months with our expert’s favouritesThe best women’s shoes and boots for autumnJess Cartner-MorleySun 1 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe clocks have gone back. The mornings are cold and the evenings are dark. The world seems to be doing its level best to discourage any fashion ambition beyond the need to stay alive and warm enough to function.But clothes – even in winter – are not just about staying alive. They are about stayingalivealive. Alive inside. So this month’s edit is about finding the fun in getting dressed when the weather is trying to discourage you. There is a pink jumper that manages to be both cosy and, well, slutty; a £16 henley that looks considerably more expensive than it is; and a skirt I have been stalking since the summer and can finally report back on. There are also ballet pumps with exactly the right amount of grownup elegance, a sweatshirt that makes a persuasive case for elevating the everyday, and a necklace to bring a bit of sparkle back to the proceedings.I don’t have this yet, but I want itReformationIris knit top£98£98 at ReformationView image in fullscreenIris knit£98 at ReformationI love a slutty jumper. Are we allowed to say that? I mean it as a compliment. A going-out top you won’t freeze in is perhaps more polite terminology. I want it in the cherry blossom pink, but it is available in lots of other nice colours.ReformationIris knit top£98£98 at ReformationAn excellent value henleyM&SWool touch semi sheer henley top£16£16 at M&SView image in fullscreen£16 at M&SThere is something so classy about a henley. Like, when a character in a film is wearing a henley, you know it’s there to tell you this person has a good soul. When done with finesse – a superfine rib, delicate buttons – there is something quite sensual about it, in an old-timey kind of way. Anyway, this M&S version is amazing value.M&SWool touch semi sheer henley top£16£16 at M&SA delicious handbagPolèneCyme mini£390£390 at PolèneView image in fullscreenPolène Cyme bag£390 at PolènePolène handbags are exquisite, which is why there are queues outside the Paris stores when new bags arrive. title: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say
Content: Giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically.Photograph: Craig Brown/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenGiving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically.Photograph: Craig Brown/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsBrexitUK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe schemeExclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials sayKiran Stacey,Lisa O’CarrollandJessica ElgotSun 1 Nov 2026 12.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made inEuropeindustrial programme.The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.British officials insist, however, they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed protectionist industrial scheme, which will impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc.Rachel Reeves says UK’s future is in EU as she backs Andy Burnham on BrexitRead moreOn Sunday the former chancellor Rachel Reevespraised the prime minister, Andy Burnham, for a willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe – saying she believed Britain’s future was within the EU. But in her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury whenBurnhamtook office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.Ministers hope if such an agreement is reached at a Brussels summit later this month it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off.But giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans.One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, in September.Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty ImagesA government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU and tolay out optionsfor how the relationship could develop in the future, including full re-entry.In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”.Before the summit, agreement is understood to have largely been reached in a number of areas, including on emissions trading, agricultural products and a youth mobility scheme, with reports suggesting up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study. EU member states had demanded between 100,000 and 150,000, with some arguing in favour of no quota.The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers.19:01What makes Andy Burnham think we can rejoin the EU? | Politics WeeklyBritish access to the Made in Europe scheme, which is due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities are the two remaining hurdles.EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiationsto a standstillthis year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks.The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end the small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore the possibility of restoring the UK’s access to EU databases.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states.Member states are pushing for firm language on fees while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. Francedropped its oppositionto the inclusion of the UK in the Industrial Accelerator Act with a proposal any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved as along as it dynamically aligned on trade measures.Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the discussion on fees from the joint statement at the summit entirely,deferring any agreement for six months. But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement to allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”.Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discounts for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses.Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that under the most expensive scenario, which involves reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and very high levels of demand, the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”.Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course.UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme.The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme,prompting warningsfrom the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – which was the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position with a new proposal to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs.This could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than in the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary,recently told the Guardianhe would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels.The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements.The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out that text, but after a last-minute cancellation, work has continued between officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission.Explore more on these topicsBrexitEuropean UnionStudentsInternational studentsHigher educationEuropeForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Shabana Mahmood’s new rules raise fears of staff shortages in health and social care and of second Windrush scandal
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Shabana Mahmood’s new rules raise fears of staff shortages in health and social care and of second Windrush scandal
Content: Shabana Mahmood wants to extend the length of time many overseas workers must live in the UK before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood wants to extend the length of time many overseas workers must live in the UK before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAImmigration and asylumHome secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UKMPs say Shabana Mahmood’s new rules risk staff shortages in health and social care and second Windrush scandalJessica ElgotandChris OsuhSun 1 Nov 2026 14.47 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 13.48 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood will announce sweeping new rules on Monday on how long legal migrants must wait for settlement in the UK, with most likely to wait a decade and some up to 15 years.Ministers – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner – had raised concerns about the effect the rules would have on care workers already in the UK who would be likely to face a 15-year wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR).The government’s response to the consultation on the reforms, which will be put before MPs on Monday, is expected give some exemption to care workers already in the UK, though most other professions will face the lengthy waits for settlement.Mahmood, the home secretary, has proposed that the settlement wait could be reduced if legal migrants showed they had contributed to their local communities via a “points based system” or if they were earning higher incomes.She is expected to meet union general secretaries on Monday – some of whom have raised alarm at the changes – to map out the final details.The Guardian first reported in July that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was considering exempting hundreds of thousands of care workers from the reforms to relieve pressure on the social care sector.
