The Home Officehas grantedabout 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more people coming as their dependants.Under the plans published for consultation, the standard qualifying period for settlement would double from five to 10 years, while some workers in occupations below graduate level, including care workers, could face a 15-year qualifying period, subject to proposed exemptions and reductions.In June, Rayner described making care workers already in Britain wait up to 15 years for permanent residence as “un-British”. In September, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the plans would have been “tough” for her family, who came to Britain as refugees.In a letter to Mahmood and the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, seen by the Guardian, parliamentarians and organisations representing migrant workers, racial equality campaigners and health professionals describe the proposals as “an iteration of Windrush era policies”.TheWindrush scandal, exposed by Guardian reporting in 2017, involved mainly Black Britons being wrongly detained, deported and denied access to work and essential services, despite having the right to live in Britain.In their letter, dated 29 October, the signatories urge ministers to “stop history from repeating itself” by abandoning the proposals or, at a minimum, introducing extra safeguards.Signatories argue that changing the rules for people who have planned their lives around existing settlement requirements would be unfair and could encourage essential workers to leave the country.They warn that proposed exemptions for some public-service workers may fail to protect staff employed by independent health and social care providers, as well as workers’ family members.The letter urges ministers to follow the recommendations of the Windrush Lessons Learned Review, conductedby Wendy Williams, which called for improvements in the development and scrutiny of immigration policy, including greater consideration of its impact on affected communities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Labour MPs Bell Ribeiro-Addy, Diane Abbott, Clive Lewis and Rachael Maskell are among the signatories, alongside the Green MPs Ellie Chowns, Carla Denyer, Siân Berry and Hannah Spencer. Organisations backing the letter include the Work Rights Centre, Action for Race Equality, Care England and the Society of Radiographers.The signatories write: “Windrush was a scandal borne from racist immigration policies … this situation is not historic when this same wrong persists, and the same groups are targeted by current immigration proposals.”The signatories warn the health and care sector is already “dangerously under-staffed” and that the proposed changes risk “worsening the health and wellbeing of everyone in the UK”.The letter argues that the government could struggle to meet cancer treatment and NHS waiting-list reduction targets without retaining and expanding the workforce, particularly in professions heavily reliant on internationally trained staff, like radiography.It raises particular concerns about adult social care, adding: “International workers are essential to maintaining current levels of care. Without them, services will contract, and unmet need will increase.”Launching the consultation on earned settlement last year, Mahmood described Britain as a “multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy” that demanded “contribution and integration”. She added: “To become a part of this country, permanently, is therefore not a right but a privilege – and one that must be earned.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumShabana MahmoodRefugeesHome OfficeWindrush scandalCare workersSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion with third place in Mexican GP | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 20-year-old Italian clinched the title with four rounds to go in a race that was won by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The 20-year-old Italian clinched the title with four rounds to go in a race that was won by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen
Content: Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton lift new world champion Kimi Antonelli.Photograph: Eloisa Sanchez/ReutersView image in fullscreenMax Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton lift new world champion Kimi Antonelli.Photograph: Eloisa Sanchez/ReutersFormula One 2026Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion with third place in Mexican GP20-year-old clinches title with four races to goVerstappen wins race ahead of HamiltonGiles Richardsat the Autódromo Hermanos RodríguezSun 1 Nov 2026 17.27 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 18.57 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKimi Antonelli etched his name into the Formula One record books as world champion and as a deserved and popular winner whose verve and extraordinary skill has been thrilling to watch, turning what many thought might have been an unlikely title tilt into a triumphant march, sealed with tears of joy at the Mexican Grand PrixIn taking his debut F1 title for Mercedes, the 20-year-old Antonelli, with his tousled hair and charming boyish looks, is the youngest driver to claim the sport’s crown and the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari won in 1953. It is Mercedes’ first drivers’ championship since Hamilton last won in 2020 and the team’s 10th.‘He’s done an insane job’: Antonelli’s rivals united in praise for ‘incredible’ championRead moreThe youngster closed it out unsurprisingly with the cool command the greats of the sport display by taking third place in Mexico City, a race won after no little drama by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, from the ­Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton, who was left fuming with his teammate Charles Leclerc, who finished fourth.Afterwards Antonelli was clearly moved and said it was a moment that would live for ever but had left him almost speechless. His race engineer, Peter Bonnington, spoke perhaps for everyone who has watched the Italian this season, noting that this was just the beginning for Antonelli.“It is a very special day, a young man has broken the record for the youngest world champion,” he said. “It is the first of many I reckon, I am just super happy for him, stoked.”On any other day this feisty affair in Mexico City, with Verstappen superb and a dramatic Ferrari inter-driver spat to savour, would have been ­considered quite an entertaining affair but for all that it really belonged to Antonelli.He brought what has been a hugely successful campaign to a close as the sport’s 36th world champion at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez in only his second season in F1 and with four meetings still to go. Sebastian Vettel was the previous youngest winner of the drivers’ championship, aged 23 in 2010, when Antonelli was just four years old.The Italian has been on top for almost the entire season, having taken the lead after the third round in Japan. With the Mercedes proving to be the class of the field in the opening half of the year under the new regulations, Antonelli made the most of it and established a dominant lead. He won five of the first six races, outracing his teammate George ­Russell, who had been the pre-season favourite.Antonelli went on to take nine wins in a season where he failed to score points only twice, on both occasions because of mechanical failures. Even as Mercedes were pushed by Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull, Antonelli retained a stranglehold on his lead, including sealing a win from 19th on the grid at his home grand prix at Monza.Russell and Hamilton were his nearest contenders but neither was able to significantly narrow the gap. They had to win in Mexico to keep the title alive but Antonelli’s third place would have clinched it even had they done so.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli crosses the chequered flag to finish third in Mexico.Photograph: Daniel Becerril/ReutersAntonelli did exactly what was required of him here, kept his cool and did not put a foot wrong in a race that was run at a frenetic pace. Leclerc made a great start and tried to pass Hamilton for the lead at turn four took but cut the corner to do so.He did not give the place back and was investigated, with Hamilton ­furious his teammate had cost them a one-two in the race and let Verstappen ultimately into the lead. The stewards found Leclerc had gained an advantage in leaving the track and he was given a five-second penalty to take during his pit stop.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was a decision which left ­Hamilton unhappy. “The problem is he’s got clean air and doesn’t have to manage like the rest of us. He should just give the place back,” he said. “The stewards are basically handing Charles this win.”Later when the race was stopped he made his displeasure clear again. “We’ve got big problems. Big, big problems,” he said. A lively debrief at Ferrari is in store.A red flag was called after Valtteri Bottas crashed out with a big impact at turn one. It prompted a restart from which a feisty Hamilton moved up to second and Antonelli into third, typically not willing to quietly do the minimum to take the title. It allowed him to seal glory with a podium place, where the two greats hoisted the kid on to their shoulders.Kimi Antonelli claims the Formula One crown – his season in picturesRead moreThe victory might be something of cold comfort to Verstappen given Antonelli secured the title, but ­comfort it will be to the Dutch driver and his team who will be buoyed by what was a hugely impressive run from fifth on the grid as they look to enter next season strongly. It has set up the mouthwatering prospect of Verstappen and Antonelli and ­hopefully Hamilton competing consistently at the front in 2027.The title for Antonelli represents a vindication of the enormous faith Mercedes had placed in the boy from Bologna, whom the team brought into their young driver program when he was 12. He was promoted to take Hamilton’s place last season, which proved a difficult year for the rookie but since then he has adapted to competing at the very sharp end with alacrity and great skill.He went into the race in Mexico needing only ninth place or better and despite only qualifying in fourth delivered a nerveless drive ­indicative of the form he has shown across the year. A moment to remember but surely not the last for this ­fascinating, precocious talent.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
Content: A still from a social media video appears to show the result of drone strikes on an oil refinery in Russia’s Samara oblast on Friday.Photograph: social media/ReutersView image in fullscreenA still from a social media video appears to show the result of drone strikes on an oil refinery in Russia’s Samara oblast on Friday.Photograph: social media/ReutersUkraineUkraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineriesKremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sitesLuke Hardingin KyivSun 1 Nov 2026 12.20 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 19.30 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure fromDonald Trumpahead of the US midterm elections, as a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky ended on Sunday night.Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.The Wall Street Journal hadreported that Ukraine had given in to pressurefrom the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper thatthey never agreed to a demandfrom Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on Russia restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv was now “simply ignoring” US wishes.Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce shows de-escalation is possible, says ZelenskyyRead moreZelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he said, as part of Ukraine’s continuing “long-range sanctions”.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows smoke rising from the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery in the Samara region of Russia after a reported Ukrainian drone attack on Friday.Photograph: European Union/Copernicus/Sentinel-2/ReutersZelenskyy said his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four Ukrainian regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the ​deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram.Kyivexperienced power cuts lasting eight to 10 hours on Sunday after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sqkm (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sqkm (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”The latest attacks came beforea six-day local ceasefirebrokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, came to an end in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Hundreds of residentswere reunited with their loved onesover the weekend in northern Ukraine, with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success.“The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended,” said Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, hailing what had been an “important step in our joint humanitarian efforts”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleshky. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between ⁠Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would ⁠pave the ⁠way ​for broader peace efforts.“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, and Kremlin officials said on Sunday thatVladimir Putinwas willing to talk directly to Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged.He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces, which the Kremlin does not control but says it has “annexed”.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS foreign policyVolodymyr ZelenskyyMelania TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz  | Iran | The Guardian
description: Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Content: Young Iranians walk past a large anti-US wall mural in Tehran on Sunday. Iran’s foreign minister has said he hopes the US chooses ‘diplomacy over other paths’ to end the crisis.Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYoung Iranians walk past a large anti-US wall mural in Tehran on Sunday. Iran’s foreign minister has said he hopes the US chooses ‘diplomacy over other paths’ to end the crisis.Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesIranNegotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of HormuzThird day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopeningPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorSun 1 Nov 2026 12.49 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 13.25 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOfficials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday withQatartrying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.TheUnited Arab Emiratesenvoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.View image in fullscreenIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the country was ready for both defence and diplomacy.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.View image in fullscreenThe US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution.Photograph: Erik S Lesser/AFP/Getty ImagesSpeaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranStrait of HormuzQatarUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Tributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crash | Spain | The Guardian
description: Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
Content: Dr Marta Shahbazi ‘was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist’, said the Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge.Photograph: MRC Laboratory of Molecular BiologyView image in fullscreenDr Marta Shahbazi ‘was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist’, said the Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge.Photograph: MRC Laboratory of Molecular BiologySpainTributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crashDr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biologyHaroon SiddiqueSun 1 Nov 2026 14.36 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in theSpanish train collisionon Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.Dr Marta Shahbazi, 41, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.The LMB said the mother of two had recently won the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology’s scientific excellence prize. She had been due to be presented with the award during its conference in El Rompido, Andalucía.In a LinkedIn post, the LMB said it was deeply saddened by her death, which was “a profound shock and a huge loss”, adding: “Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies.”It said she was a role model who had written eloquently about balancing her family and career, describing herself as a “mother scientist”.Dr Roser Vento-Tormo, a group leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute outside Cambridge, wrote: “Marta Shahbazi was a beautiful person: a close collaborator, a treasured friend, and an inspiration to me both as a scientist and as a mother.“As a scientist, we shared so many dreams. We co-supervised two students together, and I cannot describe how much joy it was to work alongside her.“Some of our work will still be published in the coming months, and anyone who reads it will feel the passion she poured into everything she did …“My thoughts are with her family. Anyone who knew Marta could see how deeply they were a unit, and how much they meant to her.”The Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), based in Santiago de Compostela,Spain, paid tribute to Shahbazi as “a brilliant young researcher”.The disaster was Spain’s second high-speed rail crash this year. Both collisions occurred on the line between the central city of Madrid, Spain’s capital, and Seville, in the Andalucía region in the south of the country.Three days of national mourning were observed from Thursday. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described the incident as a “tragedy” andhas promised an investigation.Explore more on these topicsSpainTrain crashesUniversity of CambridgeMedical researchBiologyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Teenage violinist wins BBC Young Musician 2026, after first all-female final | BBC Young Musician | The Guardian
description: Judges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity
Author: Imogen Tilden
Headline: Judges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity
Content: ‘My absolute dream…’ Sofia Demetriades, winner of 2026’s BBC’s Young Musician.Photograph: BBC Studios/Celf CalonView image in fullscreen‘My absolute dream…’ Sofia Demetriades, winner of 2026’s BBC’s Young Musician.Photograph: BBC Studios/Celf CalonBBC Young MusicianTeenage violinist wins BBC Young Musician 2026, after first all-female finalJudges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturityImogen TildenSun 1 Nov 2026 16.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA teenage violinist has won theBBC Young Musiciancompetition 2026, in the first all-female final in the competition’s 48-year history.The judges, Joanna MacGregor, Ben Gernon and Errollyn Wallen, hailed Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity.The 18-year-old is from Leicestershire, and in her first year of undergraduate studies at the Royal Academy of Music.The brainchild of Humphrey Burton, the biennialBBCcompetition was set up in 1978 and has produced finalists such as Sheku Kanneh-Mason, Alison Balsom, Stephen Hough and, in 2004, Nicola Benedetti, who was the last violinist to win.Demetriades was one of several hundred to send in a video application, before 40 young players were selected to attend live auditions in Bath Spa University to gain one of eight places in the quarter-finals – which took place on Demetriades’ 18th birthday. Among her fellow quarter-finalists was the first accordion player to reach the final stages, 14-year-oldSylvester Maschi.View image in fullscreenRecorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni, violinist Sofia Demetriades and saxophonist Kezia Colton, finalists of BBC Young Musician 2026.Photograph: BBC/Betsan EvansEach of the three finalists performed a concerto with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales, conducted by Alpesh Chauhan in a concert at Bristol Beacon. An 18-year-old saxophone player,Kezia Colton, performed Takashi Yoshimatsu’s 1994 Cyber Bird Saxophone Concerto, while 17-year-old recorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni played Graham Fitkin’s Recorder Concerto.Fitkin’s virtuosic concerto involves six different recorders, ranging from the giant contrabass, about 1.6 metres high, to the tiniest sopranino. It was originally commissioned by Debretzeni’s teacher, Barbara Law, and it was given itspremiere performance in 2017by 2014’s Young Musician finalist, Sophie Westbrooke. And there was a further connection this year to previous competitions – 2022’s overall winner, the percussionistJordan Ashman, joined Kezia Colton onstage for Yoshimatsu’s concerto.“Kezia plays with incredible verve and spirit, said Wallen. “Her performance was sassy and cool,” said Gernon, “but her more intimate playing is incredibly strong too.”The judges hailed the “electricity, aliveness, and beautiful intensity” that Debretzeni brought to Fitkin’s concerto. “She took us on a musical journey … we were inside every note,” said Wallen.“Before the competition I hadn’t planned on being a musician,” said Debretzeni. “I wanted to study psychology … but this has been so inspiring it’s made me want to pursue music. It’s been literally life-changing.”Demetriades was acclaimed as a simply extraordinary musician by MacGregor. “She performs with her eyes, achieving dizzying technical feats but she looks as if she’s enjoying it,” she said.“Sofia’s innate sense of colour, musical style and architecture combines with an effortless technique, and a joy for whatever music she’s playing. In a competition full of gifted and dedicated young musicians, Sofia’s sensitivity and sophistication stood out in every round. I’m very excited to watch her musicianship develop even further in the years ahead.”The winnerreceives the trophy, a cash prize of £3,000towards music studies as well as recording and broadcast opportunities on Radio 3, including with one of the BBC ensembles. All three finalists will work withYoung Classical Artists Truston managing their future careers.“I am so honoured and thrilled to have been a part of BBC Young Musician,” said Demetriades. “I loved playing in the quarter-final on my 18th birthday. I didn’t think I could top that, but to go on to be crowned winner is my absolute dream! It was pure delight to share the stage with BBC NOW, Alpesh Chauhan and my fellow finalists – I really hope to play alongside them again soon.”The final and the three previous stages are available to watchon BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsBBC Young MusicianClassical musicBBCAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: How Rachel Reeves has mapped out the economic agenda for Andy Burnham’s government | Rachel Reeves | The Guardian
description: On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her
Content: Rachel Reeves takes questions after her Mais lecture in March. She argued that major cities outside London had underperformed compared with European counterparts.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenRachel Reeves takes questions after her Mais lecture in March. She argued that major cities outside London had underperformed compared with European counterparts.Photograph: Yui Mok/PARachel ReevesAnalysisHow Rachel Reeves has mapped out the economic agenda for Andy Burnham’s governmentJessica ElgotDeputy political editorOn Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked herReeves says UK’s future is in the EUSun 1 Nov 2026 12.47 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 16.11 ESTShareWhich senior politician has argued that “Brexit did deep damage” and that the government seeks “not to turn back the clock but to look toward a new and stable, future relationship?”It was not Andy Burnham, who has been the torchbearer for thinking the unthinkable on Brexit since he became prime minister. Instead, these are the words of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, ina lecturesix months ago.Reeves has taken a more thoughtful approach on how to come to terms with life outside government than some of her fellow former ministers.A speech at Harvard on Monday will be her first public intervention on her own record and on Britain’s future, wisely left until afterJohn Healey’s first budget.She will say no one in government could “be in any doubt” about her view on the damage of Brexit – and her belief that one day the UK should return to the EU fold. “Economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe,” Reeves will say.The speech, which will examine how governments can meet the public’s appetite for radicalism while maintaining credibility with financial markets, will say that pursuing a closer relationship with the EU, even rejoining, may be credible as well as radical.“Economically, it is the credible choice. Britain’s values, and a serious assessment of the geopolitical scene today, tell us it is the radical choice too,” she will say, giving Burnham “credit for his willingness to face reality head on”.The Treasury, where the blueprints for the Remain campaign’s “Project Fear” were drawn up, has always been the heart of pro-European sentiment in government and Reeves its biggest champion underKeir Starmer.Her sentiment seems more aligned though with that of Burnham, who cast her out of government, than with Healey, her successor as chancellor. He has joked about his own age when asked if the UK would rejoin the EU “in his lifetime”, saying it was his job to “try and make the most of Britain’s position now”.Within Westminster, there are more than whispers from some MPs that they have judged Reeves’s legacy and influence too harshly. Healey’s first outing at the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok saw its economists lavish praise on his predecessor, saying the UK’s deficit reduction plan “stands out” among G7 peers.It is particularly striking how the themes of Reeves’s lecture have become the agenda for Burnham’s government. In it, she argued: “Today, what most distinguishes Britain from our closest peers is the relative underperformance of our major cities outside London, compared to their European counterparts.”Reeves, who is the MP for Leeds West and Pudsey, said the north of England had “waited for far too long, for a government that matches warm words with concerted ambition”.Her call to “liberate our regions from stifling Whitehall orthodoxies” sounds strikingly Burnhamesque. The main policy announced in the speech? A plan to begin giving regional leaders a share of national taxes “which have, for too long, been allocated by central government”.That work now forms the centrepiece of Healey’s budget. If this government has its own theory of growth – Brexit and devolution – it is awkward at best that it removed the key backer of both under Starmer.But Reeves’s main theory of growth was investment, in pursuit of which she raised employers’ national insurance.That is the other reason for Burnham’s government to be grateful to Reeves – and for which she has received no credit. Those tax raises – despite being unpopular – gave a sense of a government willing to make hard choices while taking the risk to borrow for public investment. The fiscal rules were changed to allow for a multi-year commitment to an eventual £100bn in new capital spending.The cash is now beginning to flow into NHS infrastructure, roads, housing, rail upgrades and energy and industrial investments. Reeves will lay out her theory in her Harvard speech this week that the shift to an investment-led growth model “required sacrifices” that a Starmer-led government failed to get the public to back.“The challenge is to make the politics and economics, those dual tests of credibility and radicalism, line up,” Reeves will say.She will not say – although others have – that much of the problem with Starmer’s government was the man himself, rather than the agenda.Burnham, if he avoids an early election, may start to see some of that investment bear fruit in public and market confidence, both in upgraded public services and in Britain’s appeal as a location for private investment.There is much that could derail all this – not least further international turmoil – but when Burnham’s government counts its success on public services, Europe, devolution and growth, Reeves will be able to claim some credit.Explore more on these topicsRachel ReevesAndy BurnhamBrexitJohn HealeyEconomic policyKeir StarmerBudget 2026analysisShareReuse this content

title: Tommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership void | Tommy Robinson | The Guardian
description: With heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movement
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: With heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movement
Content: Tommy Robinson and his supporters outside Southwark crown court.Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTommy Robinson and his supporters outside Southwark crown court.Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/Getty ImagesTommy RobinsonTommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership voidWith heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movementBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSun 1 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.30 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe verdict was met with a groan from Tommy Robinson’s supporters, who had sat behind the dock throughout his harassment trial.It took more than 11 hours of jury deliberations to find the far-right activist guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists, enough time for a band of lieutenants and hangers-on to get their hopes up that he might be acquitted.Yet as Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, potentially faces up to 10 years in prison, another narrative has now taken hold. A miscarriage of justice has taken place, according to messages pumped out across his own media platforms and the ecosystem of self-styled “citizen journalists”. Some carried wild commentary during the trial, including from Robinson himself, who wondered aloud about a “Muslim” member of the jury.Other voices have since joined in, including Reform UK members and Rupert Lowe, the leader of the Restore Britain party and Nigel Farage’s main rival for hard-right voters. “Tommy Robinson has been found guilty – it is my view that the system has, again, treated him unfairly. We live in dark times,” tweeted Lowe, the MP for Great Yarmouth.Evidence at Southwark crown court heard how Robinson used what the prosecution described as “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” against Daily Mail reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after they reported on his alleged role influencing the 2024 Southport riots.They were forced to employ security or leave their homes, while a statement from Young’s daughter told of encounters outside the family address with men believed to have been sent by Robinson, a self-styled champion of women’s safety.Robinson also admitted “paying” for the personal number of the editor of the Daily Mail, Ted Verity, who was left a message in which Robinson threatened to make the paper’s journalists and their families “famous”.While Robinson will learn his fate on 16 December, there are now wider implications for Britain’s far right. If he goes to jail again, the far right will be deprived of its most effective and – arguably – most charismatic leader, with little or no apparent replacement.The obvious heir apparent is anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, AKA Danny Tommo, the leader of the Patriot Platform movement that has brought groups of masked men on to the streets of Dover and other towns this year. He, however, is in custody ahead of a trial over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the Channel. He has denied wrongdoing.View image in fullscreenDaniel Thomas, AKA Danny Tommo, and supporters outside the Daily Mail offices in London.Photograph: Denise Laura Baker/Getty Images“With the Robinson conviction and Thomas being away there is definitely a leadership void in the anti-migrant space, with no obvious significant figure who can step in,” said Joe Mulhall, director of research at Hope Not Hate, which has closely monitored the recent targeting of asylum accommodation and Robinson’s own rallies.“It’s a really disparate scene made up of lots of little groupuscules, and I think the most likely thing we will see are lots of ad hoc actions being taken by various self-styled ‘patriot groups’. That can be harder to monitor and police, but this conviction is clearly a big blow for the movement nationally.”The wind has also been taken out of the sails of the anti-migrant movement by other police arrests, including in connection with vandalism attacks targeting houses in multiple occupation (HMOs).Of continuing concern to observers of the far right is the role of Elon Musk, who Robinson once again thanked for bankrolling his legal expenses after the multibillionaire owner of X was credited with supporting the activist’s terror chargesacquittal last year.One day alone at Southwark court cost £20,000, Robinson told supporters, a drop in the ocean to Musk. Perhaps not surprisingly, others on the far right have been eyeing up that aid.Question marks now hover over a supposed pivot by Robinson and others around him towards encouraging a voter registration drive by their supporters, though Mulhall points out that Robinson had already appeared to be struggling with this year’s takeoff of protests.“Patriot Platform suddenly emerged and you could see him [Robinson] scrambling to try to keep up with a support base who had already become quite impatient with what they viewed as his money-making grift,” Mulhall said. Over recent weeks, Robinson’s X feed has been taken up with reposting old footage of him confronting journalists and others in a bid to reinforce his direct action credentials.One figure who is looking over his shoulder at Robinson, however, is Farage. The Reform UK leader responded with sarcasm when asked about the conviction, and he has clearly changed his party’s policy on permitting members who support Robinson.Divisions could reignitebetween figures such as Richard Tice, vocal in the past about not wanting to haveanything to do with Robinson and “his lot”, and Reform members embracing the narrative that he has become a martyr.Meanwhile, Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison, in the worst case, although sentencing guidelines provide a wide range of flexibility to Mr Justice Cavanagh, who will first consider culpability.A specialist criminal law barrister told the Guardian that at least two “high culpability” factors could be considered. Robinson telling journalists he was coming to get them could amount to “conduct intended to maximise fear or distress”, while hiring an investigator suggested a “high degree of planning and/or sophisticated offence”.“In terms of harm, I suspect it will be seen in the most serious category, particularly as at least one victim moved house as a result,” the barrister said. “When it comes to the type of sentence, Robinson’s problems are that his track record of previous offences raises questions about the prospect of rehabilitation. There is also a lack of strong personal mitigation and he presents an ongoing risk, namely to journalists who say something he disagrees with.“The judge might decide that, given the current prison overcrowding crisis, a suspended sentence will suffice. If it’s suspended for the full three years in line with guidelines, it could well have a greater impact on reining in his behaviour.”This article was amended on 1 November 2026 to correctly refer to the 2024 Southport riots; an earlier version had described these as the Southend riots.Explore more on these topicsTommy RobinsonFar rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: English children’s homes are in crisis. Does Denmark hold the answers? | Children | The Guardian
description: UK children’s minister Josh MacAlister has travelled to Copenhagen to see what can be learned from Danish system
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: UK children’s minister Josh MacAlister has travelled to Copenhagen to see what can be learned from Danish system
Content: Josephine Schneider’s House in Frederiksberg, Denmark.Photograph: Ole Jensen/Ole Jensen/Getty Images for The GuardianView image in fullscreenJosephine Schneider’s House in Frederiksberg, Denmark.Photograph: Ole Jensen/Ole Jensen/Getty Images for The GuardianChildrenEnglish children’s homes are in crisis. Does Denmark hold the answers?UK children’s minister Josh MacAlister has travelled to Copenhagen to see what can be learned from Danish systemJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentSun 1 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a quiet suburb on the outskirts of Copenhagen sits a large white house, set back from the road behind a purple-leaved plum tree. It looks much like the rest of the buildings on the street and there is little outward sign this is Josephine Schneider’s House, considered one of the best children’s homes in the world.Danish children’s homes are often cited as the gold standard of children’s residential care globally. They are now being studied by the British government as it tries to create a roadmap out of the crisis in which its own children’s home system has become mired.Last year there were 669 children living in illegal, unregistered children’s homes across England, with councilspaying more than £125m of taxpayers’ money to keep them there.Overall spending on children’s homes soared 96% in five years to over £3.1bn in 2023-24, while standards have dropped,private equity firms are cashing inand a growing number of children are being sent to homes hundreds of miles away.The situation is dire, the children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, admits. “We now have this shadow system of unregistered, illegal homes, which is certainly not providing therapeutic support and the costs are huge,” he said. “We need big changes, a major shake up, and I spend as many hours as I can a week on children’s social care reform.”View image in fullscreenJosh MacAlister and Mads Sørensen, deputy director of Josephine Schneider’s House.Photograph: Patricia GlindorfEarlier this week, MacAlister visitedDenmarkto see how its children’s homes operate and what can be exported back to England, as part of a Department for Education review into how the sector can be improved.The140-year-old Josephine Schneider’s House, which houses 12 children and young adults aged six to 23, is starkly different from many British equivalents.In the centre of the house is a spacious kitchen staffed by the head chef, Rasmus, who cooks the children’s meals, lunch boxes and after-school snacks – pizza rolls are a particular favourite. He works with the children himself, encouraging them to help make the food and come grocery shopping.The Copenhagen house that’s probably the best children’s home in the world | Clare Considine and Helen RussellRead moreThe rest of the staff are all degree-level professionals in social pedagogy, a discipline focusing on psychology, child development and ethics, and they strive to recreate a traditional family home by cooking, eating and socialising with the children.“We don’t have an in-house therapist but everything we do is therapeutic,” said Mads Sørensen, deputy director of the home.One member of staff sleeps in the house at night and wakes the children up each day at 7am. “We ask them how they like to be woken up, to help them feel safe and create that predictability, make their nervous system calm a bit,” Sørensen said.Many of the children here have suffered physical, emotional and social neglect, and issues such as self-harm, insomnia and eating disorders are common.Unlike children’s homes in England, where many children report being isolated and cut off from family and friends, here children are encouraged to have friends stay at the weekends and holidays, there are regular parents evenings, including a Christmas banquet.View image in fullscreenIn the centre of the house is a spacious kitchen, with the children encouraged to help make the food.Photograph: Ole Jensen/Ole Jensen/Getty Images for The GuardianEach child also has a team of two to three staff members working with them on their education and wellbeing. In a semi-independent flat on the top floor live the older residents, aged 17 and above, who have their own living area and kitchen as they start to transition into adulthood.The young people buy their own food and do their own chores, under the guidance of staff, preparing them for independent life beyond the home. They are allowed to stay in the home up until the age of 23, and encouraged to return for regular visits beyond that age.This is a far cry from children’s homes in England, which teenagers must leave as soon as they turn 18, part of the cliff-edge loss of support that iscausing the early deaths of care leavers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMacAlister said he may change this. “Getting rid of the really binary date of birth point to decide where you live is something I’m really persuaded by,” he said. “I hear of children being forced to move when they turn 18, even if they’re in the middle of sitting their A-levels. We have to move away from that.”He also wants to import some of the culture from Danish children’s homes, particularly their focus on personal growth and maintaining family relationships.“A lot of residential care in England is actually about adults containing their own anxiety and concerns about teenagers, and that’s a really poor model,” MacAlister said. “The first question is always ‘how do we protect ourselves from risk?’ which is not what we should be asking first. It’s very different here in Denmark.”The quality of staff is crucial, and something at the heart of the ongoing review, which is being led by Emmanuel Akpan-Inwang, the director of Lighthouse Pedagogy Trust, which runs a children’s home in Sutton based on pedagogy principles.“What’s interesting about Denmark is working in a children’s home is a career that people really want to do,” he said. “It’s competitive. Homes are able to select really great people. They support and train them. They stay in the sector for long periods of time.“But we can’t simply lift and shift the system to England. The Danes have spent more than 40 years developing it. But we can learn from it.”At Josephine Schneider’s House, many staff members have been there 10 years or longer. In the UK, about 53% of children’s home staff have worked in the sector for three years or less. Poor pay, working conditions and a lack of training force many to leave the sector early.But underpinning Danish children’s homes is extensive state funding – a third of homes are publicly owned, 42% are not-for-profit and 27% are private profit.By contrast, in England, 83% of children’s homes places are now privately run, with some operators recording profit margins of more than 20%.The government has passed laws giving itself the power to intervene and cap profits by private providers but has yet to use it, with MacAlister saying they need to wait for a new “market oversight body” to provide full transparency of exactly how much money is being made before they can push ahead.The government of Wales is moving more quickly, and will ban all for-profit providers in children’s social care by 2030. But MacAlister said it would not be easy to replicate this in England, where numbers are much bigger.“We need to massively boost local authorities so they can take back control of the whole purchasing process, curb demand by making sure more children can live in foster homes or kinship arrangements, and shape a system on our terms, not one that is driven by profit,” MacAlister said.Explore more on these topicsChildrenSocial careDenmarkEuropeSocial exclusionChild protectionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s a force’: Obama answers call to boost Democrats – and rattle Trump | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Former president has given series of blistering speeches to help candidates in key races – and deployment has proved a hit with party’s progressive wing
Author: David Smith
Headline: Former president has given series of blistering speeches to help candidates in key races – and deployment has proved a hit with party’s progressive wing
Content: Obama at a rally for Senator Jon Ossoff and governor conteneder Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia this week.Photograph: Robin Rayne/Zuma/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenObama at a rally for Senator Jon Ossoff and governor conteneder Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia this week.Photograph: Robin Rayne/Zuma/ShutterstockUS midterm elections 2026‘He’s a force’: Obama answers call to boost Democrats – and rattle TrumpFormer president has given series of blistering speeches to help candidates in key races – and deployment has proved a hit with party’s progressive wingDavid Smithin WashingtonSun 1 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.44 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThat could have been awkward.Barack Obama, campaigning for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, acknowledged that his fellow Democrat has criticised some aspects of the Obama presidency.“Yeah, Abdul didn’t agree with some things we wanted to do – that our administration was doing – when I was president,”he told a rally in Detroit. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” The crowd erupted in laughter. “I’d say about five times a day, she says, ‘You knucklehead. Why you do that?’”It was an elegant attempt to bridge the gap between the old Democratic party and the new. The US midterm elections have brought anti-incumbent sentiment to the fore. Some candidates have activelyshrugged off their party labels, eager to cast themselves as outsiders running against the Washington establishment.Against that backdrop, who wants a 65-year-old former president who left office nearly a decade ago with his promise of hope and change still only partly realised? It seems thatDemocratsdo.View image in fullscreenBarack Obama with Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit last Saturday.Photograph: Dominick Sokotoff/Shutterstock“Yes, we can!” chanted the crowd this week inside an arena in suburban Atlanta, Georgia, reviving the cadence ofan Obama 2008 campaignthat now feels like an artefact from a vanished age.With days to go before midterm elections that willdecide the balance of powerin Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump’s second term, Democrats have turned to their most formidable orator for a series of blistering speeches in the campaign’s closing days.America’s first Black president has mercilessly mocked Trump’s autocratic pretensions and derided his foreign policy misadventures in the Middle East.“This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said in Georgia. “It’s the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it.”For party strategists, the decision to deploy Obama in the campaign’s closing stretch was a calculated gamble. Unlike Trump, who has spent weeks staging grievance-filled rallies in traditional Republican strongholds, Obama maintained a selective public profile until the final weeks, allowing a new generation of Democratic candidates to establish their own identities before delivering a late burst of star power.David Litt,a former Obama White House speechwriter, said: “What you’re seeing is him coming in to support a new generation of Democratic leaders who have emerged organically, rather than trying to be involved from day one. He still has both a credibility and an ability to drive turnout that, if you’re a candidate in a close race, you can absolutely benefit from – especially among young voters and Black voters.”The former president possesses a rare currency in modernUS politics, according to Litt: the ability to command attention, and unnerve his successor.“Obama is good at getting attention, and attention is hard to get these days,” he continued. “The other thing is he continues to live in Trump’s head rent-free.Donald Trumpis out there on the stump, and in theory, he should be talking about his accomplishments. Instead he’s relitigating his decisions involving ballroom renovations, because he can’t help but get triggered by a single sentence from a former president.”That sentence came at a rally in Cleveland, Ohio, when Obamaobserved that Trump’s gold-encrusted renovationshave left the White House looking as if “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”.View image in fullscreenObama campaigns with Ohio Democrats in Cleveland last week.Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty ImagesThe comment triggered a mini-culture war in rightwing media – not because Obama had invoked a murderous Iraqi dictator, but because he had dared to suggest that a popular restaurant chain was a symbol of vulgar excess.Trump waved his arms to mimic a lettuce leaf,accused Obama of snobbery and said: “Every piece of lettuce he eats has to be perfect, and I’m not that choosy.” He defended his gilded White House decor and claimed Obama had left the executive mansion “deteriorated”.Trump’s treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, a wealthy former hedge fund manager,even staged a photo-opoutside a Cheesecake Factory in Washington, ordering a french-dip cheeseburger in an apparent attempt to rebut accusations of elitism and urging “the Martha’s Vineyard set” to sample the chain’s multi-page menu.To Obama, the outcry merely proved his case. In Atlanta, he said: “They mobilised a whole-of-government response to a joke, not to inflation, but to a joke. They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory.”For Litt, the Republican outrage betrayed a glaring double standard. “This is a party that spent years complaining, ‘Oh, you’re not allowed to say anything offensive any more,’” he said. “It turns out all these people who would die on the hill of allowing someone to use offensive language suddenly think [the] Cheesecake Factory is a line you just can’t cross.”In rural east Tennessee, Corbin Trent, a media strategist and former communications director for Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, scoffed at Republican attempts to portray Obama’s remarks as elite condescension toward working people.He said: “They thought they were going to do this liberal elite stuff. I live in rural America. You’ve got this guy, Donald Trump, who presents himself like a mafioso, running our country like a mob – how can he enrich himself? There’s no accountability. You’re reminded of it every time you go to the grocery store, fill up your gas tank, turn on the TV and see that we’re bombing more places.”Democrats have also mobilised former vice-president Kamala Harris for their midterm effort, while ex-presidentBill Clinton campaigned with David Jolly, who is running for governor of Florida. But Obama has been unusually active in presidential, congressional and gubernatorial elections since he left the White House.In 2024 he backed Harris in the final stretch of the presidential race, which Trump ultimately won. When Obamaopened his presidential centrein Chicago in June, all living former presidents were in attendance – but Trump was not.Yet within the broader Democratic coalition, Obama’s legacy remains complicated. For a younger generation of activists who came of age during Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns and the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the former president is remembered as much for his institutional constraints and moderate compromises as for his inspirational rhetoric.Norman Solomon, a co-founder of the progressive group RootsAction, said: “It’s like a great oil painting. If you walk up to it and look real close, it’s not going to look so great. If you look too close at Obama’s record – the collapse on peacemaking in Palestine, tripling troops in Afghanistan, presiding over the greatest upward transfer of wealth in anybody’s lifetime – it does not look so great.“Then he leaves the White House and jets off to an island owned by a billionaire [the Obamas spent a post-presidency vacation on private islands owned by the British billionaire Sir Richard Branson in 2017]. That is not solidarity.”Solomon acknowledged, however, that in the immediate crisis of 2026, Obama’s tactical value is undeniable. “Almost anybody is going to look great compared to Trump. InMichigan, where there’s been resentment between African American and Arab American communities, it’s helpful for Obama to present a wiser outlook on what’s at stake.”Other progressives welcome Obama back on the campaign trail, seeing his involvement not as a concession to the old order, but as evidence that the former president recognises how far the party has moved to the left.View image in fullscreenObama with Jon Ossoff.Photograph: Edgar Su/ReutersJoseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution, a group that grew out of Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign, said: “Obama hitting the campaign trail is a net positive because it’s strategic. He helps pull in key demographics including African American voters.“But more broadly, I interpret Obama being on the campaign trail as a validation of the progressive movement’s momentum. He is the epitome of the establishment, and he is out there pounding the pavement for progressives, saying our agenda isn’t radical – it’s mainstream. It’s an affirmation of how powerful our movement has become.”Geevarghese also highlighted Obama’s ability to shield minority candidates from xenophobic attacks. “Obama represents a candidate who overcame the opposition’s ‘othering’ – when they called him un-American and used his middle name, Hussein. In the case of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who is weathering some of those same attacks, having Obama on the trail validates his candidacy and bolsters him within the American mainstream.”Since 2016, the DSA has grown from 6,000 members to over 130,000 nationwide, scoring high-profile mayoral victories withZohran Mamdaniin New York while looking to expand its congressional caucus.Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the DSA, said: “Today, Obama appearing alongside progressive candidates shows where the decisive shift is happening. Voters want real results toward an alternative to the factors that produced Donald Trump. Barack Obama coming out and campaigning with candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan shows a recognition of where voters are.”Yet Obama, like Trump, remains a political unicorn: a figure who defies easy categorisation. That remains a strength.Nina Turner, a former Ohio state senator and prominent progressive voice, said: “President Obama, because of his uniqueness, transcends the anti-establishment movement.”View image in fullscreenObama meets Democratic supporters in Georgia.Photograph: Erik S Lesser/AFP/Getty Images“He is still an extraordinarily positive figure among the Democratic base,” she added. “Even on the progressive side, for those of us who were disappointed with the ultimate analysis of his presidency – the drone wars, running on hope and change but not making a whole lot of change – he still has ‘that thing.’ He’s a force.”“The critique of President Obama is he was very much establishment: he ran on hope and change, but didn’t make a whole lot of change,” said Turner. “People were hopeful, though, and it’s the hopeful portion of his candidacy that still looms large – even as people critique his presidency, particularly on the progressive side of the ledger. Overall him being out there will be good for Democrats of all generations.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026Barack ObamaDemocratsDonald TrumpUS politicsObama administrationTrump administrationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican loses | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Incumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJ
Author: Chris Hippensteel
Headline: Incumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJ
Content: Senator Dan Sullivan makes an appearance at the Alaska Federation of Natives Convention in Anchorage, Alaska, on 22 October.Photograph: Kerry Tasker/ReutersView image in fullscreenSenator Dan Sullivan makes an appearance at the Alaska Federation of Natives Convention in Anchorage, Alaska, on 22 October.Photograph: Kerry Tasker/ReutersUS midterm elections 2026Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican losesIncumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJChris HippensteelSun 1 Nov 2026 15.10 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.39 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’sUS Senaterace if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.The justice department argued in its lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before election day, that there could be “voter confusion” over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the November ballot, whichRepublicansfear could take away votes from the incumbent and influence the race’s outcome in favor of the Democratic nominee, Mary Peltola.The justice department said it planned to appeal Sunday’s ruling: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.Sullivan, in aninterview with CNNon Sunday morning, said that he would accept the results of his upcoming election.According to a recent New York Times investigation, aides from Peltola’s campaignrecruitedanother man who shared Sullivan’s name to join the race in a ploy to peel away votes from the Republican incumbent.Since those revelations,Republicans, including Donald Trump, have called for Peltola to be disqualified from the race and criminally prosecuted. Peltola has continued to deny any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign, recently telling a reporter at a campaign event that she had “no idea” if any of her staff were involved.Asked by CNN’s Jake Tapper if he would only accept the election results if he won, Sullivan responded: “No, I’m going to accept the election results.”Earlier in his interview with Tapper, Sullivan also said he wasn’t focused on how Peltola’s campaign might be legally challenged. He was focused instead on winning the race outright. He nonetheless expressed doubt that Peltola had lacked any knowledge of the effort to put a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.“She’s continually lying to the Alaskan people,” Sullivan said. “And I guarantee you, she’s lying right now.”Meanwhile, the Washington Postreportedthat Republicans tried to boost unviable Democratic candidates in the Alaska primaries as well. A Republican Super Pac boosted two candidates for Senate who did not live in Alaska, and praised them as “progressives” similar to Bernie Sanders.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026AlaskaUS SenateUS politicsRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Dark money made darker’: funding labyrinth conceals donors to Republican campaigns | US political financing | The Guardian
description: One man’s campaign finance operation in Wisconsin exemplifies the opacity of the US political financing system
Author: Jason Wilson
Headline: One man’s campaign finance operation in Wisconsin exemplifies the opacity of the US political financing system
Content: Activities raise questions about the attitude of Republicans to campaign finance in the run-up to the November midterm elections.Photograph: Brooks Kraft/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenActivities raise questions about the attitude of Republicans to campaign finance in the run-up to the November midterm elections.Photograph: Brooks Kraft/Corbis/Getty ImagesUS political financing‘Dark money made darker’: funding labyrinth conceals donors to Republican campaignsOne man’s campaign finance operation in Wisconsin exemplifies the opacity of the US political funding systemJason WilsonSun 1 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 08.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer of 2024, a non-profit called the Green Dragon Coalition wired the last $20,000 of a $445,000 grant to aSuper Pac. Its tax return for that year would describe the purpose of the transfer as “educational”.The same day, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records, the Super Pac spent $8,000 attacking Celeste Maloy, the Republican congresswoman for Utah’s second district, four days before the primary that would decide whether she kept her seat. It had already spent more than $400,000 promoting her challenger, Colby Jenkins, who was running to her right with the endorsement of the rightwingUtahsenator Mike Lee.One man was involved at every stage, and his name is on the paperwork for the charity that raised the money, the non-profit that passed it on, the Super Pac that the non-profit donated to and the campaign this money eventually supported.His name is Thomas Datwyler, and his businesses are mostly headquartered in a rented address in Hudson,Wisconsin, a town of 15,000 near the border with Minnesota. Datwyler operates at an industrial scale, acting as treasurer of more than 350 federal political committees in the current election cycle, including 115 congressional campaigns and 100 Super Pacs, and as an officer of more than two dozen non-profits.The extent of Datwyler’s activities over several political cycles raises questions about the attitude of Republican campaigns and candidates to campaign finance in the run-up to the November midterm elections, and the evolution of so-called “dark money” electoral funding.Across the 2024 and 2026 cycles,Super Pacswhose books Datwyler also keeps have spent more than $2m supporting 14 candidates that are also his clients, or attacking their opponents, according to FEC filings. In several of those races the money reached the Super Pac through charities and social welfare groups for which he is a treasurer.Datwyler-tied groups have been funded by donors connected to the rightwing megadonor Leonard Leo, along with the Conservative Partnership Institute and the personal foundation of the Claremont Institute’s board chair, the Thomas Klingenstein Fund, among others.Money raised from these conservative donors has gone into organisations that Datwyler runs the books for, and those organisations have passed money on to Super Pacs that spent in Republican primaries. Non-profit tax filings do not show which donors’ funds made up any particular onward transfer.View image in fullscreenLeonard Leo of the Federalist Society in New York City on 16 November 2016.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APAlong the way, the same firms are paid by both the campaigns and the groups that are legally required to be independent of campaigns in order to maintain their tax-exempt status. In Florida’s 19th district, a campaign and the supposedly independent Super Pac backing it share 14 vendors, according to FEC filings.Federal law prohibits coordination between Pacs and campaign committees, but proving it is challenging. The FEC is a reluctant cop, and while Datwyler has attracted significant controversy and state-level investigations, what he does may not be illegal.Trump beware: US voters are concerned about government corruptionRead more“Somebody in Datwyler’s position is well aware of where all the cracks and crevices in the system are, how to sort of exploit the rules in a way that maximises his clients’ ability to secretly influence elections,” saysSaurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the non-profit Campaign Legal Center.“There’s a reason why the same handful of people – and Datwyler’s probably the chief among them – tend to come up in connection with these dark money operations. It’s because they have the knowhow of how to do it. And they’re willing to be the public face on each of these entities.“The actual donors providing the money don’t want to be publicly outed as the source of the outside money pouring into the race.”Datwyler wrote to the Guardian that “AxCapital [where he is CEO] is grateful that so many clients entrust our team to facilitate their participation in the democratic process. As an industry leader, we have strict internal firewalls, strong safeguards, and robust policies to ensure full compliance with all laws, regulations, and requirements.”The Green Dragon pipelineThe Green Dragon entities exemplify a pattern that recurs across Datwyler’s network.TheGreen Dragon Coalitionis a 501(c)4 social welfare non-profit, and one of three entities registered in Delaware in 2023 with sequential IRS employer numbers, all listing the same address in Hudson, Wisconsin. The other two were theGreen Dragon Society, a 501(c)3 charity, and theConstitutional Conservatives Fund, a Super Pac.Datwyler is treasurer of all three, and is the only officer that any of the organizations pay: the Green Dragon Coalition paid him $25,012 during the 2024 cycle and the Green Dragon Society paid him $29,066.This is just a fraction of the compensation Datwyler has received across various arms of the political operation he works on. Tax filings indicate that he received at least $487,545 in the 2023-2024 cycle from non-profits. FEC filings indicate that during the last two election cycles at least $793,470 flowed to Datwyler directly, or to two Delaware-registered consultancies, 10Six Consulting and Same Day Processing, that share aWisconsinaddress with the vast majority of his political and charity organizations.Meanwhile, AxCapital, where Datwyler is CEO, brought in $4.9m across both cycles. AxCapital was created in a 2022 merger of HenryAlan and Datwyler’s 9Seven Consulting.The Green Dragon Coalition’s $445,000 “educational” grant to the Constitutional Conservatives Fund in 2024 is recorded in the Pac’sFEC receiptsin five payments between 15 March and 21 June 2024. In turn, the Pacspent $447,347supporting Jenkins. Datwyler was also treasurer ofColby Jenkins for Congress, a role he had held since October 2023, and of the candidate’s joint fundraising committee. Datwyler is therefore keeping the books for the charity, the social welfare group, the Super Pac attacking the incumbent and the campaign it was attacking her on behalf of.View image in fullscreenColby Jenkins speaks during Utah’s second congressional district debate on 10 June 2024 in Salt Lake City.Photograph: Scott G Winterton/The Deseret News via APThe Green Dragon Coalition’s 2024 revenue was $917,002, of which$750,000 – or about 82% – came from the Concord Fund, the Leonard Leo-network group formerly called the Judicial Crisis Network. The Green Dragon Society, a 501(c)3, also took $250,000 from Purple Action, a 501(c)4 whose officers include tech mogul and former Trump administration “crypto czar” David Sacks, and $200,000 from the Conservative Partnership Institute, and $90,000 each from “dark money” vectors DonorsTrust and Fidelity’s donor-advised fund. TheThomas D Klingenstein Fundgave the 501(c)3 $75,000 in 2023, before the 2024 payments to the Super Pac.Lawson Bader, the president and CEO of DonorsTrust, said the organisation was “unfamiliar with the Constitutional Conservatives Fund, and the fact that the Green Dragon Coalition has an affiliated 501(c)4”. Grants from donor-advised funds to a 501(c)3 “cannot be used for political purposes”, he said, adding that DonorsTrust “would reconsider future grant recommendations made to organizations that violate the rules governing charitable activities”.A Fidelity Charitable spokesperson said: “Use of Fidelity Charitable grants for political contributions or campaign activities is prohibited. The terms all non-profits receive when grant funds are issued to them include explicit language to that effect.”The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualizedRead moreThese are not the only money flows from major conservative funders through Datwyler-connected entities.In 2024 American Majority Action, a 501(c)4 founded by conservative activist Ned Ryun, gave Integrity Minnesota, for which Datwyler served as treasurer, $250,000 for “voter registration and activation plans”. (A 2020Campaign for Accountability complaintasked the IRS and two state agencies to investigate whether Ryun’s groups spent more than half their money on politics, which would violate IRS laws governing 501(c)4 groups. Campaign for Accountability communications director Michael Clauw told the Guardian that the IRS did not respond to the complaint or take any action.)American Majority Action did not respond to a request for comment.Integrity Minnesota also received $50,000 that year from Restoration of America, which theChicago Sun-Times reported in October 2024was part of “a sprawling empire of organizations pushing far-right agendas and election denialism”, funded by at least $150m from shipping-supplies billionaire Richard Uihlein.The Guardian contacted Restoration of America for comment.And a separate Datwyler vehicle, Aurora Venture, received $300,000 from Ardleigh Impact Corp, a Delaware 501(c)4 with one director, no employees and no website, registered to the Springfield, Virginia, home of Staci Goede, a former Republican State Leadership Committee finance chief who is the treasurer of 26 federal political committees this cycle.TheDaily Beast reported on 16 May 2024that Ardleigh had moved more than $2.5m to Republican Super Pacs within months of being formed, raising the suspicion that it may be a straw donor.The Guardian contacted Goede for comment.The money pipeline functions such that none of these organizations are named as donors in the FEC filings of the Super Pacs.The Guardian contacted the Concord Fund, Thomas Klingenstein and the Conservative Partnership Institute for comment, and emailed Purple Action at an address that returned the message undelivered. None responded.This cycle, the Green Dragon Coalition has put a further $177,500 into the same Super Pac in seven payments since 5 December 2025, the most recent on 21 April 2026. The Pac’s independent expenditures so far this cycle total $15,000 in support of Barry Moore, the Alabama congressman currently running to replace Tommy Tuberville, who is departing the US Senate to run for the Alabama governor’s seat.The Guardian contacted Barry Moore for comment.Elsewhere, the Pac’s expenditures have gone to organizations connected to Datwyler’s associates.Itspayments to L4 Consulting LLCtotal $164,809 across 13 installments between 2 January and 5 June 2026, with the disbursements booked as “PAC strategy consulting” and “fundraising consulting”.
