L4 is run by Dan Hauser, who is president of both Green Dragon entities and takes no salary from either.Hauser wasreported in October 2025to have been a paid senior adviser to the Utah senator Mike Lee, another Datwyler client, during the same period. In the 2024 cycle, L4 took $207,560 from the same Super Pac. Green Dragon’s charity separately paid L4 $128,033 for “event production”.The Guardian contacted Hauser for comment.Ghosh, the campaign finance reformer, pointed out that while non-profits have to disclose donors to the IRS, with the exception of private foundations and some political non-profits, they do not have to disclose them to the public.“So if the entire object is to conceal the sources of the money, the [501](c)4 on its own can accomplish that objective. The only thing the [501](c)3 layer adds is that [501](c)3 donations are tax deductible for the donor,” he said.Ghosh added: “But that’s a little riskier because if they are using the [501](c)3 to first obtain a tax deduction and then that money is being used to influence elections, that’s one of the few things that federal tax law does prohibit.”Either way, he said that “that’s a transparency nightmare. It becomes this problematic daisy chain where the [501](c)3 is sending money to the [501](c)4, theoretically not to support its political advocacy. But again, who can say exactly whether that’s happening or not? These are opaque entities. They are black boxes.”Alyssa Bowen, executive director of True North Research, put the same structure more bluntly. “It’s like dark money made darker,” she said. “It’s almost like he’s running science experiments to find out all the ways you can conceal who’s donating.”She said the charity layer carried a second advantage for the giver. “The Pacs are legally required to disclose your donors, but you’re not [required to do so] for a 501(c)3 or [501(c)]4. And then there’s also the tax benefits – donors receive tax benefits for donating to a 501(c)3,” she said. “So it’s twofold for these donors that are trying to make sure that they’re not held accountable for some of the more political spending that they do.”Parallel pipelinesA similar pattern is visible across four other 2026 races. In each, Datwyler is treasurer of the campaign and of the Super Pac spending in that race, and in each he held both roles before the spending began.TheLove America Uphold Freedom Pacspent $248,091 for Catalina Lauf in Florida’s 19th district between 13 and 24 July 2026, which is all the independent spending it has ever made. It is registered at Datwyler’s own address, and amended its registration on 11 July to add the domain LAUFPAC.com, two days before the advertising started.It shares 14 vendors with Lauf’s campaign, seven of them substantive digital firms, over overlapping periods – which engages the FEC’scommon-vendor conduct standardindependently of who the treasurer is.The Guardian contacted the Lauf campaign for comment.View image in fullscreenCatalina Lauf speaks to the crowd during the Save America tour on 3 January 2021 in Sugar Hill, Georgia.Photograph: David J Griffin/Icon Sportswire via Getty ImagesOn shared vendors, Ghosh said this is “more pressing than just having a treasurer in common. The use of vendors in common for things like media production, placement – that’s exactly the kind of spending that would be the subject of prohibited coordination. If the vendors they’re using are actually taking what they learn from their work for the campaign clients and then utilising that information or passing that information to their Super Pac clients, that’s exactly what the law prohibits.”TheDefending Conservative Values Pacwas registered on 9 May 2026 and spent $485,213 against Blake Moore, the incumbent Karianne Lisonbee is challenging, between 29 May and 20 June – again, 100% of its spending, and again in Utah’s second district. TheShow Me Valor Pacwas registered six weeks after Taylor Burks’ campaign, with Datwyler as treasurer, and spent $166,051 supporting him. TheAmerican Honor Pacspent $162,800 for David Flippo in Nevada’s second district; Datwyler is its treasurer, custodian of records and only named officer, and its entire 2026 income – $155,000 – came from Stephen Flippo.TheAmerican Liberty Foundationis simultaneously the name of a 501(c)3, a 501(c)4 and a Super Pac, all with Datwyler as treasurer, the first two presided over by Raymond Yonkura, Jim Jordan’s chief of staff for nearly a decade. The Super Pac spent $294,021 for Jenny Costa Honeycutt in South Carolina’s first district in June 2026, funded by $355,000 from the social welfare arm, $250,000 from the Geo Group’s Pac and $250,000 from a group called Voice of the Children of Israel.What those campaigns knew is the open question for True North’s Bowen. “It’s concerning that all of these organisations and entities are using him, because what do they know about his past?” Bowen said, referring to Datwyler. “Is that why they’re using him – or are they totally unaware?”She was skeptical that one person could service so many committees properly. “It feels far-fetched that he could be doing a good job,” she said.‘Stunning … inexplicable’In the current electoral cycle, Datwyler has already attracted controversy.The Delaware Republican party reportedly claims hewent unresponsive and then leftin January 2026 amid five straight months of negative federal cash balances, missing a filing deadline and drawing an FEC warning of “civil money penalties, an audit or legal enforcement action”; he says he resigned because the party had not paid him.In Alabama he is the sole officer of a Pac registered to a rented mailbox that has reportedly drawnlegal threatsover its attack mailers. A former state senator, Dell Hill,reportedly saidin April that he had launched the Pac, whose registration names only Datwyler. Datwylerreportedly saidhe was “strictly the accountant doing the books” and had “nothing to do with producing the ads”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne of the Republican incumbents it targeted, the state representative Matt Simpson,lost his primaryin May.In a telephone conversation, Simpson said of Datwyler: “If he found loopholes to try to exploit for his purposes, then that’s the nature of the business that we’re in. You can’t lie, though. That’s the problem that I have with it.”He gave the Guardian a copy of a later mailer in which the Pac said a false claim about Simpson’s positions “was a printing error”.The Guardian contacted Phillip Pettus, another incumbent the Pac targeted, for comment.A Texas campaign Datwyler keeps books fordrew a watchdog complaintin May 2026, and Andy Ogles, whose campaign he still runs the books for,confirmed in 2024that, at that time, the FBI was investigating his campaign finances.View image in fullscreenRepublican representative Andy Ogles, of Tennessee, at the US Capitol on 3 February 2026.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesThe complaint has not moved because the FECneeds four votes to open an investigationandhas had only two commissionerssince October 2025. Donald Trump’s two nominees have sat with the Senate rules committee since 11 February with no further action.In May this year, the Campaign Legal Center asked the commission to investigate Datwyler again, over a $250,000 payment to one of his Super Pacs from the private prison company Geo Group, ICE’s largest contractor.Datwyler has not been charged with any offence, and several of the investigations closed without findings. His firm’s general counsel has called the allegations against him “baseless attacks”.The incidents are part of a longer pattern of scandal and regulatory scrutiny.To date, Datwyler has been named as a respondent in24 complaintsbefore the FEC. Two ended in penalties, both for conduct that predated his appointment as treasurer. The other 22 were dismissed or closed without a penalty, at least three of them after commissioners deadlocked 3-3.In January 2023 the FECfined Josh Mandel’s Senate campaign$15,080 for failing to promptly reportcontributions totalling $147,601received between 14 and 30 April 2022, before the 3 May Ohio primary.Datwyler’s successor as Mandel’s campaign treasurer, Elizabeth Curtis,wrote to the FECabout “the stunning number of inexplicable reporting errors made by Mr Datwyler … ignoring the FEC and potentially incurring significant fines without notifying the Committee”.The Guardian contacted Curtis for comment via a consultancy website contact form.View image in fullscreenJosh Mandel speaks at a campaign event in Cortland, Ohio, on 21 April 2022.Photograph: Gaelen Morse/ReutersIn 2023, the FEC fined four campaigns for failing to file required notices of late contributions in the 2022 elections while Datwyler was their treasurer:Mandel’s Senate campaign ($15,080) and the House campaigns ofRodney Davis($5,820),Ann Wagner($3,560) andJoe Kent($3,304), for a total of $27,764. Fines against the campaigns ofRich McCormickandKyle Sinclairalso named Datwyler as treasurer, for failures that predated his appointment.Those were not the only cases. A Guardian review of FEC enforcement records found 13 cases in which a committee was penalised for failures that occurred, at least in part, while Datwyler was its treasurer, with penalties totalling $110,791. The largest came in April 2024, when Rodney Davis’s campaignagreed to pay $43,475, in a settlement Datwyler signed, after it failed to refund $479,783.82 in general-election contributions within the permitted time once Davis had lost his 2022 primary.The largest penalties to name Datwyler concerned reporting from before he took over.In March 2024, Mike Braun’s Senate campaignagreed to pay a $159,000 civil penaltyover improperly reported loans from the 2018 race.The FEC’s file on the matterrecords that Datwyler became the campaign’s treasurer on 29 January 2019, after the period in question, and that the campaign blamed its former treasurer for the errors. Commissioners deadlocked 3-3 on a separate allegation, that the campaign had misreported receipts and disbursements.A representative for Datwylerreportedly saidhe “served as treasurer at the time the issue was corrected, reviewed, and resolved, not at the time of the underlying activity”.Trump loyalist Jim Jordan linked to group that received ‘dark money’ from ICE detention contractorRead moreIn July 2022 Jim Jordan’s campaignagreed to pay $60,000for failing to accurately disclose $1.2m in receipts and disbursements in five reports covering late 2018 to mid-2020. The FEC’s referral lists Datwyler as its treasurer from 15 July 2020, and the campaign told the commission he had “identified hundreds of errors” in its earlier accounting and filed corrected reports.He was the shared treasurer of Joe Kent’s 2022 congressional campaign and of a Super Pac backing it – an arrangementthe Guardian examined in February 2025, when campaign finance experts questioned the campaign’s routing of more than $1m through a company they described as a possible shell.Liberty OhioIn December 2021 Mike Dowling, a former FirstEnergy executive defending himself in a shareholder lawsuit over the $60m scheme that secured passage ofOhio’s HB6 energy bailout,subpoenaedtwo dark-money groups at the centre of that scandal: Partners for Progress and Generation Now, the latter of which hadpleaded guilty to racketeeringthat February.He asked for their communications with a list of people and organisations that included Liberty Ohio Inc, a non-profit for which Datwyler was treasurer, as well as Datwyler himself and the group’s secretary, Scott Guthrie. The same list named Ohio’s governor and lieutenant governor and every current and former member of the state legislature. Neither Datwyler nor Liberty Ohio was served with a subpoena or was a party to the lawsuit.The lawsuitsettled in August 2022, with $180m paid to FirstEnergy by insurers to resolve the derivative claims, less $36m in court-awarded legal fees. The defendants admitted no liability or wrongdoing.Both Datwyler and Guthrie were working at the time on Josh Mandel’s Senate campaign, with Datwyler as its treasurer and Guthrie as its manager. Mandel subsequently lost the 2022 Republican primary to JD Vance, who was subsequently elected Senator for Ohio, and then vice-president as Donald Trump’s running mate.Committees for which Datwyler served as treasurer spent more than $7m across the race – more than $5.4m of it from theUSA Freedom Fund, a Super Pac registered to his own post office box, which put$831,281 behind Mandeland a further $4.6m into attacking his three main rivals:$3m against Mike Gibbons,$1.5m against JD Vanceand$36,530 against Jane Timken.The Guardian can reveal other striking transactions involving Datwyler during that campaign. Between September 2021 and June 2022, Team Josh – the joint fundraising committee for Mandel’s campaign and his leadership Pac – transferred $1.1m in seven installments to the federal account of the Shelby county Republican party, a committee registered not in Ohio but atDatwyler’s post office box in Hudson, Wisconsin. The federal account of a second Ohio county party,Delaware, sent a further $362,458.Those two transfers were the entire declared income of the Shelby county account, amounting to $1,471,200. It then spent$1,398,811 on independent expenditures supporting Mandel, amounting to 95 cents of every dollar it took in, andwound itself upthat December. Datwyler was treasurer of all three committees, and of Mandel’s campaign.The Guardian contacted Scott Guthrie for comment. An email to Josh Mandel was returned undelivered.State-level enforcementTwice, state authorities have probed Datwyler as opposed to his clients.The most developed coordination allegation against him is in Tennessee. In 2024, the state’s registry of election finance referred a complaint to the attorney general over the Republican primary in the fourth senate district, where a dark-money Pac spent more than $600,000 to defeat the incumbent, Jon Lundberg. Datwyler was treasurer and officer of that Pac, East Tennessee Conservatives; he was also treasurer of the congressional campaign of Diana Harshbarger, whose son Bobby was the challenger.The attorney general’s report found that Datwyler had helped Bobby Harshbarger set up his campaign in April, after being introduced by the congresswoman’s chief of staff. According to the report, Datwyler sent him guidance on appointing a treasurer, obtained a tax number for a bank account and opened a fundraising account with Republican donation processor WinRed, and that the Pac he ran then spent heavily against Lundberg.Investigatorscould not reach a conclusion, mainly because Datwyler declined, through counsel, to be interviewed or to produce documents. Two registry members said he should be subpoenaed. “The system’s not working the way it needs to on the dark money side,” the registry’s chair, Tom Lawless, said, “and I don’t know if we’ve got the tools to do anything for it.” Datwyler’s lawyer, Eric Brown,reportedly saidthat “news reports confirm that the AG report found no factual or legal basis to support the allegations of improper coordination”.The registrydismissed the complaintin May 2025 at the request of Ken Yager, the Republican state senator who had filed it. “It’s just one of those where nobody was here to prosecute it,” Lawlesssaid at the time.The Guardian contacted Bobby Harshbarger for comment.A second Tennessee complaint went further. Lawyers for the Civic Engagement Forum and Datwylerconceded to the registrythat the group had operated as a political campaign committee and should have registered and disclosed its spending, and offered $2,500 to settle. The registry’s chair, Tom Lawless, said the offer was not high enough. In July 2025, the registrydeferred a decisionand ordered the group to register and file its disclosure reports, and in September itaccepteda revised offer of a $6,000 penalty and closed the case.Datwylerreportedly toldthe attorney general’s investigators that he had no personal knowledge of the Citizen Engagement Forum, a second group named in the complaint.In April 2024 Emily’s Listasked the FEC to investigatean Arizona group with a Democratic-sounding name, the Turn AZ Blue Pac, which had disclosed neither its spending nor its donors and which was listed with Datwyler as its treasurer. Through a lawyer, Datwyler told the commission he “is not, nor has he ever been, the treasurer” of the group, andthe FEC’s dismissal reportrecords that he swore he had never heard of it before the complaint. The commission dismissed the case in April 2025.View image in fullscreenEmily’s list asked the FEC to investigate the Turn AZ Blue Pac, which listed Datwyler as its treasurer. He said he had never heard of the group before the complaint.Photograph: Presley Ann/Getty Images for Emily’s ListThat July, a Nevada leadership Pac formed to back the Republican Senate candidate Jim Marchantasked the justice departmentto investigate Datwyler for alleged wire fraud over a $500 cheque written from its account to his compliance firm, AxCapital, after he had stepped down as its treasurer. The complaint, written by the Republican election lawyer Dan Backer, alleged “a long history of running roughshod over federal campaign finance law”. It said Datwyler first described the payment as a bank error made through an online bill-pay system, then said he would refund it; the Pac’s own FEC filings record a$500 “compliance refund” from AxCapitalon 22 April 2024. Eric Brown, general counsel of Axiom Strategies, which owns AxCapital,reportedly saidthe firm faced “baseless attacks” and that the letter was “nothing more than a stunt”. No charges have followed.Backer told the Guardian this week that he believed the $500 was refunded “only after filing the [justice department] letter”; his letter is dated 26 July 2024. Asked whether the justice department had responded, he said: “Law enforcement agencies generally do not comment on pending investigations.” He said Datwyler had “cost the GOP vast sums of money” and was “just not cut out for this line of work at this level”, and that aggrieved former clients rarely act because “no one ever wants to spend the money or put their reputation out there, to sue or to file an FEC complaint”.The Guardian also contacted the Tennessee complainant, the state representative Michele Reneau, and Emily’s List for comment. They did not respond.In Maryland, Datwyler waslisted as the treasurerof “Dan Cox for US Congress”, a committee registered in the name of a candidate who had not filed to run. In Ohio’s Mahoning valley, county party chairs of both partiescould learn nothingabout a group attacking local officials beyond his name on the treasurer designation.In Texas, a Super Pac Datwyler kept books for reportedlyspent almost everything it raised on credit card feesand nothing on campaigning, according to its own FEC filings.Perhaps most notoriously, George Santos’s campaignnamed him treasurer in January 2023and his lawyer told the FEC the appointment was unauthorised – a position the same lawyerlater retracted, writing that he had lost confidence in his client’s account.Santos, the New York Republican who fabricated most of his biography, was expelled from the House in December 2023 andsentenced to more than seven yearsin April 2025 for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. He served 84 days before Donald Trumpcommuted the sentencein October.SecrecyDatwyler is steadfast in maintaining secrecy on behalf of funders.Asked in October 2024 about $200,000 that arrived at a Super Pac opposing Sheldon Whitehouse from his Wisconsin address, Datwylersaid a Florida couple were the primary fundersand declined to name them.Occasionally, Datwyler’s denials have been undone by his own filings.Asked in October 2025 about attack mailers in a Utah school board race, hesaid the address on them “is not associated with us at all”; hours later, the Pac filed state paperwork listing him as its primary officer.Time after time, however, investigations that reached committees he kept have ended without action against him. Three executives of Navatek, a Hawaii defence contractor,pleaded guiltyover schemes that included routing $150,000 of company money through a sham entity, the Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers, to 1820 Pac, a Super Pac backing Susan Collins for which Datwyler was treasurer. The Pac told the FEC the contribution was lawful. Commission lawyers later recommended finding that it had failed to refund the money once its source came to light, but the commissioners never voted on that, and in January 2025, with the statute of limitations running out, theydismissedthe allegation against the Pac and Datwyler in his official capacity. The Pac’s FEC reports show no refund.On Datwyler’s overall operation, Saurav Ghosh said: “What you’re describing is both incredibly common and incredibly problematic for our elections.”Explore more on these topicsUS political financingRepublicansSuper PacsUS politicsWisconsinfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I can’t afford to lose £3,000’: the ‘gameshow’ that made contestants gamble their own money | Television | The Guardian
description: A Derren Brown-style experiment? A Ghostwatch stunt? Wild rumours have swirled around Bradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot all week. The hoax has finally been revealed – and its message is terrifying
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: A Derren Brown-style experiment? A Ghostwatch stunt? Wild rumours have swirled around Bradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot all week. The hoax has finally been revealed – and its message is terrifying
Content: A blurred reality in Million Pound Shot.Illustration: Channel 4View image in fullscreenA blurred reality in Million Pound Shot.Illustration: Channel 4Television‘I can’t afford to lose £3,000’: the ‘gameshow’ that made contestants gamble their own moneyA Derren Brown-style experiment? A Ghostwatch stunt? Wild rumours have swirled around Bradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot all week. The hoax has finally been revealed – and its message is terrifyingHannah J DaviesSun 1 Nov 2026 17.05 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.14 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn late October, some canny viewers began to wonder whether there was something strange about Channel 4’s latest gameshow. Bradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot had been billed as a new big-money contest with a twist, but information about its pilot episode was strangely minimal. Television and radio producer Chuck Thomaswondered on Xwhether it could be a Derren Brown-style psychological experiment; a Ghostwatch-esque stunt; or even a dark TV comedy in the vein of the genre-bending series Inside No 9. Indeed, the timing – one day after Halloween – also seemed to point viewers towards some kind of parody or one-off drama.As more information was revealed about the show – including that its players would stake their own money, in a UK television first – Thomasconsideredwhether this was in fact “an elaborate anti-gambling stunt”. It was an opinion shared by journalist Alistair Ryder, whopostedthat it was “more likely to be a stealth anti-gambling drama disguised as a gameshow than a modern Ghostwatch”, adding that the programme “could make for uncomfortable viewing in a completely different way”.Both were right: Bradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot was a fake, designed to highlight the manipulative tactics used by the gambling industry. And even for those who watched the programme live tonight (Channel 4 provided press screeners a few days beforehand), the ruse was likely fairly apparent from the outset. One contestant, Mark, declared that he would stake all of the money he had to his name – £1,000 – while another, Reece, intended to use money borrowed from friends and even credit cards and loans for a chance to win the show’s titular top prize. Said Walsh, in a departure from the usually upbeat language of TV quizzes: “There could be a lot to win … but there could also be a lot to lose.” Either this was the biggest recession indicator ever, or there was something more afoot.View image in fullscreen‘A lot to lose’ … contestants on Million Pound Shot.Photograph: Channel 4Walsh compered the show in the usual breezy style he displays on ITV’s The Chase (when Reece made his first bet – using a chip-and-pin machine mounted in his lectern – Walsh asked: “Did you leave a tip for me?”). But what followed was markedly different from what we usually see in these sorts of shiny-floor productions. Reece began to lose badly, betting more than he could afford on trivia rounds and ending up £2,400 in the red. At a critical moment where he could have cashed out of the game, he was offered a bonus ball – a free bet – for the “million pound shot” roulette game. “I can’t really afford to lose £3,000,” said Reece, a teacher on an annual salary of £30,000. “But then, if you have another free £3,000 … ” He played on, losing catastrophically. But, said Walsh, he could always buy another ball with his own money …It was here that Million Pound Shot’s artifice would have begun to truly give way for anyone watching live. A heckler in the crowd asked whether there was “no one else that thinks that this is wrong?!” The woman was an actor – as was Reece, Mark, another contestant Helen and even the floor manager. But – as both viewers at home and press watching in advance would have then realised – the audience were totally unaware. Pity the people who thought they had signed up for a fun outing, only to find themselves at the centre of a downbeat TV experiment.But, depressing as it may be, Million Pound Shot had an important message. Psychologist Dr Steve Sharman explained to the studio audience that the game’s “bet balls” echoed the way the gambling industry makes money feel abstract, encouraging people to spend far beyond their means. Losses, he explained, are often disguised as wins, using an example of similar-sounding winning and losing notifications from the Ladbrokes app which “messes with the reward circuitry in our brain”. (Entain, which owns Coral and Ladbrokes, say customers only receive promotional offers if they have opted in to marketing, and that it blocks marketing where it identifies safer gambling concerns, even if a customer has opted in. It strongly rejects any suggestion that Coral deliberately targets customers showing signs of gambling harm with free bets. They say all games on Ladbrokes are certified to the regulator’s technical standards, which ban games from celebrating a return less than or equal to the stake.)Pressing a buzzer gave Reece the illusion of control, in the same vein as fixed-odd betting terminals and online games, while the free bet hooked him back in just as he should have quit, echoing tactics used by the likes of , William Hill. (Evoke, owners of William Hill, say they strongly reject any suggestion that they disregard consumer protections to keep customers playing regardless of the potential risks. They say their approach to restricting marketing and take-up of new bonus offers is informed by the Gambling Commission’s requirements and their own assessment of indicators of gambling harm. They say they have invested in specialist teams to identify potential signs of gambling harm and take appropriate action, including stopping customers from gambling.) Gambling reform campaigner Will Prochaska told Walsh that problem gamblers were nine times more likely than others to be offered a free bet, with half of the sector’s profits coming from just 5% of its customers.Elsewhere, according to Prochaska, at least £1bn a year is spent by the industry on advertising in the UK – to replace customers who quit, turn to crime to fund their gambling, or even take their own lives. Walsh’s language, we learn, had been lifted directly from those adverts, such as Sky Bet. (Flutter UKI, which owns Paddy Power & Sky Bet, say they operate in a legal, licensed and highly regulated market and they take their obligations incredibly seriously. They say advertising is a benefit of being part of a regulated market. They say that like any other business, their brands offer promotions to attract customers and free bets are part of that offer.)View image in fullscreenBradley Walsh on Million Pound Shot.Photograph: Gary Moyes/Channel 4The most impactful aspect of Million Pound Shot was arguably an interview with the man who inspired the character of Reece,Patrick Foster, who struggled with gambling addiction for 13 years, racking up estimated debts of around £250,000. He began gambling in betting shops at university, before turning to the internet: “Suddenly I had a betting shop and a casino in my pocket, and I could do it any time, any place, at the click of a button.” At one stage, Foster had 76 accounts with different online platforms. Like Reece, he was also a teacher. So severe was his addiction that he lied to his students’ parents and borrowed money from them, too. A high-risk attempt to get the money back led him to contemplate suicide. His wife Charlotte says: “The gambling industry has an awful lot to answer for.”Foster’s story has been highly publicised before. And many of the gambling industry’s dirty tricks have long been dissected by journalists like the Guardian’s Rob Davies, who wrote in his 2022 book Jackpot that such companies “have an incentive to ensure you don’t twig that you’re steadily haemorrhaging cash”. Million Pound Shot might also feel too heavy-handed – a clearly signposted experiment that lays everything on extra thick.And yet, it highlights an extremely dangerous problem that’s all too often trivialised. A closing ident tells us that £17.5bn was lost by Britons to gambling in 2025, with one in every 14 suicides linked to gambling. Reform is surely long overdue. “It’s serious, it’s real and it’s happening now,” says Walsh of the events dramatised in Million Pound Shot. If it makes even one person think differently about how they gamble, this brash and blatant hoax will surely have been worth it.A Betting and Gaming Council spokesperson said: “Our members operate in one of the most tightly regulated gambling markets in the world, with strict rules on advertising, customer protection, promotional offers and game design. These protections have been strengthened significantly in recent years. Practices such as losses disguised as wins have been banned for years, while operators are required to stop marketing to customers where strong signs of harm are identified.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.org.In the UK, support for problem gambling can be found via the NHSNational Problem Gambling Clinicon 020 7381 7722, orGamCareon 0808 8020 133. In the US, call theNational Council on Problem Gamblingon 1-800-MY-RESET. In Australia,Gambling Help Onlineis available on 1800 858 858 and the National Debt Helpline is at 1800 007 007Explore more on these topicsTelevisionBradley WalshChannel 4featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘Let’s take Alexa out into the garden and smash it with a shoe’: Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan take aim at Hollywood, AI ... and each other | Television | The Guardian
description: As deadpan spoof documentarian Philomena Cunk returns with a new series on cinema, her creators discuss meeting J-Lo, their worst ever jobs – and why artificial intelligence is like mad cow disease
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: As deadpan spoof documentarian Philomena Cunk returns with a new series on cinema, her creators discuss meeting J-Lo, their worst ever jobs – and why artificial intelligence is like mad cow disease
Content: I’m with stupid … Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenI’m with stupid … Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianTelevisionInterview‘Let’s take Alexa out into the garden and smash it with a shoe’: Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan take aim at Hollywood, AI ... and each otherTim JonzeAs deadpan spoof documentarian Philomena Cunk returns with a new series on cinema, her creators discuss meeting J-Lo, their worst ever jobs – and why artificial intelligence is like mad cow diseaseSun 1 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShe has tackled Britain, conquered the world and even grappled with life itself. Now Philomena Cunk is back on our screens – looking as miserable and confused as ever – to take on her biggest subject yet: cinema.Cinema, the iconically stupid presenter explains, is not just mankind’s greatest achievement but also a world where “men can be heroes, women can get off with heroes, and nobody ever goes to the toilet – unless you’re watching a specialist film from Japan”. So if you’ve ever wanted to know why “Citizen Ken” always has carrots in his pockets, where the word auteur comes from (“They felt theyoughtaget all the credit”) or how Benedict Cumberbatch reacts to the hardest-hitting questions of his career (such as “Who are you?”), this is quite literally the only place you’ll ever find the answers.It has been 13 years since Diane Morgan and Charlie Brooker’s comic creation hit our screens, growing from an amusing segment on Brooker’s show Weekly Wipe into one of the most beloved figures on TV. To celebrate this new three-part series we’ve brought Morgan and Brooker together to chat about everything from defecating robots to dinner dates with Kanye West, and what it feels like to imagine a blue horse (there’s weirdly quite a lot about this).It’s a busy time for them both. Brooker is preparing for the launch of Blackmere, his deadpan detective show due on Netflix early next year, which he says will be in the vein of Airplane! and The Naked Gun. “The title will end up annoying me and that’s all my own fault,” he says. “It’s how Americans say ‘Black Mirror’ and I thought: that’s actually a really good name for a policeman.” As for Morgan, she is on a roll at the moment: her sitcom Ann Droid, about a robotic care assistant, garnered rave reviews, and she recently survived five episodes of Prime Video’sLast One Laughing. “People thought Cunk would be good training for that because she never laughs,” she says. “What they don’t realise is that I do crack up during the interviews, they just cut those bits out.”When we meet, Morgan has also just gone viral for chatting to J-Lo at the Stella McCartney show in Paris. So, before we get to anything else, what on earth were they chatting about?Diane MorganWell she’d just done a film with Brett Goldstein, so I told her that I used to do standup with him and that I enjoyed the film.Charlie BrookerIs that the best you could do?DMWell it’ssomethingisn’t it? What should I have said? Asked her what she’s doing later?Who’s the most unlikely person you’ve been in conversation with, Charlie?CBOh, I know the answer to this! It’s Kanye West. It was a couple of years ago. I actually had dinner with him. I don’t know if this is an anecdote for public consumption, really, but … it was quite a bizarre and sad occasion. I ended up thinking: “He’s not well.”View image in fullscreenReel deal… Diane Morgan as Philomena Cunk.Photograph: BBC/Pacesetter Productions/Olly CourtneyWhy did you meet up?CBHe wanted to meet because he’d seen a Black Mirror episode and liked it very much …DMWas it one of the earlier funny ones?CB[Deliberately ignoring her] I can tell you which one it was. It was calledMetalhead. It’s got your mate Maxine Peake in it and a robot dog.DMHonestly, how dead inside would you have to be to get a robot dog instead of a lovely little rescue dog?CBBut a robot pet wouldn’t die! That’s the reason I don’t have a pet in London, because I get very sad pre-emptively imagining that pet getting squashed.DMWhen you say you “imagine” it, what do you mean? Because you told me once that you had that thing where you can’t see images in your mind [aphantasia]. So if I say: “Picture a blue horse”, everyone else pictures it but you can’t.CBI think I can picture things. It’s just not like on telly where they have a flashback.DMIt is for me. It’s full surround sound, and so much detail.CB[Closing his eyes] If I think of a blue horse, I don’tsee it… It’s more like my brain is describing it to me.DMThat’s fascinating, isn’t it? The man who wrote Black Mirror can’t picture a blue horse! Whereas mine’s got reins on, it’s got facial expressions, it’s going … [Morgan blows an enormous raspberry while circling her head round in a convincingly horse-like manner].CBOK, what’s it doing right now? Is it lifting its tail? Can you see its bum?DMWell I can now. Now you’ve said that.This is actually exactly the kind of material my editor asked for in this piece.CBDid they say: “Can it be mainly about their psychic projections of horses?”DMIt is interesting, though. Have you been diagnosed with that or …CBDiagnosed withwhat?DMNo imagination.CBCritics might say I have, yes.DMDo you have dreams?CBI definitely see things in dreams and imagine that they’re real. Once I had a dream where a little circle appeared to signal a reel change, like when you’re watching an old film on TV. And the dream itself was about teachers at the school who were assassinating people. So fuck you with your “you can’t see anything in your mind’s eye” nonsense. I think our brains all have different operating systems, like Windows or Mac OS or Linux.DMThere’s actually a man who got to 40-odd and discovered he only had half a brain.CBWas his name Jacob Rees-Mogg?DMHe was actually an accountant. And he’d been living totally fine with half a brain. They were like, how can this be? Because you think of all the areas of the brain, like, the hippocampus and, er, the other areas of the brain … I just think that’s incredible. That basically you don’t really need a brain. I actually think your brain’s more like an aerial. So we are actually in the cloud and we’re being livestreamed to the receptors in our skulls. And when you die, your body dies, but your consciousness just goes back to the cloud.CBThat’s beautiful, actually. What’s the point of that, though?DMWell, what’s the point of anything? Don’t go pulling at that thread! Right, come on, let’s start!Did you have any idea Philomena Cunk would be such an enduring character?DMNo, I was told by people on the programme that I would get a huge backlash because I wasn’t Charlie. They said brace yourself for a lot of shit on social media. Because people just want Charlie. Anything that isn’t Charlie is just people going: “Where’s Charlie, this is fucking shit!”CBAnd now it’s the other way round!View image in fullscreenMirth control … Diane Morgan and Charlie Brooker.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianWas Diane’s auditionfor Philomena Cunkthe first time you met?CBYeah! Oh, actually, no! Because she’s got an anecdote about me being horrible at the Edinburgh festival.DMEveryone in my family used to read your Guardian column. It started with my dad. He rarely laughed at anything, but he would be crying tears reading your column. And I’d be like: “What’s so funny?” So he’d read a bit of it and we’d all laugh, as a family, together. And then they started printing your photo.CBAnd that ruined it for you?DMIt meant I recognised you at the Edinburgh festival. So I went over and was like: “You’re Charlie Brooker!” And you said: “Yeah, what do you want?” So I said: “I read your column, it’s really funny.” And you said: “So?”CBSurely I was joking. Sometimes when people come up and say: “I really love Black Mirror”, I reply, “What’s wrong with you?” It’s just a joke!DMLooking back, of course it was a joke. But I didn’t know that then. I was mortified. I thought: “He hates me!” and I was crushed. I couldn’t even think about him for years. When the auditions came up for Philomena, I knew I wanted it more than anything … but that Charlie hated me. Whereas actually you didn’t give a shit.Philomena Cunk was supposed to be a posh character originally, right?CBWe used to get people going: “Oh you’re mocking working-class accents,” because of the Barry Shitpeas character. So the idea was to add an airhead, middle-class, yummy-mummy, Chelsea-tractor cupcake blogger to the show. Hence the name Philomena Cunk.DMYou’d never get someone called Philomena in Bolton – you’d get your head kicked in.CBI was watching all the audition tapes and wasn’t quite sure who the character was.DMLuckily I’d got the guts up to ask if I could do it in my own accent because I thought that was funnier.CBWhen I saw you doing it in your flat, fucking depressed, unimpressed-with-everything tone, I was doubled over with laughter.DMAh, that’s so sweet … you’re forgiven for the Edinburgh thing now.CBThe strange thing about Cunk is she’s sort of weirdly in charge of things, even if she’s speaking to a professor or whatever …DMWe interviewed Michael Bay for this new series and the crew were a bit terrified of him because they’re big, big fans. But I wasn’t bothered. Because [whispers] I don’t really watch a lot of films. It actually helps that I don’t know or care who these experts are. Actually, I think we confused Michael Bay because I asked him how much he paid for his trainers and he thought I meant actual people who trained him. He said I was asking odd questions.DMI often talk about my mate Paul, though, so that might get confusing.View image in fullscreenCharlie Brooker (centre) and Diane Morgan with Cunk on Cinema executive producer Sam Ward.Photograph:  /BBC/Pacesetter Productions/Matt KennedyThere are lots of jokes about AI in these new episodes – mainly Cunk challenging experts by saying she’s asked AI. Do either of you use AI?CBI use it when I’m somewhere I don’t know and want to find, say, a good barbecue restaurant that doesn’t serve pork. And then when you turn up it no longer exists. But other than that, no. I would never use it to help write something.DMThey’re trying to force it on you, aren’t they? But I won’t even let it do that [Mimics flicking something away].CBI’m a bit annoyed that there’s new technology and I don’t like it. I think it’s more that I don’t like the people who are making it. Having said that, I think the idea that it’s going to take over the world and destroy us all is a bit far-fetched.Ithasstarted speaking its own language, though, according to reports…CBYeah, but it’s just been fed on scraps of itself, hasn’t it? It’s a bit like when we started feeding cows on scraps of cow, and in the end they all got mad cow disease. So AI might look like it’s talking in some advanced language but actually all it’s saying is [sticks out tongue and waggles his head]: “Braaaappurgglefluuuurrrk!”View image in fullscreenJape expectations … Diane Morgan and Charlie Brooker.Photograph: Antonio Zazueta OlmosDid you ever think technology would advance this rapidly?CBNot really. Our Alexa recently updated and started speaking in a very human voice, which really freaked my son out. It was like, “Hey, yeah man, we can do that if you like” … a bit uncanny valley. We’ve had to change its voice back to the previous setting. When really what we should be doing is taking it out into the garden and smashing it with a shoe.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDiane, you don’t use AI, but in a way you’ve written quite a pro-AI comedy withAnn Droid?DMHave I? Oh yeah. I suppose I have. [Anxiously] Is that what people are saying?CBIt’s what he’s saying, right now!DMIt wasn’t supposed to be a statement on anything. It was just supposed to be a funny show about a robot and an old woman. It’s different when it’s your own show. On another person’s show you just say the words and if it’s shit then it’s not your fault. But with this everything rests on you. I remember when I first had the idea. I pitched it to the BBC and then I suddenly thought: “Oh shit, they’re going to make me be the robot aren’t they?” And they did. So I spent a year freaking out about it. Because obviously if you’re on telly pretending to be a robot and it doesn’t go well then it’s going to look really daft isn’t it?So you went to robot school …DMI did! With a guy called Dan.What did he teach you?DMNever blink, mainly. He also taught you not to bob your head. To always walk like this [gets up and glides across the room in a chillingly robot-like manner].Would you fancy robot school, Charlie?CBWell I am quite stiff. I’ve got a very bad back. I’d quite like to be a robot, though. They don’t have to defecate.Is that something they taught you at robot school?DMNo we didn’t cover that.‘Suddenly I was a celebrity. I didn’t want to be!’ Sue Johnston on fame, loneliness and her new robot palRead moreDid robot school require you to go full method with your character?DMI mean, I practised at home. But I didn’t spend a day as a robot. My job’s not that weird.Whatisthe weirdest job you’ve ever had?CBI know what Diane is going to say …DMThe worming tablets factory?CBYeah! Did you ever eat them?DMEat what? A worming tablet? Of course I didn’t. They’re for dogs. And I’m not a dog. Also, I’ve not got worms. You’ve not done horrible jobs like that, have you?CBWhen I worked at CeX we had a lot of people coming in trying to sell stolen laptops. And a boss who would make us do things, like, one day I had to clear out the back room.DM[Sarcastically] Oh, that sounds terrible.CBIt was! It was full of shit and a dead cat!And look where you both are now!DMI owe it all to Charlie! He totally made everything happen for me. All my subsequent career in comedy is down to him … I owe him everything!CBAh, that’s lovely. You’ve had to be really nice to me there and it’s all on tape!Would you like to say anything nice back?CBI’d say that Diane has naturally funny bones. And skin and eyes. She operates on a unique comic frequency – it’s rare to find a performer like that. She’s totally tuned in to the words which means in turn the writing room can tune into her. She elevates everything. Can I be sick now? I don’t like saying nice things.Cunk on Cinema will air on BBC Two and iPlayer from 12 November.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionCharlie BrookerDiane MorganTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Like many authors, I’m bombarded by scam fan mail. I wasn’t prepared for what would happen when I wrote back | Joe Dunthorne | The Guardian
description: The novelist receives passionate AI-written emails almost every day – but when he decided to take up one sender’s offer to find him new readers, the story took a darker turn
Author: Joe Dunthorne
Headline: The novelist receives passionate AI-written emails almost every day – but when he decided to take up one sender’s offer to find him new readers, the story took a darker turn
Content: Joe Dunthorne.Photograph: Hayley BenoitView image in fullscreenJoe Dunthorne.Photograph: Hayley BenoitJoe DunthorneLike many authors, I’m bombarded by scam fan mail. I wasn’t prepared for what would happen when I wrote backThe novelist receives passionate AI-written emails almost every day – but when he decided to take up one sender’s offer to find him new readers, the story took a darker turnJoe DunthorneSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s no humble way to say it: I get a lot of fan mail. Almost every day, multi-paragraph emails arrive from passionate and well-informed readers in Barcelona and Frankfurt, Chicago and Warsaw. They have appealing names like Bella Monroe, Thalina Rose and Tricia Claxton. Some of them are straightforward enthusiasts while others are more irreverent, like the one who signs off her messages “warm chaos”. Some love the “deadpan genius” of my novels while others admire my nonfiction’s “moral courage”. What they all have in common, though, is that they are entirely fake and trying to con me out of money. They promise to promote my work at their city-wide book clubs or spread the word among their reading communities, if only I transfer a few hundred dollars to cover costs.In the age of generative AI, scam emails have achieved a new level of personalisation. Most writers I know are receiving a steady stream of emails like this. The messages are often sophisticated enough to bypass a spam filter and reach our inboxes, leaving us no option but to read them and ask the painful question: would any real, living person feel this strongly about my work? Or, as one writer friend put it, the reason I know they’re fake is because they’ve actually read all my books.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markThe AIs that write these scams really have read all our books. We are being manipulated by a version of ourselvesWhat makes it worse is that the AIs that help write these scams reallyhaveread all our books. Last year, Anthropicagreed to pay $1.5bn in compensationto the thousands of authors whose copyrighted work they’d used to train their AI, Claude. In July, a group ofpublishers filed a lawsuit against Googlefor utilising “one of the most prolific infringements of copyrighted materials in history” in order to train their AI, Gemini. So when writers receive these AI-assisted scam messages, we know we are being manipulated by a version of ourselves.A few months ago, for example, I received a gushing email from Ottessa Moshfegh. The bestselling, Booker-shortlisted author of My Year of Rest and Relaxation–to my mind one of the most potent voices in contemporary fiction – was taking time away from producing her inimitable prose to write me a fan letter. I thanked her for getting in touch. We got chatting and I asked about her work-in-progress. She said that her new novel was “preoccupied with interior life: how emotions register, how they fail to, and what that absence or excess does to identity over time”. I thought we were making a real connection when she said that, really, the best way to understand her work was to explore her Amazon page. Sigh. Never meet your heroes. Other writers have received similar messages from fake Donna Tartt and fake Sally Rooney. It must be strange for the real Moshfegh, Rooney and Tartt to know that their novels have been harvested by tech corporations in order to create the ghost versions of themselves who now haunt the inboxes of their peers.double quotation markIt must be strange for Rooney and Tartt to know that ghost versions of their novels now haunt the inboxes of their peersThe correct response to all this is, of course, to simply report the email, block the sender and move on. But there is a part of me that fantasises about dramatically unmasking the scammer, revealing the villain beneath. So when I received an email from the founder of the Berlin Book Club, I decided to see how far I could get. I agreed that Ididneed help reaching new audiences. Iwaswilling to pay for her connections and expertise. Soon we started discussing payment methods. She wanted me to use CashApp or make a direct bank transfer but I was insistent that I could only send hard cash. We went back and forth for a couple of days. I impressed on her that I had, at that very moment, 500 US dollars in crisp notes in an unmarked envelope and that I lived quite near the post office. She finally relented and gave me a physical address. Neither of us commented on how unusual it was for the founder of the Berlin Book Club to have a postal address in the Philippines. I went on Google Maps and was able to find the street in question, a rural two-lane road with palm trees, a junk shop, an evangelical church and a large building hidden behind high white walls.The Philippines – along with Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia – is one of the countries most affected by organised crime networks running industrial-scale “scam farms”. Last year,authorities raided a facility in Bamban, north of Manila, freeing nearly 700 people who had been trapped there and forced to work as scammers. Inside the building, it resembled a hybrid between a call centre and a prison, rows upon rows of computers and green screens, and tiny dorms with bunk beds. About half of the workers were Filipino, while the others had been trafficked from China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan, Indonesia and Rwanda, their documentation withheld. The bosses, meanwhile, splashed around in the swimming pool next door. When another nearby compound was raided, they found it had its own brothel, karaoke suite and torture room. Across south-east Asia, these scam compounds are a multi-billion dollar industry, run largely by Chinese crime syndicates who routinely use violence and sexual abuse to keep workers in line. With the enormous sums of stolen money flowing through the industry, some compounds are the size of small towns or, perhaps more accurately, labour camps – with thousands of workers.double quotation markNeither of us commented on how unusual it was for the founder of the Berlin Book Club to have a postal address in the PhilippinesThe scammers are encouraged to make use of the latest technology, not just generative AI but also face masking apps, so that they can conduct video calls wearing whatever face suits the task. The big focus is on “pig butchering”: long-term romance scams where people are tricked into falling in love with a wealthy, glamorous foreigner who then advises them to invest in fake cryptocurrency. When a large scam compound in Cambodia was seized by the Thai army, they discovered that its facilities resembled a TV studio. There were costumes, wigs and different sets for filming different scams. There was a fake Brazilian police station and a replica Vietnamese bank. Scammers were trained to keep their targets on the hook for months, even years, inventing private and personalised narrative worlds through which they could drain all of the victim’s money. In aninterview with the BBC, one former scam compound manager sounded not unlike a novelist when he described the process. “[It’s] all about exploiting emotion,” he said. “You create a dream.”For my part, I did not send any cash to the Philippines. Instead I shared the details I’d received with the country’s cybercrime agency. Although, in the words ofWinston Casio, the spokesman for the presidential anti-organised crime commission in the Philippines, the ongoing problem is that the criminals have “the financial capability to corrupt just about anybody in public office. The amount of money they have is their potent tool against law enforcement.” When authorities shut down the Bamban compound, for example, they discovered that it was being run byAlice Guo, the local mayor. Similarly, the idea that AI companies might go out of their way to halt the criminal misuse of their technology seems just as doubtful – and for exactly the same reason. It’s making them fantastically rich.All of which is to say that my fantasy of unmasking the villain was just that, a fantasy. At least now, when I receive fake fan mail, I can attempt to understand the probable reality behind the quirky name and upbeat tone. On the other side of the screen, there is someone frightened and far from home, sitting in a sound-insulated booth with a dozen phones splayed out on their desk – while behind them their manager walks by, a taser at his hip.Explore more on these topicsJoe DunthorneScamsPublishingSocial mediaEmailfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I’m sick of smug celebrities on the podcast circuit. No wonder there’s a fuss when someone speaks the truth | Imogen West-Knights | The Guardian
description: It was so refreshing to hear Aaron Sorkin admit he was bad at parts of directing after his movie flop. If only others could be as frank, says writer Imogen West-Knights
Author: Imogen West-Knights
Headline: It was so refreshing to hear Aaron Sorkin admit he was bad at parts of directing after his movie flop. If only others could be as frank, says writer Imogen West-Knights
Content: Aaron Sorkin, director of The Social Reckoning (pictured) has been candid about his directing skills.Photograph: Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures/APView image in fullscreenAaron Sorkin, director of The Social Reckoning (pictured) has been candid about his directing skills.Photograph: Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures/APOpinionAaron SorkinI’m sick of smug celebrities on the podcast circuit. No wonder there’s a fuss when someone speaks the truthImogen West-KnightsIt was so refreshing to hear Aaron Sorkin admit he was bad at parts of directing after his movie flop. If only others could be as frankSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.56 ESTShareBy most accounts,Aaron Sorkin’s new film The Social Reckoning, a follow-up to his 2010 smash-hit The Social Network, is a flop. The film criticMark Kermode’s response to seeing itwas that Sorkin, who is widely regarded as one of the greatest living screenwriters, is “not a great director”.It seems that Sorkin agrees. Because Sorkin is very famous, he has had to do the rounds talking about the film in the media, which led to his appearance on the Hollywood Reporter’sAwards Chatter podcast earlier this week, in which he addressed these kinds of criticisms head on. “I’m very worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts that you can’t learn,” he said. “In addition to having absorbed none of the science of filmmaking, I have – and this is a problem in a visual medium – I have no visual sensibility at all, it turns out.”It’s not the first time a director has made a confession in this vein. Sam Raimi, for instance, memorablytold the Nerdist podcast in 2014that the reason Spider-Man 3 sucked is that he “messed up plenty” because he “didn’t really believe in all the characters”. But someone like Sorkin, a man with five Primetime Emmy wins and four Academy Award nominations, can afford to fess up to some failings. And it’s a pretty funny thing to say, as he does on this podcast, immediately after the host waxes lyrical about all his glittering career highlights and staggering creative ability.On the one hand, I think the world would be a better place if more people admitted that they are not that good at their jobs. I’d have loved it if the guy I hired to hang some pictures in my last flat, and who positioned several of them as if they were trying to escape through the ceiling and then merrily gouged a hole in one wall before claiming the wall itself was made of some substance previously unknown to masonry, had just held his hands up and said: “Look. My bad. I am not very good at this.”View image in fullscreenAaron Sorkin on the set of Molly’s Game with Jessica Chastain in 2017.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyBut it got me thinking about the whole podcast circuit.Podcasts, and the increasingly widespread “video podcast”, have become a cornerstone of the film publicity world. There are the big hitters such as the A24 Podcast and The Big Picture, but there are also endless podcasts you’ve never even heard of, where figures from the entertainment world have to engage in hours of conversation every time they have a new project out. Unlike the old requirement for a celebrity to commit to a couple of broadsheet interviews or a 10-minute slot for some late-night arts programme, the new demand forhoursof sprawling chat just ends up being undignified for all involved.I’ve interviewed actors and directors, and while most of them are media-trained and polite enough to seem engaged in talking about their work, it cannot be fun for them to meander around the houses again and again on the same subject. Making people talk about the same thing over and over is quite literally the basis of certain forms of torture.I hate to think of the kinds of things I might claim about my own work if I was subjected to hours of repetitive chatter about it. Do we really need to hear actors and directors do so much extemporaneous talk about what they do? Especially when so few of them – mea culpas of this Sorkin kind excepted – are saying anything other than “yeah it was a great experience, I love movies and this new movie of mine in particular”?I understand that the publicity circuit is a built-in part of making creative work in our digital age. People have to hear about the film for people to buy tickets to the film. The microphones are not going away. But I think that if we must have them, let’s have more strange admissions of incompetence or, even better, straight-up lies,to enliven the conversation.The only person who seems to be squeezing some personal enjoyment from the media merry-go-round is Robert Pattinson, who onceclaimed he watched a clown die in a car explosionin an interview for the Today show while promoting Water for Elephants in 2011.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo, more power to Sorkin, but next time maybe claim that you, I don’t know, secretly run a Facebook group for fans of the 1996 chimp comedy Dunston Checks In.Have a little fun with it.Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalistExplore more on these topicsAaron SorkinOpinionPodcastsThe Social NetworkSam RaimiRobert PattinsoncommentShareReuse this content

title: The UK’s legal cannabis market is booming – so why can’t this talented artist get any to treat his epilepsy? | Kojo Koram | The Guardian
description: Companies have rushed to supply the drug as a wellness treatment, but patients with serious illnesses aren’t able to get NHS prescriptions, says author and academic Kojo Koram
Author: Kojo Koram
Headline: Companies have rushed to supply the drug as a wellness treatment, but patients with serious illnesses aren’t able to get NHS prescriptions, says author and academic Kojo Koram
Content: Artist Louis Petit, who has epilepsy and needs medicinal cannabis, with his mother, Emma Matthews, at his  studio in Haggerston, London.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArtist Louis Petit, who has epilepsy and needs medicinal cannabis, with his mother, Emma Matthews, at his  studio in Haggerston, London.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The GuardianOpinionCannabisThe UK’s legal cannabis market is booming – so why can’t this talented artist get any to treat his epilepsy?Kojo KoramCompanies have rushed to supply the drug as a wellness treatment, but patients with serious illnesses aren’t able to get NHS prescriptionsSun 1 Nov 2026 07.33 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 11.52 ESTShareIn 2022, a prodigiously talented young artist named Louis Petit was preparing to return to the UK, having been effectively exiled in the Netherlands as a teenager so he could access the medical cannabis he needed to control his epilepsy. Six years earlier, Louis, then 12, had been diagnosed with a rare form of the neurological disease when medical cannabis was still illegal in the UK.But in Rotterdam, where it was legal, doctors helped him discover that a medical cannabis oil called Bedrolite, in combination with the right mix of anti-epileptic treatment, could slow and eventually stop his seizures. This was something his neurologists in the UK had previously considered impossible.By the time Louis won a place at City and Guilds of London Art School in 2022, the UK government had legalised medicinal cannabis, pressed by parents needing the drug to treat their epileptic children –most notably Charlotte Caldwell and Hannah Deacon.Louis assumed his troubles were behind him. “It seems naive now, but I think both me and my mum thought Britain would welcome me back, saying, ‘Thank God you’re better’,” Louis told me. But Louis has never been able to get a prescription for medical cannabis through the NHS. Instead, like almost everyone who needs the drug in this country, his only access has come through the expensive private sector. And now the producer of Bedrolite, a Dutch company, Bedrocan, hasdeclared bankruptcy.This means there is a high chance that, in the near future, the drug that keeps Louis well will stop being available privately, in a huge blow to all patients who rely on it. If this was people with diabetes facing a shortage of insulin, or people with high blood pressure running out of beta blockers, politicians would be falling over themselves to be seen trying to secure the long-term supply. But because this is epilepsy and cannabis – a medicine that has been stigmatised by a 50-year “war on drugs” – successive governments have avoided the issue, allowing this current crisis to develop, despite patients warning for years that they can’t be just abandoned to the private market.View image in fullscreenLouis Petit in Great Ormond Street hospital in 2018.Photograph: Family HandoutWhen the then home secretary, Sajid Javid,legalised medicinal cannabis in 2018, he stood up in parliament and promised patients who needed cannabis medication that their arduous fight was finally coming to an end. “Having been moved by heartbreaking cases involving sick children,” Javid said, “it was important to me that we took swift action to help those who can benefit from medicinal cannabis.”But these benefits reached a fraction of those who needed help. Since the first few patients received their prescriptions on the NHS, the vast majority of others – including Louis – have been met with a wall of refusal fromthe healthcare system, with doctors’ requests for public funding to prescribe cannabis medication rarely granted in practice.Until 2025, there werefewer than five prescriptionsfor unlicensed cannabis-based products such as Bedrolite given out across the entire NHS. In the absence of an accessible NHS route, the private market has become the only option for treatment for most patients,costing them anything up to £4,000 a monthfor their medicine.The result of medicinal cannabis being handed over wholesale to the private sector is that cannabis has quietly become one of the new growth sectors in Britain, with many cannabis companies getting rich from the boom.Remote online prescriptions,48-hour door-to-door deliveryandtargeted advertisementson social media have all helped grow the private customer base.But while private suppliers offer customer-friendly products such as cannabis vape pens and gummies on prescription, Bedrolite is a cannabis oil that was modified specially for children with drug-resistant epilepsy, and can’t be replaced with general cannabis. There is a much larger market for presenting cannabis as the new must-have wellness treatment for the on-the-go millennial suffering from anxiety, sleep issues or chronic pain medicine than there is for trying to treat acute but rare ailments such as complex epilepsy or multiple sclerosis.And there is little commercial incentive for private companies to spend huge amounts of money on the expensive, large-scale, clinical, randomised control trials that are needed to get more cannabis medication licensed and mainstreamed on the NHS. Successive governments washed their hands of this issue once legalisation eased the immediate pressure from families with sick loved ones who were campaigning against an outright ban.This dynamic leaves us in the paradoxical position whereby medical cannabis has become one of Britain’s new growth industries at exactly the same time that the most vulnerable patients, who desperately need the medication, cannot access it.“It’s been one shock after another since we came home,” said Louis’s mother, Emma. “If his neurologists’ funding request to NHS England had been approved last year, his Bedrolite supply would be guaranteed. There is enough stock in the Netherlands to last into 2028. But it’s not available to those without NHS prescriptions.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInitially, it was feared that the drug would stop being on sale in the UK before Christmas, but last week one UK drug manufacturer, Target Healthcare,told familiesit will secure a six-month stockpile of Bedrolite, offering temporary relief. However, what happens in six months’ time is anyone’s guess.The possible consequences of epileptic patients such as Louis suffering a forced withdrawal from the medication they use to control their seizures could be severe. The UK government needs to intervene and negotiate with Bedrolite’s manufacturer to secure the supply for all patients who need it in Britain.But beyond this emergency, the UK government needs to stop ignoring the medical cannabis industry and put in place the necessary investment and regulatory frameworks for it to become an accepted prescription on the NHS.Even before the recent bankruptcy of Bedrocan,families and campaignershave been insisting that patients shouldn’t be forced to live at the mercy of the volatile private market, all because politicians are too scared of the negative headlines that might come from mainstreaming a still-stigmatised drug such as cannabis on the NHS.“Health shouldn’t be an issue of whether you are wealthy enough to afford it or even be able to access it,” Louis said to me as we parted. We will see over the next couple of months if the politicians in charge of this country agree.Dr Kojo Koram is professor of law and political economy at Loughborough University and the author of The Next Fix: The Winners and Losers in the Future of DrugsDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsCannabisOpinionEpilepsyDrugscommentShareReuse this content

title: Why Scottish nationalists should see Burnham as a real threat – and an opportunity | Rory Scothorne | The Guardian
description: The PM’s goals may spell bad news for the SNP. But his EU bridge-building could also resurrect its dreams of independence, says historian Rory Scothorne
Author: Rory Scothorne
Headline: The PM’s goals may spell bad news for the SNP. But his EU bridge-building could also resurrect its dreams of independence, says historian Rory Scothorne
Content: Scottish first minister John Swinney and his deputy,  Jenny Gilruth, at the SNP conference in Aberdeen on 16 October.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenScottish first minister John Swinney and his deputy,  Jenny Gilruth, at the SNP conference in Aberdeen on 16 October.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAOpinionScottish independenceWhy Scottish nationalists should see Burnham as a real threat – and an opportunityRory ScothorneThe PM’s goals may spell bad news for the SNP. But his EU bridge-building could also resurrect its dreams of independenceSun 1 Nov 2026 04.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.36 ESTShareFifty years ago this month, a group of leftwing Scots gathered in the Golden Lion hotel in Stirling for the inaugural conference of a new political party. The “Scottish Labour party” had formally split from Labour at the beginning of 1976, driven by disillusionment over the party’s timid proposals for a new Scottish assembly. They were led by the firebrand MP for South Ayrshire, Jim Sillars, who promised to take Scotland’s Labour tradition back to its roots in both socialism and home rule.Sillars’ new party was a media sensation in Scotland, and quickly joined by public intellectuals such asTom Nairn,Hamish HendersonandNeal Ascherson. It offered something new and exciting: a fusion of the two movements that were battling for Scotland’s soul in a decade that had already been defined by electoral clashes between Labour and the Scottish National party.The party struggled, however, to enthuse the working-class voters on whom Sillars had gambled his future. It did attract a handful of Trotskyist activists from the International Marxist Group, and at the October 1976 conference, Sillars orchestrated a heavy-handed purge of the far left, causing proceedings to degenerate into near-violence. At one point, a member of the party’s national organising committee summoned up Ayrshire’s mining heritage against the “entryist” threat, yelling: “We should get our fucking pit boots on and wade into them!”Andy Burnham was not quite as forthright earlier this month, when, midway through the SNP’s conference in Aberdeen, he delivered hisown speech in Motherwell, offering to cooperate on further devolution within Scotland. The conference itself was far more peaceful, the SNP having already shed its “fundamentalist” wing with the breakaway of Alex Salmond’s Alba party (which Sillars, it’s worth noting,also endorsed). The National Economic Council meeting on Friday between Burnham, John Swinney and the Welsh first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, emphasised the shared agenda of three governments seeking to combine devolved power with reindustrialisation – precisely what the SLP was calling for in 1976. But the SLP, which never recovered from its public meltdown in Stirling, made another contribution to the cause that matters intensely to the relationship between Burnham and the SNP.Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK | Simon JenkinsRead moreKeen to make national self-determination palatable to socialists, Sillars’ party sought to remove any hint of separatism from its politics by embracing the new European Economic Community, arguing for “independence in Europe”. With goods, people and services moving freely across borders, independence would no longer mean separation, but simply real equality between self-governing, co-dependent nations.View image in fullscreenJim Sillars, centre, visits a factory while campaigning in the Glasgow Govan byelection in 1988, which he won for the SNP.Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesAfter the SLP’s collapse, Sillars found his way into the SNP, rising through the ranks to become deputy leader in 1991. “Independence in Europe” came with him. The SNP made some of its first breakthroughs in the 1970s as a Eurosceptic party, distinguishing itself from the three pro-EEC Westminster parties by campaigning against membership in 1975 with theslogan“No voice, no entry”. But by the 1990s, it had completely reversed this position, helped by the new European Union’s growing emphasis on the rights of small nations and minority cultures.The SNP’s newfound Europeanism reflected and reinforced that of the country it came to govern. It was helped, too, by Scotland’s tendency to define itself against English politics, which became more Eurosceptic over the same period. When the SNP’s success produced areferendum on independence, Europe was one of the central issues. An independent Scotland, voters were told, would be a new state, and would therefore have to reapply to join the EU. Scots voted against independence partly to protect their European passports. Two years later, they voted overwhelmingly toremain in that larger union too.But England, with 10 times Scotland’s population, swung the result the other way. Scotland was thus asked, over the period of just two years and two votes, to choose between its membership of the UK and of the EU – but in the wrong order. Immediately after theBrexitvote, support for independence briefly surged, but then dropped. Scots realised they did not fancy yet another wrenching break-up. It was only with the arrival of Boris Johnson as prime minister, the conclusion of a hard Brexit, and the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic that “yes” moved into a consistent lead.Today, yes and noare neck and neck, but many independence campaigners remain concerned about how another referendum campaign might unfold. The fundamental political case for independence has always been that British politics is overwhelmingly Anglocentric, and Scotland’s interests are marginalised. While Brexit has deepened this structural complaint, it has also transformed the economic arguments against independence: if Scotland were to vote for independence and rejoin the EU tomorrow, it would suddenly face a hard border with the rest of the UK, whichbuys more of Scotland’s exportsthan every other country in the world put together – including the whole EU.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome nationalists argue that, under such circumstances, Scotland could be granted the same status as Northern Ireland, which has found a middle ground between European and UK markets. But Northern Ireland has been given special treatment because of the simmering threat of a return to open conflict over the partition of Ireland; Scotland is not a remotely serious candidate for civil war over its borders with England or Europe and would be highly unlikely to be treated with the same sensitivity by the global community.Scottish nationalism’s problem is also its greatest selling point: it is not motivated by any deep ethnic grievance, and as such its supporters are hard to mobilise into the kind of bloody-minded self-sacrifice that might justify some deeper rupture with England. It is founded, instead, on a modern, peaceful and democratic discontent with Westminster’s gradual abandonment of everything that seemed to make Britain worthwhile: good jobs, functioning public services, international cooperation and a vaguely shared moral compass.Burnham is therefore a meaningful threat to the SNP, for this is precisely the nostalgic vision of Britain that he promises to restore – with messaging skills that can finally rival the SNP’s and promises of “regional empowerment”. Yet it offers an opportunity as well. It is hard to imagine that Burnham, whether he has three years in power or a decade, will truly be able to resurrect the lost world of dignified work, British industry and social security that he conjures up in his speeches. But it looks increasingly plausible that he may have to rebuild some of Britain’s relationships with Europe as a precondition of his wider agenda. That would repair the one bridge that Scotland truly needs intact for a successful sprint towards independence, should the rest of Burnham’s project falter.Rory Scothorne is a historian and writer based in EdinburghExplore more on these topicsScottish independenceOpinionDevolutionScottish politicsScottish National party (SNP)Andy BurnhamBrexitScotlandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Forget maxxing your life. 2027 must be the year we relax – and start minning | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: Maxxing is selfish, desperately try-hard and often futile. Instead of pushing your endeavours to the limit, minning means doing them less, if at all, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: Maxxing is selfish, desperately try-hard and often futile. Instead of pushing your endeavours to the limit, minning means doing them less, if at all, writes Polly Hudson
