Content: Stop … ginmaxxing is so over.Photograph: Dziggyfoto/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenStop … ginmaxxing is so over.Photograph: Dziggyfoto/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionSocial etiquetteForget maxxing your life. 2027 must be the year we relax – and start minningPolly HudsonMaxxing is selfish, desperately try-hard and often futile. Instead of pushing your endeavours to the limit, minning means doing them less, if at allSun 1 Nov 2026 11.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 14.56 ESTSharePublic service announcement: fellow citizens, we have maxxmaxxinged. It has been close for a while, but now we have gone over the edge – reached, and passed, maximum maxxing. The tipping point was a week in which we sawreports of Namemaxxing. If you can’t decide between two baby names, pick them both. Suggestions included blending Maeve and Avery to create Mavery, or Leo and Giovanni to make Leovanni – Futupid. Then Dictionary.comrevealed its word of the yearand, yes, you guessed it: maxxing. It’s fully exhausting, in every way, but mainly in that -maxx has been fully exhausted. For the good of us all, 2027 has to be the year of minning. (The second “n” is important, otherwise pits may be deluged.)Maxxing is selfish, desperately try-hard and often futile – surely nobody who ever set out to funmaxx achieved it (see: New Year’s Eve),not even Dua Lipa. Minning is much more noble: it’s about making the world, rather than only yourself, better. Instead of pushing your endeavours to the limit, it means doing them less, if at all.Andy Burnham could have leapt ahead of this trend when he unveiled his crackdown on headphone dodgers by declaring that he was loudcastminning. Other plagues against society with the potential to be similarly addressed are slow walking (dawdleminning), noisy eating (chewminning), not indicating when driving (mindreadminning), and absent-mindedly checking your phone mid-conversation (scrollminning). And let’s not forget dropping litter (binminning), turning up to a friend’s without warning (pop-inminning) and being over competitive (winminning.) Overall, this movement is about being as good a human being as possible (sinminning) but it’s also an opportunity to cut out habits such as drinking too many spirits (ginminning) and even negative familial relationships (kinminning).‘Maxxing’ is Dictionary.com’s word of the year: ‘It’s cooler than saying you’re doing more’Read moreBack in the days when all of this was fields and we only used one x in “max”, it was clear that max volume is too loud, max capacity too crowded, and max power too draining. Somewhere along the way we lost sight of that. Let’s take a deep breath, and enjoy the relief of leaning into minning. First person to suggest they’re doing maxxminning will be taken to the tower and made an example of.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Life is full of suffering – but leaning into moments of pleasure can allow the nervous system to rest | Nadine Levy | The Guardian
description: The simplicity of breathing; the sweetness of laughter; the privilege of lying on a bed. Buddhism teaches us how to enjoy the small pleasures
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The simplicity of breathing; the sweetness of laughter; the privilege of lying on a bed. Buddhism teaches us how to enjoy the small pleasures
Content: ‘The point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure but to lean into it when it naturally arises.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure but to lean into it when it naturally arises.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesMaking sense of itBuddhismLife is full of suffering – but leaning into moments of pleasure can allow the nervous system to restNadine LevyThe simplicity of breathing; the sweetness of laughter; the privilege of lying on a bed. Buddhism teaches us how to enjoy the small pleasuresMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.17 ESTShareThere is a particularBuddhist storythat reassured me I had found the right path.The story goes that Prince Siddhartha Gautama was deep in spiritual practice – arduous, unforgiving practice. He had tried everything from breath-holding to extreme fasting. But none of it brought the freedom from suffering he sought.As is sometimes the case in those moments, he was graced with a memory. He remembered being a child, sitting under the shade of a rose apple tree while his father worked nearby. As he sat there, free from preoccupation, his mind settled and his experience became infused with a deep sense of pleasure and ease.This memory gestured at what later became a fundamental Buddhist idea: put simply, extreme self-denial is not the path to freedom. More radically, could it be that a certain kind of pleasure – a more refined pleasure – might help point the way?Surviving desire: what Buddhist thought teaches us about our war on want | Making sense of itRead moreI’ve always been intrigued by pleasure, its limits but also its invitation. The pleasure Siddhartha remembered was not wily or sneaky, waiting to trick him into attachment, but rather carried him towards freedom of heart.Admittedly, the Buddha distinguished this kind of pleasure from sensual pleasures, which can become tangled with craving, acquisition and a mistaken belief that happiness lies in getting more.But the point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure but to lean into it when it naturally arises.As humans, we are strangely adept at trying to elicit and extract pleasure, to plan for it and prolong it, but not so good at receiving it when it is right in front of us.Stress candiminishour sensitivity to pleasure. Psychologists use the term “anhedonia” to describe the diminished capacity to anticipate or experience pleasure, a phenomenon associated with a range of mental health conditions.As a teenager, I had a free-spirited friend who wholeheartedly called out, “I love bed!” before she went to sleep. We could hear her down the corridor.I loved bed too; we all did. But would we admit it?She noticed the sheets, the relief of placing a tired body down, the privilege of a pillow. Boy, she knew how to receive pleasure when it was being offered.The Buddha observed that all experience is associated with a tonal quality – pleasant, painful or neutral. In Buddhism, we call thisvedanā,or feeling tone. And then there is all the manhandling we do with feeling: judging it, willing it to stay, tweaking it.When working with mindfulness students who are having a hard time, I often do a pleasure check.I ask, sometimes provocatively, “What are you doing in your free time?” Then: “Are you able to read a good novel? Could you go for a massage or a meandering walk in the sun?” What I am really asking is: can you be with pleasure intentionally, even amid suffering?These conversations also make it plain that access to pleasure is not enjoyed equally. The time, safety and space necessary to notice and receive pleasure are affected by our social and material circumstances. But when pleasure does arise amid turbulence, allowing it to register can offer the nervous system a chance to rest, even for a moment.We feel this viscerally: a slower breath, a softening, a release. And if we are quiet, we might notice our minds relishing it – “How terrific, I love this.” Or as the US novelistKurt Vonnegutput it: “If this isn’t nice, I don’t know what is.”Can we let pleasure simply hold our attention without trying to prolong it?Pleasure arrives with different inflections. Some forms leave us aching for more. Others are more sublime, spiritual even – the kind the Buddha spoke of: the mind that gathers and settles. The simplicity of the breathing body. The sweetness of simply existing.I once had a teacher who started meditation sessions with: “It feels good to be in the body.” It was a low bar for pleasure but somehow I felt it.Then there is the pleasure of living a life of non-harm, of treating ourselves and others with dignity, love and respect. Subtler still is the pleasure of laying down the burden, even for a moment, of having to be and do.It’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdom | Muhammad AbdulsaterRead moreI remember marvelling that in my mother’s final weeks, days in the hospital could still brim with pleasure. Among the many unpleasant experiences, there was the sweetness of laughter, a leg massage, a feeling of togetherness, and a daughter’s recognition of the comfort and familiarity of being with her mum.Each evening, I would think how strange it was that there was so much pleasure in despair.And here receptivity was key. I suspect without it, I might have seen only what was painful and missed the pleasure braided through.Every time I sit to meditate, I consciously luxuriate in the pleasure of breathing.Of course, pleasure dissipates, and unpleasant and neutral sensations arrive too. Yet in Buddhist practice, these too are met with the samereceptive attention: “Oh, this is unpleasant, and it will change.” Sometimes there is even a kind of pleasure in this honesty.And, for the record, I still love bed.Dr Nadine Levy is a senior lecturer at theNan Tien Institute. She coordinates its health and social wellbeing program and the graduate certificate in applied mindfulnessExplore more on these topicsBuddhismMaking sense of itReligionMeditationPhilosophyHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on listening to people with learning disabilities: a matter of life and death | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Covid pandemic shed an unforgiving light on health and social care inequalities. The lessons have yet to be absorbed
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Covid pandemic shed an unforgiving light on health and social care inequalities. The lessons have yet to be absorbed
Content: ‘While many carers and health workers may provide remarkable support and treatment, professionals are not immune from society’s prejudices.’Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreen‘While many carers and health workers may provide remarkable support and treatment, professionals are not immune from society’s prejudices.’Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAOpinionDisabilityThe Guardian view on listening to people with learning disabilities: a matter of life and deathEditorialThe Covid pandemic shed an unforgiving light on health and social care inequalities. The lessons have yet to be absorbedSun 1 Nov 2026 12.25 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 15.40 ESTShareThe fear that so many felt as the death toll rose during the Covid pandemic was magnified for Fiona Walker. “I know from experience they wouldn’t have valued my life,” she says, in anew reporton the treatment of people with learning disabilities during the crisis.The 1.5 million people in the UK with learning disabilities, and their families, had reason for concern. Death rates in England werefour to six times higherthan average for people with learning disabilities. As is now well established, the pandemic did not create inequalities; it exposed and intensified them. People with learning disabilities die on average 19.5 years earlier than people without, and deaths arealmost twice as likelyto be classed as avoidable.Learning the lessons means listening to people with learning disabilities and their family carers. Ms Walker and others were commissioners for the newHow We Survive and Thrivereport led by Learning Disability England, working with researchers from the University of Birmingham and Manchester Metropolitan University. It describes how families were abandoned by planners in the pandemic, though carers and communities gave welcome support. While care homes were failed, the needs of those living in family homes or community settings were often simply overlooked.Recommendations include prioritising patients with learning disabilities and finding ways to increase rather than decrease support in a future crisis. But other improvements would help now as well as in the next public health emergency: ensuring people are included on the GP learning disability register, and providing accessible information and reasonable adjustments. Reactions to treatment can be wrongly taken as a refusal of care, when they really point to the need for easier to understand information, or the presence of a carer who can explain to or advocate for the patient. As Mencap has pointed out, such adjustments can be the difference between life and death.While many carers and health workers may provide remarkable support and treatment, professionals are not immune from society’s prejudices. The shockingimposition of “do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation” decisionson people with learning disabilities in the pandemic may have partially reflected initial advice from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice). It said that patients should be assessed as scoring high for “frailty” – potentially affecting whether they received critical care – if they needed support with personal care, whatever the reason. Nice had towithdraw it. Testimony from patients with learning disabilities and their families suggestsdangerous assumptionsabout patients’ quality of life also played a role. Those will be overcome only through sustained training and accountability.Alarmingly, however, families and campaigners fear that progress made in recent decades is now being undone. Alongsidecuts to social care packages and local supportcome profound challenges in healthcare. Important initiatives such as theLearning from Lives and Deaths scheme, examining the care received by people with learning disabilities and autism before their deaths, andmandatory trainingfor healthcare staff on treating such patients, face growingfunding pressures. Thenumber of learning-disability nurseshas fallen by a third since 2009 and student numbers are collapsing. That must be reversed. Learning disabilities should not mean a shorter life.Explore more on these topicsDisabilityOpinionCoronavirusCovid inquiryHealthNHSeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the US midterms and election interference: Trump’s attempted heist is already under way | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Voters are turning against the Republicans. But the clearest possible message is needed to safeguard democracy
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Voters are turning against the Republicans. But the clearest possible message is needed to safeguard democracy
Content: ‘The January 6 insurrection showed how acute the peril to American democracy had become. It is more so now.’Photograph: Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘The January 6 insurrection showed how acute the peril to American democracy had become. It is more so now.’Photograph: Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionUS politicsThe Guardian view on the US midterms and election interference: Trump’s attempted heist is already under wayEditorialVoters are turning against the Republicans. But the clearest possible message is needed to safeguard democracySun 1 Nov 2026 12.30 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 14.56 ESTShareThe psychologist Jennifer Freyd identified a pattern often used by perpetrators: deny, accuse, and reverse victim and offender. More than one observer has noted that Donald Trump employs that pattern politically. With polls suggesting Republicans are likely to lose the House and perhaps the Senate too in the midterms, the man who refused to accept Americans’ democratic verdict in 2020is hawking a narrative of cheating Democratswho will steal seats via illegitimate votes.The January 6 insurrection showed how acute the peril to American democracy had become. It is more so now. This time, Republican efforts to undermine the results began well in advance. In 2020, Mr Trump’s vice-president, Mike Pence, the attorney general, William Barr, and others refused his most outrageous demands; now the justice department is supine. And the supreme court’sgutting of the Voting Rights Act, which safeguarded against the worst kinds of racial discrimination, means that states no longer require pre-approval for decisions that could well tilt a race. Districts have already been redrawn.Courts have so far blocked executive orders unconstitutionally claiming election powers that clearly lie with states. But the blizzard of efforts ensures that Republicans do not need to succeed every time. A few thousand or even hundred votes in key places could have a profound effect on the outcome. The all‑out push also intimidates potential voters. Whatever happens to the federal criminal investigation intoalleged non‑citizen voting in California, and whether or not Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers are actually stationed near polling placesas mooted, legitimate voters may fear drawing attention to undocumented relatives. Finally, all these threats and initiatives establish the false story of a stolen election, to be taken up more powerfully after votes are cast.Mr Trump repeated his call for the prosecution of Mary Peltola, the Democratic senate candidate in Alaska, after the New York Times reported that her campaign had sought to confuse voters by recruiting another candidate with the same name as her Republican opponent, despite its denials. The state’s Republican governorhas not committed to certifying the resultif she wins. Putting up similarly named candidates is an old trick, as well as a dirty one. Though not inherently illegal, it is unethical and could potentially lead to criminal charges. It isnot grounds for contesting the result of this race. But it is a gift to Republicans claiming that Democrats are pursuing election fixes – when the clear evidence is that the threat to US democracy comes from Mr Trump and his enablers.There are two key checks to their wide-ranging and concerted efforts. The first is that, despite facing horrific abuse and death threats, election officials – including Republicans – have beenassiduously preparing to resist anti-democratic efforts. That is tempered, however, by the determined Republican push to control election boards, with a growing number ofelection deniersin place.The second is that asurge in early votingsuggests that the obvious threat to democracy is motivating citizens to participate, and to ensure that their ballots count. Recent elections elsewhere – notably Brazil, where Mr Trump’s favoured far‑right candidate was rejected – show that a decisive message from voters is harder to challenge than a marginal one. The best defence of democracy is to show that people care about it. And the clearer the verdict, the better the prospects of upholding it.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionDonald TrumpUS economyRepublicansHouse of RepresentativesUS SenateeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: This government should rebuild adult education as a democratic bulwark | Education | The Guardian
description: Letters: John Holford, Alan Wells, Jol Miskin and Isobel Hunter Readers respond to an editorial that championed the freedom to learn at any age
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: John Holford, Alan Wells, Jol Miskin and Isobel Hunter Readers respond to an editorial that championed the freedom to learn at any age
Content: ‘Despite the best efforts of teachers and volunteers, the number of adults with poor literacy skills has not apparently gone down.’Photograph: Don McPhee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Despite the best efforts of teachers and volunteers, the number of adults with poor literacy skills has not apparently gone down.’Photograph: Don McPhee/The GuardianEducationLettersThis government should rebuild adult education as a democratic bulwarkJohn Holford,Alan Wells,Jol MiskinandIsobel HunterReaders respond to an editorial that championed the freedom to learn at any ageSun 1 Nov 2026 12.29 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.31 ESTShareYour editorial makes a strong case for lifelong adult education (The Guardian view on adult education: learning should be for all ages, 25 October). But like thereportby the all party parliamentary group on further education that it refers to, it overlooks one vital dimension: we need adult education to defend democracy.For most of the last century, adult education’s role in creating democratic civil society was widely accepted, not least by policymakers. The Ministry of Reconstructionmade the case in 1919: “universal and lifelong” adult education was “a permanent national necessity, an inseparable aspect of citizenship”.It would cultivate “an open habit of mind, clear-sighted and truth-loving, proof against sophisms, shibboleths, claptrap phrases and cant”. Later official reports agreed. The result – built up over decades – was a rich and broad adult education provided not only in further education but also through voluntary organisations and universities.In just a few years from the mid‑1980s, this was swept away. Since the 1990s, the central purpose of adult education – at least for policymakers – has become serving the economy. Wider concerns, from democratic citizenship to personal fulfilment, have been marginal at best. The infrastructure of provision has been vandalised. Funding been cut to the bone, while the organisations that provide courses – once genuine partners whose voices were taken seriously – have been treated as “delivery boys” for the current Whitehall fad.Bringing democratic purpose and practice back into adult education, rebuilding a vibrant infrastructure of providers and listening to the voices of students and professionals could make adult education a bulwark of democracy again. It would involve a radical turn away from “40 years of neoliberalism”, which Andy Burnham tells us he would welcome. It would help the country’s societal resilience in the face of authoritarianism. Above all, it would make people’s lives truly richer.John HolfordEmeritusprofessor of adult education, University of NottinghamYour editorial mentions that up to 8 million adults have low literacy skills. This number appears to have remained unchanged since the first adult literacy campaign over 50 years ago. The campaign led to the setting up of a national agency by the then government, focused on introducing adult literacy programmes. TheBBCtook it so seriously that it showed a TV series, On the Move, every Sunday to help adults join programmes. The independent national agency lasted for 30 years under various names, ending up as the Basic Skills Agency, which closed in 2008. I was the chief executive from 1978 to 2006.Despite the best efforts of teachers and volunteers, the number of adults with poor literacy skills has not apparently gone down. One of the major reasons for this failure is that 20 or so years ago, the government changed the target audience from adults who struggled with basic skills to anyone without an A-C grade in GCSE English.Many of these were young adults, and did not struggle with reading and writing in same way as those in the original target audience. This change increased the target audience to over 25 million adults at a stroke. It also helped officials to claim enormous success.Adults who struggle with these basic skills are not easy to reach. They’re often embarrassed and want to keep this secret; many are poor. There are no quick fixes. So unless the government starts to target initiatives where there is the greatest need, the numbers will never change.Alan WellsFormer director,Basic Skills AgencyYour editorial correctly points out that it isn’t only young adults who need to learn new skills; it’s all adults. And it’s not just narrowly about skills. I worked for the Workers’ Educational Association (WEA) for 30 years until 2018. During that period there were ups and downs to do with funding and government support, or lack of it, but by comparison with today those years were glorious.In my city of Sheffield, you would have found courses in most localities. The offer was broad – from art, literature, writers’ workshops and history to information and communications technology, politics, weaving and yoga. The focus and curriculum was on education with a social purpose, and there was an absolute commitment to encouraging adults who’d been denied opportunities first time round and giving them a second chance.This type of education brought people together, broke down barriers, helped people’s mental health, and developed knowledge and confidence. It built skills too: teamwork, speaking and listening, writing, constructing an argument etc.And today? Well, I searched the current WEA offer in South Yorkshire and was shocked to find a very short list of courses: Driving Theory, CV Writing, Work Ready, Conversation with Crafting (ESOL), and Ace the Interview. And that’s it!This is scandalous. The austerity years pretty much crushed adult education and any notion of lifelong learning. Is the education secretary looking at this? She should be.Jol MiskinSheffieldYour editorial on adult education rightly argues that lifelong learning can improve health and wellbeing as well as earning potential. But it overlooks an institution that has been broadening horizons and opening up opportunities for more than 175 years: the public library.Adult education does not only happen in classrooms. Libraries offer a more informal, familiar environment that can be particularly valuable for those who carry negative experiences of education.Every day, the UK’s 4,000 libraries help people build digital skills, learn a language, discover a hobby, find work or pursue a new or long-held interest – independently or with support and guidance from trained staff. Libraries complement more formal adult education by reaching people who might otherwise miss out and connecting them with further opportunities.As the next phase of devolution reshapes adult skills provision, we should make sure public libraries are firmly part of it.Isobel HunterCEO, Libraries ConnectedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The decision to bar Andreas Malm from entering the UK is farcical and chilling | Higher education | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Ahmad Elabbar reflects on what such a decision means for academics who are working on today’s most difficult and urgent topics
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Ahmad Elabbar reflects on what such a decision means for academics who are working on today’s most difficult and urgent topics
Content: ‘Malm is a challenging author … but he is without a doubt one of the world’s leading environmental historians and scholars of climate change.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Malm is a challenging author … but he is without a doubt one of the world’s leading environmental historians and scholars of climate change.’Photograph: AlamyHigher educationLettersThe decision to bar Andreas Malm from entering the UK is farcical and chillingDr Ahmad Elabbarreflects on what such a decision means for academics who are working on today’s most difficult and urgent topicsSun 1 Nov 2026 12.29 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.30 ESTShareUK higher education is in a confusing and fraught enough state without the government banning distinguished authors on our reading lists such as Andreas Malm (Climate academic Andreas Malm barred from entering UK, 30 October).Last Thursday I gave a lecture on negative emissions and geoengineering, and recommended The Long Heat, which Malm co-authored with Wim Carton, to my students.The recommendation was obviously not meant as an endorsement of Malm’s position in that book, or of any of his views – Malm is a challenging author who holds controversial positions on a range of issues. But he is without a doubt one of the world’s leading environmental historians and scholars of climate change. His books are on my reading lists, and those of many of my colleagues.You’d be hard pressed to find anyone working on climate change today who hasn’t, in one way or another, engaged with his work. A ban on his entry to the UK is farcical, and raises chilling prospects for all academics working on today’s most difficult and urgent topics.Dr AhmadElabbarUniversity of CambridgeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A new strategy is needed to address the harms related to cocaine and other drugs | Drugs | The Guardian
description: Letters: Dr Will Haydock calls for a new govrnment plan with clear priorities, while a reader in Ecuador points to the devastating impact of UK cocaine use there
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Dr Will Haydock calls for a new govrnment plan with clear priorities, while a reader in Ecuador points to the devastating impact of UK cocaine use there
Content: ‘Every time a user purchases cocaine, they are actively contributing to the murderous activities of transnational organised crime networks.’Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Every time a user purchases cocaine, they are actively contributing to the murderous activities of transnational organised crime networks.’Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesDrugsLettersA new strategy is needed to address the harms related to cocaine and other drugsDr Will Haydockcalls for a new govrnment plan with clear priorities, while a reader in Ecuador points to the devastating impact of UK cocaine use thereSun 1 Nov 2026 12.29 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.31 ESTShareThe reports published as part of your investigation into cocaine lay bare the widespread harms linked to the drug that people are experiencing (Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges, 25 October;‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse, 26 October).Similar concerns can be identified in relation to other drugs – including alcohol – and the situation could not be more urgent. Deaths related to drug use have been rising for over a decadeto unprecedented levels, and the emergence of synthetic opioids in the UK has prompted the National Crime Agency to warn that “there has never been a more dangerous time to take drugs”. The latest figures on drug-related deaths will be publishedon 4 November, and are likely to confirm a stubbornly shocking and tragic level of harm.Fortunately, there is clear evidence that substance use treatment and recovery services, as provided by a range of charities across the country,are an effective and efficient way to help people turn their lives around, with knock-on positive effects on families, communities and public services.Treatment and recovery services will have a crucial role to play if the government is to achieve its aims on policy issues such as violence against women and girls, the crisis in the criminal justice system, homelessness and young people’s employment and mental health.Yet for over two years, the government has been largely silent on addiction. What we need now is a new drugs strategy with clear priorities. The 2021 drugs strategy provided investment and set specific ambitions for drug and alcohol treatment. This was transformational for our field, which is now supportingthe highest number of adults in treatment since reporting began.To achieve his own ambitions, the prime minister must show comparable focus and leadership. If we get our response to alcohol and other drugs right, we can save and improve hundreds of thousands of lives.Dr Will HaydockChief executive, Collective Voice (national alliance of drug and alcohol treatment and recovery charities)Yourarticle on cocaine use in Britaintreats it as a domestic social problem and fails to mention the most important consequences. Every time a user purchases cocaine, they are actively contributing to the murderous activities of transnational organised crime networks.Here inEcuador, cocaine trafficking sustains these networks, whose presence contaminates every aspect of our lives: through their “ownership” of key players in politics, business, the police and the judiciary, and assassinations of those who refuse to play the game; through the frequent deaths of innocent people caught up in the crossfire of wars between rival gangs; and through the devastating effects on small businesses, crippled or driven out of business by protection rackets.Cocaine users in Britain should reflect on the fact that their “recreational” activity is helping to finance these crimes. Law enforcers should consider that every time they let someone off with a caution for a first offence, or turn a blind eye to cocaine use at social events, they are equally culpable.Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The UK must stick to its spending pledge on international aid | Aid | The Guardian
description: Letters: Meeting the 0.3% floor is a test of whether it is serious about its commitment to international cooperation, says Callum Northcote
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Meeting the 0.3% floor is a test of whether it is serious about its commitment to international cooperation, says Callum Northcote
Content: ‘It’s estimated that 62 million fewer people will be supported by UK aid worldwide in 2026-27 compared with 2019.’Photograph: Foreign/PAView image in fullscreen‘It’s estimated that 62 million fewer people will be supported by UK aid worldwide in 2026-27 compared with 2019.’Photograph: Foreign/PAAidLettersThe UK must stick to its spending pledge on international aidMeeting the 0.3% floor is a test of whether it is serious about its commitment to international cooperation, saysCallum NorthcoteSun 1 Nov 2026 12.28 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.30 ESTShareThat the UK might miss its 0.3% target on international development spending is rubbing salt into an open wound (Report, 26 October). The UK’s development budget, which tackles global challenges and is a lifeline to millions around the world, has been repeatedly cut over the past five years – it’s estimated that62 million fewer peoplewill be supported by UK aid around the world in 2026-27 compared with 2019.When theLabourgovernment announced it was cutting aid to 0.3% of gross national income, it committed to ensuring that this would be the floor, with the intention to increase funding again over time. This must hold true if the government is serious about rebuilding its international reputation. The government has instead used clever accounting techniques at the expense of communities around the world – and what it promised voters it would be spending their money on.Currently, the government continues to use the official development assistance (ODA) budget on housing refugees in the UK. The government is absolutely right to be supporting refugees here in the UK, but we must review the choice to fund this from a constrained aid budget.Recent rule changes mean that as the cost of housing refugees goes down, the money saved will not, however, go back to the development budget but be absorbed by the Treasury. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office should be the aid budget’s “spender of last resort”. This is a simple fix that will ensure millions of children around the world will not miss out on support due to the cuts, and means the money will be used for its original intention rather than plugging holes elsewhere.Ensuring we meet our 0.3% floor is a major test of whether the government is serious about its commitment to international cooperation – it’s essential that it does all it can to pass it.Callum NorthcoteHead of global systems reform, Save the Children UKHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
