The deal was first reported by Sky News.The deal followed reports last year that the UK government had picked Teesworks as the site for a new artificial intelligence datacentre, and planning applications had been submitted for a project that would span nearly 500,000 sq metres.The deal “reflects the constructive work between all those involved to enable this vital infrastructure … and will support the growth of AI and digital technologies, and enable the region’s next phase of industrial and economic development”, Matt Pearce, the head of land at National Grid, said.“We are committed to working closely with our partners to progress the development as quickly as possible,” he added.Ben Houchen, the mayor of the Tees Valley combined authority, told Sky News: “Everyone who has tried to build a datacentre in this country knows the biggest problem is getting enough power to the site quickly.View image in fullscreenBen Houchen: ‘If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability … it needs somewhere to physically put it.’Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian“While we’ve been stuck in the queue, the US, the Gulf and parts of Europe have been getting on with it and hoovering up the investment. Having up to 3.2GW of capacity here means we can finally compete for those projects.“If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability, with sensitive data stored safely on British soil, it needs somewhere to physically put it, and I’d much rather that was Teesside than Texas or Abu Dhabi.”Last week, the government published a draft national policy statement on datacentres, describing them as “as fundamental to our economy as the railways and electricity networks on which we have long depended”.“We must take control over the development of datacentres in this country and ensure that the country and host communities benefit from them,” it said.However, the rapid construction of datacentres in the UK has been met by strong opposition, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging fromAuchtertool, a village north of Edinburgh, toBrick Lanein east London.In October, the Guardian reported thatAI companies told ministers they had 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentresin the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.The London-listed infrastructure services group Balfour Beatty was reported to be in line to deliver the Teesworks substation for National Grid, with the utilities firm Steel River Power (SRP) also heavily involved in the project.Balfour Beatty and SRP were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsNational GridUtilitiesEnergy industryNorth of EnglandAI (artificial intelligence)Datacentres - UKInfrastructurenewsShareReuse this content

title: Green party must avoid being taken over by hard left, says former leader | Green party | The Guardian
description: Adrian Ramsay says some new members would be ‘more at home’ in Your Party or Socialist Workers party
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Adrian Ramsay says some new members would be ‘more at home’ in Your Party or Socialist Workers party
Content: Adrian Ramsay: ‘I think there’s a real crossroads point for the party at the moment.’Photograph: Alishia Abodunde/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAdrian Ramsay: ‘I think there’s a real crossroads point for the party at the moment.’Photograph: Alishia Abodunde/Getty ImagesGreen partyGreen party must avoid being taken over by hard left, says former leaderAdrian Ramsay says some new members would be ‘more at home’ in Your Party or Socialist Workers partyJessica ElgotDeputy political editorSun 1 Nov 2026 09.35 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.34 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdrian Ramsay, the former co-leader of the Green party of England and Wales, has said the party must fix its internal democracy to avoid a takeover by the hard left, saying that some new members “might be more at home” in Your Party or the Socialist Workers party.Ramsay, who has been critical of the handling of the row over a “Zionism is racism” motion passed at theGreen partyconference, said there were a “small number” of individuals who used “divisive” tactics to influence the party’s agenda.“I think there’s a real crossroads point for the party at the moment,” he told the BBC. “And one option is to dig in … but I think that there’s a risk it brings with it a quite divisive approach to politics, which you’ve seen from small groups of people on the hard left of politics who go around different parties to try to influence how those parties are run.”He said there were some new members who had joined the Greens after the failure of other leftwing movements, such as George Galloway’s party or Jeremy Corbyn’s Your Party, who had their roots in hard left organising.“There is also a small number of people who have joined, perhaps from the very hard left of politics, who might be more at home in the SWP or with George Galloway or with Your Party. [They] not only want to adopt some very hardline positions on certain issues, but have a very different culture to how they go about it,” he said.He said those members were “seeking to change the direction of the party” and the leadership needed to reassert the core values and ways of working of the Green party, which was “much more about consensus building, much less about highly fractional, highly tribal politics, and of course about the environment”.Zack Polanski says application of Zionism is racist and no state has right to existRead moreFlaws in the party’s internal democracy meant small groups could have an outsized influence he said.“It was 0.4% of members who voted for this [the Zionism is racism motion] and I don’t think that’s reflective of party members as a whole, it’s certainly not reflective of those I speak to,” he said, adding there should be a ballot or survey of the wider membership.Ramsay, the MP for Waveney Valley, welcomed the party’s growth in membership and said he was not calling forZack Polanskito stand down as leader over the handling of the row.He also said he was not intending to quit the party himself. “I’ve got no intention of going anywhere. What I want to see happen is this issue be clearly addressed,” he said.But it was critical the party disavowed the Zionism motion sooner than the two-year cycle which party rules allow for, he said, and that the party changed its internal rules to give the wider membership more control over policy, rather than the small numbers who attend the party’s annual conference.A spokesperson for Greens Organise – the grassroots group that backed Polanski’s leadership – said: “Adrian Ramsay put forward his case for the future of the Green party a year ago, and lost – by a landslide 84%.“Over 150,000 members have joined the party under Zack’s leadership, and helped bring the party unprecedented electoral success.“They deserve representatives who focus their energy on fighting for the radical solutions to the crises our country faces.”Ramsay said he believed it was also clear the party needed to refocus on its core missions around climate and nature, as well as the cost of living crisis.“I think that will unite our members. I think it will ensure we still have a wide appeal as a party,” he told the BBC Newscast podcast.Asked if he viewed Zionism as racist, he said: “No … I’ve made clear my position on the motion, as lots of other Greens have done.”He said the situation in Gaza was “appalling” but that the motion was contradictory to the Green party manifesto from 2024.“We support equal rights for both Palestinians and Israelis, and Greens have always supported self-determination for all people.”He said he had told Polanski directly he should have been present for the debate and vote, despite fighting a byelection in Holborn and St Pancras. “I do think he should have been there and he should have expressed his view clearly,” he said.Ramsay said the party needed “to find a way for this motion to be changed or rescinded sooner than the two years that Zack is talking about … changing the fact that a policy can’t be reviewed until two years is up”.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyAdrian RamsayZack PolanskinewsShareReuse this content

title: Sadiq Khan calls for cap on numbers of robotaxis on London streets | Self-driving cars | The Guardian
description: Mayor questions impact on air quality, congestion and jobs as government poised to allow driverless vehicles in capital
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Mayor questions impact on air quality, congestion and jobs as government poised to allow driverless vehicles in capital
Content: A Wayve autonomous vehicle leaves a depot on 3 September 2026 – the first day Wayve and Uber launched autonomous passenger rides in London.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Wayve autonomous vehicle leaves a depot on 3 September 2026 – the first day Wayve and Uber launched autonomous passenger rides in London.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersSelf-driving carsSadiq Khan calls for cap on numbers of robotaxis on London streetsMayor questions impact on air quality, congestion and jobs as government poised to allow driverless vehicles in capitalGwyn TophamTransport correspondentSun 1 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 11.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon’s mayor has called for a cap on the numbers of robotaxis on its streets, with the UK government poised to allow fully driverless vehicles to operate in the capital.Sadiq Khan said politicians had failed to “grasp the pace of change” from the technology, which could threaten jobs and increase congestion in the city, and questioned whether the rules for autonomous cars were fit for purpose.His comments came after Chinese robotaxis, now being tested in London, were unveiled byFreenow by Lyft, a rival to Uber.In September Uber started offering limitedpassenger services in Wayve’s self-driving cars, albeit with a safety driver in the front seat, under licence from Transport for London (TfL).Freenow by Lyft is hoping to launch fully driverless Baidu robotaxis as early as next year, under a national licensing scheme.However, the companies, as well as Waymo – which operates robotaxis in San Francisco and other US cities – are primarilyfocusing on Londonand Khan said the city needed to be able to limit the rollout.“What we don’t want is a situation where there’s a big bang without proper regulation in place. We’ve got to make sure the regulation is fit for purpose before we have a mass rollout of things like automated vehicles,” said Khan.He added: “I think the pace of change when it comes to tech and innovation has not been fully grasped by politicians. There’s got to be incremental movement when it comes to things like robotaxis or automated vehicles.“We’re lobbying the government forTfL, for London, to have more powers than it currently has on things like automated vehicles.“There are big questions that haven’t been answered yet: what impact will this have on air quality, on congestion, on those people whose livelihood is being a private hire vehicle driver or a black-taxi driver.”Uber begins self-driving robotaxi trial in ManchesterRead moreDrivers’ unions have held protests at the London HQs of Wayve and Waymo in recent weeks, with many Uberdrivers fearing for their future.Khan added: “Is there going to be a cap? At the moment there’s no cap on the number of private hire vehicles or taxis. We’ve lobbied for those powers as well.“London isn’t San Francisco. We’re a city of almost 10 million, 400 villages, narrow roads, and it’s really important to get this right.”Under current regulations for fully autonomous vehicles, TfL can only give or refuse consent for their use within London and not manage or license robotaxi services, making the capital’s authorities somewhat less enthusiastic than ministers to accelerate towards the new technology.However, Freenow by Lyft said the UK’s national framework for driverless cars was an important factor.Danny O’Gorman, UK and Ireland general manager, said it was “great news for us to really invest in the market. But in terms of how it’s going to be regulated, once the service is up and running, that’s something that still needs to be ironed out.”O’Gorman said the company was working closely with TfL and “wanted to do things the right way”. About 24 autonomous Baidu Apollo Go vehicles are being tested in the London borough of Brent.The spacious Chinese cars, which incorporate a massage seat and a built-in touchscreen in the back for passengers, are in fully autonomous service in cities in China and the UAE, and appeared to be handling the streets safely in a test drive in October for the Guardian.But many test trips still require human intervention, with roadworks proving difficult. For autonomous vehicles (AVs), “an interesting challenge in London is following the rules of the road”, when many drivers ignore them, O’Gorman said: “You get beeped at a lot for following the speed limit.”Freenow by Lyft is promising a purpose-built AV depot in the UK. O’Gorman said a large proportion of displaced taxi drivers could be employed there in remote operating and servicing jobs.The company has traditionally worked with black cabs and, he said: “The larger risks to that industry are the driver age profile: two-thirds are over 50 and they’re retiring, and the vehicle’s too expensive.“AV is not going to be really competing in that space and it’s going to take a long time for us to scale up to vehicle numbers that threaten anything to do with that.”Explore more on these topicsSelf-driving carsMotoringRoad transportRobotsLondonUberWaymonewsShareReuse this content

title: Attempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot police | France | The Guardian
description: Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania
Content: A riot police officer in Paris is hit by a molotov cocktail during a charge against demonstrators at the end of the nationwide day of protests in France.Photograph: Sameer al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA riot police officer in Paris is hit by a molotov cocktail during a charge against demonstrators at the end of the nationwide day of protests in France.Photograph: Sameer al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceAttempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot policeYouth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and AlbaniaJon Henleyin ParisSun 1 Nov 2026 11.24 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.22 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a police officer and Germany’s interior minister has called for harsh penalties after peaceful and mainly youth-led protests across Europe ended in violence.In Portugal, police – some with dogs – cleared protest camps with baton charges, while security forces inSwitzerlandwere attacked with paving stones.Protests over the education system, deteriorating public services, declining prospects, unaffordable housing and the spiralling cost of living haveshaken a number of countriesthis autumn.Violence erupted inthe French capital as well as Marseille, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Lyon and Toulouse on Saturday night after an estimated 320,000 demonstrators, some in Halloween costumes, took to the streets.View image in fullscreenProtesters in Halloween costumes gather in the La Plaine square in Marseille. Officials say 320,000 people took part in protests across France.Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters in Halloween costumes at an unauthorised demonstration in Marseille over the high cost of living.Photograph: Coust Laurent/ABACA/ShutterstockAs the rallies ended, masked and hooded rioters arrived and caused what the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as an “extraordinary” level of violence. More than 770 people were arrested.In Paris, the prosecutor’s office said incendiary devices were thrown at a group of about 15 gendarmes and police officers and a formal investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.Injuries reportedly included second-degree burns in an incident captured on mobile phone video and shared on social media and broadcast on French television.The level of physical violence and looting was significantly lower than on 17 October, when 2,600 people were arrested and as many as 3,000 shops pillaged inone of the worst nightsof urban unrest in France’s recent history.View image in fullscreenRiot police in action in Paris. More than 770 people were arrested across France for public order offences.Photograph: Bernard Jules/ABACA/ShutterstockIn Germany, looters and rioters ⁠rampaged through Frankfurt, the country’s financial hub, damaging stores and injuring more than 100 police officers.“The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable,” said Alexander Dobrindt, the hardline interior minister. He singled out “violent leftwing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community”, adding: “Tough penalties must follow this breach of the peace.”Dobrindt told the tabloid newspaper Bild that deploying a heavy police presence across multiple locations had been effective. “Excesses of ​violence like those ‌in Paris were ​prevented thanks to our ​highly committed police forces,” he said.View image in fullscreenA protester in a Batman costume salutes in front of a fire started by rioters in Frankfurt. German authorities have promised a strong response.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersMore than 100,000 protesters marched in over 30 German cities on Saturday to demand better ⁠education and lower living costs in protests led by the “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z will sort it) campaign.Hooded rioters ⁠damaged 17 Frankfurt shops, looting five of them, and threw missiles including petrol bombs, according to Roman Poseck, the state interior minister for Hesse.More than 100 of the 1,300 police officers deployed in the city were injured and 54 suspects, ‌aged from 13 to 29, were arrested. “I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMost of those arrested were German nationals, the minister said, adding that police estimated they had been confronted with “between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background”.Violence also broke out Saturday night in Cologne, where police used water cannon to disperse the crowd, and in Berlin, where protesters attacked police with bottles and fireworks. Gen Z regelt posted a statement distancing itself from all violence.View image in fullscreenRiot police clear Lisbon’s Rossio Square of activists protesting over housing affordability.Photograph: Manuel de Almeida/EPAInPortugal, riot police removed protesters by force from Rossio Square in Lisbon at about 4.30am on Sunday after thousands of people angry at the housing crisis marched through the city on Saturday and set up camp.The protesters want Portugal’s minority centre-right government to withdraw a ⁠bill that makes ⁠evictions easier and ends rent caps on new leases. A smaller camp in Porto was also cleared by force.InAlbania, masked protesters hurled stones and firebombs at police in the capital, Tirana, on the margins of a demonstration demanding the resignation of the prime minister, Edi Rama, over perceived corruption.Youths threw paving stones and firebombs at police and set fire to rubbish bins at the end of a largely peaceful protest. The interior ministry said on Friday that 350 people had been hurt in the protests, including 200 police, with 269 minors arrested.View image in fullscreenAn anti-government protest in Tirana turned violent with protesters hurling stones and petrol bombs at police.Photograph: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIn Switzerland, hundreds of protesters gathered in Zürich and Basel on Saturday night for unauthorised demonstrations – both of which ended in violence – under the slogan: “We’ve had enough in Switzerland, too.”In Zürich, police used water cannon, teargas and rubber bullets to disperse rioters attacking them with fireworks, bottles and stones,Swiss media reported. A police patrol car was damaged and rubbish bins and electric bikes set on fire.In Basel, police said about 150 people gathered in the city centre at around 9pm. Shop windows were smashed, facades tagged with graffiti and bins and bikes set on fire, with incidents also reported in Geneva.Explore more on these topicsFrancePortugalAlbaniaGermanySwitzerlandProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat was torched in an arson attack. Should it be rebuilt? | Adolf Hitler | The Guardian
description: With the far right resurgent in Germany, experts are divided as to whether the dictator’s former mountaintop retreat is better restored or left a ruin
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: With the far right resurgent in Germany, experts are divided as to whether the dictator’s former mountaintop retreat is better restored or left a ruin
Content: The fire at mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, on 24 October.Photograph: Berchtesgaden/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe fire at mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, on 24 October.Photograph: Berchtesgaden/AFP/Getty ImagesAdolf HitlerHitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat was torched in an arson attack. Should it be rebuilt?With the far right resurgent in Germany, experts are divided as to whether the dictator’s former mountaintop retreat is better restored or left a ruinDeborah Colein BerlinSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the last structural relics of Adolf Hitler’s dictatorship was conceived to project indomitable power. Last month it was destroyed in a suspected arson attack. Will it, and should it, be rebuilt?The historic Nazi mountaintop retreat known as the Eagle’s Nest is perched on an Alpine peak at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft), with stunning views over southernGermanyand Austria. In German, its design is known asÜberwältigungsarchitektur, intended to overwhelm and intimidate.Now, despitethe efforts of 200 firefighters battling through the night, only charred ruins remain of the former guest lodge, tourist magnet and remembrance site destroyed in the blaze which started on 23 October. It is closed indefinitely.“Even if a British air force bomb had struck the building on 25 April 1945, as it did most of the other structures in what was then the ‘Führer’s no-go zone’ on the Obersalzberg near Berchtesgaden, Hitler’s former tea house … could scarcely have been more severely damaged than it was by the fire,” Munich’s Süddeutsche newspaper said.View image in fullscreenA brass-plated lift, built into the rock, took 41 seconds to bring visitors up to the Eagle’s Nest.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyThe fire has triggered a debate about whether, and how, to rebuild at the toxic site for the next generation of visitors, while mitigating the never-quite-banished risk of creating a shrine for neo-Nazis.While the places associated with Hitler’s victims, including the former concentration camps, are preserved in perpetuity, the question of how to treat the perpetrators’ artefacts remains fraught, particularly given the resurgence of the far right in Germany and inEuropemore broadly.Local authorities believe the fire was deliberately started by a 33-year-old suspect with a history of mental illness. The site, which is owned by the German state of Bavaria, attracts more than 300,000 people each year but was closed to visitors that day. No one was injured.View image in fullscreenThe Eagle’s Nest is known more prosaically in German as theKehlsteinhaus, for the mountain it rests on.Photograph: DEA/W. BUSS/De Agostini/Getty ImagesBavarian state culture minister Markus Blume has said a commission of experts in heritage conservation, construction and Germany’s culture ofHolocaustremembrance would be enlisted to help determine the future of the Eagle’s Nest.Given the building’s inextricable links to the Nazi regime and its crimes, Blume said, “any reconstruction must do justice to this historical responsibility”.The marvel of Alpine engineering, which took3,800 workers just over a year to build, is known more prosaically in German as theKehlsteinhaus, for the mountain it rests on.After a coach ride on serpentine roads through five tunnels, visitors rode a brass-plated lift, built into the rock, for 41 seconds to reach its portal.View image in fullscreenThe Eagle’s Nest pictured in 2019.Photograph: Maurice Savage/Alamy“The prestige project and the road leading to it cost about 30 million Reichsmarks, equivalent to about 130 million British pounds today,” said Nazi-era historian Felix Bohr, author of Before the Downfall: Hitler’s Years in the Wolf’s Lair, which is being published in the UK in November.“Hitler loved architecture that made other people look small. He insisted on being involved in the planning and construction of propaganda buildings.”The lodge was completed in 1938, and mainly used to welcome and impress state guests, diplomats and select foreign journalists.Just a short distance down the mountain at the Obersalzberg complex was Hitler’s own residence, the Berghof, where he spent about a quarter of his 12 years in office.View image in fullscreenThe Eagle’s Nest pictured in 1940.Photograph: Hulton Deutsch/Corbis/Getty Images“Important decisions about prosecution and crime, about war and genocide were taken there,” said Sven Keller, director of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, an educational facility at the site.“The surrounding mountain scenery was used as a backdrop for the construction of Hitler’s ‘Führer’ image. It offered spectacular, awe-inspiring views, and demonstrated technical prowess to subjugate even this rough natural environment.”Inside, it had many of the trappings of Nazi bling, including Untersberg marble donated by Mussolini, Venetian mirrors and plump green leather armchairs recalling an English country manor house.Hitler is known to have visited the Eagle’s Nest only 14 times until 1939 and then never again due to the second world war’s outbreak, when the tea house no longer matched the warrior-statesman image he wished to project, Bohr said. Close associates including his companion Eva Braun still used it regularly, however.View image in fullscreenHeinrich Hoffmann, Eva Braun and Adolf Hitler at the Berghof in 1942.Photograph: Prisma by Dukas Presseagentur GmbH/AlamyAfter the war, Obersalzberg became a recreation centre for occupying US troops, but the last vestiges of the Berghof were torn down and hundreds of trees were planted in its place – a fateful decision that has served as a cautionary tale.“The Americans and the Bavarian state tried to prevent it from becoming a pilgrimage site for old Nazis and Hitler admirers. It didn’t work. If anything, a hidden site in the woods is even more interesting and mysterious,” Keller said. Nazi swastikas were often found carved into the tree bark.He said a 180-degree pivot toward clearly marking the site and exposing its history, including how it fit into the Nazi power apparatus, proved the healthier approach.“Public accessibility creates transparency whereas barriers or fences encourage rumours and legends,” Keller said. “Today, a popular public trail crosses the site, and mundane activities such as hiking keep it from becoming a sacred space (for neo-Nazis).”View image in fullscreenHitler with Eva Braun at the Berghof in June 1942.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyKeller said transparency should be the watchword going forward.“I cannot imagine that those responsible would opt for [a] simple reproduction of Nazi architecture, but it also can’t be left as a ruin – those tend to be even more fascinating,” he said.“Instead, we should find ways to integrate the material remains and new information and education, showing the temporal layers, including the use as a tourist destination since the 1950s. The fire added a new layer to the history to Obersalzberg, and this should be visible too.”New political realities in Germany and Austria, where the far-rightAlternative für Deutschland(AfD) andFreedom Partylead the respective national polls, will have to be taken into account as well, he said.View image in fullscreenA US soldier at the Eagle’s Nest, 4 May 1945.Photograph: Eric Schwab/AFP/Getty ImagesBohr said that troubling context led him to oppose any reconstruction of the Eagle’s Nest. “Hitler’s megalomania should remain a ruin. My suggestion would be to secure the remaining structure as far as possible and to use it to convey the history of the site,” he said.“Particularly in view of the strength of the AfD and the rise of right-wing extremism in Germany, the focus should be on coming to terms with Nazi ideology, not on restoring its stage sets.”Explore more on these topicsAdolf HitlerNazismGermanyEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in Delhi | India | The Guardian
description: Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
Content: Rahul Gandhi and fellow leaders of the opposition Congress party wave at supporters during the protest on Sunday.Photograph: Vipin/APView image in fullscreenRahul Gandhi and fellow leaders of the opposition Congress party wave at supporters during the protest on Sunday.Photograph: Vipin/APIndiaTens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in DelhiLed by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter rollHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiSun 1 Nov 2026 11.11 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 01.20 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against theNarendra Modigovernment continue to gather momentum.Led by the Congress party, India’s opposition alliance has brought together supporters from across the country, amidgrowing angerover a large-scale revision of the country’s voter roll that has seen 130 million names erased.Opposition leaders have alleged the process gives Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) an electoral advantage, and have called for the resignation and impeachment of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. The BJP has denied the claims.Addressing tens of thousands of party workers and supporters, the opposition leaderRahul Gandhisaid Kumar had “carried out the biggest crime. He has tried to silence the voice of people, strangulate our country.”Gandhi said the opposition, united under the acronymIndia(Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance), would not let “democracy be finished in the country” and warned Modi: “You can’t run anywhere.”View image in fullscreenTens of thousands of people attended the march in Delhi on Sunday – short of the million the Congress party leaders had predicted.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersThe protest was one of the largest shows of opposition strength in years, taking place amid a wider resurgence of anti-government dissent which has been systematically crushed over the 12 years of the Modi regime.The biggest challenge to the regime has come from youth-led protests that erupted over the summer – led by a movement that began satiricallycalling itself the “Cockroaches”– and forced the resignation of one of Modi’s cabinet ministers. Cockroach-led protestshit the streets againlast month, also in opposition to the revision of the electoral rolls known as special intensive revision (SIR).The opposition, in particular the Congress party, has become emboldened in the wake of the youth mobilisation. However, a significant trust deficit remains between the establishment opposition parties and the Cockroach movement. On Sunday, while Cockroach leaders had extended their support to the opposition rally, they did not attend themselves.Congress leaders had publicly predicted that a million people would attend the rally, but in the end the numbers were in the tens of thousands and empty seats were visible in the protest arena.The somewhat lacklustre turnout demonstrated the challenge still faced by Congress and its opposition allies in being seen as a formidable and viable challenger to the Modi government.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (India) bloc gather at the rally under the slogan 'Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao' (save votes, save the country).Photograph: Mihir Singh/EPAThe opposition, led by Gandhi, has lost the last three general elections to the BJP as the parties have widely failed to counter the BJP’s muscular Hindu nationalist rhetoric. The Modi government has systematically gone after political opponents, leaving little space for dissent.The majority of those gathered at the protest site on Sunday were party workers and organisers who had been bussed in, and there was very little evidence of a mobilisation of the young people who have been participating in the Cockroach-led protests. According to the opposition, many of their buses were stopped from enteringDelhiby police barricades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShalini, a restaurant owner from Goa, said she was there “not for the opposition but because I am against the BJP and how they are trying to remove any avenue of dissent in this country. I’m not particularly for any opposition party.”She said many questions still remained about the viability and support of that opposition, but she sensed a “groundswell of dissatisfaction with the BJP and the opposition is cashing in on it – good for them”.‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streetsRead moreThe issue of the revision of the electoral rolls first emerged last year, but recently erupted into a national scandal after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper revealed irregularities and discord within the election commission over its implementation.Millions of allegedly eligible voters have discovered their names have been left off the electoral rolls, with Muslims and minorities disproportionately targeted. This week, Human Rights Watch said the accusations raised “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections”.Arwind Chaudhery, 48, said he too was not aligned with any party. “I am here because SIR has undermined our democracy and the situation has got so bad, it is beyond repair or rectification,” he said. “So it is natural that people will be driven out to protest and that is a ray of hope.”The BJP have sought to dismiss the opposition protests as anarchy. The party’s president, JP Nadda, said Sunday’s rally would be the “nail in the coffin” for the opposition alliance. He said the protest was “not ​an act of respect for democracy. ‌It is a calculated conspiracy ​to plunge the nation into anarchy, ​all in the name of democracy.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaProtestSouth and central AsiaRahul GandhiNarendra ModiDelhinewsShareReuse this content

title: Piles of rubbish, power cuts and potholes: anger grows over Johannesburg’s run-down infrastructure  | South Africa | The Guardian
description: The problems run deep in South Africa’s largest city. Will voters punish the ANC in next week’s local elections?
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: The problems run deep in South Africa’s largest city. Will voters punish the ANC in next week’s local elections?
Content: Recyclers collect rubbish in Gandhi Square in Johannesburg. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThe problems run deep in South Africa’s largest city. Will voters punish the ANC in next week’s local elections?ByRachel Savagein JohannesburgSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne week before the local elections inSouth Africa, the pavements and roads of the Johannesburg township Alexandra were filled with piles of rubbish, rotting in the heat. At the Jukskei River, its banks choked with rubble and litter, foul-smelling brown water flowed out of a culvert.“We’ve got way too many challenges,” said Semadi Manganye, the chief executive of Alexandra Water Warriors, an environmental NGO that organises clean-ups of the river and plants trees on its banks. “If it’s not electricity, it’s water. If it’s not water, it’s waste.”View image in fullscreenAlexandra Water Warriors volunteers cleaning up plastic pollution from the Jukskei River.Photograph: Jérôme Delay/APManganye acknowledged the challenges of providing public services in a city whose population grew by 10% to 4.8 million between the 2011 and 2022 censuses. “I have an understanding of why they’re failing,” he said. “But we’ve got to mitigate against this – we knew that it was going to happen.”On 4 November, up to29 million South African voterswill go to the polls for local elections amid deep discontent with the water cuts, power outages and potholes that plague the country’s 257 municipalities. Their problems are so deep that even the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, hasadmitted: “Too many of our municipalities are failing to meet the needs and expectations of the people they are meant to serve.”View image in fullscreenDiscontent over waste and public services will play a main role in the local elections in South Africa.Photograph: Emmanuel Croset/AFP/Getty ImagesIn the last financial year (2024-25), only 39 local governments, 15% of the total, received a “clean” audit from the country’s auditor general. Two-thirds are “financially distressed”, according toa parliamentary budget office report.Nowhere are the problems more pressing than in Johannesburg, South Africa’s largest city and commercial capital. The city has been ruled by a series of unstable coalitions, with 10 changes of mayor in the past decade. Authorities have admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog. It is estimated that a quarter of the water bought by the municipal water body Johannesburg Water islost to leaks.View image in fullscreenA person washing in flood water in a busy market area in central Johannesburg.Photograph: Per-Anders PetterssonAt a public meeting in Rabie Ridge, a township in the city’s north-east, about 400 people berated the incumbent mayor, Dada Morero, and executives from Johannesburg’s electricity utility, City Power.One person said she had had no power for six months. Another said her mother had been forced to turn to loan sharks after receiving energy bills as high as 6,000 rand a month when her monthly pension was 2,000 rand.“If there is any organisation that is dysfunctional it is this organisation … it is failing,” one man said, drawing huge cheers from the audience.Even some affluent northern suburbs are going without piped water for weeks at a time. After a month-long outage about six months ago, people in parts of Melville and Westdene have been unable to predict when they will get water since September.View image in fullscreenPeople walk past a hole where a water pipe has broken at an intersection in the Yeoville area of central Johannesburg.Photograph: Per-Anders Pettersson“The word I’d use is desperate, because literally there’s been almost no water at all,” said Kate Spiller, a semi-retired management consultant. “During the day, there’s dribs and drabs. And then sometimes in the middle of night, my husband’s been able to fill a couple of five-litre bottles and then it’s gone dry again.”Spiller and her husband drive 10 minutes almost daily to a mosque that has a borehole to fill up about a dozen five-litre bottles, which they use to take bucket showers. “It’s incapacitating … you’re always planning, you’re always thinking: ‘We need to get water, we’d better make a plan,’” she said.“Overall, Johannesburg is providing the necessary services to our communities,” Morero said in an interview after the Rabie Ridge meeting. “Isolated areas where they don’t have [services], we are focusing on right now.”He acknowledged parts of the inner city were without power, due to a “collapsed” substation, but blamed “vandalism” and criminals. “From time to time, with the JPMD [Johannesburg Metropolitan police department] we try to push back, but there are also syndicates who are also organised and affecting our infrastructure,” he said.However, experts have said many city politicians and officials are themselves corrupt. An October report by theGlobal Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crimesaid: “Governance failure in the CoJ [city of Johannesburg] has given birth to a criminal ecosystem.”View image in fullscreenWater pooling on a street in central Johannesburg from a broken pipe. It is thought a quarter of water is lost to leaks.Photograph: Per-Anders Pettersson“People in charge of the supply chain system can easily get backhanders,” said Rashid Seedat, a former city official and the executive director of the Gauteng City-Region Observatory, a research organisation.“Of course, corruption is the metro police officer taking a bribe of 200 rand [and] a 200m rand tender. It’s across the board and endemic in the entire system and acceptable.”The Democratic Alliance, South Africa’s second-largest political party, has mounted an energetic campaign in Johannesburg, under the 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor Helen Zille, to try to unseat the African National Congress (ANC) and its coalition partners, the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the populist Patriotic Alliance.Zille, who is white, has previously caused controversy, particularly among black voters, including fortweets in 2017that said colonialism was not completely negative. However, viral stunts that have drawn attention to Johannesburg’s infrastructure issues, such as Zille snorkelling in an enormous flooded pothole, have helped to put the DA ahead of the ANC in the polls (voters choose parties and councillors, who in turn elect the mayor).View image in fullscreenHelen Zille in a water leak that has been in place for over three years in Douglasdale, Johannesburg.Photograph: Jacques Nelles/DAThe DA has polled between 29% and 36% in October, compared with 22% to 27% for the ANC, which is fielding three possible mayoral candidates amid factional infighting. However, this may not be enough for Zille to form a coalition, analysts say.“In order to understand Joburg, you actually have to zoom out a bit and look at all of Gauteng [province],” said Ziyanda Stuurman of Africa Practice, a consultancy. “Over the last decade, and especially since 2021, there’s been this very clear working relationship between the ANC, EFF and ActionSA across the three municipalities [Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni].“Once in-principle coalition arrangements are agreed to, you’ve seen the EFF back ANC and ActionSA mayors across all three cities and there’s been a negotiation keeping in mind all three.”Stuurman said a coalition similar to recent ones could lead to five more years of decline in Johannesburg. “It’s been much more horse-trading than it actually has been about the city’s best interests.”Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaAfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Investors pull billions in funds from Binance after record $6.3bn hack | Binance | The Guardian
description: Cryptocurrency exchange has begun to allow withdrawals after theft believed to have come from North Korea
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Cryptocurrency exchange has begun to allow withdrawals after theft believed to have come from North Korea
Content: Binance told customers it was testing its networks and assets to ensure deposits were safe.Photograph: Romain Doucelin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBinance told customers it was testing its networks and assets to ensure deposits were safe.Photograph: Romain Doucelin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBinanceInvestors pull billions in funds from Binance after record $6.3bn hackCryptocurrency exchange has begun to allow withdrawals after theft believed to have come from North KoreaLauren AlmeidaSun 1 Nov 2026 13.53 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 13.08 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInvestors have pulled $3.6bn (£2.7bn) in funds from the cryptocurrency exchangeBinanceas it recovers from a record hack in which billions were stolen from customer accounts.The platform was hit by a $6.3bn theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history. Experts identifiedNorth Korea as the probable culprit.Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach but on Sunday announced it hadbegun a phased reopening.By Sunday afternoon, the platform had processed $4.6bn in withdrawals and $1bn in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of about $3.6bn – representing 2.1% of its $171bn in total assets under management.The numbers were confirmed by the company in its latest proof of reserves snapshot. A full report is expected on Monday.How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programmeRead moreBinance said: “After an initial spike, withdrawal volumes have declined and are stabilising as expected, while deposit volumes have remained substantial.”The crypto exchange told its customers that market conditions were stable and that its team was “testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets”.“We know how important safe and reliable access to your funds is and will share details of the next phase as soon as we can,” it said on X.In the first phase Binance restored withdrawals for 15 networks and assets, including ethereum, USDT and USDC tokens on the ethereum blockchain, as well as some others held on the BNB Smart Chain blockchain. Later on Sunday, dealing in the Dogecoin and Avalanche currencies resumed on their own platforms.The platform said it had replenished 90% of the ⁠amount stolen. The remaining 10% of tokens were less liquid, meaning they ⁠may take ​longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday.How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe?Read moreRichard Teng, Binance’s co-chief executive, said separately that the company was “committed to covering the ⁠remaining 10%” and users would not bear the financial impact of the hack.On Saturday the FBI confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused ofhacking into Sony Picturesas revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.“The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29,” the law enforcement agency said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors” were “using to launder these stolen assets”.Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate.Binance said it had set aside about $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses. “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1bn secure asset fund for users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its futures insurance fund and own corporate treasury, Binance said ​on X.The hack came as many observers expressed worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.The sheer scale of the hack has put aspotlight on the capacity of North Korea– which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.Explore more on these topicsBinanceHackingBitcoinNorth KoreaBlockchainCryptocurrenciesCybercrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading | China | The Guardian
description: A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Content: Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenXi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesChinaAnalysisThe US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleadingEduardo PorterA truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilitiesSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.22 ESTShareDonald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless theFederal Reservecuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.But neitherChinanor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.View image in fullscreenThe port in Qinzhou, China, on 22 October 2026.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionairesRead moreThe paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order.He described the strategyas building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging itsoverwhelming dominanceover the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year,it stunnedthe Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.View image in fullscreenA girl visits an installation about rare earth production at the National Museum in Beijing, China, on 24 March 2026.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersIt has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains manyother restrictions. While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hitother countriesfor a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency hasestimated thatif China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.Where does the supply chain war go from here? TheTrump administrationis pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.China, on the other hand, has announced a range ofhigh-tech export restrictions, covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.View image in fullscreenWorkers at a photovoltaic power-generation project site on 27 October 2026 in Wenling, Zhejiang province, China.Photograph: Zhou Xuejun/VCG/Getty ImagesChina will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.Explore more on these topicsChinaUS economyDonald TrumpTrump administrationTrump tariffsCritical mineralsTariffsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Fashion and tradition: how John Smedley is innovating in a tough market | Manufacturing sector | The Guardian
description: In the final article in a series on high-end British manufacturing we look at a clothing brand that dates to the 18th century but is increasingly on-trend
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: In the final article in a series on high-end British manufacturing we look at a clothing brand that dates to the 18th century but is increasingly on-trend
Content: The knitwear manufacturer John Smedley has a commitment to craft skills.Composite: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenThe knitwear manufacturer John Smedley has a commitment to craft skills.Composite: Guardian Design/GettyManufacturing sectorFashion and tradition: how John Smedley is innovating in a tough marketIn the final article in a series on high-end British manufacturing we look at a clothing brand that dates to the 18th century but is increasingly on-trendMaking jeans again: the Hiut Denim factory in CardiganRolls-Royce rides high on craze for customisationLuxury leather: from wallets to cigar casesSarah ButlerSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTina is wielding a large pair of scissors with authority, slicing with immense skill and precision.With 38 years of experience, she is an important member of the 230-strong manufacturing team producing fine knitwear for the John Smedley brand. Using a chalk, a semi-circular guide and a sharp pair of scissors, she cuts necklines in the knitted garments ready for the final trim to be attached.The brand’s site in the Peak District,Derbyshire, is the oldest continuously operating factory in the world, with a maze of buildings, one of which dates to 1784. Inside is a mix of hi-tech Japanese knitting technology, skilled artisans such as Tina, who finish garments by hand, and some machines which date back more than 60 years and have to be kept going with bespoke parts. Another smaller Smedley factory, in Armthorpe, South Yorkshire, also finishes the garments.The company – which holds royal warrants from King Charles and Queen Camilla – has faced difficult times in the luxury market in recent years, but is surviving by mixing heritage with innovation: from launching new designs and forging celebrity partnerships to investing in the latest equipment.Most UK fashion manufacturing closed down more than 30 years ago as brands moved to cheaper offshore manufacturing locations such as China, India and Bangladesh.There are 3,515 manufacturers of clothing in the UK, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics collated by UKFT, 315 fewer than a decade before. The number of people working in the industry is now just 15,000 according to the ONS, compared with 173,000 30 years ago.Smedley has stayed true to its roots. It not only knits and puts together garments, but dyes cotton yarn, and washes, steams and packs the finished products, all in a beautiful wooded valley in Lea Bridge, near Matlock.Water comes from a brook that runs under the factory with much of the steam for its processes generated by ancient-looking boilers as well as some shiny new silver ones.Together, the workers produce 4,500 items a week not only under the John Smedley name, but under contract for high-end brands including Lanvin, Margaret Howell and Daks.View image in fullscreenThe actor Bill Nighy has worn John Smedley’s three-button polo shirt since he was 17.Photograph: Charlie GrayIn 2024, it invested more than £4m in updating machinery to become more efficient and increase the range of styles it can make.Jess McGuire-Dudley, the 41-year-old marketing expert who stepped up to be managing director last year after a decade at the company, says the family owners are “open to change”. “As long as it is in an appropriate way, that’s always embraced,” she says.While some of its methods may be age-old, she says Smedley is increasingly on trend. The company is not struggling to attract new workers as, McGuire-Dudley says, young people are interested in craft skills and the sustainability aspect of making goods closer to home.To help attract and retain people, the company has refurbished housing on its site to offer cheap accommodation alongside other staff benefits including pilates classes and a running club.However, McGuire-Dudley says the factory is racing to train its younger workers as its most skilled employees near retirement age. The apprenticeship can take up to two years.The commitment to craft skills is part of the founding philosophy that has protected John Smedley when other British-made brands have fallen away.“He always had a vision of the highest quality produced for the top end of the market,” she says. “That is what we have tried to stay true to.”The battle for survival is also self-funded by the business, which is owned by about 65 members of the founding family and chaired by the eighth-generation John Smedley descendant Ian Maclean.View image in fullscreenJohn Smedley’s Derbyshire factory: ‘Sure, we could do things more cheaply overseas, but it wouldn’t be what the family want to support.’Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianThe first in a line of John Smedleys was brought in to manage the original factory, owned by the family of Florence Nightingale. The Smedleys took control of the business, then making spun cotton and muslin, in 1818, eventually adapting it to spin wool and cotton yarns and then knit them into clothing.By the mid-1800s the company had made a name crafting underwear, with some claiming that the term long johns takes its name from John Smedley. The John Smedley brand itself was first registered in 1876 and by the end of the century it had diversified into men’s clothing.In 1932, Smedley’s knitting machines began making the three-button polo shirt, still one of its bestsellers. By the 50s and 60s the brand’s fame was at its height, with celebrities such as Marilyn Monroe, the Beatles and Audrey Hepburn photographed wearing John Smedley roll necks.Today, John Smedley sells around the world via its website and a string of stores in Japan, as well as in two London boutiques and luxury outlets including Selfridges, Harrods and Brown Thomas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe urbane British actor Bill Nighy recently collaborated with the label on two collections, having worn its three-button polo shirt since he was 17. The brand also created a cheaper diffusion line, JS, which was sold in John Lewis in 2024 and is now sold via the Smedley website and in Japan.The flurry of activity aims to reverse a fall in sales and profits. A drop in the value of the yen hit sales to Japan, a key market, responsible for half of international trade.John Smedley’s sales fell 5% to £16.8m in the year to 31 March 2025, while the group slid to a £720,000 pre-tax loss, having made a £270,000 profit the year before, according to accounts filed at Companies House.McGuire-Dudley and her team have responded with an improved online presence and by revving up European trade with more direct sales adding a dedicated French website. It has opened a new showroom in Milan where it is testing pop-up sales events.The deal with Nighy, the JS line and a new website helped to drive the first year of UK sales growth in more than five years in the 12 months to the end of March 2026.“The market is still extremely tricky,” says McGuire-Dudley. “This year we are in the midst of a turnaround. The last several months have been profitable. There is a sense it is all coming through but it is a slow burn as we are having to recoup massive volume losses from Japan.”While the recent rise in the yen may help sales in Japan, she says: “We can’t run a business on hope. We have had to pivot.”View image in fullscreenJess McGuire-Dudley, CEO of John Smedley, in the company’s boardroom.Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian“We are starting to prove those ideas are working. The new financial year will be transformational I think.”The company has benefited from the support of its family shareholders who have held out against buyout offers to support British manufacturing.Robert Marsden-Smedley, an eighth-generation family member and board director, says:“When my father was chairman we had a couple of approaches. That was tempting and we felt they were trying to buy it with a view to asset stripping and what was left would not be us.”Family commitment is needed as UK manufacturers face a raft of higher costs with increases in employers’ national insurance contributions and the legal minimum wage adding £700,000 to Smedley’s bills last year.McGuire-Dudley says: “From a manufacturing point of view it was slightly shortsighted. Many manufacturers smaller than us went under.“Energy and labour costs can wipe out profitability straight away and you don’t have any control over them.”Marsden-Smedley says the family is determined to prioritise its Derbyshire factory and UK manufacturing over short-term profit.“The family is very proud of what we have got here. Sure, we could do things more cheaply overseas but it wouldn’t be what the family want to support. It’s a responsibility. I feel part of our job is being custodians of the business today to pass it on to the next generation in as good a state or a bit better.”Explore more on these topicsManufacturing sectorLuxury goods sectorFashion industryDerbyshireInternational tradeBrexitCraftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: High street ‘slot farms’ could avoid budget tax rise through bingo hall loophole | Gambling | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of adult gaming centres in England have bingo licences that still qualify them for discounted business rates
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Hundreds of adult gaming centres in England have bingo licences that still qualify them for discounted business rates
Content: The chancellor this week increased duty on slot machine takings from 20% to 25% – but venues with bingo licences could escape the rise.Photograph: Mark Waugh/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe chancellor this week increased duty on slot machine takings from 20% to 25% – but venues with bingo licences could escape the rise.Photograph: Mark Waugh/AlamyGamblingHigh street ‘slot farms’ could avoid budget tax rise through bingo hall loopholeHundreds of adult gaming centres in England have bingo licences that still qualify them for discounted business ratesRob DaviesSun 1 Nov 2026 07.04 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of high street “slot farms” could continue claiming a discount on their business rates, unless the government closes a loophole that allows them to pose as bingo halls.John Healey singled out adult gaming centres (AGCs) in his first budget this week, in which he increased duty on slot machine takings from 20% to 25%, claiming he was “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.How £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budgetRead moreAs well as raising the duty, which willalso affect bookmakers and casinos, he said AGCs and vape shops in England would no longer be eligible for a discount on business rates aimed at leisure and hospitality businesses.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been avocal critic of AGCsand posted on Instagram after the budget to back the policy, a key plank of his pitch to improve British high streets.However, many shops owned by the UK’s two largest slot farm companies, Merkur and Admiral, could escape the tax tweak, Guardian analysis suggests.This is because they have obtained bingo licences for venues that appear to offer slot machines almost exclusively.GamblingCommission records suggest that hundreds of slot machine venues may have exploited this loophole.View image in fullscreenMany shops owned by the UK’s two largest slot farm companies, Merkur and Admiral, could escape the tax tweak.Photograph: allanbellimages/AlamyWhen the Guardian visited four owned by Merkur and one owned by Admiral, all advertised bingo in their shop windows. However, the shops appeared to offer mainly slot machines inside. Bingo was available only on tablets stacked in one small corner of the room, allowing the venues to operate under a bingo licence.In at least one case,captured in covert filming, a member of staff said nobody ever used the bingo tablets, and they appeared not to be in working order. The remainder of the venue was dedicated to slot machines offering a £2 spin every 2.5 seconds for a jackpot of £500. These category B3 machines are associated with higher levels of gambling-related harm than most other products, according to several studies.One so-called bingo venue is the Merkur Slots shop in Stockport, where Wendy Hughes, who had terminal cancer,lost £2,000 over two spellslasting 16 hours. Merkur was fined £100,000 after the Guardian revealed the details of Merkur’s exploitation of Hughes, who has since died.TheStockportbranch of Merkur is among more than 200 arcades that are licensed as bingo venues, according to Gambling Commission records, despite appearing to be geared towards slot machine play. Some data is duplicated, making it hard to measure exact numbers.Operators could also now convert their remaining AGC licences to bingo.The Labour MP Alex Ballinger, a co-chair of the gambling reform all-party parliamentary group, welcomed the tax increase on slot machines but urged the government to be vigilant about the loophole. “We must ensure these licences cannot be used to sidestep the new business rates rules,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe urged the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to proceed with proposals to tighten the licensing rules, amid a consultation. “The government has already recognised this problem, and I am confident ministers will work with the regulator to close loopholes and ensure enforcement going forward,” he said.View image in fullscreenThe chancellor says he is ‘raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street’.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesThe business rates expert Paul Turner-Mitchell of the real estate intelligence company Altus Group said the outcome of the tax change could hinge on how the Treasury defined an AGC and how local councils chose to enforce the rules. “A bingo licence alone does not settle its business rates treatment,” he said.Merkur and Admiral did not respond to a request for comment.Joseph Cullis, the president of the arcade operators’ trade body Bacta, said the industry would be hit hard by the tax changes.“My great-grandfather started our family business back in 1962, and we’ve spent more than 60 years building it into what it is today,” he said. “Like many of the family-run businesses I represent across the sector, this decision will force us to reconsider investment and make difficult decisions about our future. Even larger operators will now be forced to scale back their plans.”Explore more on these topicsGamblingBusiness ratesBudget 2026Tax and spendingStockportEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It seems weird for an MC – but lyrics have never been a thing for me’: De La Soul’s honest playlist | De La Soul | The Guardian
description: Rapper Pos of the hip hop greats favours Barry White for the bedroom and sobs to Stevie Wonder, but which cheese-rock hit does he love on the sly?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: Rapper Pos of the hip hop greats favours Barry White for the bedroom and sobs to Stevie Wonder, but which cheese-rock hit does he love on the sly?
Content: Soul power …Pos (left) and his De La colleague Maseo.Photograph: NBC/Todd OwyoungView image in fullscreenSoul power …Pos (left) and his De La colleague Maseo.Photograph: NBC/Todd OwyoungHonest playlistDe La Soul‘It seems weird for an MC – but lyrics have never been a thing for me’: De La Soul’s honest playlistRapper Pos of the hip hop greats favours Barry White for the bedroom and sobs to Stevie Wonder, but which cheese-rock hit does he love on the sly?As told toRich PelleySun 1 Nov 2026 04.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withMy father could sing really well – he was in a choir and had this coolness. He would walk around singing Love and Happiness by Al Green and, because he looked so much like him on the cover, I actually thought he was Al Green.The first single I boughtUnderlove by Melba Moore from Abraham & Straus, this department store in Long Island that had a mini record store inside. I later realised it was produced by Kashif, and I would fall in love with everything he produced.The song I do at karaokeI’d like to have a go at Everybody Wants to Rule the World or Shout by Tears for Fears.The best song to play at a partyWhen someone throws down All I Do by Stevie Wonder, you can see it in people’s faces – this is a classic piece of soul music.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toIt seems weird for an MC – I can tell you every drop and hi-hat, but lyrics have never been a big thing for me. When I play with Mos Def, Black Thought or Gorillaz, I’m amazed that they can seemingly remember the lyrics to every song on Earth. I can just about remember Top Billin’ by Audio Two.The song I can no longer listen toI don’t really fall out of love with songs. There are lots that get played too much, but at some point I usually grow back in love with them. I don’t want to name anyone in case they come and beat me up.The song I secretly likeI’ll play These Dreams by Heart in my dressing room when I think no one else is listening. It reminds me of the big hair era.The song that gets me up in the morningI always try to start my day by saying: it’s going to be a lovely day. I even had Lovely Day by Bill Withers as my alarm, ready to go off at 6am.The song that changed my lifeI was living in the Bronx. My brothers would have mixtapes, but when I heard Planet Rock by Afrika Bambaataa and the Soulsonic Force, it made me really want to do this rap thing. I remember saying: “What the fuck is this?” and my mom telling me off for cursing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe best song to have sex toAny Barry White record. Or Let’s Get It On by Marvin Gaye. Have I ever tried making love to my own music? Hell no.The song that makes me cryI love the love Stevie Wonder gives the other person in I Love Every Little Thing About You – saying, basically, the only person I put before you is God, and nothing could top my love for you. I tear up when I hear that record.The song I’d like played at my funeralI Am I Be byDe La Soul.Stakes Is High, remixed by J Dilla and featuring Mos Def and Truth Enola, andCabin in the Sky, the band’s ninth studio album, are both out now.Explore more on these topicsDe La SoulHonest playlistHip-hopfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dafne Keen and Harriet Walter on working with Patrick Stewart: ‘I’ve never seen anyone so ecstatic’ | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: The late actor’s co-stars in Logan and Anthony and Cleopatra remember dog impressions, marching band-conducting and a fervent belief in fun
Author: Harriet Walter
Headline: The late actor’s co-stars in Logan and Anthony and Cleopatra remember dog impressions, marching band-conducting and a fervent belief in fun
Content: ‘Always alive in the moment’: Harriet Walter and Patrick Stewart in Anthony and Cleopatra at the RSC, 2006.Photograph: Alastair Muir/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Always alive in the moment’: Harriet Walter and Patrick Stewart in Anthony and Cleopatra at the RSC, 2006.Photograph: Alastair Muir/ShutterstockPatrick StewartDafne Keen and Harriet Walter on working with Patrick Stewart: ‘I’ve never seen anyone so ecstatic’The late actor’s co-stars in Logan and Anthony and Cleopatra remember dog impressions, marching band-conducting and a fervent belief in funDafne Keen andHarriet WalterSun 1 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 03.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDafne Keen: ‘He asked me: have you noticed no-one ever sneezes in films?’I had the unbelievable privilege of working with Patrick when I was 11 [in Logan]. He was a man of extraordinary warmth, wit and generosity. He possessed that increasingly rare ability to make everyone around him feel as though they were being let in on something wonderful. To work alongside him was to be reminded, every day, of what it means to love what you do, and to share that love with others. He imparted lessons in a way that was so wise, you didn’t even realise you were being taught.To describe Patrick simply as a remarkable man would feel an injustice to the sheer breadth of what made him so. He was a master of his craft, certainly, but also a teacher, a raconteur, a mischief-maker and, above all, a profoundly generous human being. He carried his knowledge lightly, his humour generously, and his affection for the people around him with a warmth that was impossible to miss.He had a seemingly inexhaustible supply of jokes that could make the longest, most arduous days on set pass in minutes. I remember walking around one of the house sets with him and remarking that the only thing missing from the home was a dog. Without missing a beat, Patrick began barking and behaving like one, until I was absolutely roaring with laughter. It was that sort of instinctive silliness, a complete willingness to abandon any notion of grandeur or self-importance, that made being around him such a joy.View image in fullscreen‘He had a way of making you feel included’: Dafne Keen in LoganPhotograph: 20TH CENTURY FOX/AllstarHe was equally gifted at talking to children and professors alike, shifting his linguistic code to meet whoever happened to be in front of him. I remember the little snippets of Shakespeare, Ibsen, Chekhov and Pinter he would spontaneously grace us with, sharing passages from the works he loved as though letting us in on a private little world.
