He could move from the most sophisticated literary conversation to the most ridiculous schoolyard mischief without ever seeming to change gear.Patrick was an incredibly protective scene partner and colleague. He had a way of making you feel included, listened to and respected, even when you were just a clueless 11-year-old finding your feet in the pressure-filled adult world of a film set. I remember him noticing me looking longingly at his Professor X wheelchair, and secretly approaching me to explain that if you pushed the stick hard enough, it went very, very fast. He then proceeded to invite me on it, encouraging me to go faster. I remember him hatching little plans with me, things we could sneak into scenes to make the set feel more like a playground and less like the intimidating grown-up world it could sometimes be.On one of our first days together, after an incredibly intense take, he turned to me and asked, entirely seriously, “Have you ever noticed, no one ever sneezes in films?” I stared at him for a moment before agreeing that he was quite right. “We should try to sneeze in this one,” he said. And so we made a pact to try to sneak a sneeze into a take. It was such a Patrick observation: at once completely absurd and rather brilliant. He was an artist with an extraordinary attentiveness to the world around him, someone who noticed the smallest details and understood that there was always something worth questioning, even in the most familiar conventions of his craft.That was perhaps one of the loveliest things about him. He never seemed to outgrow the joy of playing, or to lose sight of the fact that, at its heart, acting should be fun. He had this extraordinary ability to make you feel that you weren’t simply there to do a job, but to be part of something, to contribute, to experiment and, above all, to enjoy yourself.There is something incredibly moving about the idea that an actor of his stature never made a child feel small, inexperienced or peripheral. He let you in on the secret. He made you feel like a fellow conspirator, a teammate.I learnt so much from him. He was, however briefly, my colleague and my acting professor, and he will forever be my Professor X. Someone who built a little safe haven for me on the often alien world of a film set, who made room for play, curiosity and mischief, and who taught me more than I think he ever realised. I will carry my admiration for him, and my gratitude for the time I was lucky enough to spend in his company, for the rest of my life.Harriet Walter: ‘He enjoyed fame in the best possible way’A memory: Patrick, wearing a team baseball cap to disguise the inimitable sculpture of his head, moving anonymously through the crowds at an American Football match in Michigan. Later during halftime he stepped up to the podium, bald pate boldly exposed, to conduct the University of Michigan Marching Band in a medley of TV theme tunes. I’ve never seen anyone so ecstatic. Fame came relatively late to Patrick and it was therefore enjoyed in the best possible way.Later that night we performed together in Antony and Cleopatra.He was still buzzing. But then he was always alive in the moment and taught me that the sexual chemistry between the famous pair was more to do with their minds and their verbal sparring than in any fantastic costumes or scenery. His curiosity and courage earned him a full eventful and rewarding life. I was blessed in knowing him.Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartMarvelRoyal Shakespeare CompanyHarriet WalterTheatreShareReuse this content

title: The best theatre to stream this month: the Gisèle Pelicot trial becomes an all-star play that ‘just floors you’ | Stage | The Guardian
description: An unmissable documentary play, Tom Stoppard’s Arcadia with luminous Isis Hainsworth and ecstatic dance in a Norwegian museum are among November’s highlights
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: An unmissable documentary play, Tom Stoppard’s Arcadia with luminous Isis Hainsworth and ecstatic dance in a Norwegian museum are among November’s highlights
Content: ‘It is the facts’ … Gisèle Pelicot, subject of The Pelicot Trial.Photograph: Christoph Rutenkolk/EPAView image in fullscreen‘It is the facts’ … Gisèle Pelicot, subject of The Pelicot Trial.Photograph: Christoph Rutenkolk/EPAThe best theatre to stream this monthStageThe best theatre to stream this month: the Gisèle Pelicot trial becomes an all-star play that ‘just floors you’An unmissable documentary play, Tom Stoppard’s Arcadia with luminous Isis Hainsworth and ecstatic dance in a Norwegian museum are among November’s highlightsChris WiegandSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Pelicot TrialSwiss director Milo Rau’s ripped-from-the-headlines approach to theatre has included shows about wars in Iraq and Congo and the exploitation of migrant workers. His four-hour documentary play (created with Servane Dècle) about the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot has been performed around the world and will be staged by the Young Vic at London’s County Hall on 30 November. The production swiftly sold out butwill be livestreamed in full. The cast includes Adjoa Andoh, Rosie Jones and Olivia Williams. “It was the act of witnessing that really got me,”said Young Vic boss Nadia Fallof the show. “It isn’t scenes and costumes in a set like a traditional piece of theatre. It is the facts. It just floors you.”ITA Music Vol 1: New OriginalsIt’s already one of Europe’s coolest theatre companies, anavant garde hit factorythat stormed the West End withThe Yearsand Oedipus. Now,Internationaal Theater Amsterdamhas launched its own record label to release the “most requested” music from its recent productions. The first compilation includes tracks by Thijs van Vuure from an adaptation of James Baldwin’s novel Giovanni’s Room.Available on Spotify.View image in fullscreenA night in the museum … DuEls.Photograph: Antero HeinDuElsThe moving mosaic of schoolboys he painstakingly choreographed forthe viral Storm videohas brought Damien Jalet on to the smartphones of a huge new audience. OnSadler’s Wells Digital Stage, you can now see the great innovator twisting scenes of ecstasy and agony with performers among the statues of Oslo’s Vigeland Museum, in the hour-long film DuEls (made with Erna Ómarsdóttir). Highlights include a tangled trio familiar from horror hitSuspiria. Endlessly intriguing, not least in how the movement changes your appreciation of figures frozen in time: a choreographer illuminating sculptors.View image in fullscreenIsis Hainsworth in Arcadia at the Old Vic.Photograph: Manuel HarlanArcadiaWhen director Carrie Cracknell was cast in a student production of Tom Stoppard’s The Real Thing, she considered herself “no match for his dazzling dialogue, speed of thought or emotional depths”. But Cracknell mastered all of that, and much more, in her Old Vic revival of the chewy Arcadia, which traverses two different centuries to explore matters of the universe and the heart, with a first-rate cast including the luminous, Olivier-nominated Isis Hainsworth. If only all plays left you with quite so much to think about. OnNT at Homefrom 26 November.Salt.In 2017, the performance artistSelina Thompsonarrived at the Edinburgh fringe with a mallet, protective goggles and blocks of salt rock that she duly hammered in a one-woman show whose audience members each took home a piece. Thompson left Edinburgh that year with several awards for her extraordinary account of the transatlantic slave triangle and how she retraced its route, from the UK to Ghana to Jamaica. The performance inspiredthis film on BBC iPlayer, which preserves its sense of ritual, commemoration and intimacy – and adds Thompson’s reflections on its creation.Explore more on these topicsStageThe best theatre to stream this monthTheatreDanceDamien JaletMilo RauGisèle PelicotGisèle Pelicot rape trialfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Romeo + Juliet at 30: how Baz Luhrmann made teens fall in love with Shakespeare | Baz Luhrmann | The Guardian
description: The maximalist, heart over head adaptation of the romantic tragedy made stars of its leads and became an English teacher’s most trusted weapon for Bard-averse students
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The maximalist, heart over head adaptation of the romantic tragedy made stars of its leads and became an English teacher’s most trusted weapon for Bard-averse students
Content: Claire Danes and Leonardo DiCaprio in Romeo + Juliet.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd./AlamyView image in fullscreenClaire Danes and Leonardo DiCaprio in Romeo + Juliet.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd./AlamyBaz LuhrmannRomeo + Juliet at 30: how Baz Luhrmann made teens fall in love with ShakespeareThe maximalist, heart over head adaptation of the romantic tragedy made stars of its leads and became an English teacher’s most trusted weapon for Bard-averse studentsAdrian HortonSun 1 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.26 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRomeo + Juliet is not the most renowned or beloved of Shakespeare’s plays, but it is perhaps the most foundational. The 16th-century tragedy, a story of love-addled teenagers and white-hot resentment, is often an English student’s first introduction to the bard’s oeuvre – more accessible and relatable to teens, with its plaintive lust and histrionic mood swings, than the more austere machinations in, say, Macbeth, Hamlet or Othello. And if Romeo + Juliet is the young person’s entry to Elizabethan English, perhaps no version of it is more worthy of the term “gateway drug” than Baz Luhrmann’s 1996 film version, which reimagined Verona’s family feud as a tropical gang war and launched an army of teenage crushes with the faces ofLeonardo DiCaprioand Claire Danes.To see or not to see? Every single Shakespeare play – ranked!Read moreThe maximalist interpretation of Shakespeare’s most lovelorn work, released 30 years ago this week (!), retains Elizabethan verse but announces its divergence from rigid classicism from the jump. Oursceneis set in fair Verona beach by a news anchor via TV set, relaying the woe of two star-cross’d lovers before clips of civil strife. Fresh off his breakout success in 1992’s Strictly Ballroom, the Australian director boldly mapped the medieval story on to 90s tabloid fixations – grainy footage of violence in the streets, magazine headlines of capos and criminals, helicopter views of car chases and riots that recalled the media circus around the OJ Simpson chase two years prior. It is a movie that could have only been made in the 90s; Luhrmann’s vision of two warring families as rival gangs, replete with their own economic operations and marked territory, tapped into the era’s preoccupation with gangland as a source of transportive art, from movies to hip-hop, and as a conservative fixation for ideas on intrinsic criminality.Luhrmann and his wife, costume designer Catherine Martin, reimagined Verona as a sun-scorched beach city, incorporating real locations – Mexico City’s famed Immaculate Heart of Mary Church and Chapultepec Palace, Veracruz’s Boca del Río – to convey an urban den of simultaneous reverence and decay. The Montagues, with their heedless hollering and open Hawaiian shirts, and the Capulets, urban cowboys in Cuban-heeled boots, nearly vibrate with loathing and brandish guns marked by Catholic iconography. Perhaps compensating for the at times impenetrable verse, Luhrmann cut and spliced and twirled the camera in a frenetic, at times literal firework display of manic energy. The film’s raucous shootouts and parties now read as an obvious precursor to Euphoria high school – these kids dressed up and showed out, popped ecstasy and ripped around town in souped-up cars. Watching a single scene, even the lovers’infamous fish tank meet-cute, has the feel of chugging an energy drink.As such, the blatantly youth-aimed film had plenty of detractors in its time. Critics dismissed it as vulgar and garish, but audiences turned out en masse; Romeo + Juliet made over $147m against a $14.5m budget, boosted in part by a period-defining soundtrack with needle drops from The Cardigans, Everclear, Radiohead and Garbage. (And of course, the song from that oft-replayed fish tank scene, Des’ree’sI’m Kissing You, became the ubiquitous soundtrack for couple-shipping montage videos on 2000s YouTube). By the time I first viewed the film in 2009 – like many, in high school English class, as part of my teacher’s bid to get us invested in Shakespeare – it was already considered a classic.That my teacher’s bid worked is largely due to the performances of the film’s two luminous stars, both brimming with the type of uncut, untameable desire known only to youth. Romeo + Juliet, of course, was a movie about teenage obsession that sparked a million teenage obsessions with DiCaprio (including from yours truly, who cried in English class not over the lovers’ double suicide –soooomelodramatic of them! – but over the realization that youth is fleeting and I would never be with anyone so beautiful. Devastating!) But it is a 17-year-old Danes, in a role originally intended for a text-accurate 13-year-old Natalie Portman (correctly deemed too childlike next to a 21-year-old DiCaprio), that shines on a rewatch. Her beauty is wide-open and uncomplicated, her face shaded with feelings as fresh and fleeting as morning dew. When her face falls, upon realizing her lover’s suicide, you feel, too, the ear-ringing fall of one’s first galling disappointment, the lurch of a sickening comedown.View image in fullscreenClaire Danes as Juliet in Romeo + Juliet.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyThat is the genius of Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet: it is a feelings-first movie, a portrait of teenage melodrama where all emotions exist only at full volume. That’s true for the highs – when the lip-locked lovers careen across a pool, or when Harold Perrineau’s Mercutioenters the scenewith a high-kick in full silver drag to Kym Mazelle’s Young Hearts Run Free – as with the lows. In Luhrmann’s vision, Mercutio’s death at the hands of John Leguizamo’s Tybalt, a devilish sharpshooter with a soul patch, lands as equally tragic and torturous as the lovers. Perrineau stumbles, processes and curses both houses with such fervor as a real hurricane swept into Veracruz, that the rest of the film feels muted without him. And still, Romeo’s agonized poisoning, which frankly puts DiCaprio’s more famous death in the North Atlantic to shame, lands as a timeless gut-punch. So much youthful idealism and beauty, wasted on such petty grievances.Luhrmann’s masterpiece more than transcended the more straightforward Shakespeare adaptations of the era, such as Kenneth Branagh’s Much Ado About Nothing (1993) and Hamlet (1996), Trevor Nunn’s Twelfth Night (1996) and Michael Hoffman’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream (1999). It arguably inspired the many modernizations kicked off by the runaway success of 1999’s 10 Things I Hate About You and continued by Easy A and She’s the Man. It quite evidently inspired a recentBroadway revival, starring Rachel Zegler and Kit Connor, that borrowed the Romeo + Juliet styling and the film’s stir-crazy bombast. But nothing has quite captured the imagination, or imparted the hot blood coursing in Shakespeare’s literary characters, like those two cursed houses in Verona beach. Thirty years on, we are still waiting for the next truly great, pop culture-shifting Shakespeare moment.Romeo + Juliet is available to watch on Hulu and HBO Max in the US, and on Disney+ in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsBaz LuhrmannRomeo and JulietClaire DanesLeonardo DiCaprioWilliam ShakespearefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Strauss: An Alpine Symphony album review – monumental work’s mystic vision guides Petrenko  | Music | The Guardian
description: Vasily Petrenko and the Royal Philharmonic’s take on Strauss’s tone poem is full of darkness and light, with an impressionist’s eye for details
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Vasily Petrenko and the Royal Philharmonic’s take on Strauss’s tone poem is full of darkness and light, with an impressionist’s eye for details
Content: Thrills and spills… conductor Vasily Petrenko.Photograph: Ben WrightView image in fullscreenThrills and spills… conductor Vasily Petrenko.Photograph: Ben WrightMusicReviewStrauss: An Alpine Symphony album review – monumental work’s mystic vision guides PetrenkoRPO/Petrenko(Harmonia Mundi)Vasily Petrenko and the Royal Philharmonic’s take on Strauss’s tone poem is full of darkness and light, with an impressionist’s eye for detailsClive PagetSun 1 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 06.41 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is the third recording of Richard Strauss’s monumental tone poem to appear in the last year, and in some respects the most interesting. Vasily Petrenko and theRoyal Philharmonic Orchestraadopt an expansive view, taking three minutes longer to clamber up and down the composer’s musical mountain than Edward Gardner or Nicholas Collon’s recent recordings. And yet nothing here seems to drag its feet.View image in fullscreenVasily Petrenko/RPO: Richard Strauss: An Alpine SymphonyThe natural world through which the intrepid hikers pass may be the emphasis of the ascent, but it’s the mystic vision and elegy on the summit where the conductor’s focus lies – that and the uneasy darkness into which Strauss’s day of thrills and spills ultimately descends.There’s a softness to the nocturnal opening that hints at mysteries to come, while a sense of awe pervades the headstrong plunge into the woods. Yet the pastoral episodes – the waterfall, the alpine meadow with its shepherds and cowbells, and especially the bellowing horns and thundering percussion of the tumultuous storm – are painted with an impressionist’s eye for detail.Recorded at the Royal Albert Hall in 2025, it’s a work that really suits the auditorium’s resonant acoustic and is presented here in spectacular sound by Mike Hatch and his team at Floating Earth. At 53 minutes, though, a filler might have been nice.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Tosca review – ENO’s new staging abandons Puccini’s realism for baffling and near-constant violence | Opera | The Guardian
description: Annilese Miskimmon’s new production of Puccini’s complex drama unmoors it from its church and state settings, but there are few gains, only losses in her radical reading. Christopher Purves’ brutish Scarpia, however, is terrific
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Annilese Miskimmon’s new production of Puccini’s complex drama unmoors it from its church and state settings, but there are few gains, only losses in her radical reading. Christopher Purves’ brutish Scarpia, however, is terrific
Content: Luxurious, stark … Axelle Fanyo and Christopher Purves in Tosca.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLuxurious, stark … Axelle Fanyo and Christopher Purves in Tosca.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianOperaReviewTosca review – ENO’s new staging abandons Puccini’s realism for baffling and near-constant violenceColiseum, LondonAnnilese Miskimmon’s new production of Puccini’s complex drama unmoors it from its church and state settings, but there are few gains, only losses in her radical reading. Christopher Purves’ brutish Scarpia, however, is terrificFlora WillsonSun 1 Nov 2026 05.48 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 07.55 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour years since English National Opera unveiledits previous Tosca(a hyper-stylised affair directed by Christof Loy), the curtain goes up on another new production, this time by ENO’s artistic directorAnnilese Miskimmon. The appeal of Puccini’s work to any company – never mind one urgently committed to stabilising itself – is clear. Tosca isone of opera’s most bankable titlesand a complex, compact drama about power with endless potential for contemporary “relevance”.It’s also an opera rooted in the specifics of three real locations – at least according to the original text and stage directions. Where other operas’ settings are regularly reimagined, Tosca’s ultra-realism has proved exceptionally immovable. Miskimmon’s decision to strip Amanda Holden’s translation of all references to particular places and – still more unusual – to set the entire opera in a single space might thus have been a radical creative departure.In practice, however, the curtain rises on what looks like a variation on the standard theme: a plain, mid-century modern church complete with Madonna and mural-in-progress, a troupe of cleaning ladies and a sacristan-cum-caretaker in dungarees. But a battered baby grand and the baffling arrival and immediate departure of a string quartet should, it seems, give the game away that (as per the programme) we are actually looking at a concert hall – albeit one in which the sacristan still pauses work to sing his Angelus.View image in fullscreenIntense … (from left) Christopher Purves, Chaz’men Williams-Ali and Axelle Fanyo in Tosca at London Coliseum.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAmong the various dramaturgical problems this approach unfortunately introduces, we lose Puccini’s visceral collision of church and state at the end of act one and his subtle layering of onstage and offstage worlds in act two. It’s hard to say what we gain instead beyond near-constant violence. Women are hauled around by their hair and the Marchioness Attavanti gets a cameo to scream through the Te Deum. Corpses accumulate on stage as Scarpia’s heavies amble around. Multiple musical instruments are smashed, the impact diminishing slightly each time.There were moments when the sheer musical sumptuousness generated by the ENO orchestra underBen Glassbergoverwhelmed anything happening on stage, and when vicious snaps of brass conjured a real sense of terror. There were times when the chorus roared desperately into life, adults and children alike intensely engaged. There were others whenAxelle Fanyo’s beauty of tone in the title role – covered and luxurious, served in a liquid torrent – rendered temporarily irrelevant the endless onstage foot traffic.Chaz’men Williams-Alisounded uncomfortable as Cavaradossi, struggling to make an impact from the back, when pitted against onstage “offstage” musicians and alongside so many larger voices. ButChristopher Purveswas a terrific, brutish Scarpia – his posture as starched as his uniform, his baritone stark and chilly, his diction hard as nails. This is not, I’m afraid, a vintage Tosca – but Purves’s Scarpia just might be.At theColiseum, London, until 11 DecemberExplore more on these topicsOperaTheatreToscaEnglish National Opera (ENO)Classical musicGiacomo PuccinireviewsShareReuse this content

title: Love the C word? You might be Australian. Hate it? You might be American | Australian books | The Guardian
description: Academics and lexicographers are exploring how swearing is tied to national cultural identities – and how the internet may cause new, creative cursing to ‘flourish’
Author: Steve Dow
Headline: Academics and lexicographers are exploring how swearing is tied to national cultural identities – and how the internet may cause new, creative cursing to ‘flourish’
Content: The use of the C word on TV shows like Colin from Accounts mirrors the way once-taboo profanities are being used every day.Photograph: Joel Pratley/BBC/CBS Studios/Paramount+ ©2024View image in fullscreenThe use of the C word on TV shows like Colin from Accounts mirrors the way once-taboo profanities are being used every day.Photograph: Joel Pratley/BBC/CBS Studios/Paramount+ ©2024Australian booksLove the C word? You might be Australian. Hate it? You might be AmericanAcademics and lexicographers are exploring how swearing is tied to national cultural identities – and how the internet may cause new, creative cursing to ‘flourish’Get our weekend culture and lifestyle emailSteve DowSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.03 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom Kath & Kim’s “pack of shunts” to Colin from Accounts’ call to “go and trim your fuckin’ hooves for netball, cunt!”, the way Australian TV shows have incorporated creative vulgarities into their dialogue mirrors the way people like to swear – and linguistic researchers say younger generations of Australians in particular see once-taboo profanities as signifiers of cultural identity.But a fondness for the C word in Australian TV doesn’t make Australians the world’s biggest swearers.Researchpublished in 2025 by linguists Martin Schweinberger of the University of Queensland and Kate Burridge of Monash University showed the nationality that swore the most often online were Americans, followed by the British, with Australians ranking third.However, Australia’s online swearing came second for breadth and creativity, with Britain topping this “better indicator” showing “richness of repertoire”, Schweinberger says. The Brits topped the list for many finely grained phrases that were “a little bit weird”, he says. “One was ‘knob-gobbler’. I thought, that’s beautiful.”“Australians were [also] very creative in the number of forms they use [such as] bloody, crap, idiot, damn. Whereas Americans, when they use vulgarity, they focus on fuck and shit,” he says.View image in fullscreenBronson called Ines ‘a cunt’ at the commitment ceremony in Married at First Sight Australia in 2019. The word wasn’t bleeped out.Photograph: Channel NineOverall, the British used “cunt” much more than Australians online, according to the study, but importantly the database used statistics collected in 2012 that did not include Australian blogs or social media posts. While Schweinberger agrees “cunt” has “lost its misogynistic meaning in Australia”, he adds: “I wouldn’t be sure about that in the US because they really shy away from it. It’s a very harsh word there.”Amanda Laugesen, a lexicographer and the director and chief editor of the Australian National Dictionary, says popular culture “does help to break down taboos”.“If you are hearing more of that in popular culture or online, it does help to shift the nature of what we think is acceptable.”Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morningKath & Kim pushed boundaries in 2003 on the ABC when Kim shouted, “Chardonnay, Chardonnay, you pack of shunts” – but by 2019, contestants on Australian versions of The Bachelor and Married at First Sight were uttering the word “cunt” without being censored in the edit.“TV stations were playing on controversy,” Laugesen says. “They made a big deal about it in the commercials that somebody was going to say this word.”Laugesen is about to release a second edition ofRooted: An Australian History of Bad Language, noting that since the book’s first publication in 2020 evidence has emerged of “young [Australian] people identifying the amelioration of the C word and the creative uses of the C word as being particularly Australian, which is fascinating”, citing the example of the portmanteau “shitcunt” for a particularly bad person.View image in fullscreenAmanda Laugesen predicts Australians’ ‘creativity with swear words’ will continue to ‘flourish’.Photograph: Ashley St George/The GuardianLaugesen is referring to a 2025thesisby the Monash University PhD philosophy student Dylan Swayne Hughes which used online survey data and recorded commentary from 49 students and seven teachers across three Victorian high schools. In it, Hughes writes: “For some participants, cunteven seems to have undergone a process ofenregisterment, becoming evaluated as a significant part of Australian culture and identity.”“Some of the older feminists I’ve spoken to still felt that was a misogynistic word,” Laugesen says. “But as with many words, that baggage and meaning shifts across time, so it’s lost that kind of cultural meaning or even people thinking of it as a bodily descriptor. Now it’s really just an insult.”Laugesen sees our broader use of swearing as a “performance of Australianness” arising from Australians’ self-perception as “more informal” and “anti-authority” compared with other predominantly English-speaking countries. Emerging from convicts, bushmen and “digger” soldiers in the first world war, vulgar vernacular is celebrated in Australia today in phrases such as “I’m not here to fuck spiders” (meaning “I don’t have time to waste”) or “cunning as a shithouse rat”, she says.“Language is very much tied to ideas of Australian identity in a way that you wouldn’t say, I think, of the US or the UK,” she says. “There’s an argument to say, what else does Australia have in terms of an idea around itself, around the Australian character and Australian values? Language is one of those things we use to make up an idea of what is Australian.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSaved for SundayEase your Sunday scaries with the best of Guardian Australia’s culture and lifestyle journalism.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWTF? Americans and Britons swear more than Australians online, research findsRead moreIn 2027, Schweinberger and Burridge plan to publish new research drawn from theinternational corpus of Englishglobal linguistics project, which will show that among 14 English-speaking countries, New Zealanders swear most frequently face to face, closely followed by Ireland and Australia, with the UK and US behind at fifth and sixth.Burridge says social swearing – in person – is a form of “verbal cuddling”, rooted in Australians’ love of banter and informality. “The main function of swearing is as a solidarity marker,” she says, noting the British-born Australian journalist Richard Twopeny’s observation in his 1883 book Town Life in Australia: “The lower-class colonial swears as naturally as he talks.”View image in fullscreenKath & Kim pushed boundaries in 2003 on the ABC with ‘Chardonnay, Chardonnay, you pack of shunts’.Photograph: Netflix“The English-speaking world is also becoming a lot more laid back now so there’s a blurring between public and private boundaries,” says Burridge. “But the lines have always been blurry in Australia.”Laugesen predicts Australians’ “creativity with swear words will likely continue to flourish”, with school students now seeing “racist, sexist and homophobic slurs as much more taboo than traditional swear words”.Social media “has become even more toxic”, however, with more abuse allowed by tech companies as free speech in the 2020s, with a lack of government regulation allowing “people to say pretty much anything online”.View image in fullscreenBut Laugesen says she would be “loathe to censor bad language”, noting taboos around swearing “have been used to close down voices and stop people from speaking out or challenging authorities”. She cites, as one example, the offensive language crimes that remain on the books in Australia, which are “disproportionately targeting Indigenous Australians”.“The history of bad language has been entwined with what it has meant, and means to be, Australian,” she says.“But all too often this has been defined along white, masculine lines. This is not to say we should reject our swearing reputation, but … we might want to think about what that says – and what we want it to say – about our values and identity.”Rooted: An Australian History of Bad LanguagebyAmanda Laugesen is published by NewSouth in Australia, $34.99Explore more on these topicsAustralian booksAustralian televisionTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why you should treat charisma as a red flag | Psychology | The Guardian
description: Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself
Content: Illustration: Elia BarbieriView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia BarbieriThe big ideaPsychologyWhy you should treat charisma as a red flagToday’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourselfAlex CurmiSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.26 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth isround!”It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. Disagreements on topics like these frequently damage relationships, alienate friends and estrange loved ones.How did things get so bad? I believe the answer is, in part, that we’re constantly exposed to a novel form of charisma.As a psychiatrist, I’ve always been fascinated by this quality: the magnetism that brings out a deep sense of trust, loyalty or enthusiasm in others. The psychology of charisma tells us that it is not necessarily a magic, undefinable X-factor, but rather a set of skills and behaviours. Sometimes people have it naturally, sometimes people learn it.double quotation markIn our nomadic past, if a person was merely superficially charming, you found out quicklyI have some experience with this. When I started my podcast a few years ago, I struggled (as I still do) with my monotonous voice. All the content creation experts said the same thing: switch up the pitch, pace and volume of your speech to maximise audience engagement. Slick production is optional, charismatic communication is not. Storytelling, body language, moral outrage and more can be mastered to help would-be internet personalities put a spell on their audience.It’s been a huge lesson for me to discover how difficult it can be to discuss big topics in the mental health space responsibly, even as a trained professional. It’s also become shockingly clear how easily someone can distort the truth on, say, antidepressants, psychotherapy or ADHD when they have no experience or knowledge in that area – as long as they come across confidently and convincingly.The dangers of charisma are nothing new, of course. History is filled with examples of people using charm to advance their interests. Dictators, cult leaders and con artists are all proof that an otherwise reasonable person can succumb to a well-executed charm offensive.The difference now is one of scale. The 2024 US election, for example, was widely described as the “podcast election”, as both candidates (Trump more successfully) consented to numerous softball interviews on the medium. They reached millions, not with policy, but with good vibes. And you don’t have to be a public figure to leverage charm in this way – any video with the right allure can go viral, regardless of that person’s intentions or expertise.Why are we so easily taken in by charisma? Like many aspects of our psychology, we can understand it more clearly through the lens of our evolutionary past.Our ancestors spent most of their time (approximately 94% of human history) as hunter-gatherers, living in nomadic tribes that may have consisted of as few as 20 people. Groups that small, pitted against the forces of nature, needed strong leadership. Like many animals, humans have status hierarchies. High-status hunter-gatherers likely had many of the traits we still associate with charisma today: great eye contact, body language that signalled certainty, a persuasive voice.The difference being that, back then, you had the opportunity to observe your peers all day, every day: their flaws, their virtues, their competence, often while facing lethal danger. If a person was merely superficially charming, you found out quickly. Charisma would only win out if accompanied by other important qualities, including sound judgment, good character and wisdom.That’s not the case now. Technology allows us to shield the unpalatable parts of ourselves much more easily, selecting only the best bits for public consumption. Our brains did not evolve to process handpicked slices of someone else’s behaviour, detached from the rest of their lives, so we’re vulnerable to being duped. One frightening example is that of Ruby Franke, the parenting vlogger with millions of subscribers who wasjailed for child abuseafter two of her six children were found beaten and malnourished.We spend a lot of time worrying about how the minds of teenagers are warped by the online world. We’re keenly aware how prone they are to manipulation by seemingly impressive figures. What we fail to realise is, we’reallteenagers when it comes to the internet. Algorithmic social media has only been around for about 15 years, and we remain largely unconscious of how routinely it bypasses our better judgment. Is there any way to grow out of this newly acquired susceptibility?The best form of defence against the excesses of charisma is critical thinking. We should regard it as being like a collective immune system, and it should be central to our culture and the way we educate our young people. They should be taught how to evaluate sources, interpret information and recognise bias. Similarly, separating confidence from substance ought to be considered a basic life skill. Looking at counter-arguments when we are emotionally pulled to someone’s perspectiveshould be routine, and changing our mind when it is emotionally difficult should be celebrated.It would also be helpful for the average person to learn the fundamentals of confident communication. Not only can this help you express yourself when you have something of real value to offer, but it also teaches you to see through a person who would happily use such tactics to deceive or seduce.All told, charisma should actually be a red flag that encourages us to be more sceptical of an individual, not less. When someone can convincingly hold court on important topics like finance, healthcare or the Middle East, we should ask questions. What experience do they have? Do they have a history of dishonesty? What do they stand to gain from this view? What need in me might this person be speaking to? For my part, the next time I discuss something important, I will go easy on the pitch, pace and volume, and try to let the facts speak for themselves.Alex Curmi is a psychiatristand host ofThe Thinking Mindpodcast.Further readingThinking, Fast and Slowby Daniel Kahneman (Penguin, £16.99)The Age of Magical Overthinkingby Amanda Montell (Thorsons, £12.99)The Anxious Generationby Jonathan Haidt (Penguin, £12.99)Explore more on these topicsPsychologyThe big ideaSocial mediaDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Historian Lucy Worsley looks back: ‘The story of my life has been – the bookworm shall go to the ball’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The presenter recalls being a ‘weird little nerd’, almost becoming a scientist – and the most revealing costume she’s worn for work
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The presenter recalls being a ‘weird little nerd’, almost becoming a scientist – and the most revealing costume she’s worn for work
Content: FlashbackFamilyHistorian Lucy Worsley looks back: ‘The story of my life has been – the bookworm shall go to the ball’The presenter recalls being a ‘weird little nerd’, almost becoming a scientist – and the most revealing costume she’s worn for workHarriet GibsoneSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLucy Worsley dressed as a witch, holding a broomstick, in 1977 and 2026Lucy Worsley in 1977 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian. Styling: Andie Redman. Hair and makeup: Céline Nonon at Arlington Talent. Archive photograph: courtesy of Lucy WorsleyBorn in Reading in 1973, Lucy Worsley is a historian and TV presenter. She ­graduated with a first in history from Oxford, before completing a PhD in art history at the University of Sussex. Worsley spent 21 years as chief curator of Historic Royal Palaces, overseeing the Tower of London, Hampton Court and Kensington Palace, among others. She has p­resented numerous documentary series, including Six Wives, Royal History’s Biggest Fibs and most recently Victorian Murder Club. She lives in London with her husband. Her latest book,Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History, is out now.This is meat the age of four. It was my career ambition to become a witch. My back-up options were spy and nun.We were living in Canada at the time. Dad was an expert in cold places – glaciers and permanently frozen ground – and he was embarking on a year’s swap with an academic at the University of Ottawa. My mother made the costume for me to go trick or treating with the family across the road. In my basket are sweets and I look very pleased and very proud.Because of my father’s job, we moved around a lot. I wasn’t naturally good at making friends, because I’m quite shy. New schools could be intimidating, but I always had a safe space when reading books. Whenever I ask my parents what I was like as a child, they say, “We don’t know, because you were always reading a book and not talking to us.” Deep down, I was a secret showoff. I was flamboyant when adopting somebody else’s clothes or character or persona.double quotation markMy youth and inexperience became my superpowers because people could see I was going to do things differentlyOutside school I had Guides, played musical instruments and acted in plays. Nobody there knew I was an A-grade student, so I was able to pass for normal. But at my state school in Nottingham, I couldn’t hide. I was a weird little nerd, and my studiousness marked me out in a way that I didn’t have the social skills to conceal. Even though I was lonely, I soldiered on because of my political views. For example, the pupils were going to have a “wear what you like” day to protest about the teachers who were always going on strike. I disagreed, and thought the teachers should strike, so I went in my school uniform – a horrendously stupid choice as everybody laughed at me.I always loved history, but my father, being a scientist, wanted me to take a different path. To please him, I chose science subjects for my A-levels. Halfway through, my mum said, “You’re not enjoying this. You need to do what you want to do, which is history.”Great Pottery Throw Down judge Keith Brymer Jones looks back: ‘Men like seeing me be emotional’Read moreAt university, I studied ancient and modern history. It was a period in which I went mildly off the rails: staying up late talking to people who were just like me, organising the rag parade, playing in orchestras, rowing and doing all the extracurricular activities. I didn’t work hard until the very end of my three years, as I was too busy having a lovely time.As soon as I saw the advert for the role of chief curator at Historic Royal Palaces, I thought, “That’s my job!” It was a lengthy recruitment process, with interviews in different palaces, and at one point I got in a tizzy looking for the right entrance at the palace of St James. A sentry was standing in a box, so I said, “Please tell me where the right way is. I’m desperate.” He wasn’t allowed to talk to me, but in the end he took pity and rolled his eyes in the direction I should go.The role was high-profile and there was an expectation of what someone doing that job would be like. Historically, it had been done by men, always of a certain seniority – people very much in command of themselves. By comparison, I was 29 years old, small and pale. I had bought a long, dark coat, which I thought made me look grown up. But my youth and inexperience eventually became my superpowers, because everybody could see there was something different about the way I was going to do things. I came to realise that my authority is in building a relationship of trust with the person I’m talking to, not making them think that I know more.My TV career beganwhen BBC Look North came to make a film about Bolsover Castle in Derbyshire, where I was working. We ended up spending the day together, with me showing them how they could tell the story. That night I was struck by how much I enjoyed the experience. I began appearing as an expert “talking head” on various shows, and in 2008 I did a show about Henry VIII. More followed. The world was changing – I wasn’t Simon Schama or David Starkey – and we were ready for more women to talk about history.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe struggle to look “authoritative” that I’d experienced earlier came up again in my TV career. I would get notes such as, “She needs to wear tailoring. She needs a dark coat.” It felt wrong. I am known for wearing costumes – using whatever it takes to tell a story. Like a primary school teacher, I have no dignity. But that is also the skill that is available to me. The dressing up might be considered frivolous by critics, but clothes tell us about hierarchy and social structures. They are also fun to look at, which is important when making TV.double quotation markI slip through the streets in a  cap and glasses, but one in a thousand people have weirdly impressive facial recognition skillsEach day is different on set, but some are stranger than others. In one of my early shows, I was dressed as a medieval peasant foraging in the woods. My costume was a brown blanket. It was November and really cold, but I didn’t have the confidence to say, “This isn’t working for me.” In the end, I just burst into tears. Crying does work, but it’s better to speak up: I did a programme about the American Revolution once, and said to the producer, “I’d really like to be in the Independence Day procession that goes through Philadelphia on 4 July.” I imagined I’d be in a modest costume with buttons and a hat, maybe playing the cymbals. It turned out I was part of a twirling team and my costume was a skin-tight leotard. The rest of the team were 22-year-old girls. I got changed, but agreed with the cameraman that he would only shoot me from the neck up.Being recognised iswonderfuland terrible, as I’m a showoff but also shy. I’m capable of slipping through the streets of London in my baseball cap and glasses, but one in a thousand people have weirdly impressive facial recognition skills and clock me. Once a lady recognised me from my teeth alone. I also have a distinctive voice. Someone overheard me speaking in a swimming pool and said, “I know that voice!” I thought, “I’m naked, I’m dripping. I don’t want to engage with you just now, but thank you.”The story of my life has been “the bookworm shall go to the ball”. I’ve had a wonderful career. But since turning 50, I’ve realised I work too hard. I’m endlessly asking myself, “Do you really love your work? Or is it just the capitalist patriarchy that’s making you think you love your work because that’s good for the economy?”I don’t have the answers. But that’s the job of the historian. To ask the questions – and, for me, to put on the costumes. So has the girl in the photo grown up at all? Perhaps not.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackPhotographyTelevisionHistoryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘My family are all Trumpian, so I’ve had a lot of practice talking to people who are far right’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: She thinks the answer to the climate crisis is cutting CO2, he favours population control and North Sea oil and gas extraction. Can they make it through a meal together?
Author: Erica Buist
Headline: She thinks the answer to the climate crisis is cutting CO2, he favours population control and North Sea oil and gas extraction. Can they make it through a meal together?
Content: Sam and Roger. All photographs: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSam and Roger. All photographs: David Levene/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘My family are all Trumpian, so I’ve had a lot of practice talking to people who are far right’She thinks the answer to the climate crisis is cutting CO2, he favours population control and North Sea oil and gas extraction. Can they make it through a meal together?Erica BuistSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam, 29, central LondonView image in fullscreenOccupationCompliance officerVoting recordSam is American so can’t vote in the UK yet, but when she can she intends to vote GreenAmuse boucheShe is an expert knitter. She started when she was five and makes socks, mittens, hat, jumpers – if you know Sam, she’s knitting you somethingRoger, 80, north-west LondonView image in fullscreenOccupationRetired accountantVoting recordNever Labour or Tory. He’s always voted for “outliers” such as the Greens, and now ReformAmuse boucheIn 1978, he was an internal auditor and was sent to Angola during the civil wargoing on. He bribed soldiers with cigarettes to let him get to the frontline because he “wanted to hear the guns”For startersRogerI got there early and had a pint of beer, and when Sam arrived we got on famously right from the start. We were both surprised at how much we had in common.SamI wasn’t very nervous – my family are all Trumpian, so I’ve had a lot of practice talking to people who are far right.RogerI started with a beautiful dressed crab with two slices of soda bread and a chunk of butter. For main I had fish and chips, and we were too full for dessert.SamI really enjoyed the dressed crab, then I had a wild mushroom risotto with broccoli stems, and a Coke.View image in fullscreenThe big beefRoger​​ I don’t like net zero – I think it’s all happening too quickly. We’re doing all of this electrification too early. I think we should use the resources we’ve got: continue to extract more oil and gas from the North Sea until it’s all gone, and then you can have your electric cars.Dining across the divide: ‘He says net zero is a waste of money as we’ll hit 3C anyway. I think that’s nihilistic’Read moreSamI think the climate crisis is a big problem, and the number one priority to reduce the effects would be to stop producing CO2. It’s been proved that a decrease in beef production and an increase in plant consumption would really help.RogerThe way to fix the climate crisis is to control the population. I think the UK is dangerously overdependent on imports of people, as well as food, energy and other things. We should encourage local production, expand our fishing fleet and exploit North Sea fossil fuels until they’re exhausted.SamI pointed out that his desire to drill for more oil contradicts his opinion on self-sufficiency in food production because the more CO2that is emitted into the atmosphere, the higher the temperature gets and the less water there is available for agriculture.View image in fullscreenSharing plateRogerI am a xenophobe and proud of it. Nothing to apologise for, as it’s a natural human trait of risk awareness. I believe many of the terrorist outrages in the UK in the past 25 years have been perpetrated by foreigners, and a few by the offspring of foreigners.SamHe talked a lot about banning Muslims. I grew up in a very white, Christian, Republican area of Colorado and I heard a lot of fear-based rhetoric. I had absolutely never met a Muslim person until I moved to Glasgow, and realised none of it was true. It seems like Roger’s operating from a place of fear.View image in fullscreenFor aftersRogerI think Nigel Farage accepting a £5m donation was OK, but failing to declare it is troubling. There was nothing to lose by declaring it.SamIn the US there used to be a limit on how much a person could donate to a political campaign, and now there is absolutely no limit. I just feel that’s wrong. I don’t think one person should be able to have that much sway and that much buying power over an election. And that principle is the basis of my aversion to that, apart from the fact that it broke the rules.View image in fullscreenTakeawaysRogerI think she’s a thoroughly charming, intelligent person. And she’s an immigrant, but I think it’s human to look for sameness before differences first, so the discussion was very amicable. I liked the fact that we could agree on so much, especially green stuff – apart from North Sea oil.SamThe majority of Reform voters I’ve met are not particularly sophisticated or educated people, and I guess it’s bad of me to stereotype them like that, because he was an accountant and refined and well-spoken. We arranged to keep in contact.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeRoger and Sam ate at theBull & Last, London NW5.Want to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect venison casserole – recipe | Stew | The Guardian
description: Venison casserole is as autumnal as fallen leaves, a glass of red and a fire in the grate. But who makes the best version?
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Venison casserole is as autumnal as fallen leaves, a glass of red and a fire in the grate. But who makes the best version?
Content: Felicity Cloake's venison casserole 05aPhotograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake's venison casserole 05aPhotograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.How to cook the perfect ...StewHow to make the perfect venison casserole – recipeVenison casserole is as autumnal as fallen leaves, a glass of red and a fire in the grate. But who makes the best version?Felicity CloakeSun 1 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 08.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBecause I don’t eat it very often, I always forget how much I like venison. Or, rather, how much I like it in certain contexts: the natural leanness of a wild animal doesn’t naturally lend itself to soloing in juicy burgers or sausages, but, when slow-cooked, it’s fabulous – rich in flavour, and soft enough to eat with a spoon, should you so desire. It also tends to be good value both in season and frozen for the rest of the year, and, as red meat goes, a pretty climate-friendly option (though not straightforwardly so,as this piece explains) that pairs beautifully with seasonal spuds and kales, and is even better when made ahead of time and reheated. In fact, it’s the perfect autumn and winter entertaining option, even if the only people you’re entertaining are yourselves, the dog and the cast of Celebrity Traitors.The meatFew recipes specify the cut, perhaps because venison is so often sold in chunks, so the assumption is that it’s going to be used for just this purpose, and rarely do the vendors elucidate further than saying the meat is for “stewing” or simply “diced”.Caroline Conran, whose recipe in her 1978 British Cookingis attributed to nameless “ghillies” (Scottish hunting guides), suggests using leg or haunch, whileGary Rhodes is firm in his beliefthat “venison for stewing should come from the haunch, or you can use neck”. Meanwhile,David Eyrecalls for a whole shoulder inThe Eagle Cookbook, which, like the haunch, feels like a great extravagance, even though, in truth, it is my favourite – the shoulder is better marbled than either the haunch or the diced venison I buy, which, once slow-cooked, makes for a richer, stickier result. That said, you can counteract the meat’s leanness by adding other fats, of which more later, so the only cut you should steer clear of, simply because it’s too tender for such treatment, is the saddle.View image in fullscreenJohn William, AKA “the deer man” of Raasay, soaks the meat overnight in “gutsy red wine”. All thumbnail images by Felicity Cloake.John William, “the deer man” of Raasay, whose recipe is includedin Sue Lawrence’s A Taste of the Scottish Islands, soaks the meat overnight in “gutsy red wine”. I cannot speak for Raasay venison, and I imagine William knows what he’s talking about, but my testers and I don’t detect much difference with the wild Devon meat I use. Indeed, chemist Hervé Thisconcludedthat one would have to marinade meat for several days for the alcohol to have a noticeably tenderising effect, while the flavour penetration of any marinade is mere millimetres. By all means, marinate if you like, then, but I think you’re better off trusting in the mingling of flavours that takes place in the pot.Rhodes tells readers of his book More Rhodes Around Britain that, “I like to cut the meat into large pieces rather than dice. It takes a little longer to cook, but the texture and taste are better.” Sceptical though I am that it will cook through, after trialling it I find myself inclined to agree; two-bite chunks remain juicier in the middle.The vegetablesEveryone starts their stew with onions (though you could use shallots instead, not least because their sweetness would be welcome here), but after that is where the recipes start to diverge. Rhodes and Eyre go for a classic triumvirate with carrot and celery, and the latter, like William, also includes leek. Clarissa Dickson Wright champions beetroot,writing in the Game Cookbookshe co-authored with Johnny Scott that “the brilliant food writer Claire Macdonald discovered there is an enzyme in [it] that breaks down the fibres in venison. When I was staying at Kinloch Lodge, the blissful hotel on Skye, she told me it would tenderise even the toughest old stag.” Again, wild animals are particularly hard to generalise about, especially one that might be anything from a 9kg muntjac to an 190kg red deer, but, on this evidence, I wouldn’t be rushing to add chunks of beetroot for anything other than flavour – its sweet earthiness is delicious with the meat.View image in fullscreenClarissa Dickson-Wright’s venison casserole features lots of beetroot, because it helps break down enzymes and ‘would tenderise even the toughest old stag’.Indeed, I’m going to focus on sweetness: even more than beetroot, we love the fruitiness of boththe prunes in the Claire Macdonald Game Cookbook, and Clarissa Dickson Wright’s redcurrant jelly (in truth, most fruity jellies would work, should you have something similar hanging out in the cupboard). And if you’re a fan of sweet-and-sour combinations, may I encourage you to consider popping in some of Macdonald’s pickled walnuts as well – as one of my testers put it, along with the prunes, they “completely blended into the gravy and gave it a lovely richness and depth of flavour – neither too sweet nor too salty”.I like to include as many vegetables in a casserole as possible, hence the onions, carrots and leek here, all of which will echo the sweetness of the prunes and preserve. If rich, sweet and savoury doesn’t appeal, bear William’s recipe in mind; with its chopped red pepper and tomatoes, it has a lighter, more southern feel, though if you do go down that road, maybe add some of Eyre’s garlic, too (I’d be tempted to include a glug of red wine to beef it out a bit as well, but then I don’t know the meaning of the world light).The seasoningThough bacon might seem to belong in the “meat” paragraph above, it’s purely here for its delicious, savoury fat, fat that the free-roaming deer hasn’t had the chance to build up on its wild perambulations. If you don’t care for pork, an extra slug of oil, plus a dash of William’s Worcestershire sauce, should prove a satisfactory replacement.Rhodes adds bay, Dickson Wright and Eyre thyme, Eyre parsley stalks and Conran juniper berries, a classic seasoning for venison and one that I love. But seeing as we already have the jelly, I’ve stuck with thyme here, because I think its austere, savoury aromatic quality works with fruit and meat.The liquidDickson Wright, who probably couldn’t move for deer carcasses and pheasant skeletons while writing her Game Cookbook, instructs me to make a game stock, which drives the dog wild for the hour it takes in the pressure cooker (expert guidance viaCatherine Phipps’ excellent Modern Pressure Cooking). Should you also have bones going to waste, it’s worth your while doing the same, though both the beef stock in Conran’s recipe and the vegetable version in Macdonald’s won’t do any harm, and we don’t find we miss anything in Eyre’s version, which tops up red wine with water.View image in fullscreenClaire Macdonald’s twice-cooked version features prunes and pickled walnuts.Wine, in fact, features in almost every recipe, and with good reason: its fruit, acidity and tannins combine with the browned meat and bacon to produce a richly savoury sauce. If you’d prefer to leave it out, use the same amount of beef stock and add either a glass of port, as Conran does, or an extra spoonful of redcurrant jelly and a squeeze of lemon. You’ll notice I’ve been generous with the quantity, because a couple of the recipes I try don’t have enough gravy for my testers’ liking – and what’s the point of a casserole without gravy, as one tartly (and ungratefully) observes.The cookingEveryone except Conran bakes their casseroles – you can, of course, use the hob for the recipe below, but I find it much easier to keep things at a constant low simmer in the oven. To my surprise, the venison doesn’t need as long as I’d imagined either: two hours at 160C proves quite sufficient for both Eyre and Dickson Wright’s offerings, and though you can stick it in a very low oven overnight, as William recommends (no doubt particularly useful if you have an AGA or similar), there’s really no need. In the interests of making the most of the fuel, I’d strongly urge you to consider baking some potatoes at the same time.View image in fullscreenDavid Eyre’s venison and pancetta casserole calls for a whole shoulder of venison, ‘which feels like a great extravagance’.A final piece of advice: should you have the luxury of time, Macdonald’s tip that “twice cooking is almost obligatory for casseroles; the flavours are vastly better than if the casserole is made and eaten straight away”, is a good one. Take it out of the oven after 90 minutes, then, when you’re ready to eat it the next day or the day afterwards, put it back in there at the same temperature for half an hour. It also freezes well.Prep20 minCook2½ hrServes4100g streaky bacon800g venison, preferably boned shoulder, if available2 tbsp neutral oil, or lard or dripping2 tbsp plain flourSalt and black pepper1 large onion, peeled and chopped1 leek, trimmed, washed and chunkily sliced1 carrot, coarsely diced2 sprigsfresh thyme, or ½ tsp dried thymefr300ml red wine8 stoned soft prunes, halved1 tbsp redcurrant jelly, or other fruit jellyHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Chop the bacon into wide pieces. Drain any liquid from the venison and, if it isn’t already diced, cut it into large, two-bite chunks.View image in fullscreenHeat the oil in an ovenproof casserole dish for which you have a lid on a medium-high flame.Fry the bacon in the hot fat until it releases its fat and begins to turn golden.View image in fullscreenMeanwhile, toss the venison with the flour and a good pinch of salt and pepper.View image in fullscreenScoop out the bacon with a slotted spoon and put in a large bowl, then add a few pieces of the venison and brown on all sides – don’t overcrowd the pan or you won’t achieve that deep, brown colour that brings with it such flavour. Scoop each batch out as soon as it’s done and add to the bacon bowl.View image in fullscreenWhen all the venison is browned, turn down the heat to medium-low and add the onion, leek, carrot and a pinch of salt. Fry, stirring regularly, until the veg have softened and are starting to colour; stir in the thyme towards the end.View image in fullscreenScoop the vegetables into the meat bowl, then add a splash of wine to the pan, and stir to dislodge and dissolve any bits from the base.View image in fullscreenStir in the prunes and fruit jelly, then return the meat and vegetables to the pan, and add the rest of the wine and just enough water mostly to cover the meat – a few bits will stick out of the top like icebergs, but, without knowing the diameter of your pan, it’s impossible to give a precise amount of water.View image in fullscreenBring to a simmer, then cover and put in the oven for 90 minutes if making ahead of time, or two hours if serving immediately. If reheating later, return the stew to the oven and cook at the same temperature for 30 minutes. Check the seasoning, stir in a little extra water if it’s too dry for your liking, then serve with mashed potato and greens.Venison – love it, hate it, or somewhere in between? Is it theethical red meat, or is thispure greenwashing and speciesism, as Peta claims? Why don’t we eat more of it in this country (Bambi?) and, if you love it, what’s your favourite way to prepare it?Explore more on these topicsStewHow to cook the perfect ...GameFoodMeatWinter food and drinkAutumn food and drinkClarissa Dickson WrightrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Moods, Leeds LS2: ‘Puzzling, if not quite a car crash’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: The crumpet has the texture of a damp Always Ultra
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The crumpet has the texture of a damp Always Ultra
Content: Moods, Leeds: ‘An all-day restaurant and bar with a tattoo parlour and hair salon attached.’Photograph: Shaw & Shaw/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMoods, Leeds: ‘An all-day restaurant and bar with a tattoo parlour and hair salon attached.’Photograph: Shaw & Shaw/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewMoods, Leeds LS2: ‘Puzzling, if not quite a car crash’ – restaurant reviewThe crumpet has the texture of a damp Always UltraGrace DentSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 07.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve done some fairly rash things in my time, but I’ve never popped into anywhere for king scallops with ’nduja and come out with a swallow tattoo on my neck, though what is this life without adventure? Which is whereMoodscomes in: the space is an all-day restaurant, bar, tattoo parlour and hair salon in Leeds, offering violetta potato with ox cheek, a short back and sides, and the chance to tattoo “Mum” on your lower left arm, all in one Grade II-listed building.It occupies the former First White Cloth Hall on Kirkgate, built in 1711 for the trade of white undyed cloth. This cavernous ark, with roof timbers dating back to the 1470s, lurked on Historic England’sHeritage at Risk registerfor more than 20 years, during which time it was under almost constant threat from the bulldozers. It tookthe National Lottery Heritage Fund,Leeds Civic TrustandRushbond, a Leeds-based developer with a penchant for rescuing buildings, to drag it out of danger. Then Will and Hayley Moody arrived, slotting in theirBuzz Club Tattoo Studioand ahair and beauty salon called Self, and now, on the ground floor, there’s Moods, a kitchen reportedly run by Craig Rogan. Laugh at the tattoo/hair/dinner triumvirate, if you want (I know I did), but it’s a grim joke that we treat our old buildings like this, and that hospitality is in a state so wild thatthisseems to be the solution. Bring on the bright new future of ye olde small plates, buzzcuts and half-sleeve emporiums, all under 400-year-old timbers.View image in fullscreen‘If there are traces of the advertised yuzu and dill in here, they are destroyed by the sheer volume of cream’: Moods’ oak-smoked salmon with rye bread.Moods is incredibly cool, which I know immediately because of the gorgeous amounts of disdain with which I’m treated by the receptionist when I pop by at 2.30pm to try the all-day menu. She looks at me bamboozled, as many Gen Z-ers do, as if I have announced myself as an intergalactic equerry from Zarg requesting the keys to a plutonium source. Eventually, I’m tucked away by a wooden dresser that’s used as a base for cleaning supplies and cutlery. Only 42 other better tables are lying empty.The all-day menu looks rather fabulous, though. There is a wild mushroomcrumpetwith Old Winchester and black truffle honey at £14. There is mead-glazed pancetta with potato rösti and mushroom ketchup, as well as fried chicken brioche with elderflower and pickled cucumber. And all of it cooked by Rogan,Simon Rogan’s son, trained by his father atL’Enclumeand atFera at Claridge’s. He’s channelling this greatness via osmosis; I can smell it in the air. Well, that and Jangro spray sanitiser.View image in fullscreenMoods’ post-noon brunch menu looks ‘rather fabulous’ and includes the likes of salt-baked beetroot salad.Doubtless Moods is a fabulous place to drink cocktails at the long open bar in the centre of the room, where the signature peach melba comes with caramelised peach vodka and ice-cream foam. But the food proper turns out to be more of an uphill struggle. I order that crumpet, envisioning ceps, girolles, perhaps a random morel, on a home-baked sourdough crumpet with good butter. What arrives resembles nothing so much a Warburtons Giant Crumpet topped with chopped chestnut mushrooms fried in butter and a few herbs, and a big handful of cress. The buttery mushroom liquor has soaked into the crumpet while it waited, and it now has the texture of a damp Always Ultra. And where is the Old Winchester?Next up, oak-smoked salmon with rye bread for £16: two tiny triangles of fish are draped over a shedload of creme fraiche– at least seven tablespoons of the stuff –a bit of roughly chopped kohlrabi, long pieces of chopped apple and yet more cress. If there are traces of the advertised yuzu and dill in here, they are destroyed by the sheer volume of cream. It is puzzling, if not quite a car crash. Then again, I was in an actual car crash once, and I definitely enjoyed theSugar Puffsthey gave me with my 10am discharge papers a lot more.View image in fullscreen‘Channelling Simon Rogan’s greatness via osmosis’: Moods’ lemon raspberry muffin.Writing all this off as a bad start, I return the next morning for breakfast, hoping to make more sense of the place. From the outset, things do not look good. Breakfast, a staff member mutters, doesn’t start until 10am, even though the doors open at eight, the music is on, the coffee machine is on and the cakes are being unloaded. There are also at least 11 staff bumbling about. How about just a coffee then, I ask. A white americano, please? God, I’m needy. By this point, I’m reducing myself to a small speck of a woman the size of a postage stamp, and I’m upsetting nobody. A black americano arrives, and then someone takes pity and allows me to order porridge, which turns up half cooked with a ramekin of what they call bramble preserve (AKA blackberry jam). I ask brightly if I might meet the famous chef, mainly out of mischief, but he’s not here. I might go back when the place is in a better mood.Moods98 Kirkgate, Leeds LS2, 0113-390 4552. Open all week, brunch 8am-4pm, bar small plates noon-9pm. Brunch from about £15 a head; bar small plates from about £8 each, all plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This is how we do it: ‘We don’t have penetration – but it’s by far the best sex I’ve ever had’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Penetrative sex is painful for Nina, but intimacy with Noah is fun, hot and loving
Author: Elena Angelides
Headline: Penetrative sex is painful for Nina, but intimacy with Noah is fun, hot and loving
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘We don’t have penetration – but it’s by far the best sex I’ve ever had’Penetrative sex is painful for Nina, but intimacy with Noah is fun, hot and lovingHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toElena AngelidesSun 1 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNoah, 26double quotation markThe mechanics of how we have sex don’t matter to me. I still feel the same degree of pleasureSex with Nina is by far the best I’ve ever had. Our intimate life is incredibly communicative, but it wasn’t always that way. We were friends who lived in a house-share together, and decided to start a relationship. We hit an early roadblock – penetrative sex was very painful for her.After that first time, we both shut down. We were each coming to it with our own worries. In the past, I felt anxiety about whether I was doing sex right, so I was left worrying that I had done it all wrong. Nina felt concerned that penetrative sex would feel better for me, and that without it our sex wouldn’t be good enough. We still tried penetrative sex for a bit, but it clearly wasn’t working. It started to feel ridiculous that we were even trying.We had some productive conversations, and scribbled all our concerns down on a mind map. We looked it up, and Nina’s symptoms marry up withvaginismus, so we educated ourselves about that. We built our sex life organically from the ground up. We would kiss and grind on each other, and we knew that felt good.double quotation markWith previous sexual partners, I didn’t feel confident I was doing it right, because we stuck to the formula we had seen in filmsOver time, she has seen how much I enjoy sex with her, which has eased her worries that I might crave anything else. The mechanics of how we have sex don’t matter to me. I still feel the same degree of pleasure the way we do it, and I am so happy to have Nina as my partner in life and in the bedroom.Nowadays, I would say our sex life is quite mobile – we might both be on our backs or facing each other, and I might touch her from the front or wrap my arm around and touch her from behind. We can change it up more than other couples, because the positions of penetrative sex are more restrictive.With previous sexual partners, I didn’t feel confident I was doing it right, because we stuck to the same formula we had seen in films. We didn’t play around and feed back about what felt good for us. But because Nina and I have built our sex life together, it’s created a place of comfortableness and love.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreNina, 23double quotation markWe tried penetrative sex but it really hurt me and I didn’t experience any pleasureI’d only had one sexual encounter before Noah. I dated this guy for a few months. It was exclusively finger penetration, which I found incredibly painful. It was my first inkling that penetrative sex would be difficult. He didn’t communicate about what he was doing when he put his fingers inside me, and I didn’t feel comfortable with him at all.When Noah and I slept together the first time we tried penetrative sex, but it was a complete disaster. It really hurt me and I didn’t experience any pleasure whatsoever – I may as well have been sticking something up my nose! I felt insecure – Noah had more sexual experience than me and I thought he might want someone who could have penetration and call things off – but he’s just a lovely, kind human.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markI remember he joked: ‘It doesn’t really matter where the willy goes!’As time went on, I started to realise he wasn’t going to end things and stopped worrying about it so much. I remember he joked: “It doesn’t really matter where the willy goes!” We have been together for three years now and he makes me feel entirely secure.This is how we do it: ‘At our age we get to wake up and say: What are we doing today? Let’s make love’Read moreI know I should probably go to the doctor and find out why penetrative sex is so painful, but I just don’t feel the urge because there isn’t anything missing from our love life.The bread and butter of our sex life is touching each other at the same time. I think nonpenetrative sex is more fluid and dynamic, and you are not limited by the positions of penis-in-vagina sex.I find it frustrating when people define sex as penetrative. There are so many ways to have sex. In TV and film, you always see couples having penetration – I would like to see more straight nonpenetrative couples represented. I would define our sex life as full – fun, hot and loving.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My wife and I are in our late 70s and have no children. Who can help us in our old age? | Family | The Guardian
description: Getting older and losing your autonomy is even harder without family around. You need to consider both the practical and emotional issues involved
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Getting older and losing your autonomy is even harder without family around. You need to consider both the practical and emotional issues involved
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyMy wife and I are in our late 70s and have no children. Who can help us in our old age?Getting older and losing your autonomy is even harder without family around.
