You need to consider both the practical and emotional issues involvedAnnalisa BarbieriSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.25 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy wife and I are in our late 70s, and have been married formore than 40 years. We didn’t have kidsand wererather traumatised after failed IVF.My wife is Asian and has no UK-based family. I do, but they are not closegeographically,nor are theypeople who would be able to give any support if needed. Friends are of a similar ageand so have their own issues to deal with. My wife and I have always been a self-reliant unit,and we’re both reasonably healthy, but I’m increasingly awarethat there will soon come a timewhen help is needed.We should make arrangements for thingssuch as alastingpower ofattorney (LPA), but there is nobodywe would trust enough and who would be willingto take on that role.As social care forolder people slips further into crisis, how can we plan for the inevitable?This must be a problem faced by a significant number of people, but it doesn’t seem to be aired.I think you’re right: this is a growing problem, and I’d be interested to hear what others have done, since, sadly, I cannot magic up someone for you.I took your issue to two people: psychoanalytic psychotherapist and CEO of Tavistock Relationships Andrew Balfour, author of Life and Death: Our Relationship With Ageing, Dementia and Other Fates of Time; and estate planning specialist solicitor Gary Rycroft to look at the legal side.double quotation markSometimes the challenges of later life rekindle earlier losses, amplifying our overall sense of lossBalfour said: “Your letter is a very poignant expression of how we might all feel about getting older and losing autonomy and the independence of youth. It sounds as if you and your wife have lived like a self-contained unit for a long time, so it must be anxiety-provoking thinking about losing that.” He also pointed out that “sometimes the losses and challenges of later life rekindle earlier losses and anxieties, amplifying our overall sense of loss”. This is worth reflecting on because you mentioned the hope you had for children, and you may now be imagining how things might have been.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy partner’s obnoxious conduct at our sons’ football matches is putting me off him | Annalisa BarbieriRead moreWe tend not to live as we used to, in close family units with relatives nearby, though relatives can also let you down. Balfour wondered if there were other people you could link to, not necessarily to find someone to become your attorney, but “maybe others at a similar point would help you feel less alone with your anxieties”.Practically, you need to separate what your needs are now (if any) from what you think they might become. Giving someone power over your health and/or finances (there are two types of LPA) is a serious business and a subject that has been in thenews of late. Rycroft explained that you can have any number of attorneys. Having more than one is a good idea, so no one person is in charge, and most people go for up to four. You might imagine both of you needing help at the same time, but that is often not the case, so Rycroft thought it might be an idea for you and your wife to initially appoint each other as your attorneys. This gives you “enhanced status” beyond simply being a spouse.You could also appoint a professional such as a solicitor. They would charge, but in time, if you met someone you trusted but didn’t want to make sole attorney, they could do it together. This is a complicated area, though, which would need specialist legal input.Age UK is a great resource for many worries about ageing, and offers a free downloadableLifeBook, in which you can record the details of your affairs. The Alzheimer’s Society provides a simplerThis Is Meform for more personal information. And Macmillan has advice on making aliving will.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is availablehere.Comments on this piece are pre-moderated to ensure the discussion remains on the topics raised by the article. Please be aware that there may be a short delay in comments appearing on the site.Explore more on these topicsFamilyAsk Annalisa BarbieriOlder peopleSocial carePower of attorneyFamily financesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A gift to scammers: why you should probably keep your birthday a secret | Money | The Guardian
description: Using a fake DOB or leaving the field blank when making an online account can offer protection from identity theft
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Using a fake DOB or leaving the field blank when making an online account can offer protection from identity theft
Content: Giving your date of birth can reveal an important piece in the jigsaw for scammers hoping to steal your identity.Photograph: kmt_rf/AlamyView image in fullscreenGiving your date of birth can reveal an important piece in the jigsaw for scammers hoping to steal your identity.Photograph: kmt_rf/AlamyScam watchMoneyA gift to scammers: why you should probably keep your birthday a secretUsing a fake DOB or leaving the field blank when making an online account can offer protection from identity theftShane HickeySun 1 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 02.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou get a call from your bank saying there has been suspicious activity on your account. They read out your name, address and date of birth so you are happy it is a legitimate caller.But you are talking to criminals who have used your date of birth as part of a web of verifying information to convince you they are someone else.People’s DOBs are often held in online accounts after being entered as part of a sign-up process for a retailer, loyalty scheme, newsletter or online competition. In arecent hack of the online retailer Asoscustomers’ dates of birth were among the details taken by scammers.Now cybersecurity professionals have warned people to resist entering a date of birth, or to put in a fake one, to limit the amount of personal data that is online, frustrating criminals’ attempts to “jigsaw” together personal profiles.‘They call every week’: the phishing attacks targeting past victimsRead moreJake Moore, an adviser for the cybersecurity company ESET, says information gathered during hacks can be sold on and used by scammers, either to trick people into trusting them, or to impersonate them.“A date of birth alone is not particularly valuable to criminals, but combined with other information, such as names and phone numbers, it can help criminals … commit identity fraud,” he says.Alexandre François, who investigates scams for the intelligence company WhoisXML API, found that eight out of 14 retailers he surveyed recently asked for a date of birth on sign-up. “Retailers may also have little incentive to remove this field, as the full date gives them the customer’s age, which is useful for marketing and targeting,” he says.What it looks likeView image in fullscreenA woman delivering a package from Asos.Photograph: True Images/AlamyYou may hear about a hack either in the news, or in an email from an organisation telling you that your data has been compromised. How the scam manifests itself will depend on what happens to the information that has been stolen.If a retailer is hacked, and the details end up on the dark web, they can be used to make phishing emails look more authentic, says Serpil Hall, a security expert from Datos Insights. Hackers can also use them to try to convince company help desks that they are talking to the victim. But it may not all happen straight after a security breach.“The process typically runs like this: a retail breach provides a name, date of birth, email and address,” she says. “Other leaked data adds credentials, phone numbers and identifiers. Public information such as social profiles, employment details and relatives adds more context. The result is an enriched identity profile with more identifiers and greater confidence when matching records.”What to doBe wary of anyone who contacts you out of the blue, even if they seem to have a lot of information.“Using a different birthday on low-risk websites can reduce exposure, but it is even better to not enter any personal fields that aren’t mandatory,” says Moore. “It is even worth using a separate email address for shopping online, too, so you can bin the email if it gets caught up in a breach and you can start again.”François says shops only need your payment card details and a delivery address. (You will, however, need to verify your age in some cases if you are buying age-restricted items, such as knives.)François says: “Strictly speaking, you only need to give your real date of birth, and your real name, where they are checked against official records and used to prove who you are: your bank or any lender, the tax office, the driving licence and passport agencies, right-to-work checks, a police notice. In those systems the date of birth works as a key. A shop is not one of them.”Leaving a birthday field blank is best, he says. “If this is not an option, use the same date across all retailers, possibly the first day of your birth month, so that you do not forget it.”Explore more on these topicsMoneyScam watchIdentity fraudScamsConsumer affairsCybercrimeHackingOnline shoppingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to improve your memory: 10 easy, enjoyable expert tips – from reading a book to getting more sleep | Ageing | The Guardian
description: Relying on technology can make us forgetful, but there are some simple ways to sharpen your recall. Memory experts describe the tricks and habits that can help
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: Relying on technology can make us forgetful, but there are some simple ways to sharpen your recall. Memory experts describe the tricks and habits that can help
Content: Use it or lose it … experts say engage the mind to increase its longevity.Illustration: Guardian Design/Guardian Design; Photographer/AgencyView image in fullscreenUse it or lose it … experts say engage the mind to increase its longevity.Illustration: Guardian Design/Guardian Design; Photographer/AgencyThe expertsAgeingHow to improve your memory: 10 easy, enjoyable expert tips – from reading a book to getting more sleepRelying on technology can make us forgetful, but there are some simple ways to sharpen your recall. Memory experts describe the tricks and habits that can helpSarah PhillipsSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMemory can worsen as we age, but it is often possible to do something about it. Here, memory experts share their advice on how to improve your power of recall.Retrain your brain“Memory is a buildable skill. You can train it, just like learning how to ride a bike or drive,” says Sania Alam, the founder ofFuturistic Learning, which provides memory-training education. Alam, based in the US, has coached memory athletes who have broken six Guinness World Records. But the times we are living in are not conducive to maintaining a strong memory. “We are in an age where we are bombarded with information,” says Alam. “At the same time, AI has come in, and social media is growing. All of these things are ageing our brains. You see people at a very young age who are beginning to have memory issues.” How can we tackle this? “My suggestion would be to get your hands on any course that teaches you memory techniques, so that you can start using your own brain instead of relying on gadgets, because these days we can’t even memorise our own number, let alone an emergency contact.”View image in fullscreen‘Keeping our brains active through learning keeps them functioning better for longer’ … boost your brain with a challenge.Photograph: Posed by model; Kathrin Ziegler/Getty ImagesLearn something new“The best way to improve your memory is to keep your brain active by learning new things and engaging in cognitively stimulating activities,” says Barbara Sahakian, a professor of psychiatry at the University of Cambridge and co-author ofBrain Boost: Healthy Habits for a Happier Life. “Find something that you would enjoy, but haven’t tried yet,” she says, suggesting chess, a new language or instrument. In 1995, Sahakianpublished an article in the British Medical Journal with Martin Orrell, emphasising the need to learn new things to reduce the risk of dementia and Alzheimer’s – in other words “use it or lose it”. “Keeping our brains active through learning and remembering, we drive the neural circuits and keep them functioning better for longer,” she says. “Studies with medical studentsstudying for examsand black-cab taxi driverslearning routesin London have shown that the hippocampus actually increases in volume. So, remember to use your brain through education and other challenging activities, so that you can keep it fit and functioning better for longer.”double quotation markThe best way to improve your memory is to keep your brain active by learning new thingsRead moreReassuringly, you don’t have to sign up to a complicated course to improve your memory but can simply open a book instead. “Reading something that interests you, whether it is fiction or nonfiction, has a positive effect on the brain, cognition and mood,” says Sahakian. “Several studies have shown that reading canreduce the riskof cognitive decline and dementia with ageing.”View image in fullscreen‘Studies have shown that reading can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.’Photograph: Hero Images Inc./AlamyAvoid distractionsAnother way that tech can disrupt memory is through its impact on our ability to focus. “We are rapidly switching our attention from one thing to the next,” says Sahakian. “This makes it difficult for people to then focus their attention and concentrate when they need to accomplish a goal. Experiments have shown that students who have mobile phones in classdo not perform as well in tests; even having a mobile phone that was off next to you acts as a distractor of your attention.”Take your brain on a journey“We have to use these specific techniques. It’s not magic,” saysKatie Kermode, a memory champion from Manchester, who started competing in 2008 and set the world record for remembering names, and numerous other titles since. When trying to memorise something, Kermode advises using the journey technique, which she learned when she was nine to memorise the order of the planets in the solar system. “A thermometer breaks, and the silver Mercury goes everywhere. The goddess Venus clears it all up and puts it into a bag and throws it. It lands on the Earth … It goes on like that, making each planet into an object or a person, and making them into a story, so they link from one to the next,” says Kermode. “In competitions we memorise thousands of digits, which I couldn’t just naturally do by sitting and repeating them to myself. You have to work a little bit, but it really helps you to memorise anything that you want to.”View image in fullscreen‘Find something that you would enjoy, but haven’t tried yet’ … learning helps the mind function longer.Photograph: Posed by models; Ronnie Kaufman/Getty ImagesSimilarly, you can create a “memory palace”, which has its roots in the work of the Ancient Greek poet Simonides of Ceos and was more recently popularised by the memory expert Tony Buzan, who died in 2019. “I tend to use ‘memory palace’ when there is a prescribed sequence and ‘journey’,” says Kermode. In everyday life, thinking of a route that you know well and placing things to remember along that route, is really helpful with recalling a shopping list, for example. “You put the first item in your driveway, then the second item could go in your hallway, and you mentally walk through it and try to remember it,” says Kermode. It can be used for remembering a speech or presentation, too. “Each topic of your speech can be in a different location, and if you’ve got sub-points to make within that topic, you can visualise that within the location.”Never miss a birthdayKermode is pretty good at recalling dates. “I’ve got techniques for remembering them, where each month has a particular meaning and/or a colour, and then each day of the month has an object,” she says. “But remembering to actually do something on that birthday – that’s a different thing that I struggle with. I would say that is a different part of the brain.”Kermode uses symbolism to turn abstract concepts into something concrete she can visualise. “If you’ve got something quite abstract to remember,” she says, “like you’re trying to remember a birthday in October, you might turn October into a pumpkin because October is an abstract word but you can use symbolism to make it more real. If you’re trying to remember a number, two looks like a swan, so 2 October could be a swan sitting on a pumpkin.” A lot of people aren’t good at visualising, says Kermode. If this is the case for you, “make it more of a story and involve more people. We even have memory competitors that can’t visualise, and they find ways around it.”Exam cramDr Michael Gruneberg, a former senior lecturer in psychology at Swansea University and founder ofLinkword Languages, recommends mnemonics, and specifically acronyms, for revision. “When I was preparing for exams, I would do the reading, so I knew my stuff, then I would pick out about eight points on a topic that I thought might come up and list them, then take the first letter of each to make up a word or a sentence.” A common example is “Richard of York gave battle in vain” for remembering the order of colours in the light spectrum (and the rainbow).View image in fullscreen‘Spaced repetition’ … for an exam, practise memorising facts at increasing intervals.Photograph: skynesher/Getty ImagesKermode swears by slides. “For each different subject, like history or geography, have a different slide deck on PowerPoint [or similar], and then each subtopic within that could be its own slide. Choose a background for the slide that represents that topic. It should be related to it, and it should be quite detailed, so you can imagine things happening inside it. For instance, for GCSE biology, one of the topics is platelets. I thought of plates, and I thought of a dinner table. So I had a picture of a dinner table with lots of plates of food, and then all the things that relate to that topic on the slide, including clotted cream as a reminder that platelets clot blood.”Flashcards can be helpful, says Kermode. “But I think what people miss is using the techniques to help them memorise information in the first place, because flashcards just help you review things at certain intervals. You have to put in the effort to memorise it in the first place.” In a lesson or lecture, Kermode writes down the key points and facts that she wants to remember, and lays them out as amind map. “So you’re not just writing a list of points, but have your key topic as the central image, and then that branches out to each subtopic.”Practice makes perfectMake sure you keep running over whatever it is you want to learn, to ensure it stays in your brain. “If it is a short-term list, then you just need to do it once or twice, and you have probably got it,” says Kermode. “If it is something you want to learn more long-term, then you need to review it regularly because otherwise we naturally forget.” Kermode suggests trying “spaced repetition”, which means practising at increasing intervals. “So the first week, you might go over it a couple of times on the first day, and the same the next day, and then a couple of days later. But then the next week you might be on to once a week, and eventually once a month.”Take notes and set alarmsGruneberg, who is 86, says to always make a note of appointment times. “There is something called ‘prospective memory’ that does not improve, to say the least. Remembering to do things, when to see the doctor, all sorts of things like that. It becomes much more necessary to write these things down as you get older.”“I use alarms all the time,” admits Kermode. “We do become reliant on it. You can try to remember it, but also set the alarm just in case. I think triggering your mind to do something at a certain point, you have to use something that you’re going to do. Say you need to go to the hairdresser straight after lunch – you could associate using scissors to get into the fridge.”Rest upSahakian ensures that she gets at least seven hours’ sleep a night. “You consolidate in your memory what you have learned during the day when you sleep at night. Therefore, it is important to sleep well and not to stay up all night cramming for exams.”View image in fullscreen‘You face a lot of brain fog when you’ve not slept’ … sleep more to stay sharp.Photograph: Catherine Falls Commercial/Getty Images“Sleep is really important for your brain to work in an efficient way, especially if you’re trying to memorise something fast,” agrees Kermode. “If you’re tired, it’s not going to work.” After competing, Kermode often feels exhausted. “There was one competition I won, and I got back home and was trying to get some money out at the ATM, and I couldn’t remember my pin because my brain was frazzled.”“You face a lot of brain fog when you’ve not slept,” says Alam. “Your mind isn’t working at its top speed, and that is because your body has a circadian rhythm that is designed around sleep. Sleep at the time you need to, so that you can stay sharp.” When trying to commit something to memory, Alam recommends taking regular naps, “so that you can give your brain that time to process the information, put it where it needs to be placed, and then it will be handy when you need it”.Explore more on these topicsAgeingThe expertsMemoryNeuroscienceSleepHealth & wellbeingMental healthHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It’s snow time: the best winter activity holidays in Europe for non-skiers | Winter sports holidays | The Guardian
description: From husky sledding and chasing the northern lights in Lapland to bear-spotting in Transylvania, here’s our pick of wild and magical snowy breaks in Europe
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From husky sledding and chasing the northern lights in Lapland to bear-spotting in Transylvania, here’s our pick of wild and magical snowy breaks in Europe
Content: E-fatbiking through the snowy forests of Ruka in Finland.View image in fullscreenE-fatbiking through the snowy forests of Ruka in Finland.Winter sports holidaysIt’s snow time: the best winter activity holidays in Europe for non-skiersFrom husky sledding and chasing the northern lights in Lapland to bear-spotting in Transylvania, here’s our pick of wild and magical snowy breaks in EuropeFiona KerrSun 1 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArctic thrills and survival skills inFinnish LaplandAt Ruka, the first skiers of the year slalomed down the slopes on 2 October. Just inside the Arctic Circle, Ruka’s long snow-sure season and cosy village atmosphere make it a popular ski resort with Finnish families. The long polar nights mean there are only a few hours of dim twilight each day, but the slopes here are floodlit, so that never stops play.The Narnia-like setting offers just as much action off the runs as on them, and in December the resort launchesRuka Guides, guided adventures from a dedicated activity centre. Spend the morning e-fatbiking through snowy forests (from €90) or cutting a hole in a frozen lake to catch fish (from €89), before learning Arctic survival skills (from €85) or snowshoeing in the evening darkness on the hunt for the northern lights (from €89).Other, more offbeat diversions include floating in a thermal suit down the freezing Kiveskoski river in meditative silence (from €135), whizzing down an alpine coaster at up to 25mph (from €11.88) and practising your sun salutation in the forest surrounded by grazing reindeer (from €45).Dasher and Dancer are a clue to the other reason Ruka is such a hit with children: the main merry man himself. Father Christmas, Mrs Claus and the elves live atSanta’s Cottage, about 30 minutes’ drive from Ruka, where they test how good little helpers are at gingerbread baking and Christmas card making, before those wannabe elves sing Santa’s favourite carol to him in Finnish, post cards at the post office and sledge down the hillside outside (from €105).All activitiesatruka.fi.Rukariutta Superior apartments sleep up to six from €362 a night (rukapalvelu.fi).Lumo Lakeside Lodges sleep up to two adults and two children from €215(rukasafaris.fi)Stargazing in the CairngormsView image in fullscreenThe Tomintoul and Glenlivet area of the Cairngorms is a designated International Dark Sky Park.Photograph: Cairngorms Astronomy GroupIn the depths of winter, the sun sets just a shade after 3.30pm in the Cairngorms national park and doesn’t rise again until about 8.50 the following morning. Those long hours of darkness combined with low levels of light pollution (the area around Tomintoul and Glenlivet is an International Dark Sky Park) makes it the perfect place for stargazing.While it’s easy to be dazzled by the Milky Way without even reaching for a telescope, the Discovery Centre in the village of Tomintoul lends out stargazing kits (pre-booking required) to help visitors delve deeper into the cosmos at one of their recommended viewing sites, such as the nearby Tomintoul Field of Hope, with its purpose-built Skyhide pavilion.The centre is also the meeting point for astronomy events (there is a close-up look at the moon on 18 November and an evening of meteor spotting when the Geminids shower is at its peak around mid-December (suggested donation £7,cairngormsdarkskypark.org).A short drive away, just north of Aviemore, storyteller Sarah Hobbs leads monthlyStargazing Storywalks. The 1½-mile after-dark amble weaves in Gaelic and Pictish tales of the night sky from thousands of years ago, from warrior queens to one-eyed giants, and ends with a cup of foraged wild tea (£20pp, Oct-March). For something a little more strenuous,Hillgoersorganises regular three-mile night walks with certified star rangers, spotting glowing planets and nocturnal wildlife (£40pp, maximum of eight in a group).The Lazy Duckcontinues the dark-sky theme with a clutch of off-grid huts among the pines of the Abernethy Forest with stargazing windows above the beds (from £187 a night in December).There are plenty of winter activities in daylight hours too, from driving theSnowRoads route, which winds along the highest public roads in Britain, to meeting the country’s only free-roaming reindeer herd (guided hill trips run Feb-Dec from £29.40pp,cairngormreindeer.co.uk).Toboggansand glaciers in ChamonixView image in fullscreenThe Grotte de Glace, carved into the Mer de Glace glacier above Chamonix-Mont-Blanc.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyAt the foot of Mont Blanc, Chamonix is famous among skiers for its gnarly off-piste terrain and intense black runs. But that dramatic landscape makes it prime territory for action off the slopes too. One of Responsible Travel’s new trips this season is a four-night self-guided snowshoeing holiday in the Chamonix valley.Using the traditional mountain spa town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains as its base, the itinerary ventures deep into the snow-covered Vallorcine valley, hiking through larch meadows and pine forests, heading up the Flégère gondola to walk along a balcony trail facing Mont Blanc, and taking in the views from the summit of Mont d’Arbois at 1,833 metres.The Mont Blanc massif is one of the most densely glaciated areas in the Alps, and while the ice is receding due to the climate crisis, taking the dinky redMontenverscog train up to the Mer de Glace is still an impressive experience. This huge river of ice winds some 5 miles between the mountains, and at the top a cable car followed by around 200 steps descends into the Grotte de Glace, a blue tunnel carved into the glacier (€49.70 for the train, gondola and ice cave visit).A more intrepid ice-spotting option is Les Contamines-Montjoie circular snowshoeing route, which climbs through pine forests to the Plateau du Truc, with its views of the d’Armancette, Miage and Covagnet glaciers.Back in Chamonix, theMont-Blanc Museumopened in July, tracing the valley’s history and Alpine exploits from the ice age to today, showcasing objects that include memorabilia from the first Winter Olympic Games (held in Chamonix in 1924) and the walking stick of Jacques Balmat, half of the two-man team that made the first ascent of Mont Blanc in 1786. That climb is only for serious mountaineers, but the cable car from Chamonix town centre is a shortcut toAiguille du Midi’s almost-as-impressive 3,842-metre peak (€43 round trip) – leaving plenty of energy to hit the nearby La Luge toboggan run (€23 for the pedestrian lift pass and one descent;ski-saintgervais.com).A four-night self-guided snowshoeing trip in Chamonix from £790pp withResponsible Travel, includingB&B accommodation, route maps, smartphone navigation app, GPS trackers and 24/7 phone supportSnowshoeing and bearspotting in TransylvaniaView image in fullscreenA Eurasian brown bear in Transylvania, Romania.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyHiking along narrow trails in thePiatra raiului national park, you’re more likely to come across bear or wolf tracks than other walkers’ footprints. The Carpathian mountains are one of Europe’s last bastions for large predators – there are thought to be more than 10,000 brown bears and around 2,500 grey wolves in Romania alone.A week-long guided trip with Exodus makes tracks into Transylvania’s dramatic karst landscape, and is an atmospheric introduction to snowshoes and crampons. Base camp is the family-run Villa Hermani guesthouse, over 1,000 metres above sea level in the village of Magura, where there’s always a warming glass of homemadepălincă(fruit brandy) waiting.Hikes climb up to the high ridge of Dealul Măgurice or to the plateau between the Piatra Craiului and Bucegi mountains, where the only thing that might break the silence is the howling of a wolf. One of the most spectacular walks heads along the Zărnești Gorge, its vertical limestone walls rising 200 metres above the icy canyon floor.When not snowshoeing through Christmas-card scenes, take in medieval churches, the cobbled old town of Brașov and the Libearty bear sanctuary, which has rescued over 120 brown bears from the cruelty of captivity. And while Bram Stoker never set foot in Romania, let alone Bran Castle (often said to be the inspiration for Dracula’s lair), you can. With its frosty turrets and towers set against the Carpathians, it looks more gothic than ever, and even better without the bloodthirsty summer crowds.Exodus’s seven-night Transylvania winter walkand snowshoetrip from£1,459pp, including all accommodation, meals, transport and activities, tour guide, snowshoes and polesIgloos and Christmas markets in InnsbruckView image in fullscreenA luxury igloo at Iglu-Dorf, near Innsbruck.Innsbruck is ringed by the Austrian Alps, meaning wherever you wander in the city – among the medieval alleys of the Altstadt or past the colourful houses along the River Inn – snow-covered mountains are the constant backdrop. Those jagged peaks are home to 12 ski areas within 15 to 75 minutes of the city by public transport, and some are worth the trip for the snow-plough-averse too.Zaha Hadid’s swooping, modernist Bergisel ski jump is a dominant sight above the town and the vertiginous view is even better from its observation deck. The architect also designed four of the Nordpark Cable Railway stations that feature fluid glass canopies mimicking natural ice formations and glaciers. They take skiers and non-skiers up to the Nordkette mountains for a bird’s eye view of the Tirolean capital.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere’s plenty more to get pulses racing without clipping on a pair of skis, from bobsleighing down the 1,399-metreOlympic trackat Igls at speeds of up to 115km/h (from €45 for bobrafting, €119 for piloted race bobsleighing) to night sledding atRangger Köpfl(€25). For more icy fun, there are igloos to spend the night in atIglu-Dorfin Kühtai, Austria’s highest ski resort (from €537 for up to three people, including cheese fondue, community sauna and breakfast).Back down in Innsbruck, Christmas market season kicks off in November, and there are seven dotted around the streets and squares, from the historic old town market to the lofty Hungerburg – be sure to trykiachl,a doughnut-like pastry served either savoury with hot sauerkraut, or sweet topped with wild cranberry jam.New skating experienceIce Magicalso launches this winter, with illuminated ice paths connecting different parts of the city, alongside light installations and projections, ice disco nights and DJs (from €8).Nordic ice-skating in SwedenView image in fullscreenIceskating in the Stockholm archipelago.Photograph: Henrik Trygg/Getty ImagesWhile Scandinavians started using animal bones to make primitive ice skates thousands of years ago, wild, or Nordic, skating as we know it (long-distance skating outdoors on natural ice for sport rather than utility) evolved in Sweden in the 1900s. Stockholm’s Skridskoseglarklubb (“Skate Sailing Club”) was formed in 1901 and today has more than 10,000 members, who share the latest ice information online to find the ideal skating locations.Nordic skates have long blades attached only at the front of the boot, used to make long, rhythmic glides; other specialist safety kit includes long, pointy poles to assess ice thickness and a backpack that doubles as a flotation device.Wild is the operative word here, and it is prudent as a beginner to skate with a pro. Stockholm-basedIce Guideruns a number of trips, from one-day introductions to multi-day tours, which head out on to Lake Mälaren or the Baltic Sea in the Stockholm archipelago (from £143 including all gear, transport and lunch).Hellasgården, less than half an hour outside Stockholm, is another popular skate spot with ploughed tracks on Lake Källtorpssjön, and there are holes cut in the ice for the bravest swimmers (and a sauna for after).While in the city centre, get your frozen kicks at the ice rink atKungsträdgården(skate rental about £7.50 an hour) or by joining the boisterous crowd at a Djurgården IF ice hockey match at the Hovet stadium.Ruby Fridaopened this summer and has doubles from £70 room-onlyA foodiewalkin the Dolomites, northern ItalyView image in fullscreenHiking through the Drei Zinnen nature park in the Dolomites.Hearty Tirolean food is made for winter:Knödeldumplings smothered in melted butter and parmesan, the ricotta- and spinach-filled pasta pockets ofSchlutzkrapfen, the cast-iron skillet hash ofBauerngröstl. Hiking through the slopes and valleys of the Dolomites’ Drei Zinnen (Three Peaks) nature park on a week-long trip with self-guided walking holiday specialists Inntravel is a good way to work up an appetite.From the charmingly traditional Hotel Drei Zinnen in the village of Sesto near the Austrian border, a network of 100km of well-groomed, partially cleared paths (meaning no snowshoes required) branches out through the Fischleintal valley and beyond into the nature park.Mountain huts (rifugios) are dotted along routes for a warming lunch: Talschlusshütte serves mountain pine and porcini mushroom risotto and classic comfortingGerstensuppe(barley soup) along the Fischleintal valley walk; while the 100-year-old Dreischusterhütte among the fir trees in the nearby Innerfeldtel valley is much loved for itsKaiserschmarrn(shredded pancake) and homemadeApfelkiachl(fried apple rings).Other routes start with a cable car ride and cut across the snowglobe landscapes of the Kreuzbergpass (stopping for a drink on the terrace at the Klammbach hut, of course) or loop around the banks of the frozen Lake Toblach.Hotel Drei Zinnen has welcomed a fair few winter explorers through its doors since it opened in 1930. One regular guest – the mountaineer and author of Seven Years in Tibet Heinrich Harrer – inspired the hotel’s original owner Hans Watschinger to transform the establishment and the village of Sesto (Sexten in German) into a winter destination. It’s still run by the Watschinger family, and today there’s daily afternoon cake and a Finnish sauna to ease walk-weary muscles, and four-course nightly feasts of Italian favourites and local South Tirolean specialities to fuel up for another day in the mountains.A seven-night Italian Dolomites Winter Walking trip from £1,076, including half-board accommodation, local bus pass and transfers (inntravel.co.uk)Husky sledding, reindeerand thenorthernlightsin NorwayView image in fullscreenFeeding reindeer in Tromsø.For as long as the lights of the aurora borealis have danced across the sky, the people living beneath them have told stories explaining the mysterious, spectral glow – are they omens or gods, communication from spirits or threat of war? For some Sámi communities in northern Scandinavia, they were the souls of the dead, souls that were not to be disturbed by looking, talking, waving or pointing at them, in case the ghostly veil snatched you into the sky or cut off your head.At 217 miles (350km) above the Arctic Circle, Tromsø is the ideal destination for northern lights chasers and learning about the indigenous Sámi people – many of whom still herd reindeer across the vast wilderness.The Oskal family have lived a way of life shaped by reindeer for generations, and their herd spends winter around the camp near Tromsø and summer roaming free in the mountains. The family now share that traditional way of life throughTromsø Arctic Reindeer, opening up their camp to visitors to sled ride, feed the herd and join the family around the fire in thelavvu(tent), forjoik(traditional Sámi song) and perhaps glimpses of the aurora overhead (experiences start at 990 kroner/£75 for reindeer feeding).At the gateway to Norway’s frozen far north, Tromsø is the launchpad for numerous activities – ice fishing and fjord cruising, husky sledding and snowmobile safaris – and the lively university town is interesting in itself. It was once the departure point for expeditions to the north pole – a history captured at thePolar Museumon the harbour front – and today also draws cultural travellers for concerts in the angular Arctic Cathedral and the international film festival in January.Three-night trip to Tromsø from £767pp, including B&B and an aurora-chasing trip, withDiscover the WorldExplore more on these topicsWinter sports holidaysAdventure travelArctic holidaysEurope holidaysWalking holidaysWinter walksMeteorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: with governments asking us to stockpile, can we learn anything from disaster films? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Content: Don’t get caught in traffic … Roland Emmerich’s film The Day After Tomorrow.Photograph: AllstarView image in fullscreenDon’t get caught in traffic … Roland Emmerich’s film The Day After Tomorrow.Photograph: AllstarNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: with governments asking us to stockpile, can we learn anything from disaster films?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical conceptsThis week’s question:if I get a dumbphone, how will I cope in a smartphone world?Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs I was building pyramids of loo roll and tinned beans in response to the government’sBe Ready campaign, launched this week, I got to thinking about what other aspects of modern life might help us to get through an emergency. Specifically, our extensive back catalogue of disaster movies, TV series and the like. We’ve imagined catastrophes hitting the human race in so many ways, with so many different outcomes. Are there any useful tips we can take from our library of entertaining, effects-laden disaster films?Which particular shows or movies should we watch in the name of preparedness? Or are they all pure fantasy, and when the planet overheats or the comet strikes, we’ll be wishing we’d spent our evenings watching dry informational programmes about water purification instead?Annabel, SheffieldSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyIn the event of a disaster, just stay with the dog. (The dog always survives.)alanfdowWe know that post apocalypse or disaster, only really good-looking people survive. There’s really no hope for me and the millions of average-looking people; we get buried under the volcanic ash, drowned by the tsunami, or otherwise suitably obliterated. My advice: roll with it until the inevitable sorting-according-to-looks happens.slobberfestA bonus for us now that earlier generations of survivors (Triffids, The Stand) didn’t have is abundant bottled water. In an “I alone survived” scenario, I recommend spending the first week or two driving lorries away from supermarkets, alternating between water and long-lasting food.adamcgfThat’s pretty much what one of the protagonists in Station Eleven by Emily St John Mandel does when he realises there’s a deadly pandemic starting.TobermoryNightlifeRaid the pharmacy first.DukeApricotApparently, we will have to spend at least an hour trying to save an unappealing American child who may perhaps say “I love you, Daddy” at some point. Perhaps, to save time and effort, these kids could be grouped together in convenient locations around the country for convenient collection at the first sign of comet, spaceship or giant wave?sparklesthewonderhenIt’s easier to teach blue-collar workers to do astronauting than to teach astronauts how to drill, apparently. And make sure you learn all your science from that near-documentary The Core.unclestinkyDon’t go swimming at a beach at a popular New England resort in summer.PeteTheBeatThere is a T-shirt with the slogan: Every Disaster Movie Starts With Somebody Ignoring a Scientist. This is, however, not entirely true. Some disaster movies starts with somebody allowing a scientist to do something. Clearly, the important thing is to be able to find out what kind of scientist you’ve got, and then encourage or suppress them as appropriate.SpoilheapSurferWhich particular shows or movies should we watch, in the name of preparedness?Children of Men, but to ensure the UKdoesn’tend up that way.dfic1999WarGames.LorLalaTake the million-to-one chance – it always works out.serapisOnly nine times out of 10. And it has to be exactly a million to one. A million and one to one – don’t bother.FormerlyPrawnExposing invaders to British bacteria has been known to work, especially if the aliens are precariously balanced on three legs.jno50The Walking Dead shows us what terrible decisions made by desperate people look like. The Handmaid’s Tale reminds us what the enemy looks like. And The West Wing is a blueprint for what we’ve lost in an uncivilised world.DorkaliciousCommon sense would suggest not living in New York, which gets very chilly (The Day After Tomorrow), or California, which is very shaky (Earthquake). But about one American in six does so. At least the short film Duck and Cover explains what to do when a nuclear holocaust is looming – basically, hide under a desk.jno50Thank you for posting this question. I’ve been “preparing” since the non-event of Y2K (1999). Movies: The Day After (1983), Threads (1984), The Postman (1997), The Road (2009), The Book of Eli (2010).Terri H, Toronto, via emailAs a self-confessed prepper, I think I might just have been captured by the 1975 BBC drama series Survivors. Probably saw it at an impressionable age, but it has stuck with me, along with some old second world war and air crash survival films. Resourcefulness is the key takeaway; when the shops are shuttered permanently, you have to grow it, make it, or trade for it – and protect what you do have in a lawless dystopian world!Phil Harmer, Llanidloes Powys, via emailThere was an infamous film in the UK called Threads, made in the 80s. Your Duck and Cover reminded me of it. We watched one calledProtect and Survive. It advised that on hearing the three-minute warning siren, one should do the following: fill the bath with water, take a door off its hinges and prop it lengthways along an internal wall, and cover said door with a mattress. The family should then shelter under the door until the all-clear is sounded. Even as a child I thought it ambitious to accomplish in three minutes, but the family in the film managed it. Problem was, they were there for a couple of weeks and their elderly granny died with no means of preserving the body, so they had to find alternative accommodation. On leaving the house they discovered the entire city was laid waste and society as they had known it was ended. To top it off, the young woman in the family was pregnant when the bomb dropped, with predictable radioactive effects on the foetus. People still talk about this film – it pulled no punches and showed no matter what governments do to protect citizens in a nuclear war, it won’t work. Give me zombies every time – I can deal with them.rumblestripsMy dad used to practise taking the door off and making a shelter. My mom used to say she’d rather die in the blast. Oh the joys of the 1980s.DrMomPAIn the film The Survivalist, the protagonist gains entry to a safe place – a fenced and armed camp of fellow survivors – by paying an entry fee in the form of vegetable seeds. I think this would approximate the reality of societal breakdown, where food is of primary importance and the alternative is eating other people, plenty of which occurs in the film. Incidentally, The Survivalist is probably the most realistic, hence pessimistic, films about the end of society as we know it. 28 Days Later is a good film, but hordes of ravening zombies chasing people down the street is frankly ridiculous and quite entertaining. The Survivalist is neither – it’s like The Road, too close to the bone (if you’ll excuse the expression) to be fun.curiouspantsThe beginning of The Road, where he tells his wife they need to fill the bath, is the only tip I remember.alexitoNever ever, ever extrapolate any information or “advice” from films. They’re actors, people who dress up and play pretend. All actors do is learn their lines and avoid the furniture, at least according to Spencer Tracy.bricklayersoptionThe best disaster movie has to be Threads. And from it we can learn that there’s literally nothing anyone can do. You don’t even want to survive, as afterwards things get even worse. Have a lovely Sunday, everyone!Alex42Explore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The kindness of strangers: In 1989 I lost a wallet with $1,000 in it. A couple went to incredible lengths to return it | Backpacking holidays | The Guardian
description: Cash was king in those days, and that money was enough to last me for a month as I slowly travelled from Australia back to the UK
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: Cash was king in those days, and that money was enough to last me for a month as I slowly travelled from Australia back to the UK
Content: ‘It wasn’t until the next morning that I realised the incredible lengths they had gone to in order to return my wallet.’Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It wasn’t until the next morning that I realised the incredible lengths they had gone to in order to return my wallet.’Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty ImagesKindness of strangersBackpacking holidaysThe kindness of strangers: In 1989 I lost a wallet with $1,000 in it. A couple went to incredible lengths to return itCash was king in those days, and that money was enough to last me for a month as I slowly travelled from Australia back to the UKRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesSimon Kelsey as told toKatie CunninghamSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.06 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a hot night in 1989 when my wallet – stuffed with $1,000 cash – fell out of my pocket.After university, I left the UK and went travelling in Australia for a year. I saw the delights of the east coast – mostly from various building sites, as I worked my way around doing long hours in the blistering sun. But I loved every minute of it. After 10 months, I had saved enough to make my way slowly back home.I was enjoying one last night out in Darwin with a gang of traveller friends with whom I was flying to Timor the next day. The intention was to island hop all the way to Singapore.The kindness of strangers: After a tearful breakup dinner, another patron paid our billRead moreCash was king in those days, and the $1,000 I had in my wallet was enough to last me a month on the road. The beers went down easy and I was completely unaware when, at some point in the evening, I lost my wallet. I was still none the wiser when I went to bed to get some sleep before the flight the next morning.At 1.30am, I awoke to a loud knocking on my door. I stumbled out of bed, bleary-eyed, and opened the door to the hostel manager and an elderly couple – who were holding my wallet.That couple had spent hours trawling every backpacker place in Darwin (they’d been to four!) before eventually finding me, care of my student ID card. Every dollar was still there.Still half asleep, and worse for wear after the evening’s drinks, I didn’t fully appreciate the extent of their kindness in the moment. I thanked them and went back to bed, but it wasn’t until the next morning that I realised the incredible lengths they had gone to in order to return my wallet. Without them, my trip would have been ruined.I’ve always wished I could thank them properly, but in lieu of that I made a pledge to myself – and in a way, to them – that I would always go that extra mile to help people when I have the chance.When I do get the opportunity to lend someone a hand, I always tell them to pay it forward. So I like to think that kind couple in Darwin have actually helped countless others, too.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.What is your name?Where do you live (city, state and country)?Tell us a bit about the kind act you've experienced?Where and when did this encounter take place?Can we publish your response?Yes, entirelyYes, but contact me firstYes, but please keep me anonymousNo, this is information onlyAre you comfortable with a journalist contacting you about this story for potential publication?YesNoWhat is your phone number?OptionalYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.What is your email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.Would you be interested in speaking to our audio and/or video teams?Audio onlyVideo onlyAudio and videoNo, I'm not interestedBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsBackpacking holidaysKindness of strangersAustralian lifestyleAustralia holidaysDarwin holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Some photos imprint upon us’: How our Saturday magazine puts together special issues about world-changing photographs | Magazines | The Guardian
description: A great picture can have an immediate and visceral effect on a viewer, as if bypassing thought. But a huge amount of thinking goes into selecting and sourcing them, and researching their backstories
Author: Gautam Malkani
Headline: A great picture can have an immediate and visceral effect on a viewer, as if bypassing thought. But a huge amount of thinking goes into selecting and sourcing them, and researching their backstories
Content: A 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando that was included in our selection of photographs that have changed how people view masculinity.Photograph: John Kobal Foundation/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando that was included in our selection of photographs that have changed how people view masculinity.Photograph: John Kobal Foundation/Getty ImagesInside the GuardianMagazines‘Some photos imprint upon us’: How our Saturday magazine puts together special issues about world-changing photographsA great picture can have an immediate and visceral effect on a viewer, as if bypassing thought. But a huge amount of thinking goes into selecting and sourcing them, and researching their backstoriesGautam MalkaniSun 1 Nov 2026 10.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan photographs still exert power in an age when millions of pictures are taken and shared every minute, and when a viewer’s first response is to question whether an image is even real?Every few months, a team of editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine puts together a special photography package in print and digital formats. It features photographs that don’t just stop the scroll, they have also prompted the rewriting of history books. They are the kind of images that have changed the world in some way or radically shifted people’s perceptions.Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad)Read moreEach issue has a particular theme. Earlier this month, the magazine featured photographs that havechanged how we view masculinity– from a 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando in a white T-shirt to a paparazzi shot of David Beckham in a sarong and a bare-chested Vladimir Putin on horseback. Previous issues have focused on photographs that havereshaped sport, forced people to confront the reality of theclimate crisisand upended theworld of fashion.Beyond the impact each image had back when it first came out, they still feel powerful and affecting today – reminding us how great photography can command a kind of reverence and stillness in the viewer. “Working on these issues, you realise that there’s something about the power of the images that’s elemental,” says Rebecca Liu, a commissioning editor on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine. “Some photos imprint upon us before we even canthinkabout them. They just immediately hit our bloodstream.”The first special issue featuredprotest imagesthat have prompted social or political change. It was initially conceived as a one-off feature in 2022 amid protests in the US that year against the overturning of Roe v Wade and demonstrations against police brutality. But the feature resonated so strongly with readers that it spawned an occasional series.That regularity means the process of putting the issues together is now fine-tuned, though not without its own drama and headaches. “Sometimes on the day of going to print we’re waiting on two or three final things to be confirmed,” says Rebecca. “It’s a massive act of organisation and coordination and a real collective effort with a lot of moving parts.”View image in fullscreenA photo of a demonstrator looking at a riot policeman during a 2016 protest in Santiago, Chile, which appeared in our special issue of protest images.Photograph: ReutersSelecting which pictures to include involves tapping the collective minds of picture editors and journalists on the magazine and across the Guardian. Different colleagues will have different criteria. How to weigh up a photograph’s social or political impact against its technical importance to the medium? Should it be an image that, in itself, has changed the world or a photograph of a world-shifting moment?“Everyone working on the magazine has a different take on it,” says Louis Siroy, the magazine’s deputy picture editor. “Some editors will ask how a particular photograph shaped society; what does it mean? Whereas I might be asking what are the important photographs or photographers that fit into that theme or category.”‘It never happened – but the picture says it did’: 28 fake images that fooled the worldRead moreFor example, the first special issue about protest photography didn’t just include the famous image of a protestor standing in front of a tank in Tiananmen Square, it also included a less famous but equally powerful photograph of a boy sitting on the shoulders of relatives above the sea of soldiers’ helmets. Taken by the photographerDario Mitidieri, the image was suggested by Louis. “That to me is a great photograph, and I was trying to bring something that wasn’t necessarily the image people are familiar with,” he says. “Hopefully these selections inspire people to value and appreciate the breadth and power of great photographs.”By drawing on colleagues’ different perspectives and experience, each special issue sheds unique light on its theme. “So while the selection can’t possibly be comprehensive and definitive, it’s still authoritative,” says Rebecca.Other images included in the initial protest photography issue include thefamous pictureof US athletes John Carlos and Tommie Smith raising their fists in a black power salute during a medal ceremony at the 1968 Olympics. There are also several photographs of protesters facing off against riot police or soldiers, including a powerful image of a young girl in Santiago, Chile, during a 2016 demonstration marking the anniversary of the country’s 1973 military coup.One of the most time-consuming challenges involves obtaining the rights to publish the images. “Some of the greatest challenges involve finding the right copyright holder for some lesser-known photographs,” says Caroline Hunter, the magazine’s picture editor.Protesters, pop stars and pioneers: 38 images that changed the way we see women (for better and for worse)Read moreEven well-known photographs can present hurdles. “Sometimes you have to get permission from the subject of the photo as well as from the photographer, particularly when it comes to photos of celebrities or fashion,” explains Louis. “It can get really hard to track down the person you need. For instance, the masculinity special featured a famous second world war photo of a US aeroplane gunner that was taken by the photographerHorace Bristol, who is now deceased. It took some time to contact the photographer’s son Henri in California and explain the context in which we wanted to use the photo. And even when dealing with well-known photographers, it still involves negotiating the rights for editorial use rather than commercial use.”Another challenge that can arise is the quality of the photographs. “We have to ensure the image is large enough or good enough quality to reproduce, especially for very old images that previously existed only as prints,” says Caroline. “Works by famous and art photographers often have specific rules around usage, so it’s important to ensure that we keep within their guidelines. We had a really good response from photographers after our recent photo specialmarking America at 250. I think this was because there were so many great, iconic images from seminal photographers.”The team also has to decide the best layout for the print and digital editions – which images to give prominence to, how they might best fit together, and the range of black-and-white and colour images. Maggie Murphy, the magazine’s art director, experiments with different layouts, sometimes on a screen, sometimes with printouts strewn across the desks.View image in fullscreenA famous image of  US athletes Tommie Smith (centre) and John Carlos (right) raising their fists in a black power salute at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, during the medal ceremony for the 200m race. The photo featured in our special issue of protest photographs that have changed the world.Photograph: STF/APAs well as the images, a huge amount of work goes into the words. Each special issue includes a short guest-written essay, and each photograph has an extended caption about that particular picture’s significance or backstory.The journalists who are commissioned to write these captions undertake extensive research. For example, the masculinity issue includes a famous 1970 advertisement depicting a pregnant man, for which the journalist tracked down the original campaign’s photographer, who is now 98. “I encourage original interviews and research wherever possible,” says Rebecca. “We want the words to illuminate something about the picture and for people to learn things. That’s not something you necessarily have to do for a 150-word caption, but we want to do it because the editorial component is so important to us at the Guardian.”Burning flags, busty blondes and bison skulls: 50 photographs that capture America at 250Read moreResearching the captions also reveals something about the nature of photography. “It really shows the importance of not just taking an image at face value,” says Rebecca. “I’m always surprised by what you discover when you look into things. You might find a complicated backstory behind the person who is photographed – perhaps their ambivalence about being pictured, for instance.”The same applies to the thought that goes into the introductory essays. The novelist Anne Enright wrote perceptively abouthow women are captured on camera, for better or for worse, in her introduction to an issue that featured photographs that havechanged the way society sees women. “As you look at a Kardashian selfie, consider how many rules had to be broken to get her to this moment of self-commodification,” writes Enright.The masculinity issue contains an accompanying essay by the poet and novelist Luke Kennard, who reflects on how the images seem to capture extremes of masculinity, with little in between: “To judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men… Even the bang average is barely represented.”Rebecca noticed that gap in representation back when the team was initially selecting which photographs to include in the issue. “I remember thinking, where are the other male bodies? It was difficult to find any – at least with the quality and artistry that we look for in these stories. You’d Google the words ‘dad bod’ and you’d just get screenshots of Seth Rogen and grainy paparazzi shots of celebrities on the beach.”The team is very mindful of the power of images to subtly reinforce or subvert people’s preconceptions. “Working on these issues makes us reflect on how much we subconsciously absorb images,” says Rebecca. “And how they feed into our imaginations.”Explore more on these topicsMagazinesInside the GuardianPhotographyNewspapers & magazinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda | Commonwealth summit | The Guardian
description: British prime minister has now agreed to structured dialogue on reparatory justice but issue remains off formal Chogm agenda
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: British prime minister has now agreed to structured dialogue on reparatory justice but issue remains off formal Chogm agenda
Content: King Charles was left bedraggled after a downpour during an Independence Day parade at the Sir Vivian Richards cricket ground in Antigua on Sunday.Photograph: Matias Delacroix/APView image in fullscreenKing Charles was left bedraggled after a downpour during an Independence Day parade at the Sir Vivian Richards cricket ground in Antigua on Sunday.Photograph: Matias Delacroix/APCommonwealth summitUK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agendaBritish prime minister has now agreed to structured dialogue on reparatory justice but issue remains off formal Chogm agendaNatricia Duncanin St John's, AntiguaSun 1 Nov 2026 17.26 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 14.50 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish officials reportedly insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned thatAndy Burnhamwould not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, theCaribbeanand the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.View image in fullscreenRalph Gonsalves said the British government was coming ‘kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue’.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”View image in fullscreenIrfaan Ali, Guyana’s president, who met King Charles this week in Georgetown, said he was happy ‘the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been’.Photograph: Chris Jackson/PAGonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed.He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”An FCDO spokesperson said: “We categorically reject this completely untrue accusation. The UK has approached this conversation in good faith, and we have at no point told any other Chogm member what should not be on an agenda.“Our position on reparations is clear but this government respects the right of others to raise matters as they wish.”‘We want a full apology for slavery’: Commonwealth at a crossroads as king heads to the CaribbeanRead moreProf Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and toconsider an apology.Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.Ali said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences.View image in fullscreenMia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said of Burnham: ‘Our views differ.’Photograph: Andrea de Silva/Reuters“How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said.Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.View image in fullscreenPhilip Davis, the prime minister of the Bahamas, Bahamas, stressed the importance of ‘justice, acknowledgment and meaningful address’.Photograph: Chris Jackson/ReutersThe Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summitRead moreKing Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protestsas they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events.On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.On Sunday Kemi Badenoch told broadcasters that an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would bea “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.“I would really like to sit down with my dear sister Kemi and explain to her so that she could get an understanding of what we are talking about,” Gonsalves said, adding that he would like to discuss how reparatory justice could help heal some of the fractures arising from Britain’s multicultural and ethnic tensions.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth summitReparations and reparative justiceCaribbeanKing Charles IIIColonialismBritish empireCommonwealth of NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading | China | The Guardian
description: A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Content: Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenXi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesChinaAnalysisThe US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleadingEduardo PorterA truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilitiesSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.22 ESTShareDonald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless theFederal Reservecuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.But neitherChinanor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.View image in fullscreenThe port in Qinzhou, China, on 22 October 2026.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionairesRead moreThe paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order.He described the strategyas building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging itsoverwhelming dominanceover the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year,it stunnedthe Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.View image in fullscreenA girl visits an installation about rare earth production at the National Museum in Beijing, China, on 24 March 2026.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersIt has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains manyother restrictions. While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hitother countriesfor a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency hasestimated thatif China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.Where does the supply chain war go from here? TheTrump administrationis pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.China, on the other hand, has announced a range ofhigh-tech export restrictions, covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.View image in fullscreenWorkers at a photovoltaic power-generation project site on 27 October 2026 in Wenling, Zhejiang province, China.Photograph: Zhou Xuejun/VCG/Getty ImagesChina will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world.
