Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.Explore more on these topicsChinaUS economyDonald TrumpTrump administrationTrump tariffsCritical mineralsTariffsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Binance resumes customer withdrawals after record $6.3bn hack | Binance | The Guardian
description: Cryptocurrency exchange says 90% of losses covered as FBI blames North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cryptocurrency exchange says 90% of losses covered as FBI blames North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor
Content: Binance is the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBinance is the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesBinanceBinance resumes customer withdrawals after record $6.3bn hackCryptocurrency exchange says 90% of losses covered as FBI blames North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitorGuardian staff and agenciesSun 1 Nov 2026 06.54 ESTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 22.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cryptocurrency exchangeBinancehas started to allow its customers to withdraw their funds from the platform, as it recovers from a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack.The exchange was hit by the theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifyingNorth Koreaas the likely culprit.Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach, but on Sunday announced that it had began a phased reopening after 2pm Singapore time.In the first phase people holding the ethereum, USDT and USDC tokens on the ethereum blockchain were able to withdraw their funds, as well as some others held on the BNB Smart Chain blockchain. Later on Sunday, dealing in the Dogecoin and Avalanche currencies resumed on their own platforms.The platform said it had replenished 90% of the ⁠amount stolen. The remaining 10% of tokens were less liquid, meaning they ⁠may take ​longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday.Richard Teng, Binance’s co-chief executive, said separately that the company was “committed to covering the ⁠remaining 10%” and users would not bear the financial impact of the hack.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programmeRead moreIt came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused ofhacking into Sony Picturesas revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.“The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement.How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe?Read moreThe FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors” were “using to launder these stolen assets”.Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate.Binance said it had set aside about $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses. “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1bn secure asset fund for users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its futures insurance fund and own corporate treasury, the company said ​on X.The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.The sheer scale of the hack has put aspotlight on the capacity of North Korea– which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.Explore more on these topicsBinanceCryptocurrenciesNorth KoreaHackingAsia PacificCybercrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pauline Hanson and James Ashby rule out running against Nationals leader Matt Canavan in Capricornia | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: ‘My political career may die,’ senator says after Michelle Landry announced she will not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia
Author: Tess Ikonomou
Headline: ‘My political career may die,’ senator says after Michelle Landry announced she will not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia
Content: Nationals leader Matt Canavan will run for the seat of Capricornia, with One Nation’s James Ashby rumoured to also be considering the bid for the lower house seat.Composite: AAPView image in fullscreenNationals leader Matt Canavan will run for the seat of Capricornia, with One Nation’s James Ashby rumoured to also be considering the bid for the lower house seat.Composite: AAPAustralian politicsPauline Hanson and James Ashby rule out running against Nationals leader Matt Canavan in Capricornia‘My political career may die,’ senator says after Michelle Landry announced she will not recontest her Queensland seat of CapricorniaGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastTess IkonomouSun 1 Nov 2026 18.05 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 16.25 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, will run for a lower houseQueenslandseat at the next federal election but will avoid having to face off against a key One Nation figure.Canavan confirmed his bid following the announcement Capricornia MP Michelle Landry will retire, leading to speculation it could be a tight race with Pauline Hanson’s national director.But in a statement,James Ashbysaid he will not run in the electorate, which encompasses Rockhampton.“I’ll play a role in the campaign here in Capricornia but my position as national director is one that I take serious [sic],” he said. “Therefore I won’t be nominating at pre-selection.”He saidOne Nationwould have a candidate for the seat, however.“Capricornia is a seat One Nation can win, so I intend to throw the resources and people behind a strong campaign,” Ashby said.Speaking at a press conference, Canavan said someone needed to step up in central Queensland and that he would “put it on the line”.“I’m happy to put my political future on the line to deliver that, to take our country back,” he told reporters on Monday.Is One Nation losing steam in Victoria? New poll points to possible shift as election nearsRead more“I might not be successful. My political career may die, but I’m not going to die wondering. We need a change in this country.”Earlier, Hanson, who sits in the senate, ruled herself out of running for the seat.“It’s still over a year out from the election, a year and a half, so I’m not making any decisions or giving any indication where I’m standing or where James Ashby, if James Ashby is going to stand,” she told reporters.Canavan was previously tipped to make a bid for the House of Representativesamid warnings from pollsters the Nationals leader has a “zero per cent” chance of holding on to his Senate spot if One Nation maintained its surge in opinion polls.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast month, Canavan said he was prepared to do “whatever it takes” to hold Capricornia for his party.Analysts consider regionalCoalitionseats in Queensland and NSW to be particularly vulnerable and up for grabs.Landry announced her decision to retire from politics last month.The Nationals senator,Bridget McKenzie, said One Nation should not be fighting to win Coalition-held seats if the party was serious about taking on Labor.“If One Nation is really serious about firing the liar, then they need to start running in Labor party seats instead of running against someone like Matt Canavan,” she told Nine’s Today show.“[I’m] not afraid of a fight – I want to save our country, and that means changing the prime minister, and that means taking Labor party seats.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsNational partyOne NationCoalitionQueenslandJames AshbyBridget McKenzienewsShareReuse this content

title: Northern Territory water plan condemned as ‘blatant and shameless’ attack on nature | Northern Territory | The Guardian
description: Move to scrap legal requirement to set aside water for environment is ‘extreme even for the NT CLP government’, green group says
Author: Lisa Cox
Headline: Move to scrap legal requirement to set aside water for environment is ‘extreme even for the NT CLP government’, green group says
Content: Northern Territory environment minister, Joshua Burgoyne (pictured) says the water proposal, condemned by Green groups, ‘does not dismantle environmental safeguards’.Photograph: Jayden O’Neill/AAPView image in fullscreenNorthern Territory environment minister, Joshua Burgoyne (pictured) says the water proposal, condemned by Green groups, ‘does not dismantle environmental safeguards’.Photograph: Jayden O’Neill/AAPNorthern TerritoryNorthern Territory water plan condemned as ‘blatant and shameless’ attack on natureExclusive: Move to scrap legal requirement to set aside water for environment is ‘extreme even for the NT CLP government’, green group saysGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLisa CoxEnvironment and climate correspondentSun 1 Nov 2026 15.02 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNorthern Territorygovernment has been accused of making a “blatant and shameless” attack on nature by planning to delete a legal requirement that water must be allocated to the environment.In what has been described as the latest in a series of attacks on the environment by the NT’s Country Liberal party, the Finocchiaro government plans to change water rules that govern how much ground and surface water industry can take.It comes as the government plans a major expansion offracking, datacentres and agricultural development.The Wilderness Society’s chief executive, Kirsty Howey, said the latest move was “extreme even for the NT CLP government”. She called on the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, to withhold commonwealth water funding if the bill passed.High court blocks plan to extract two Sydney Harbours’ worth of groundwater from the desertRead moreThe Central Land Council, which represents Indigenous people in the southern half of the NT, said the territory government was trying to “covertly” remove the last remaining protections Territorians had in the use and management of water.The council’s chief executive, Les Turner, said: “It is actively undermining community aspirations for improved and transparent water planning laws. This flies in the face of national trends and ignores the voices of Aboriginal people from across the NT.”Turner said it was “clearer than ever” that the federal government needed to strengthen its powers to intervene on projects that affected water and aquatic ecosystems.“In August, thehigh court quashed the NT government’s decisionto grant the Singleton Station licence because they found it had been unlawfully granted,” he said.“The way the law is now, we wouldn’t have been able to support native title holders to challenge the merits of such a licence in the first place.“This is especially troubling when we might be faced with future high-water-consuming developments like datacentres looking to take advantage of lax regulations and free water.”The proposed changes would scrap a legal requirement that water allocation plans set aside water for the environment to maintain rivers, springs, wetlands and water-dependent ecosystems. They are part of a larger package that would also make changes to marine pollution, heritage and mining legislation.Other planned changes include removing a rule that total water use by industry remains below a limit set in each water allocation plan, and another that requires water resource management to comply with water allocation plans.Environment groups said the bill would also weaken the definition of “estimated sustainable yield”, which is the amount of water that may be taken or used from a water resource.Howey said the government risked trading the territory’s aquifers and rivers for “short-term gain and profiteering” by the gas, agriculture and tech industries.“It’s so blatant and shameless to literally be deleting the environment’s water allocation,” she said.“The scant safeguards that did exist – and they were threadbare – have just been ripped up altogether. They’re not even pretending any more that they’ve got an interest in protecting these places.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe NT environment minister, Joshua Burgoyne, denied the bill dismantled environmental safeguards. He said the territory’s “core framework” of environment-related laws – including those relating to environmental assessments and approvals, mining licences, pollution control, water allocation planning and heritage protection – remained.“Our government remains focused on facts, not the fearmongering tactics of environmental lobby groups,” he said.The bill before the NT parliament follows araft of earlier changesthat have dismantled environment and climate protections since the CLP won government.They include scrapping the NT’s renewable energy target, abandoning a promise to implement an emissions reduction target of 43% by 2030, and creating a territory coordinator role within the bureaucracy with the power to override 32 territory laws to fast-track developments.Bree Ahrens, the executive director of the Environment Centre NT, said the proposal to rewrite water rules puts the needs of industry above nature. “This is a smash and grab bill that puts water and nature last,” she said.Ahrens called on the Albanese government to rule out handing federal assessment and decision-making powers under national nature laws to “an increasingly rogue NT government that is dismantling water safeguards”.Our place in the sun: Australia’s uptake of solar panels is already through the roof. How much higher could it get?Read moreAfter changes to Environment Protection and BiodiversityConservation(EPBC) Act last year, the federal government can transfer its decision-making powers about whether or not a development can proceed to state and territory governments.Watt declined to comment.Burgoyne said the NT government had “a track record of protecting the environment, such as extending theLimmen Bight marine park”.“We support responsible development, effective environmental and water regulation, and continuing our work to rebuild the economy and restore our unique Territory lifestyle,” he said.Explore more on these topicsNorthern TerritoryWaterConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: House prices fall for seventh consecutive month as interest rates dent demand | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Centre of downturn shifts away from Sydney and Melbourne, but after such strong growth most homeowners still sit on sizeable gains
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: Centre of downturn shifts away from Sydney and Melbourne, but after such strong growth most homeowners still sit on sizeable gains
Content: The property market has been weighed down by four interest rate hikes this year.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe property market has been weighed down by four interest rate hikes this year.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianAustralia newsHouse prices fall for seventh consecutive month as interest rates dent demandCentre of downturn shifts away from Sydney and Melbourne, but after such strong growth most homeowners still sit on sizeable gainsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettBusiness editorSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 15.58 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian home values have dropped for a seventh consecutive month, with prices in the capital cities now falling at the fastest pace in 40 years as rising mortgage rates scare off buyers.Cotality data shows the centre of the downturn is also shifting away from Sydney and Melbourne towards the mid-sized state capital cities, with Brisbane and Perth leading October’s declines.Combined values across the state and territory capital cities fell 1.4% over the month.Cotality’s research director, Tim Lawless, said the downturn was now broad-based, with capital city home values down 8.1% since March.“The mid-sized capitals, where home values recorded extreme growth conditions over the past six years, are now well and truly in a correction,” Lawless said.“Virtually every suburb across Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide has recorded a drop in value over the past three months.”Prices tableThe property market has been weighed down by four interest rate hikes this year, with afifth widely expectedwhen the Reserve Bank hands down its decision on Tuesday.Most economists anticipate double-digit falls in Australian property prices as interest rates climb, with Morgan Stanley forecasting peak-to-trough drops of up to 15%.Lawless said high interest rates were the “most significant downside influence”, while affordability challenges and a pullback in investors sparked by the government’s tax changes had also dented demand.Although the pace of decline is at four-decade highs, Lawless said that largely reflected how strong the property market had been over the period.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVictorians can now see a home’s reserve price before auction. What does this mean for buyers and sellers?Read moreAustralian home prices started todecouple from wages in the late 1980s, before a surge in the 90s and early 2000s propelled the country into a state of unaffordable housing exacerbated by investor-friendly tax settings that were only recently unwound.Over the past decade, property prices have doubled – or nearly doubled – in Adelaide, Brisbane, Perth and Hobart. They are up by more than 50% in Canberra, and more than 30% in Sydney and Darwin. Prices are up by just over 20% in Melbourne.Most homeowners are still sitting on sizeable gains despite the recent weakness. Even a 20% drop in Perth prices from their record high would only take the market back to mid-2025 levels, according to Cotality analysis.Peter Esho, an economist and the chief executive at 13x, said he believed the big housing markets of Sydney and Melbourne were “close to bottoming”, while the mid-sized capitals were at an earlier stage of the downturn.“The downturn is just part of a normal housing cycle, driven by interest rates, which are having a negative wealth effect,” Esho said.“They’re really denting sentiment, and real estate is a sentiment asset.”Esho said he did not believe the price falls would turn “systemic”, which he said would only happen if it became difficult for prospective buyers to borrow, like it did in the US during the global financial crisis, or if unemployment surged.Rental pressures have eased slightly, with national vacancy rates rising and rent growth slowing, according to Cotality.Rents were still up more than 50% over six years, adding about $245 a week to the median rental rate, fast outpacing wage growth.Analysts partly link the rising vacancy rate to changing household dynamics. Driven by affordability, more renters are sharing homes or moving in with family, unwinding the pandemic-driven shift toward smaller households with room for a home office.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsHousingInterest ratesBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former NSW Liberal leads overhaul of One Nation candidate selection process  | One Nation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Mark Jones, once on track for one of the Liberal party’s most powerful roles, is now instrumental in One Nation’s expansion
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: Exclusive: Mark Jones, once on track for one of the Liberal party’s most powerful roles, is now instrumental in One Nation’s expansion
Content: The NSW branch of One Nation said in September it had received 900 applications for candidates standing in 93 NSW seats.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenThe NSW branch of One Nation said in September it had received 900 applications for candidates standing in 93 NSW seats.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPOne NationFormer NSW Liberal leads overhaul of One Nation candidate selection processExclusive:Mark Jones, once on track for one of the Liberal party’s most powerful roles, is now instrumental in One Nation’s expansionGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotandPenry BuckleySun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 16.38 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2023, a young and ambitious Liberal moderate was on the brink of securing one of the most powerful roles in the party: state director of theNew South Walesbranch. Three years later, he is playing a key role in selecting and vetting One Nation candidates determined to beat his former colleagues.Multiple Liberal sources familiar with recruitment for the position, which involves running election campaigns and managing fundraising, confirm Mark Jones was among the final three candidates for the role before his career advancement was ultimately blocked.InternalOne Nationdocuments seen by Guardian Australia show Jones – who quit the Liberal party in January – has become integral to One Nation’s state election campaigns performing similar administrative functions.Is One Nation losing steam in Victoria? New poll points to possible shift as election nearsRead moreSince joining One Nation as a political consultant in February, Jones has helped redesign the party’s candidate selection and vetting process and sat in on interviews. He is being assisted by former Queensland National party executive Susie Douglas, who briefly worked for the Palmer United party before quitting and describing it as a cult.The changes have not stopped One Nation endorsing several state candidates with controversial backgrounds, however. These include a former Liberal who has won support from alleged underworld figures, a naturopath who has endorsed Donald Trump’s unfoundedclaim that paracetamol is linked to autismand a former shire councillor who lost his licence for drink-driving.On Sunday, the One Nation candidate for Melbourne, Matthew Collins,resigned and apologised for now deleted comments on social mediaregarding a number of issues including sexual consent and pornographic jokes. A party spokesperson said the comments were “offensive”.Guardian Australia can reveal One Nation has also overhauled its candidate selection process in NSW after being criticised by some members inVictoriafor lengthy delays and a lack of democratic decision making.Victorian applicants who were invited to short online interviews with Jones and Douglas were surprised to find the state party leader, Warren Pickering, was also in attendance. Internal documents show the three-person team was a “selection committee”. Endorsement decisions were made after police and credit checks.In NSW, 20-30 minute interviews are now being conducted by Jones and Douglas alone, who then make recommendations to a three-person selection committee that does not include them. The committee members are the NSW leader, Mike Newman, the state president, Rebecca Thompson, and the state secretary, Sam Donovan.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThese online interviews test candidate ideas for the future of the state, their knowledge of the parliamentary system and how they could contribute to a future One Nation government.“You are expected to address each of these matters,” states a document seen by Guardian Australia. “Please treat this invitation and your participation in the selection process as confidential. Please do not announce or publish your participation at this stage.”In Victoria, applicants were first screened with a 25-page form that included detailed questions including whether someone had been subject to court proceedings or accused of bullying and verbal abuse. In NSW, this has been streamlined to a much shorter online questionnaire.The NSW branch has also introduced a requirement for candidates to include a 60-second video of themselves outlining why they want to join the party, after finding Victorian candidates who looked good on paper but were not up to scratch when interviewed.These changes may not be enough to satisfy some One Nation members who would like branches to have a greater say in who is selected to represent their regions.In September, Newman said One Nation had already received 900 applications for 93 NSW seats. Earlier this month, the party called for more applications before the 31 October deadline.View image in fullscreenNSW One Nation leader Mike Newman.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPBefore interviews are conducted, applicants must sign restrictive non-disclosure agreements that are not imposed by any other parties. This stops them from publicly confirming their applications.A copy of a non-disclosure agreement used in NSW confirms candidates may be held financially liable should they share or fail to appropriately secure confidential party information.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom moderate Liberal to One Nation whispererGuardian Australia has spoken to several NSW Liberal sources who described Jones as a professional operator who retains close ties to the party.Some expressed frustration he no longer worked for the Liberals and disappointment that a moderate would help One Nation’s campaigns against his former colleagues.Jones is a former deputy chief of staff to the NSW Liberal minister Don Harwin, who was a leading moderate at the time. He was also an unsuccessful Liberal candidate for the state seat of Shellharbour in 2015.After leaving state parliament in 2019, Jones joined the lobbying firm PremierNational and worked alongside another moderate powerbroker, Michael Photios.In early 2026, Jones formed his own political consultancy firm with his wife, Shani, who also previously worked for a NSW Liberal minister and has since been contracted to One Nation.South Australian electoral records show that firm, Camelot Consulting, was paid more than $100,000 for services to One Nation during the state election in March. It is not yet known how much money Camelot has earned from the party in NSW and Victoria.Pauline Hanson denies responsibility for colouring book depicting Bluey being held at knifepointRead moreDocuments seen by Guardian Australia show Douglas is working as “candidate selection officer”. She describes herself as a “former senior vice president of the National party in Queensland”.After serving as an independent councillor on the Gold Coast, Douglas unsuccessfully contested the federal seat of McPherson in Queensland for the Palmer United party in 2013.A year later, she told the Gold Coast Bulletin that Clive Palmer’s party was “a bit like being in a cult – everyone in his group looks up to him”.One Nation, Jones and Douglas declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsOne NationAustralian politicsNew South WalesVictoriaVictorian politicsNew South Wales politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist says | Indigenous art | The Guardian
description: Chair of National Gallery’s First Nations advisory group says the technology is undermining artists’ agency and the authenticity of their work
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: Chair of National Gallery’s First Nations advisory group says the technology is undermining artists’ agency and the authenticity of their work
Content: Artist Sally Scales on AI altering First Nations art: ‘It’s a theft of the agency of the artist. It rips the authenticity out of it, because it’s not been made by anyone who has the connection … the artist’s family lineage is not there, the lived experience is not there.’Photograph: Dean Sewell/OculiView image in fullscreenArtist Sally Scales on AI altering First Nations art: ‘It’s a theft of the agency of the artist. It rips the authenticity out of it, because it’s not been made by anyone who has the connection … the artist’s family lineage is not there, the lived experience is not there.’Photograph: Dean Sewell/OculiIndigenous artAI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist saysChair of National Gallery’s First Nations advisory group says the technology is undermining artists’ agency and the authenticity of their workGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTory ShepherdSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 15.40 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI is taking First Nations art and turning it into “Temu slop”, the Pitjantjatjara artist Sally Scales has said.Scales, the chair of the National Gallery of Australia’s First Nations advisory group, says the technology is undermining the agency of First Nations artists and the authenticity of their work and represents a “a theft” of cultural knowledge.Despite Anthony Albanese’s vow to protect Australian creatives fromcopyright theft,and the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, saying there are “no plans to weaken copyright protections”, AI has already been trained – without compensation – on the works of well known Australian artistsincluding Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave.But experts are particularly worried about the risks to Indigenous cultural and intellectual property (ICIP) in a world where AI companies can hoover up anything that may be found online, including songs and paintings that include sacred and cultural knowledge. AI has altered work, removed names and then been sold, an act the peak body for Australian visual artists said was causing “cultural and economic harm”.Artists boycotted this portrait prize over AI entries. Now they’re back to take them onRead moreSearches on sites including Temu, Shein and Amazon reveal countless works described as Aboriginal paintings, as well as items such as coasters and stubby holders bearing Aboriginal-style designs, mostly without attribution to any artist.“It’s in the name, it’s artificial,” Scales said.“I’ve seen some works where I look at it and wonder if they’ve gone through a First Nations community or a person, or if it’s something generic that they’ve whipped up.“It’s a theft of the agency of the artist. It rips the authenticity out of it, because it’s not been made by anyone who has the connection … the artist’s family lineage is not there, the lived experience is not there.”Prof Kathy Bowrey, an intellectual property expert at UNSW Sydney, said one in five creators already had problems with copyright infringement without AI. But she added the issues became even more complex when the creators were First Nations people, “partly because of lack of control over ownership and respect for Aboriginal culture”.She gave an example of an organisation paying to use artwork or images of Aboriginal people themselves, then later using AI to “update” or repurpose those images without permission.“The corporate client can pay you once and then make unauthorised Aboriginal derivative work and use the faces of the artists without consent,” she said.“Not only do [the artists] not get the repeat business, but when they go to make new work they’re competing against an AI.”The National Association for the Visual Arts (Nava) said Indigenous data sovereignty “recognises the right of First Nations peoples to exercise authority over their data, cultural material and knowledge”.In a submission to the joint select committee inquiry on artificial intelligence, Nava pointed to work by the Wuthathi and Meriam lawyer Terri Janke, an international authority on Indigenous cultural and intellectual property, who has “documented AI scrapingIndigenous artcentre websites, removing artists’ names and altering their work”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJanke has also warned of the broader risk of AI reproducing cultural knowledge without regard to its accuracy or appropriate use.“Nava members have also raised concerns about AI-generated ‘Aboriginal-style’ images and designs that imitate community-specific techniques, stories, motifs and mark-making,” the submission said. “These images can be presented and sold as Indigenous or Indigenous-inspired work, spreading misinformation, causing cultural and economic harm and competing with work by First Nations artists.”Bowrey and a colleague, the creative technologies expert Associate Prof Oliver Bown, have proposed what they call a copyright plus framework, which would give creators more power over the use of their work by forcing AI companies to disclose their data sources and giving artists the right to say no to having their work scraped or mimicked. They have also proposed imposing a levy on AI companies to create a scheme to pay creative professionals and establish a cultural fund, as well as the use of takedown notices for fake content.Bowrey said they wrote the draft policy based on the parameters of what the government has said so far.Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposalRead moreA spokesperson for the attorney general said Australian creatives were “world class” and that the government was committed to supporting them.“That’s why we’re continuing to consult with creators, media organisations and AI companies on a range of options to ensure any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation,” the spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsIndigenous artIndigenous AustraliansAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Tributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crash | Spain | The Guardian
description: Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
Content: Dr Marta Shahbazi ‘was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist’, said the Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge.Photograph: MRC Laboratory of Molecular BiologyView image in fullscreenDr Marta Shahbazi ‘was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist’, said the Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge.Photograph: MRC Laboratory of Molecular BiologySpainTributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crashDr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biologyHaroon SiddiqueSun 1 Nov 2026 14.36 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in theSpanish train collisionon Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.Dr Marta Shahbazi, 41, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.The LMB said the mother of two had recently won the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology’s scientific excellence prize. She had been due to be presented with the award during its conference in El Rompido, Andalucía.In a LinkedIn post, the LMB said it was deeply saddened by her death, which was “a profound shock and a huge loss”, adding: “Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies.”It said she was a role model who had written eloquently about balancing her family and career, describing herself as a “mother scientist”.Dr Roser Vento-Tormo, a group leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute outside Cambridge, wrote: “Marta Shahbazi was a beautiful person: a close collaborator, a treasured friend, and an inspiration to me both as a scientist and as a mother.“As a scientist, we shared so many dreams. We co-supervised two students together, and I cannot describe how much joy it was to work alongside her.“Some of our work will still be published in the coming months, and anyone who reads it will feel the passion she poured into everything she did …“My thoughts are with her family. Anyone who knew Marta could see how deeply they were a unit, and how much they meant to her.”The Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), based in Santiago de Compostela,Spain, paid tribute to Shahbazi as “a brilliant young researcher”.The disaster was Spain’s second high-speed rail crash this year. Both collisions occurred on the line between the central city of Madrid, Spain’s capital, and Seville, in the Andalucía region in the south of the country.Three days of national mourning were observed from Thursday. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described the incident as a “tragedy” andhas promised an investigation.Explore more on these topicsSpainTrain crashesUniversity of CambridgeMedical researchBiologyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
Content: A still from a social media video appears to show the result of drone strikes on an oil refinery in Russia’s Samara oblast on Friday.Photograph: social media/ReutersView image in fullscreenA still from a social media video appears to show the result of drone strikes on an oil refinery in Russia’s Samara oblast on Friday.Photograph: social media/ReutersUkraineUkraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineriesKremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sitesLuke Hardingin KyivSun 1 Nov 2026 12.20 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 19.30 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure fromDonald Trumpahead of the US midterm elections, as a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky ended on Sunday night.Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.The Wall Street Journal hadreported that Ukraine had given in to pressurefrom the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper thatthey never agreed to a demandfrom Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on Russia restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv was now “simply ignoring” US wishes.Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce shows de-escalation is possible, says ZelenskyyRead moreZelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he said, as part of Ukraine’s continuing “long-range sanctions”.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows smoke rising from the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery in the Samara region of Russia after a reported Ukrainian drone attack on Friday.Photograph: European Union/Copernicus/Sentinel-2/ReutersZelenskyy said his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four Ukrainian regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the ​deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram.Kyivexperienced power cuts lasting eight to 10 hours on Sunday after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sqkm (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sqkm (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”The latest attacks came beforea six-day local ceasefirebrokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, came to an end in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Hundreds of residentswere reunited with their loved onesover the weekend in northern Ukraine, with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success.“The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended,” said Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, hailing what had been an “important step in our joint humanitarian efforts”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleshky. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between ⁠Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would ⁠pave the ⁠way ​for broader peace efforts.“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, and Kremlin officials said on Sunday thatVladimir Putinwas willing to talk directly to Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged.He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces, which the Kremlin does not control but says it has “annexed”.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS foreign policyVolodymyr ZelenskyyMelania TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say
Content: Giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically.Photograph: Craig Brown/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenGiving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically.Photograph: Craig Brown/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsBrexitUK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe schemeExclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials sayKiran Stacey,Lisa O’CarrollandJessica ElgotSun 1 Nov 2026 12.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made inEuropeindustrial programme.The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.British officials insist, however, they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed protectionist industrial scheme, which will impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc.Rachel Reeves says UK’s future is in EU as she backs Andy Burnham on BrexitRead moreOn Sunday the former chancellor Rachel Reevespraised the prime minister, Andy Burnham, for a willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe – saying she believed Britain’s future was within the EU. But in her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury whenBurnhamtook office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.Ministers hope if such an agreement is reached at a Brussels summit later this month it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off.But giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans.One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, in September.Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty ImagesA government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU and tolay out optionsfor how the relationship could develop in the future, including full re-entry.In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”.Before the summit, agreement is understood to have largely been reached in a number of areas, including on emissions trading, agricultural products and a youth mobility scheme, with reports suggesting up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study. EU member states had demanded between 100,000 and 150,000, with some arguing in favour of no quota.The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers.19:01What makes Andy Burnham think we can rejoin the EU? | Politics WeeklyBritish access to the Made in Europe scheme, which is due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities are the two remaining hurdles.EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiationsto a standstillthis year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks.The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end the small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore the possibility of restoring the UK’s access to EU databases.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states.Member states are pushing for firm language on fees while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. Francedropped its oppositionto the inclusion of the UK in the Industrial Accelerator Act with a proposal any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved as along as it dynamically aligned on trade measures.Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the discussion on fees from the joint statement at the summit entirely,deferring any agreement for six months. But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement to allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”.Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discounts for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses.Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that under the most expensive scenario, which involves reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and very high levels of demand, the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”.Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course.UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme.The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme,prompting warningsfrom the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – which was the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position with a new proposal to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs.This could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than in the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary,recently told the Guardianhe would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels.The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements.The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out that text, but after a last-minute cancellation, work has continued between officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission.Explore more on these topicsBrexitEuropean UnionStudentsInternational studentsHigher educationEuropeForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Attempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot police | France | The Guardian
description: Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania
Content: A riot police officer in Paris is hit by a molotov cocktail during a charge against demonstrators at the end of the nationwide day of protests in France.Photograph: Sameer al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA riot police officer in Paris is hit by a molotov cocktail during a charge against demonstrators at the end of the nationwide day of protests in France.Photograph: Sameer al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceAttempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot policeYouth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and AlbaniaJon Henleyin ParisSun 1 Nov 2026 11.24 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.22 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a police officer and Germany’s interior minister has called for harsh penalties after peaceful and mainly youth-led protests across Europe ended in violence.In Portugal, police – some with dogs – cleared protest camps with baton charges, while security forces inSwitzerlandwere attacked with paving stones.Protests over the education system, deteriorating public services, declining prospects, unaffordable housing and the spiralling cost of living haveshaken a number of countriesthis autumn.Violence erupted inthe French capital as well as Marseille, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Lyon and Toulouse on Saturday night after an estimated 320,000 demonstrators, some in Halloween costumes, took to the streets.View image in fullscreenProtesters in Halloween costumes gather in the La Plaine square in Marseille. Officials say 320,000 people took part in protests across France.Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters in Halloween costumes at an unauthorised demonstration in Marseille over the high cost of living.Photograph: Coust Laurent/ABACA/ShutterstockAs the rallies ended, masked and hooded rioters arrived and caused what the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as an “extraordinary” level of violence. More than 770 people were arrested.In Paris, the prosecutor’s office said incendiary devices were thrown at a group of about 15 gendarmes and police officers and a formal investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.Injuries reportedly included second-degree burns in an incident captured on mobile phone video and shared on social media and broadcast on French television.The level of physical violence and looting was significantly lower than on 17 October, when 2,600 people were arrested and as many as 3,000 shops pillaged inone of the worst nightsof urban unrest in France’s recent history.View image in fullscreenRiot police in action in Paris. More than 770 people were arrested across France for public order offences.Photograph: Bernard Jules/ABACA/ShutterstockIn Germany, looters and rioters ⁠rampaged through Frankfurt, the country’s financial hub, damaging stores and injuring more than 100 police officers.“The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable,” said Alexander Dobrindt, the hardline interior minister. He singled out “violent leftwing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community”, adding: “Tough penalties must follow this breach of the peace.”Dobrindt told the tabloid newspaper Bild that deploying a heavy police presence across multiple locations had been effective. “Excesses of ​violence like those ‌in Paris were ​prevented thanks to our ​highly committed police forces,” he said.View image in fullscreenA protester in a Batman costume salutes in front of a fire started by rioters in Frankfurt. German authorities have promised a strong response.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersMore than 100,000 protesters marched in over 30 German cities on Saturday to demand better ⁠education and lower living costs in protests led by the “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z will sort it) campaign.Hooded rioters ⁠damaged 17 Frankfurt shops, looting five of them, and threw missiles including petrol bombs, according to Roman Poseck, the state interior minister for Hesse.More than 100 of the 1,300 police officers deployed in the city were injured and 54 suspects, ‌aged from 13 to 29, were arrested. “I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMost of those arrested were German nationals, the minister said, adding that police estimated they had been confronted with “between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background”.Violence also broke out Saturday night in Cologne, where police used water cannon to disperse the crowd, and in Berlin, where protesters attacked police with bottles and fireworks. Gen Z regelt posted a statement distancing itself from all violence.View image in fullscreenRiot police clear Lisbon’s Rossio Square of activists protesting over housing affordability.Photograph: Manuel de Almeida/EPAInPortugal, riot police removed protesters by force from Rossio Square in Lisbon at about 4.30am on Sunday after thousands of people angry at the housing crisis marched through the city on Saturday and set up camp.The protesters want Portugal’s minority centre-right government to withdraw a ⁠bill that makes ⁠evictions easier and ends rent caps on new leases. A smaller camp in Porto was also cleared by force.InAlbania, masked protesters hurled stones and firebombs at police in the capital, Tirana, on the margins of a demonstration demanding the resignation of the prime minister, Edi Rama, over perceived corruption.Youths threw paving stones and firebombs at police and set fire to rubbish bins at the end of a largely peaceful protest. The interior ministry said on Friday that 350 people had been hurt in the protests, including 200 police, with 269 minors arrested.View image in fullscreenAn anti-government protest in Tirana turned violent with protesters hurling stones and petrol bombs at police.Photograph: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIn Switzerland, hundreds of protesters gathered in Zürich and Basel on Saturday night for unauthorised demonstrations – both of which ended in violence – under the slogan: “We’ve had enough in Switzerland, too.”In Zürich, police used water cannon, teargas and rubber bullets to disperse rioters attacking them with fireworks, bottles and stones,Swiss media reported. A police patrol car was damaged and rubbish bins and electric bikes set on fire.In Basel, police said about 150 people gathered in the city centre at around 9pm. Shop windows were smashed, facades tagged with graffiti and bins and bikes set on fire, with incidents also reported in Geneva.Explore more on these topicsFrancePortugalAlbaniaGermanySwitzerlandProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz  | Iran | The Guardian
description: Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Content: Young Iranians walk past a large anti-US wall mural in Tehran on Sunday. Iran’s foreign minister has said he hopes the US chooses ‘diplomacy over other paths’ to end the crisis.Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYoung Iranians walk past a large anti-US wall mural in Tehran on Sunday. Iran’s foreign minister has said he hopes the US chooses ‘diplomacy over other paths’ to end the crisis.Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesIranNegotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of HormuzThird day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopeningPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorSun 1 Nov 2026 12.49 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 13.25 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOfficials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday withQatartrying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.TheUnited Arab Emiratesenvoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.View image in fullscreenIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the country was ready for both defence and diplomacy.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.View image in fullscreenThe US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution.Photograph: Erik S Lesser/AFP/Getty ImagesSpeaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranStrait of HormuzQatarUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Tens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in Delhi | India | The Guardian
description: Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
Content: Rahul Gandhi and fellow leaders of the opposition Congress party wave at supporters during the protest on Sunday.Photograph: Vipin/APView image in fullscreenRahul Gandhi and fellow leaders of the opposition Congress party wave at supporters during the protest on Sunday.Photograph: Vipin/APIndiaTens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in DelhiLed by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter rollHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiSun 1 Nov 2026 11.11 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 01.20 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against theNarendra Modigovernment continue to gather momentum.Led by the Congress party, India’s opposition alliance has brought together supporters from across the country, amidgrowing angerover a large-scale revision of the country’s voter roll that has seen 130 million names erased.Opposition leaders have alleged the process gives Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) an electoral advantage, and have called for the resignation and impeachment of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. The BJP has denied the claims.Addressing tens of thousands of party workers and supporters, the opposition leaderRahul Gandhisaid Kumar had “carried out the biggest crime. He has tried to silence the voice of people, strangulate our country.”Gandhi said the opposition, united under the acronymIndia(Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance), would not let “democracy be finished in the country” and warned Modi: “You can’t run anywhere.”View image in fullscreenTens of thousands of people attended the march in Delhi on Sunday – short of the million the Congress party leaders had predicted.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersThe protest was one of the largest shows of opposition strength in years, taking place amid a wider resurgence of anti-government dissent which has been systematically crushed over the 12 years of the Modi regime.The biggest challenge to the regime has come from youth-led protests that erupted over the summer – led by a movement that began satiricallycalling itself the “Cockroaches”– and forced the resignation of one of Modi’s cabinet ministers. Cockroach-led protestshit the streets againlast month, also in opposition to the revision of the electoral rolls known as special intensive revision (SIR).The opposition, in particular the Congress party, has become emboldened in the wake of the youth mobilisation. However, a significant trust deficit remains between the establishment opposition parties and the Cockroach movement. On Sunday, while Cockroach leaders had extended their support to the opposition rally, they did not attend themselves.Congress leaders had publicly predicted that a million people would attend the rally, but in the end the numbers were in the tens of thousands and empty seats were visible in the protest arena.The somewhat lacklustre turnout demonstrated the challenge still faced by Congress and its opposition allies in being seen as a formidable and viable challenger to the Modi government.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (India) bloc gather at the rally under the slogan 'Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao' (save votes, save the country).Photograph: Mihir Singh/EPAThe opposition, led by Gandhi, has lost the last three general elections to the BJP as the parties have widely failed to counter the BJP’s muscular Hindu nationalist rhetoric. The Modi government has systematically gone after political opponents, leaving little space for dissent.The majority of those gathered at the protest site on Sunday were party workers and organisers who had been bussed in, and there was very little evidence of a mobilisation of the young people who have been participating in the Cockroach-led protests. According to the opposition, many of their buses were stopped from enteringDelhiby police barricades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShalini, a restaurant owner from Goa, said she was there “not for the opposition but because I am against the BJP and how they are trying to remove any avenue of dissent in this country. I’m not particularly for any opposition party.”She said many questions still remained about the viability and support of that opposition, but she sensed a “groundswell of dissatisfaction with the BJP and the opposition is cashing in on it – good for them”.‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streetsRead moreThe issue of the revision of the electoral rolls first emerged last year, but recently erupted into a national scandal after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper revealed irregularities and discord within the election commission over its implementation.Millions of allegedly eligible voters have discovered their names have been left off the electoral rolls, with Muslims and minorities disproportionately targeted. This week, Human Rights Watch said the accusations raised “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections”.Arwind Chaudhery, 48, said he too was not aligned with any party. “I am here because SIR has undermined our democracy and the situation has got so bad, it is beyond repair or rectification,” he said. “So it is natural that people will be driven out to protest and that is a ray of hope.”The BJP have sought to dismiss the opposition protests as anarchy. The party’s president, JP Nadda, said Sunday’s rally would be the “nail in the coffin” for the opposition alliance. He said the protest was “not ​an act of respect for democracy. ‌It is a calculated conspiracy ​to plunge the nation into anarchy, ​all in the name of democracy.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaProtestSouth and central AsiaRahul GandhiNarendra ModiDelhinewsShareReuse this content

title: Teenage violinist wins BBC Young Musician 2026, after first all-female final | BBC Young Musician | The Guardian
description: Judges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity
Author: Imogen Tilden
Headline: Judges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity
Content: ‘My absolute dream…’ Sofia Demetriades, winner of 2026’s BBC’s Young Musician.Photograph: BBC Studios/Celf CalonView image in fullscreen‘My absolute dream…’ Sofia Demetriades, winner of 2026’s BBC’s Young Musician.Photograph: BBC Studios/Celf CalonBBC Young MusicianTeenage violinist wins BBC Young Musician 2026, after first all-female finalJudges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturityImogen TildenSun 1 Nov 2026 16.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA teenage violinist has won theBBC Young Musiciancompetition 2026, in the first all-female final in the competition’s 48-year history.The judges, Joanna MacGregor, Ben Gernon and Errollyn Wallen, hailed Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity.The 18-year-old is from Leicestershire, and in her first year of undergraduate studies at the Royal Academy of Music.The brainchild of Humphrey Burton, the biennialBBCcompetition was set up in 1978 and has produced finalists such as Sheku Kanneh-Mason, Alison Balsom, Stephen Hough and, in 2004, Nicola Benedetti, who was the last violinist to win.Demetriades was one of several hundred to send in a video application, before 40 young players were selected to attend live auditions in Bath Spa University to gain one of eight places in the quarter-finals – which took place on Demetriades’ 18th birthday. Among her fellow quarter-finalists was the first accordion player to reach the final stages, 14-year-oldSylvester Maschi.View image in fullscreenRecorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni, violinist Sofia Demetriades and saxophonist Kezia Colton, finalists of BBC Young Musician 2026.Photograph: BBC/Betsan EvansEach of the three finalists performed a concerto with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales, conducted by Alpesh Chauhan in a concert at Bristol Beacon. An 18-year-old saxophone player,Kezia Colton, performed Takashi Yoshimatsu’s 1994 Cyber Bird Saxophone Concerto, while 17-year-old recorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni played Graham Fitkin’s Recorder Concerto.Fitkin’s virtuosic concerto involves six different recorders, ranging from the giant contrabass, about 1.6 metres high, to the tiniest sopranino. It was originally commissioned by Debretzeni’s teacher, Barbara Law, and it was given itspremiere performance in 2017by 2014’s Young Musician finalist, Sophie Westbrooke. And there was a further connection this year to previous competitions – 2022’s overall winner, the percussionistJordan Ashman, joined Kezia Colton onstage for Yoshimatsu’s concerto.“Kezia plays with incredible verve and spirit, said Wallen. “Her performance was sassy and cool,” said Gernon, “but her more intimate playing is incredibly strong too.”The judges hailed the “electricity, aliveness, and beautiful intensity” that Debretzeni brought to Fitkin’s concerto. “She took us on a musical journey … we were inside every note,” said Wallen.“Before the competition I hadn’t planned on being a musician,” said Debretzeni. “I wanted to study psychology … but this has been so inspiring it’s made me want to pursue music. It’s been literally life-changing.”Demetriades was acclaimed as a simply extraordinary musician by MacGregor. “She performs with her eyes, achieving dizzying technical feats but she looks as if she’s enjoying it,” she said.“Sofia’s innate sense of colour, musical style and architecture combines with an effortless technique, and a joy for whatever music she’s playing. In a competition full of gifted and dedicated young musicians, Sofia’s sensitivity and sophistication stood out in every round. I’m very excited to watch her musicianship develop even further in the years ahead.”The winnerreceives the trophy, a cash prize of £3,000towards music studies as well as recording and broadcast opportunities on Radio 3, including with one of the BBC ensembles. All three finalists will work withYoung Classical Artists Truston managing their future careers.“I am so honoured and thrilled to have been a part of BBC Young Musician,” said Demetriades. “I loved playing in the quarter-final on my 18th birthday. I didn’t think I could top that, but to go on to be crowned winner is my absolute dream! It was pure delight to share the stage with BBC NOW, Alpesh Chauhan and my fellow finalists – I really hope to play alongside them again soon.”The final and the three previous stages are available to watchon BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsBBC Young MusicianClassical musicBBCAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Shabana Mahmood’s new rules raise fears of staff shortages in health and social care and of second Windrush scandal
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Shabana Mahmood’s new rules raise fears of staff shortages in health and social care and of second Windrush scandal
