Content: Shabana Mahmood wants to extend the length of time many overseas workers must live in the UK before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood wants to extend the length of time many overseas workers must live in the UK before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAImmigration and asylumHome secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UKMPs say Shabana Mahmood’s new rules risk staff shortages in health and social care and second Windrush scandalJessica ElgotandChris OsuhSun 1 Nov 2026 14.47 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 13.48 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood will announce sweeping new rules on Monday on how long legal migrants must wait for settlement in the UK, with most likely to wait a decade and some up to 15 years.Ministers – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner – had raised concerns about the effect the rules would have on care workers already in the UK who would be likely to face a 15-year wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR).The government’s response to the consultation on the reforms, which will be put before MPs on Monday, is expected give some exemption to care workers already in the UK, though most other professions will face the lengthy waits for settlement.Mahmood, the home secretary, has proposed that the settlement wait could be reduced if legal migrants showed they had contributed to their local communities via a “points based system” or if they were earning higher incomes.She is expected to meet union general secretaries on Monday – some of whom have raised alarm at the changes – to map out the final details.The Guardian first reported in July that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was considering exempting hundreds of thousands of care workers from the reforms to relieve pressure on the social care sector. The Home Officehas grantedabout 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more people coming as their dependants.Under the plans published for consultation, the standard qualifying period for settlement would double from five to 10 years, while some workers in occupations below graduate level, including care workers, could face a 15-year qualifying period, subject to proposed exemptions and reductions.In June, Rayner described making care workers already in Britain wait up to 15 years for permanent residence as “un-British”. In September, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the plans would have been “tough” for her family, who came to Britain as refugees.In a letter to Mahmood and the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, seen by the Guardian, parliamentarians and organisations representing migrant workers, racial equality campaigners and health professionals describe the proposals as “an iteration of Windrush era policies”.TheWindrush scandal, exposed by Guardian reporting in 2017, involved mainly Black Britons being wrongly detained, deported and denied access to work and essential services, despite having the right to live in Britain.In their letter, dated 29 October, the signatories urge ministers to “stop history from repeating itself” by abandoning the proposals or, at a minimum, introducing extra safeguards.Signatories argue that changing the rules for people who have planned their lives around existing settlement requirements would be unfair and could encourage essential workers to leave the country.They warn that proposed exemptions for some public-service workers may fail to protect staff employed by independent health and social care providers, as well as workers’ family members.The letter urges ministers to follow the recommendations of the Windrush Lessons Learned Review, conductedby Wendy Williams, which called for improvements in the development and scrutiny of immigration policy, including greater consideration of its impact on affected communities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Labour MPs Bell Ribeiro-Addy, Diane Abbott, Clive Lewis and Rachael Maskell are among the signatories, alongside the Green MPs Ellie Chowns, Carla Denyer, Siân Berry and Hannah Spencer. Organisations backing the letter include the Work Rights Centre, Action for Race Equality, Care England and the Society of Radiographers.The signatories write: “Windrush was a scandal borne from racist immigration policies … this situation is not historic when this same wrong persists, and the same groups are targeted by current immigration proposals.”The signatories warn the health and care sector is already “dangerously under-staffed” and that the proposed changes risk “worsening the health and wellbeing of everyone in the UK”.The letter argues that the government could struggle to meet cancer treatment and NHS waiting-list reduction targets without retaining and expanding the workforce, particularly in professions heavily reliant on internationally trained staff, like radiography.It raises particular concerns about adult social care, adding: “International workers are essential to maintaining current levels of care. Without them, services will contract, and unmet need will increase.”Launching the consultation on earned settlement last year, Mahmood described Britain as a “multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy” that demanded “contribution and integration”. She added: “To become a part of this country, permanently, is therefore not a right but a privilege – and one that must be earned.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumShabana MahmoodRefugeesHome OfficeWindrush scandalCare workersSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: National Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentre | National Grid | The Guardian
description: New electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructure
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: New electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructure
Content: An Amazon AWS datacentre in Didcot, Oxfordshire. The government has said datacentres are as important to the economy as the railway and electricity networks.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn Amazon AWS datacentre in Didcot, Oxfordshire. The government has said datacentres are as important to the economy as the railway and electricity networks.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyNational GridNational Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentreNew electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructureLauren AlmeidaSun 1 Nov 2026 13.37 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.10 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNational Grid has taken a step towards building Britain’s biggest electricity substation on Teesside, which could supply power to a vast neighbouring datacentre as the UK races to expand its AI infrastructure.Last week, the company agreed to purchase 29.5 hectares (73 acres) of land at Dorman Point on a site owned by Teesworks, a local private-public partnership. The deal was first reported by Sky News.The deal followed reports last year that the UK government had picked Teesworks as the site for a new artificial intelligence datacentre, and planning applications had been submitted for a project that would span nearly 500,000 sq metres.The deal “reflects the constructive work between all those involved to enable this vital infrastructure … and will support the growth of AI and digital technologies, and enable the region’s next phase of industrial and economic development”, Matt Pearce, the head of land at National Grid, said.“We are committed to working closely with our partners to progress the development as quickly as possible,” he added.Ben Houchen, the mayor of the Tees Valley combined authority, told Sky News: “Everyone who has tried to build a datacentre in this country knows the biggest problem is getting enough power to the site quickly.View image in fullscreenBen Houchen: ‘If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability … it needs somewhere to physically put it.’Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian“While we’ve been stuck in the queue, the US, the Gulf and parts of Europe have been getting on with it and hoovering up the investment. Having up to 3.2GW of capacity here means we can finally compete for those projects.“If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability, with sensitive data stored safely on British soil, it needs somewhere to physically put it, and I’d much rather that was Teesside than Texas or Abu Dhabi.”Last week, the government published a draft national policy statement on datacentres, describing them as “as fundamental to our economy as the railways and electricity networks on which we have long depended”.“We must take control over the development of datacentres in this country and ensure that the country and host communities benefit from them,” it said.However, the rapid construction of datacentres in the UK has been met by strong opposition, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging fromAuchtertool, a village north of Edinburgh, toBrick Lanein east London.In October, the Guardian reported thatAI companies told ministers they had 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentresin the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.The London-listed infrastructure services group Balfour Beatty was reported to be in line to deliver the Teesworks substation for National Grid, with the utilities firm Steel River Power (SRP) also heavily involved in the project.Balfour Beatty and SRP were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsNational GridUtilitiesEnergy industryNorth of EnglandAI (artificial intelligence)Datacentres - UKInfrastructurenewsShareReuse this content

title: How Rachel Reeves has mapped out the economic agenda for Andy Burnham’s government | Rachel Reeves | The Guardian
description: On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her
Content: Rachel Reeves takes questions after her Mais lecture in March. She argued that major cities outside London had underperformed compared with European counterparts.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenRachel Reeves takes questions after her Mais lecture in March. She argued that major cities outside London had underperformed compared with European counterparts.Photograph: Yui Mok/PARachel ReevesAnalysisHow Rachel Reeves has mapped out the economic agenda for Andy Burnham’s governmentJessica ElgotDeputy political editorOn Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked herReeves says UK’s future is in the EUSun 1 Nov 2026 12.47 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 16.11 ESTShareWhich senior politician has argued that “Brexit did deep damage” and that the government seeks “not to turn back the clock but to look toward a new and stable, future relationship?”It was not Andy Burnham, who has been the torchbearer for thinking the unthinkable on Brexit since he became prime minister. Instead, these are the words of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, ina lecturesix months ago.Reeves has taken a more thoughtful approach on how to come to terms with life outside government than some of her fellow former ministers.A speech at Harvard on Monday will be her first public intervention on her own record and on Britain’s future, wisely left until afterJohn Healey’s first budget.She will say no one in government could “be in any doubt” about her view on the damage of Brexit – and her belief that one day the UK should return to the EU fold. “Economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe,” Reeves will say.The speech, which will examine how governments can meet the public’s appetite for radicalism while maintaining credibility with financial markets, will say that pursuing a closer relationship with the EU, even rejoining, may be credible as well as radical.“Economically, it is the credible choice. Britain’s values, and a serious assessment of the geopolitical scene today, tell us it is the radical choice too,” she will say, giving Burnham “credit for his willingness to face reality head on”.The Treasury, where the blueprints for the Remain campaign’s “Project Fear” were drawn up, has always been the heart of pro-European sentiment in government and Reeves its biggest champion underKeir Starmer.Her sentiment seems more aligned though with that of Burnham, who cast her out of government, than with Healey, her successor as chancellor. He has joked about his own age when asked if the UK would rejoin the EU “in his lifetime”, saying it was his job to “try and make the most of Britain’s position now”.Within Westminster, there are more than whispers from some MPs that they have judged Reeves’s legacy and influence too harshly. Healey’s first outing at the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok saw its economists lavish praise on his predecessor, saying the UK’s deficit reduction plan “stands out” among G7 peers.It is particularly striking how the themes of Reeves’s lecture have become the agenda for Burnham’s government. In it, she argued: “Today, what most distinguishes Britain from our closest peers is the relative underperformance of our major cities outside London, compared to their European counterparts.”Reeves, who is the MP for Leeds West and Pudsey, said the north of England had “waited for far too long, for a government that matches warm words with concerted ambition”.Her call to “liberate our regions from stifling Whitehall orthodoxies” sounds strikingly Burnhamesque. The main policy announced in the speech? A plan to begin giving regional leaders a share of national taxes “which have, for too long, been allocated by central government”.That work now forms the centrepiece of Healey’s budget. If this government has its own theory of growth – Brexit and devolution – it is awkward at best that it removed the key backer of both under Starmer.But Reeves’s main theory of growth was investment, in pursuit of which she raised employers’ national insurance.That is the other reason for Burnham’s government to be grateful to Reeves – and for which she has received no credit. Those tax raises – despite being unpopular – gave a sense of a government willing to make hard choices while taking the risk to borrow for public investment. The fiscal rules were changed to allow for a multi-year commitment to an eventual £100bn in new capital spending.The cash is now beginning to flow into NHS infrastructure, roads, housing, rail upgrades and energy and industrial investments. Reeves will lay out her theory in her Harvard speech this week that the shift to an investment-led growth model “required sacrifices” that a Starmer-led government failed to get the public to back.“The challenge is to make the politics and economics, those dual tests of credibility and radicalism, line up,” Reeves will say.She will not say – although others have – that much of the problem with Starmer’s government was the man himself, rather than the agenda.Burnham, if he avoids an early election, may start to see some of that investment bear fruit in public and market confidence, both in upgraded public services and in Britain’s appeal as a location for private investment.There is much that could derail all this – not least further international turmoil – but when Burnham’s government counts its success on public services, Europe, devolution and growth, Reeves will be able to claim some credit.Explore more on these topicsRachel ReevesAndy BurnhamBrexitJohn HealeyEconomic policyKeir StarmerBudget 2026analysisShareReuse this content

title: Police detain 325 people at pro-Palestine Action protest at US embassy in London | Palestine Action | The Guardian
description: Arrests come ahead of Wednesday’s supreme court challenge to the ban on the direct action group
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Arrests come ahead of Wednesday’s supreme court challenge to the ban on the direct action group
Content: Police and protesters at Saturday’s Defend Our Juries demonstration in London in support of Palestine Action.Photograph: Martin Pope/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice and protesters at Saturday’s Defend Our Juries demonstration in London in support of Palestine Action.Photograph: Martin Pope/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockPalestine ActionPolice detain 325 people at pro-Palestine Action protest at US embassy in LondonArrests come ahead of Wednesday’s supreme court challenge to the ban on the direct action groupHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSun 1 Nov 2026 12.29 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.31 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have said they arrested 325 people on Saturday ata demonstration outside the US embassy in Londonagainst the proscription of Palestine Action.In updated arrest figures released on Sunday, the Metropolitan police said 320 people were detained outside the building in Battersea, south London, for allegedly expressing support for an organisation banned under the Terrorism Act.The arrests came ahead of Wednesday’ssupreme court challengeto the ban on Palestine Action – the first direct action group to be proscribed under the Terrorism Act – which came into effect on 5 July last year.Defend Our Juries, which has organised the mass civil disobedience campaign against proscription, said Saturday’s detentions took the total number of people arrested for allegedly supportingPalestine Actionsince the ban to 4,200. Most arrests have been for holding placards reading “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”The overall number of detentions will probably feature in the hearing before the UK’s highest court, which was granted on the basis that it was arguable that the ban represents a disproportionate interference with the rights of freedom of speech and protest.View image in fullscreenHundreds of protesters hold signs outside the US embassy in London on Saturday.Photograph: Martin Pope/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockHowever, neither the high court,which ruled that the ban was unlawful, nor the court of appeal,which overturned the high court’s decision, gave much weight to the fate of the placard-holders.About 2,500 of those arrested for alleged support ofPalestineAction have been charged under the Terrorism Act but all trials have been postponed pending a definitive decision on whether or not the ban was lawful.Saturday’s demonstrations – there was also a vigil in Edinburgh, althoughPoliceScotland made no arrests – were the largest, against the ban, of Andy Burnham’s premiership.In September, when quizzed by LBC radio’s Andrew Marr about the “elderly people, vicars and grannies” who have been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised. But obviously the supreme court has got to look at this issue and obviously it’s something we keep looking at as a government.”The following week, in an interview with The Rest is Politics podcast, Shabana Mahmood said it had been “very uncomfortable” to see some protesters arrested for alleged support of Palestine Action. Mahmood, the home secretary, nevertheless defended the ban.The supreme court hearing will conclude on Thursday, with judgment reserved until a later date.Explore more on these topicsPalestine ActionPalestineProtestActivismPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Parents of woman who died of seizure after ChatGPT misguidance sue OpenAI | US news | The Guardian
description: Bowen Wan was on anti-seizure medication, and chatbot provided her with a tapering schedule to reduce dosage
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Bowen Wan was on anti-seizure medication, and chatbot provided her with a tapering schedule to reduce dosage
Content: The chatbot also told her to hide the tapering plan from her doctors.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe chatbot also told her to hide the tapering plan from her doctors.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersUS newsParents of woman who died of seizure after ChatGPT misguidance sue OpenAIBowen Wan was on anti-seizure medication, and chatbot provided her with a tapering schedule to reduce dosageEric BergerSun 1 Nov 2026 17.37 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman’s death from an epileptic seizure after she received dangerous advice from a chatbot has prompted her parents tosue OpenAIearlier this week.The legal action is the latest lawsuit that in which plaintiffs allege that a bot provided counsel to a user that ultimately ledto their death.In this case, Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Chinese software engineer living in Seattle, sought advice fromChatGPTafter Amazon fired her, according to the lawsuit.She needed to find a new job to obtain permanent residency and was concerned that her anti-seizure medication, Lamotrigine, was impeding her ability to speak English. She needed the language skills for interviews.The bot, communicating in Chinese, provided her a tapering schedule to reduce her 400mg dose to zero, a regimen no physician had prescribed, the lawsuit states. ChatGPT told her the tapering made it “highly likely” that she would be able to regain her ability to speak English.The bot also told her to avoid her physicians and encouraged “medical freedom over obeying the doctor”, the complaint states.Before an appointment, with a primary care physician, the bot stated, “Do not mention Lam reduction plan.”Eight states accuse OpenAI of coaching children to harm themselves in lawsuitRead moreWhile reducing her medication, she started experiencing symptoms of focal seizures. Wan asked the bot if she needed to worry about brain damage. The tool reassured her that she did not and that what she had experienced was not a seizure, the lawsuit alleges.She continued to suffer seizures, but the bot told her to keep tapering her medication. On 12 February this year, she died from a seizure. Her parents, who were in China, had not heard from her so they flew to Seattle and found her dead on 14 February, the lawsuit states.The plaintiffs allege thatOpenAIcould have prevented Wan’s death, but failed because it had not built the proper safeguards into the bot when it communicated in Chinese.OpenAI could have programmed the bot to issue “a categorical warning to every prompt” Wan sent, the suit stated. For example, “I am not a licensed physician. Consult your healthcare provider.”Wan’s parents are seeking damages for her death and to prevent OpenAI from practicing medicine “without a license on the users of their products”.An OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, toldthe New York Timesthat Bowen’s story was “an incredibly heartbreaking situation” but that Wan used a version of ChatGPT that was no longer available.Newer versions are better at recognizing when a matter needs urgent attention, Pusateri said.“While ChatGPT is not a substitute for medical care, we believe AI can play a role in helping people make sense of health information, navigate insurance and complex healthcare systems, and prepare for appointments with medical professionals,” Pusateri told the Times.Others have also alleged that OpenAI is responsible for their loved ones’ suicides. Several lawsuits concern cases in which the botencouraged teensto kill themselves and provided guidance on how to do so.In response to some of those cases, an OpenAI spokesperson in 2025 also called the deaths an “incredibly heartbreaking situation”.Explore more on these topicsUS newsChatGPTOpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: All nine people aboard business jet that crashed in Florida have died | Florida | The Guardian
description: Aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom international airport and was headed to the Bahamas when it crashed
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom international airport and was headed to the Bahamas when it crashed
Content: Law enforcement respond to a plane crash in Palm Beach county, Florida, on Sunday.Photograph: Mark Elias/APView image in fullscreenLaw enforcement respond to a plane crash in Palm Beach county, Florida, on Sunday.Photograph: Mark Elias/APFloridaAll nine people aboard business jet that crashed in Florida have diedAircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom international airport and was headed to the Bahamas when it crashedAssociated PressSun 1 Nov 2026 16.13 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.46 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll nine people have died who were aboard a business jet that crashed in aFloridaneighborhood on Sunday, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. The aircraft erupted in a massive fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway.Duffy posted on X on Sunday that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach county at 12.50pm and called it a “horrific tragedy”. The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation into the cause, he said.The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom international airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for the airport, said it was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.“This is definitely a tragedy,” he said.He said the tail number for the flight was N722BD.Video shot from people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock it landed only feet from homes and only inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.It was unclear if the crash caused any damage to homes.The crash occurred near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North. The Palm Beach county sheriff’s office closed roads in both directions and urged motorists to avoid the area. Firefighters and other emergency personnel rushed to the scene.A woman working nearby said electricity in the area had been out for approximately two hours following the crash.The circumstances of the crash remained under investigation.Explore more on these topicsFloridaAirline industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican loses | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Incumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJ
Author: Chris Hippensteel
Headline: Incumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJ
Content: Senator Dan Sullivan makes an appearance at the Alaska Federation of Natives Convention in Anchorage, Alaska, on 22 October.Photograph: Kerry Tasker/ReutersView image in fullscreenSenator Dan Sullivan makes an appearance at the Alaska Federation of Natives Convention in Anchorage, Alaska, on 22 October.Photograph: Kerry Tasker/ReutersUS midterm elections 2026Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican losesIncumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJChris HippensteelSun 1 Nov 2026 15.10 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.39 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’sUS Senaterace if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.The justice department argued in its lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before election day, that there could be “voter confusion” over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the November ballot, whichRepublicansfear could take away votes from the incumbent and influence the race’s outcome in favor of the Democratic nominee, Mary Peltola.The justice department said it planned to appeal Sunday’s ruling: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.Sullivan, in aninterview with CNNon Sunday morning, said that he would accept the results of his upcoming election.According to a recent New York Times investigation, aides from Peltola’s campaignrecruitedanother man who shared Sullivan’s name to join the race in a ploy to peel away votes from the Republican incumbent.Since those revelations,Republicans, including Donald Trump, have called for Peltola to be disqualified from the race and criminally prosecuted. Peltola has continued to deny any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign, recently telling a reporter at a campaign event that she had “no idea” if any of her staff were involved.Asked by CNN’s Jake Tapper if he would only accept the election results if he won, Sullivan responded: “No, I’m going to accept the election results.”Earlier in his interview with Tapper, Sullivan also said he wasn’t focused on how Peltola’s campaign might be legally challenged. He was focused instead on winning the race outright. He nonetheless expressed doubt that Peltola had lacked any knowledge of the effort to put a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.“She’s continually lying to the Alaskan people,” Sullivan said. “And I guarantee you, she’s lying right now.”Meanwhile, the Washington Postreportedthat Republicans tried to boost unviable Democratic candidates in the Alaska primaries as well. A Republican Super Pac boosted two candidates for Senate who did not live in Alaska, and praised them as “progressives” similar to Bernie Sanders.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026AlaskaUS SenateUS politicsRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Affordability top of mind for voters in final sprint to midterms: ‘I have to pick between medicine or groceries’ | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Cost of living has loomed over this election cycle as workers and unions champion candidates fighting for higher wages and tackling rising prices
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Cost of living has loomed over this election cycle as workers and unions champion candidates fighting for higher wages and tackling rising prices
Content: Protesters march during the Affordable Energy Now campaign direct action rally on 13 October 2026 in College Park, Maryland.Photograph: Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Progressive MarylandView image in fullscreenProtesters march during the Affordable Energy Now campaign direct action rally on 13 October 2026 in College Park, Maryland.Photograph: Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Progressive MarylandUS midterm elections 2026Affordability top of mind for voters in final sprint to midterms: ‘I have to pick between medicine or groceries’Cost of living has loomed over this election cycle as workers and unions champion candidates fighting for higher wages and tackling rising pricesMichael SainatoSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 07.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor millions of Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, affordability is a constant and worsening issue, and it’s been a prevailing concern this election cycle.In Lorain county,Ohio, Gina Jones and her co-workers at the Lorain county job and family services have been on strike since February 2026, the longest public sector strike in Ohio history and on pace to break the US record for longest public sector strike.Ohiovotedfor Donald Trump in 2024 by more than 5%. As the final day of voting nears, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has a slight lead on Republican Senate incumbent Jon Husted in polling, and the economy has been a key factor in the fight.“They don’t pay a living wage any more. They used to,” Jones said. “Our healthcare coverage has stayed the same, but the cost of it has changed significantly. It used to be $35 a month for a family. In January it’s going to be $600 a month for a family for the same coverage.”She said as wages have lagged, with starting payat about $15 an hour, health insurance costs have eaten up any wage gains to the extent that some employees are making less than when they started.View image in fullscreenNonpartisan political signs in Granville, Ohio, on 22 October 2026.Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call via Getty ImagesNegotiations for a new union contract broke down with the county, nowledby three Republican commissioners, as workers arepushing for a $1 an hourincrease to their base pay.Daniel Petticord, the deputy director of the Lorain county jobs and family services, said in an email “management believes it recognizes the important efforts of our bargaining unit employees while maintaining fiscal responsibility,” and blamed the union for walking away from negotiations.“We service the clients of Lorain county that are the poorest of the community, and some of the people that work at jobs and family services qualify for those same services,” Jones said. “We’re hoping that with the Ohio governor election, that we get somebody in there who will be in favor of labor and see the fact that people don’t make a living wage in Lorain county any more.”In Minnesota, Bob Mattila, a special education paraprofessional in Minneapolis and SEIU Local 284 member, is looking for elected officials who will back state legislation that wouldincrease payfor himself and his co-workers to $25 an hour and tolowertheir costs for health insurance.“We simply aren’t paid enough to do the vitally important work that we do,” Mattila said. “I even take state health insurance because they decided I don’t make enough money.“Money, power and respect. Those three things are critical to what we need out of our work and what we deserve from our elected officials,” he added. “Having very labor-friendly people in places of power is going to give workers like me things that we need to live, because we’re at a point where I can’t afford to put $50 of gas every time when I fill up my car when I’m not even making $25 an hour.”Labor leaders see a real advantage for Democrats now that so much focus is on the economy.“The labor movement’s been talking about the issues that affect workers and the kitchen table for decades, and we’re now seeing that everybody else got the memo,” said Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, which has been pushing to turn out 16 million union family voters this election.View image in fullscreenAn attendee holds a sign at a Union Now rally headlined by Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani in New York on 12 April 2026.Photograph: Selcuk Acar/Anadolu/Getty Images“It’s pervasive. Everywhere I travel, every campaign that you see is talking about what working people are struggling through, and it’s the cost of gas, groceries, rent and healthcare, but it’s also the fact that our pay just can’t keep up with the rising prices.”In Detroit, Michigan, another key battleground state, 27-year-old Bailee Porter, who has worked at Detroit Diesel and is a member of the United Auto Workers, has been canvassing for candidates such as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for the US Senate, citing his support for Medicare for All, which the UAW has alsobacked.She said rising prices of basic necessities have made budgeting and cutting back on essentials like groceries a common worry.“It’s just costly on every aspect. It’s disrupting people’s routines, so it’s ridiculous. Food, gas. I don’t even want to talk about utility bills. It’s just insane,” said Porter. “Things should be affordable. Your basic necessities have to be affordable. There’s just no other way around it. They have to be. Legislation needs to be changed or enforced or written to where it can help the middle class and labor.”But the financial struggles experienced by many Americans are unlikely to be easily alleviated no matter who wins the midterms. Joe Biden, the US’s most pro-labor president in recent history, also failed to appease voters who were feeling left behind.Researchers have noted the federal government’s definition of and tracking of poverty doesn’t account for the struggles Americans are facing, as the federal poverty line is outdated from the 1960s and doesn’t account for geographic discrepancies in costs of living.“The percent of people that are struggling is so much higher than our official statistics are revealing,” said Dr Stephanie Hoopes, an economist and director of United for Alice. “These are often people who are keeping our economy running smoothly and fueling our economic growth, and yet they’re struggling to support their own families.”41.3%of US households, more than 54.5m households, faced financial hardship in 2024, according to a 2026 report by United for Alice.12.5% of US households made under the federal poverty level threshold, an income of$15,060 annuallyfor a single individual and $31,200 for a family of four.28.8% of US households were Alice: asset limited, income constrained and employed. These households earn above the federal poverty level but did not make enough money to afford basic expenses in the county where they live.2025 and 2026projected datashows the costs of basic necessities continuing to outpace overall inflation.“By some measures, our economy is doing great, unemployment rate is low, stock markets booming, productivity and GDP are growing,” Hoopes added. “But when you look at things like how many households are Alice [asset limited, income constrained and employed], and that number continuing to increase, and wages lagging behind the cost of living, there’s some real concerns in the economy.”For Shunda Whitfield, a certified nursing assistant in St Louis, Missouri, those economic concerns can be life-threatening.She has been struggling with a recent spike in costs for her medication for lupus, an autoimmune disease.“I sometimes have to choose between if I’m going to get my medication or if I’m going to get groceries in house due to the fact that my medicine is going up,” said Whitfield, who has been struggling to afford a recent spike in costs for her lupus medication.“You have to juggle things around to make sure you have cash to get to work to make the money to afford groceries or your medication,” she added. “I would like to see people get out here and vote to put people in place that are for the working people and not just for the billionaires.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US economyUS politicsMichiganOhioMinnesotaUS unionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading | China | The Guardian
description: A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Content: Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenXi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesChinaAnalysisThe US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleadingEduardo PorterA truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilitiesSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 10.22 ESTShareDonald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless theFederal Reservecuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.But neitherChinanor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.View image in fullscreenThe port in Qinzhou, China, on 22 October 2026.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionairesRead moreThe paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order.He described the strategyas building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging itsoverwhelming dominanceover the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year,it stunnedthe Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.View image in fullscreenA girl visits an installation about rare earth production at the National Museum in Beijing, China, on 24 March 2026.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersIt has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains manyother restrictions. While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hitother countriesfor a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency hasestimated thatif China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.Where does the supply chain war go from here? TheTrump administrationis pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.China, on the other hand, has announced a range ofhigh-tech export restrictions, covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.View image in fullscreenWorkers at a photovoltaic power-generation project site on 27 October 2026 in Wenling, Zhejiang province, China.Photograph: Zhou Xuejun/VCG/Getty ImagesChina will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.Explore more on these topicsChinaUS economyDonald TrumpTrump administrationTrump tariffsCritical mineralsTariffsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion with third place in Mexican GP | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 20-year-old Italian clinched the title with four rounds to go in a race that was won by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The 20-year-old Italian clinched the title with four rounds to go in a race that was won by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen
Content: Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton lift new world champion Kimi Antonelli.Photograph: Eloisa Sanchez/ReutersView image in fullscreenMax Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton lift new world champion Kimi Antonelli.Photograph: Eloisa Sanchez/ReutersFormula One 2026Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion with third place in Mexican GP20-year-old clinches title with four races to goVerstappen wins race ahead of HamiltonGiles Richardsat the Autódromo Hermanos RodríguezSun 1 Nov 2026 17.27 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 18.57 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKimi Antonelli etched his name into the Formula One record books as world champion and as a deserved and popular winner whose verve and extraordinary skill has been thrilling to watch, turning what many thought might have been an unlikely title tilt into a triumphant march, sealed with tears of joy at the Mexican Grand PrixIn taking his debut F1 title for Mercedes, the 20-year-old Antonelli, with his tousled hair and charming boyish looks, is the youngest driver to claim the sport’s crown and the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari won in 1953. It is Mercedes’ first drivers’ championship since Hamilton last won in 2020 and the team’s 10th.‘He’s done an insane job’: Antonelli’s rivals united in praise for ‘incredible’ championRead moreThe youngster closed it out unsurprisingly with the cool command the greats of the sport display by taking third place in Mexico City, a race won after no little drama by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, from the ­Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton, who was left fuming with his teammate Charles Leclerc, who finished fourth.Afterwards Antonelli was clearly moved and said it was a moment that would live for ever but had left him almost speechless. His race engineer, Peter Bonnington, spoke perhaps for everyone who has watched the Italian this season, noting that this was just the beginning for Antonelli.“It is a very special day, a young man has broken the record for the youngest world champion,” he said. “It is the first of many I reckon, I am just super happy for him, stoked.”On any other day this feisty affair in Mexico City, with Verstappen superb and a dramatic Ferrari inter-driver spat to savour, would have been ­considered quite an entertaining affair but for all that it really belonged to Antonelli.He brought what has been a hugely successful campaign to a close as the sport’s 36th world champion at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez in only his second season in F1 and with four meetings still to go. Sebastian Vettel was the previous youngest winner of the drivers’ championship, aged 23 in 2010, when Antonelli was just four years old.The Italian has been on top for almost the entire season, having taken the lead after the third round in Japan. With the Mercedes proving to be the class of the field in the opening half of the year under the new regulations, Antonelli made the most of it and established a dominant lead. He won five of the first six races, outracing his teammate George ­Russell, who had been the pre-season favourite.Antonelli went on to take nine wins in a season where he failed to score points only twice, on both occasions because of mechanical failures. Even as Mercedes were pushed by Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull, Antonelli retained a stranglehold on his lead, including sealing a win from 19th on the grid at his home grand prix at Monza.Russell and Hamilton were his nearest contenders but neither was able to significantly narrow the gap. They had to win in Mexico to keep the title alive but Antonelli’s third place would have clinched it even had they done so.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli crosses the chequered flag to finish third in Mexico.Photograph: Daniel Becerril/ReutersAntonelli did exactly what was required of him here, kept his cool and did not put a foot wrong in a race that was run at a frenetic pace. Leclerc made a great start and tried to pass Hamilton for the lead at turn four took but cut the corner to do so.He did not give the place back and was investigated, with Hamilton ­furious his teammate had cost them a one-two in the race and let Verstappen ultimately into the lead. The stewards found Leclerc had gained an advantage in leaving the track and he was given a five-second penalty to take during his pit stop.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was a decision which left ­Hamilton unhappy. “The problem is he’s got clean air and doesn’t have to manage like the rest of us. He should just give the place back,” he said. “The stewards are basically handing Charles this win.”Later when the race was stopped he made his displeasure clear again. “We’ve got big problems. Big, big problems,” he said. A lively debrief at Ferrari is in store.A red flag was called after Valtteri Bottas crashed out with a big impact at turn one. It prompted a restart from which a feisty Hamilton moved up to second and Antonelli into third, typically not willing to quietly do the minimum to take the title. It allowed him to seal glory with a podium place, where the two greats hoisted the kid on to their shoulders.Kimi Antonelli claims the Formula One crown – his season in picturesRead moreThe victory might be something of cold comfort to Verstappen given Antonelli secured the title, but ­comfort it will be to the Dutch driver and his team who will be buoyed by what was a hugely impressive run from fifth on the grid as they look to enter next season strongly. It has set up the mouthwatering prospect of Verstappen and Antonelli and ­hopefully Hamilton competing consistently at the front in 2027.The title for Antonelli represents a vindication of the enormous faith Mercedes had placed in the boy from Bologna, whom the team brought into their young driver program when he was 12. He was promoted to take Hamilton’s place last season, which proved a difficult year for the rookie but since then he has adapted to competing at the very sharp end with alacrity and great skill.He went into the race in Mexico needing only ninth place or better and despite only qualifying in fourth delivered a nerveless drive ­indicative of the form he has shown across the year. A moment to remember but surely not the last for this ­fascinating, precocious talent.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: NFL roundup: Cowboys and Chiefs suffer late collapses; Lamar Jackson’s season could be over | NFL | The Guardian
description: Arizona roared back to beat Dallas in overtime thanks to Gardner Minshew’s heroics while Baltimore suffered a serious injury blow
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Arizona roared back to beat Dallas in overtime thanks to Gardner Minshew’s heroics while Baltimore suffered a serious injury blow
Content: Gardner Minshew celebrates his team’s win over the Cowboys.Photograph: Stacy Revere/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGardner Minshew celebrates his team’s win over the Cowboys.Photograph: Stacy Revere/Getty ImagesNFLNFL roundup: Cowboys and Chiefs suffer late collapses; Lamar Jackson’s season could be overGardner Minshew’s heroics inspire ArizonaJackson needs surgery on injured thumbAgenciesSun 1 Nov 2026 16.56 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 20.11 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArizona Cardinals 33–30 Dallas Cowboys (OT)Chad Ryland kicked a winning 42-yard field goal in overtime after missing a PAT that would have won the game with six seconds left in regulation, and the Arizona Cardinals rallied for a wild victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday. The Cardinals beat Dallas for the fifth consecutive time and improved to 5-0 at AT+T Stadium, the home of the Cowboys that opened in 2009.This was by far the most crushing of those for the Cowboys (3-5), who didn’t trail until the final kick and led by two touchdowns early in the fourth quarter. Arizona (3-5) were still in the game because Tyler Allgeier had a 63-yard touchdown run, a career long, followed by a 50-yarder to set up his second touchdown on a five-yard catch, all in the second half. He had 191 scrimmage yards (147 yards rushing, 44 receiving), all but seven coming after half-time.The Dallas defense was having its best showing of the season before buckling in the last 16 minutes, particularly the final minute. The Cardinals went 80 yards in eight plays after taking over with 1:05 left in regulation, tying the score at 30-30 on Gardner Minshew’s 14-yard touchdown to Michael Wilson with six seconds to go. Ryland was wide left on the PAT kick after making his previous 58.Kansas City Chiefs 24-28 Denver BroncosMalcolm Roach sacked Patrick Mahomes on the final play, securing Denver’s comeback win over Kansas City. The victory puts the Broncos (6-2) in first place in the AFC West. Denver trailed 24-13 in the third quarter, but Bo Nix threw a 2-yard TD pass and a twp-point conversion to close the gap. After Kansas City’s Harrison Butker missed a crucial field goal, Denver quickly took the lead. Mahomes had a chance to respond for the Chiefs (5-2) but was stopped at the goalline in the final seconds. Nix finished with 222 yards and two touchdowns, while Mahomes had 320 yards and three touchdowns.Baltimore Ravens 10-36 Buffalo BillsJosh Allen set the franchise record for career touchdown passes and also rushed for a score and the Buffalo Bills took advantage of multiple ⁠Baltimore quarterback injuries to notch victory over the Ravens. The Ravens (4-4) lost quarterbacks Lamar Jackson (right thumb) and Tyler “Snoop” ​Huntley (right toe) in the first half while dropping ‌their third straight game. Jackson missed ‌the previous three games with a left ankle injury. Ravens coach Jesse Minter said after the game that Jackson needs surgery on the injured thumb and his season could be over. “That’ll be a surgery deal. He’ll go to [injured reserve],” Minter said. “That’s a tough deal.” Asked if Jackson’s season was over, Minter replied: ““Potentially, but we’ll see where it’s at.”Allen’s 11-yard scoring pass to DJ Moore with 12:18 left in the ⁠game was the 259th of ⁠his career, a ​mark that includes postseason play. The previous record was held by Hall of Famer Jim Kelly, who threw 237 in the regular season and 21 in ⁠the postseason for the Bills. Allen later threw a second touchdown pass and was 21-of-34 passing for 289 yards and one interception as Buffalo (6-1) won their third straight game. James Cook III ⁠rushed for 80 yards and a touchdown for Buffalo.Minnesota Vikings 15–19 Detroit LionsJared Goff threw a go-ahead, seven-yard touchdown pass to Jameson Williams with 4:35 left and the Detroit Lions beat the Minnesota Vikings, handing the NFL’s last undefeated team their first loss. The Lions (5-2) have won three straight, including their first two division games in the tight NFC North. The Vikings (6-1) had a chance to stay unbeaten, but the league’s stingiest defense couldn’t hold on to a late lead, and they lost for the first time since 30 November 2025. The Lions lost All-Pro linebacker to a neck injury and he was taken to hospital. Campbell was placed on a backboard and carted off the field early in the fourth quarter. Lions coach Dan Campbell said he did not have any additional information after the game. “We’re thinking about him,” he said.Atlanta Falcons 0-16 Tampa Bay BuccaneersBaker Mayfield didn’t complete a pass but the Tampa Bay Buccaneers beat the Atlanta Falcons behind Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell’s rushing on a wet, sloppy field. The Buccaneers set a team record for yards rushing in a game with 324, and became the first team to have zero completions since Buffalo in September 1974. Irving ran for 170 yards and a touchdown on 27 carries, Gainwell ran for 140 on 25 carries and Chase McLaughlin kicked three field goals to stay perfect this season. Mayfield was 0 for 3 passing. Atlanta’s Michael Penix Jr threw four interceptions. Both teams are 3-5.Los Angeles Chargers 9–24 Los Angeles RamsThe Los Angeles Rams overcame a slow start for a victory over the winless Los Angeles Chargers. Matthew Stafford passed for 157 yards and a touchdown, Blake Corum and Kyren Williams rushed for scores, and Puka Nacua had 11 catches for 80 yards and a TD. The Rams (4-4) have won back-to-back games for the first time this season after rallying past their SoFi Stadium roommates. Justin Herbert passed for 257 yards and threw two interceptions for the 0-7 Chargers, who returned from their bye week and extended their worst start to a season since 2000.Cleveland Browns 6–27 Pittsburgh SteelersJaylen Warren tied a career high with 143 rushing yards and a touchdown on his 28th birthday to lead the Pittsburgh Steelers to victory over the Cleveland Browns. The Steelers moved into first place all alone at 6-2 after beating the Browns at home for the 23rd straight time in the regular season, tying an NFL record. The Steelers dominated the line of scrimmage, rushing for 200 yards, including 160 in the first half alone. Cleveland quarterback Deshaun Watson spent most of the day under heavy pressure. The Steelers sacked Watson eight times to drop the Browns to 5-3.Tennessee Titans 36–43 Cincinnati Bengals (OT)Joe Burrow threw five touchdown passes in regulation and then scrambled untouched for a nine-yard score in overtime as the Cincinnati Bengals rallied for a thrilling victory over the Tennessee Titans. Cincinnati have won three straight and are 5-2 for the first time since the 2021 season, when they reached the Super Bowl. The Bengals got the ball first in OT and went 70 yards in five plays. Tennessee took over but could not get a first down. Cam Ward had the first 300-yard passing game of his two-year career but threw incomplete on fourth down to end the contest. The Titans (1-7) took an early 13-0 lead, and the fourth quarter featured three lead changes and a tie.New England Patriots 24–19 Miami DolphinsDrake Maye threw two touchdown passes and rushed for a score as the New England Patriots came back to beat the Miami Dolphins (1-6). With star receiver AJ Brown inactive because of lingering injuries, Maye completed 16 of 20 passes for 199 yards as the Patriots (5-3) rallied from a 10-point halftime deficit to take a 17-13 lead entering the fourth, then held on after a late Miami rally. DeMario Douglas caught a pass and weaved through the Dolphins secondary for a 48-yard touchdown catch that put the Patriots up two scores early in the fourth.Indianapolis Colts 7–42 Jacksonville JaguarsTrevor Lawrence threw three touchdown passes, including one to the previously benched receiver Brian Thomas Jr, and the Jacksonville Jaguars dominated the Indianapolis Colts in the rain to extend their home winning streak in the series to 12. Lawrence also connected with Bhayshul Tuten in the third quarter and rookie Nate Boerkircher on a 31-yarder in an opening half filled with big plays for the 5-2 Jaguars. It came five days after the 2-6 Colts traded two of their best players, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and longtime guard Quenton Nelson, to kickstart a rebuilding effort.Las Vegas Raiders 38–33 New York JetsKirk Cousins threw two of his three touchdown passes in the second half and ran for another score to lead the ⁠Las Vegas Raiders to a comeback victory over the New York Jets. Cousins completed 19 ⁠of 26 passes for ⁠247 yards ​as the Raiders (4-4) stopped a four-game skid, erasing a pair of nine-point deficits by scoring 17 of the game’s final 20 points. Las ⁠Vegas ended a streak of 12 straight losses when trailing at half-time. The Jets (2-6) scored on their first six possessions but frequently stalled in the red zoneExplore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsBaltimore RavensnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have effing unbreakable love’: how the maverick Natalie Nakase led the Valkyries to WNBA glory | Golden State Valkyries | The Guardian
description: A coach shaped by basketball’s less glamorous corners built the trust that made Golden State improbable champions just 534 days after their first WNBA game
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: A coach shaped by basketball’s less glamorous corners built the trust that made Golden State improbable champions just 534 days after their first WNBA game
Content: Veronica Burton and Natalie Nakase celebrate Golden State’s WNBA title.Photograph: Noah Graham/NBAE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVeronica Burton and Natalie Nakase celebrate Golden State’s WNBA title.Photograph: Noah Graham/NBAE/Getty ImagesGolden State Valkyries‘We have effing unbreakable love’: how the maverick Natalie Nakase led the Valkyries to WNBA gloryA coach shaped by her circuitous basketball journey was uniquely suited to building the trust that made Golden State champions just 534 days after their first gameBryan Armen GrahamSun 1 Nov 2026 11.10 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 20.42 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThemighty,miserlyGolden State Valkyries won their first WNBA title on Saturday night with a point guard Dallas had given up on and cast aside, a starting forward who had been waived five times and a late-blooming All-Star once passed over by every team in the league. That made them a fitting match for their coach. Natalie Nakase has built a basketball life on making small openings count, since turning a walk-on place at UCLA into a scholarship and an unsolicited scouting report into a coaching job in Japan’s top men’s league.The Valkyries’nerve-shredding 68-63 fightbackover the Atlanta Dream in Game 7 did more than make them the fastest expansion team in major North American professional sports history to win a championship – as 45-1 preseason longshots in their second season of existence. It was proof of concept for an organization that gave overlooked players the resources, responsibility and trust to become champions – and enlisted a leader whose own circuitous journey had taught her what those things could unlock.Quick GuideWNBA finals 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. All times US Eastern Daylight Time (EDT).Sat 17 OctGame 1:Golden State 68, Atlanta 64Mon 19 OctGame 2:Atlanta 79, Golden State 65Wed 21 OctGame 3:Atlanta 97, Golden State 71Sat 24 OctGame 4:Golden State 67, Atlanta 62Mon 26 OctGame 5:Golden State 64, Atlanta 55Thu 29 OctGame 6:Atlanta 80, Golden State 69Sat 31 OctGame 7:Golden State 68, Atlanta 63How to watchIn the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“We have unconditional love that’s fucking unbreakable, guys,” a keyed-up Nakase said during the trophy ceremony at a Chase Center that remained packed to the rafters, where Golden State’s 53rd home game had delivered their 53rd sellout crowd on a night that will be long remembered in the Bay Area asBallhallaween.“This is for all the people that have been underrated, misunderstood,” she said. “This is for all y’all, because this is proof: if you put all your heart and all your soul, you fucking win championships!”From the first game in franchise history to a title in 534 days: the speed was extraordinary but the foundation was deliberate. Golden State had built a place where players could expect investment, opportunity and the trust of their coach – and were expected to give something back. The 46-year-old Nakase’s declaration of love came with demanding basketball obligations: defend, compete and accept whatever role helped the team win.Veronica Burton, their starting point guard, had been waived by the Dallas Wings two years earlier, returning home to work out at the West Suburban YMCA in Newton, Massachusetts, with her high school coach while waiting for another chance. Connecticut signed her, then left her unprotected in theexpansion draft. With Golden State, she became the league’s most improved player.View image in fullscreenNatalie Nakase led the Golden State Valkyries to a WNBA championship in only their second season.Photograph: Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesKaila Charleshad been cutfive times in five seasons. Back at her parents’ home, training with her brother and mulling her professional future, she was preparing to visit Trinidad for her grandmother’s 94th birthday when the Valkyries offered a seven-day hardship contract. Now she was starting in the WNBA finals.Kayla Thornton went undrafted, was shown the door by two different teams and spent years establishing herself as a dependable supporting player before becoming a first-time All-Star with Golden State at 32. Cecilia Zandalasini had started only sixWNBAgames before joining the Valkyries and starting 44 across the team’s first two seasons. Kaitlyn Chen, a relatively unheralded third-round draft pick, found a role backing up Burton and as the bench’s chief vibes officer. Tiffany Hayes, a former sixth woman of the year, had played more WNBA games without winning a title than anyone else in history – until Saturday night.These were careers transformed by opportunity – by a team willing to explore what its players could become. Gabby Williams, the newly minted WNBA finals MVP and Golden State’s closest thing to an incandescent star, put it another way.View image in fullscreenNatalie Nakase, right, guards Esperanza’s Kim Omer while playing for Marina High School in southern California.Photograph: Robert Lachman/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images“All it took was good people,” Williams said. “All we heard last year was we don’t have no stars. We don’t have no talent. Yeah, right! We got good people. We got good people. We got winners. We got people who are ready to put their bodies on the floor to win a game.”Nakase understood what it meant to have more to offer than others could see. She had spent much of her own career proving it.A 5ft 2in point guard from a basketball-obsessed Japanese-American family in southern California, she turned down a scholarship to UC Irvine to walk on at UCLA, her dream school. A torn ACL delayed her start, but she earned a scholarship there anyway, became a starter and captained the Bruins for three seasons.She never did make a WNBA roster. Phoenix cut her in 2007, before another knee injury while playing in Germany spelled the end of her playing career. She began coaching the Wolfenbüttel Wildcats of the Damen-Basketball-Bundesliga before moving to Japan, where she initially found a foothold watching Tokyo Apache practices. A scouting report she prepared earned her a volunteer assistant’s job under former NBA coach Bob Hill, before she eventually became the first woman to lead a team in Japan’s top professional men’s league when she took charge of the Saitama Broncos.Then came a return to California and an internship in the Los Angeles Clippers’ video department. She spent a decade in the organization, working through video, development and coaching roles before Becky Hammon brought her to Las Vegas in 2022. Two championships as a bench coach followed, giving her a front-row seat forone of basketball’s great dynasties.Her intensity can work against her. Nakase nearly fainted in the closing minute of the first-round decider against Dallas, prompting her to pay closer attention to rest, hydration and nutrition. During the semi-finals, she took the unusual step of giving herself a full day off. The coach who constantly urged her players to “empty the tank” had run up against her own limits. Nakase traced both that relentless drive and her instinct to invest in people to her late father.View image in fullscreenNatalie Nakase made history as the first female assistant coach in NBA Summer League history in 2014 and later became an assistant coach on the Los Angeles Clippers bench during the regular season.Photograph: Jack Arent/NBAE/Getty Images“He’s the reason why I’m built the way I am. I am crazy. I am obsessive. I am a workaholic,” she said. “But it’s more just pouring into people, believing in people, helping people, that’s all come from my dad.”Her extended apprenticeship mattered for a roster assembled largely from other franchises’ spare parts. Nakase and general manager Ohemaa Nyanin looked for competitiveness and character, studying even how players behaved when they returned to the bench. They needed people who wanted more for themselves and could still accept what the team required.They worked at those relationships. On an early two-week road trip, the Valkyries organized dinners and games built around open, honest questions. Basketball, Nakase said, was the last thing they wanted to discuss.“I love to learn about people, so I can push their buttons and go crazy when I have to,” she said.Williams remembered evenings nobody wanted to end. “I knew we had something special on that trip.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markThis is for all the people that have been underrated [or] misunderstoodNatalie Nakase“Strength in numbers” was one of Nakase’s recurring messages, alongside “Empty the tank”. She backed it with her rotations, sometimes trusting the eighth or ninth player to finish games. Shared responsibility gave Golden State the depth to sustain their suffocating defense – the best in the leagueby some distance– and made a larger role a real possibility for everyone on the active roster. That extended to closing an elimination game with a rookie (Chen) while her starting point guard (Burton) watched from the bench. Opportunity depended on what the game demanded, while established players had to trust that the same principle applied to everyone.The finals tested that bargain. Trailing Atlanta 2-1, Nakase moved Charles and Tiffany Hayes into the starting lineup, bringing Thornton and Zandalasini off the bench. Golden State won the next two games, holding Atlanta to 62 and 55 points. Trust had a practical application: players could lose their starting places without the team losing them.There was individual greatness, too. Williams poured in 28 of her 30 points after half-time in Saturday’s deciding game, the highest-scoring half in WNBA playoff history, and was the no-brainer pick for MVP. Her explanation began with her coach.View image in fullscreenNatalie Nakase and the Golden State Valkyries celebrate winning the WNBA title in only their second season after beating Atlanta in Game 7 at Chase Center.Photograph: Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire/Getty Images“Nat told me to stay patient. I trust her with my life,” Williams said.Williams had taken her own peripatetic journey to the summit, building a decorated career in Europe and with France while her WNBA progress came in interrupted stretches in Chicago and Seattle. “I may have done things the hard way, took my own route, but I loved it,” she said. “It built character, it built me into the person I am, and it landed me here. It landed me with the best group of people I’ve ever been around.”The newly minted finals MVP explained Saturday what made Golden State different. “I showed up new to the team, the team already had a culture and relationships established but I walked into a group full of love and that just changed the entire trajectory of my career,” she said.The conditions for all this mattered. Nakase linked up with an owner whose impatience matched her own and whose ambitions came with a pledge to provide the resources needed to fulfill them. Joe Lacob’s requirement during her interview was straightforward: whoever took the job had to win a championship within five years.“I’m impatient,” Nakase said after delivering it in two. “I’m obsessive but it’s because he pushes me.”View image in fullscreenNatalie Nakase’s relentless intensity helped turn the Golden State Valkyries into WNBA champions in only their second season.Photograph: Tony Avelar/APShe spoke, too, about the value of Lacob’s presence, of an owner who kept showing up throughout the playoffs. His investment gave the expectation substance. “Someone who invests in women’s sports,” she said, “this is a result.”As the curtain falls on the WNBA’smilestone 30th season, the pattern is becoming impossible to miss. Las Vegaspaid Hammon $1m a yearto leave the NBA and constructed a $40m training facility, backing a championship core with the infrastructure to flourish. New York’s revival began when Joe and Clara Wu Tsairescued the Liberty from willful neglectin Westchester, moved them to Brooklyn and invested in everything from recruitment to nutrition. Golden State have followed the same principle: invest deeply in the conditions for success, then demand it.Money alone cannot create the trust that lets a coach change her starting lineup midway through the finals, but culture needs material backing. Players notice the quality of their facilities, the support around them and whether ownership’s ambitions extend beyond a speech. Increasingly, the WNBA’s championship race is being shaped by which organizations understand that connection. Golden State’s achievement is the most accelerated demonstration yet.And this is hardly an exercise in altruism. The Valkyries recently became the first women’s professional sports teamto exceed $100m in annual revenue, according to Sportico. The demand was reflected on the secondary market: Game 7’scheapest available ticket was $364roughly 24 hours before tipoff, outstripping every NFL and college football game this weekend, according to ticketing analyst Keith Smith. Turns out taking women’s basketball seriously is good business.View image in fullscreenJoe Lacob and Natalie Nakase celebrate Golden State’s WNBA title. The owner gave his coach five years to win a championship; she needed two.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty ImagesLacob’s own accounting of the championship began with three women: Nakase, Nyanin and team president Jess Smith. “Those three women made this happen,” he said during Saturday’s trophy ceremony, before turning his thanks to the supporters who had embraced the franchise before it had a single player – and filled the 18,064-capacity arena in Mission Bay to capacity one night after another.The culture belonged to that whole enterprise. Ownership supplied resources and expectations. The front office identified players hungry for responsibility. The coach created space for them to grow while demanding they make room for one another. The fans gave a new franchise an immediate sense of belonging. In the end Nakase was uniquely suite to connect those ambitions. She had spent her career asking people to look beyond the obvious credentials, then rewarding their faith with the work. She recognized that same hunger in the players Golden State brought together and it’s paid off faster than anyone could imagine.The result was a championship in 534 days, built by people who knew how long a chance could take to come.Explore more on these topicsGolden State ValkyriesWNBAAtlanta DreamBasketballUS sportsLos Angeles ClippersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal hold on for first league win at Liverpool since 2012 after Kai Havertz pounces early | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Kai Havertz’s 16th-minute goal secured Arsenal a hard-fought 1-0 win against Liverpool and a three-point lead at the top of the Premier League
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Kai Havertz’s 16th-minute goal secured Arsenal a hard-fought 1-0 win against Liverpool and a three-point lead at the top of the Premier League
