title: National Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentre | National Grid | The Guardian
description: New electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructure
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: New electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructure
Content: An Amazon AWS datacentre in Didcot, Oxfordshire. The government has said datacentres are as important to the economy as the railway and electricity networks.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn Amazon AWS datacentre in Didcot, Oxfordshire. The government has said datacentres are as important to the economy as the railway and electricity networks.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyNational GridNational Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentreNew electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructureLauren AlmeidaSun 1 Nov 2026 13.37 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 12.10 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNational Grid has taken a step towards building Britain’s biggest electricity substation on Teesside, which could supply power to a vast neighbouring datacentre as the UK races to expand its AI infrastructure.Last week, the company agreed to purchase 29.5 hectares (73 acres) of land at Dorman Point on a site owned by Teesworks, a local private-public partnership. The deal was first reported by Sky News.The deal followed reports last year that the UK government had picked Teesworks as the site for a new artificial intelligence datacentre, and planning applications had been submitted for a project that would span nearly 500,000 sq metres.The deal “reflects the constructive work between all those involved to enable this vital infrastructure … and will support the growth of AI and digital technologies, and enable the region’s next phase of industrial and economic development”, Matt Pearce, the head of land at National Grid, said.“We are committed to working closely with our partners to progress the development as quickly as possible,” he added.Ben Houchen, the mayor of the Tees Valley combined authority, told Sky News: “Everyone who has tried to build a datacentre in this country knows the biggest problem is getting enough power to the site quickly.View image in fullscreenBen Houchen: ‘If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability … it needs somewhere to physically put it.’Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian“While we’ve been stuck in the queue, the US, the Gulf and parts of Europe have been getting on with it and hoovering up the investment. Having up to 3.2GW of capacity here means we can finally compete for those projects.“If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability, with sensitive data stored safely on British soil, it needs somewhere to physically put it, and I’d much rather that was Teesside than Texas or Abu Dhabi.”Last week, the government published a draft national policy statement on datacentres, describing them as “as fundamental to our economy as the railways and electricity networks on which we have long depended”.“We must take control over the development of datacentres in this country and ensure that the country and host communities benefit from them,” it said.However, the rapid construction of datacentres in the UK has been met by strong opposition, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging fromAuchtertool, a village north of Edinburgh, toBrick Lanein east London.In October, the Guardian reported thatAI companies told ministers they had 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentresin the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.The London-listed infrastructure services group Balfour Beatty was reported to be in line to deliver the Teesworks substation for National Grid, with the utilities firm Steel River Power (SRP) also heavily involved in the project.Balfour Beatty and SRP were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsNational GridUtilitiesEnergy industryNorth of EnglandAI (artificial intelligence)Datacentres - UKInfrastructurenewsShareReuse this content

title: AI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist says | Indigenous art | The Guardian
description: Chair of National Gallery’s First Nations advisory group says the technology is undermining artists’ agency and the authenticity of their work
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: Chair of National Gallery’s First Nations advisory group says the technology is undermining artists’ agency and the authenticity of their work
Content: Artist Sally Scales on AI altering First Nations art: ‘It’s a theft of the agency of the artist. It rips the authenticity out of it, because it’s not been made by anyone who has the connection … the artist’s family lineage is not there, the lived experience is not there.’Photograph: Dean Sewell/OculiView image in fullscreenArtist Sally Scales on AI altering First Nations art: ‘It’s a theft of the agency of the artist. It rips the authenticity out of it, because it’s not been made by anyone who has the connection … the artist’s family lineage is not there, the lived experience is not there.’Photograph: Dean Sewell/OculiIndigenous artAI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist saysChair of National Gallery’s First Nations advisory group says the technology is undermining artists’ agency and the authenticity of their workGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTory ShepherdSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 15.40 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI is taking First Nations art and turning it into “Temu slop”, the Pitjantjatjara artist Sally Scales has said.Scales, the chair of the National Gallery of Australia’s First Nations advisory group, says the technology is undermining the agency of First Nations artists and the authenticity of their work and represents a “a theft” of cultural knowledge.Despite Anthony Albanese’s vow to protect Australian creatives fromcopyright theft,and the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, saying there are “no plans to weaken copyright protections”, AI has already been trained – without compensation – on the works of well known Australian artistsincluding Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave.But experts are particularly worried about the risks to Indigenous cultural and intellectual property (ICIP) in a world where AI companies can hoover up anything that may be found online, including songs and paintings that include sacred and cultural knowledge. AI has altered work, removed names and then been sold, an act the peak body for Australian visual artists said was causing “cultural and economic harm”.Artists boycotted this portrait prize over AI entries. Now they’re back to take them onRead moreSearches on sites including Temu, Shein and Amazon reveal countless works described as Aboriginal paintings, as well as items such as coasters and stubby holders bearing Aboriginal-style designs, mostly without attribution to any artist.“It’s in the name, it’s artificial,” Scales said.“I’ve seen some works where I look at it and wonder if they’ve gone through a First Nations community or a person, or if it’s something generic that they’ve whipped up.“It’s a theft of the agency of the artist. It rips the authenticity out of it, because it’s not been made by anyone who has the connection … the artist’s family lineage is not there, the lived experience is not there.”Prof Kathy Bowrey, an intellectual property expert at UNSW Sydney, said one in five creators already had problems with copyright infringement without AI. But she added the issues became even more complex when the creators were First Nations people, “partly because of lack of control over ownership and respect for Aboriginal culture”.She gave an example of an organisation paying to use artwork or images of Aboriginal people themselves, then later using AI to “update” or repurpose those images without permission.“The corporate client can pay you once and then make unauthorised Aboriginal derivative work and use the faces of the artists without consent,” she said.“Not only do [the artists] not get the repeat business, but when they go to make new work they’re competing against an AI.”The National Association for the Visual Arts (Nava) said Indigenous data sovereignty “recognises the right of First Nations peoples to exercise authority over their data, cultural material and knowledge”.In a submission to the joint select committee inquiry on artificial intelligence, Nava pointed to work by the Wuthathi and Meriam lawyer Terri Janke, an international authority on Indigenous cultural and intellectual property, who has “documented AI scrapingIndigenous artcentre websites, removing artists’ names and altering their work”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJanke has also warned of the broader risk of AI reproducing cultural knowledge without regard to its accuracy or appropriate use.“Nava members have also raised concerns about AI-generated ‘Aboriginal-style’ images and designs that imitate community-specific techniques, stories, motifs and mark-making,” the submission said. “These images can be presented and sold as Indigenous or Indigenous-inspired work, spreading misinformation, causing cultural and economic harm and competing with work by First Nations artists.”Bowrey and a colleague, the creative technologies expert Associate Prof Oliver Bown, have proposed what they call a copyright plus framework, which would give creators more power over the use of their work by forcing AI companies to disclose their data sources and giving artists the right to say no to having their work scraped or mimicked. They have also proposed imposing a levy on AI companies to create a scheme to pay creative professionals and establish a cultural fund, as well as the use of takedown notices for fake content.Bowrey said they wrote the draft policy based on the parameters of what the government has said so far.Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposalRead moreA spokesperson for the attorney general said Australian creatives were “world class” and that the government was committed to supporting them.“That’s why we’re continuing to consult with creators, media organisations and AI companies on a range of options to ensure any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation,” the spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsIndigenous artIndigenous AustraliansAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Why you should treat charisma as a red flag | Psychology | The Guardian
description: Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself
Content: Illustration: Elia BarbieriView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia BarbieriThe big ideaPsychologyWhy you should treat charisma as a red flagToday’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourselfAlex CurmiSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.26 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth isround!”It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. Disagreements on topics like these frequently damage relationships, alienate friends and estrange loved ones.How did things get so bad? I believe the answer is, in part, that we’re constantly exposed to a novel form of charisma.As a psychiatrist, I’ve always been fascinated by this quality: the magnetism that brings out a deep sense of trust, loyalty or enthusiasm in others. The psychology of charisma tells us that it is not necessarily a magic, undefinable X-factor, but rather a set of skills and behaviours. Sometimes people have it naturally, sometimes people learn it.double quotation markIn our nomadic past, if a person was merely superficially charming, you found out quicklyI have some experience with this. When I started my podcast a few years ago, I struggled (as I still do) with my monotonous voice. All the content creation experts said the same thing: switch up the pitch, pace and volume of your speech to maximise audience engagement. Slick production is optional, charismatic communication is not. Storytelling, body language, moral outrage and more can be mastered to help would-be internet personalities put a spell on their audience.It’s been a huge lesson for me to discover how difficult it can be to discuss big topics in the mental health space responsibly, even as a trained professional. It’s also become shockingly clear how easily someone can distort the truth on, say, antidepressants, psychotherapy or ADHD when they have no experience or knowledge in that area – as long as they come across confidently and convincingly.The dangers of charisma are nothing new, of course. History is filled with examples of people using charm to advance their interests. Dictators, cult leaders and con artists are all proof that an otherwise reasonable person can succumb to a well-executed charm offensive.The difference now is one of scale. The 2024 US election, for example, was widely described as the “podcast election”, as both candidates (Trump more successfully) consented to numerous softball interviews on the medium. They reached millions, not with policy, but with good vibes. And you don’t have to be a public figure to leverage charm in this way – any video with the right allure can go viral, regardless of that person’s intentions or expertise.Why are we so easily taken in by charisma? Like many aspects of our psychology, we can understand it more clearly through the lens of our evolutionary past.Our ancestors spent most of their time (approximately 94% of human history) as hunter-gatherers, living in nomadic tribes that may have consisted of as few as 20 people. Groups that small, pitted against the forces of nature, needed strong leadership. Like many animals, humans have status hierarchies. High-status hunter-gatherers likely had many of the traits we still associate with charisma today: great eye contact, body language that signalled certainty, a persuasive voice.The difference being that, back then, you had the opportunity to observe your peers all day, every day: their flaws, their virtues, their competence, often while facing lethal danger. If a person was merely superficially charming, you found out quickly. Charisma would only win out if accompanied by other important qualities, including sound judgment, good character and wisdom.That’s not the case now. Technology allows us to shield the unpalatable parts of ourselves much more easily, selecting only the best bits for public consumption. Our brains did not evolve to process handpicked slices of someone else’s behaviour, detached from the rest of their lives, so we’re vulnerable to being duped. One frightening example is that of Ruby Franke, the parenting vlogger with millions of subscribers who wasjailed for child abuseafter two of her six children were found beaten and malnourished.We spend a lot of time worrying about how the minds of teenagers are warped by the online world. We’re keenly aware how prone they are to manipulation by seemingly impressive figures. What we fail to realise is, we’reallteenagers when it comes to the internet. Algorithmic social media has only been around for about 15 years, and we remain largely unconscious of how routinely it bypasses our better judgment. Is there any way to grow out of this newly acquired susceptibility?The best form of defence against the excesses of charisma is critical thinking. We should regard it as being like a collective immune system, and it should be central to our culture and the way we educate our young people. They should be taught how to evaluate sources, interpret information and recognise bias. Similarly, separating confidence from substance ought to be considered a basic life skill. Looking at counter-arguments when we are emotionally pulled to someone’s perspectiveshould be routine, and changing our mind when it is emotionally difficult should be celebrated.It would also be helpful for the average person to learn the fundamentals of confident communication. Not only can this help you express yourself when you have something of real value to offer, but it also teaches you to see through a person who would happily use such tactics to deceive or seduce.All told, charisma should actually be a red flag that encourages us to be more sceptical of an individual, not less. When someone can convincingly hold court on important topics like finance, healthcare or the Middle East, we should ask questions. What experience do they have? Do they have a history of dishonesty? What do they stand to gain from this view? What need in me might this person be speaking to? For my part, the next time I discuss something important, I will go easy on the pitch, pace and volume, and try to let the facts speak for themselves.Alex Curmi is a psychiatristand host ofThe Thinking Mindpodcast.Further readingThinking, Fast and Slowby Daniel Kahneman (Penguin, £16.99)The Age of Magical Overthinkingby Amanda Montell (Thorsons, £12.99)The Anxious Generationby Jonathan Haidt (Penguin, £12.99)Explore more on these topicsPsychologyThe big ideaSocial mediaDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A gift to scammers: why you should probably keep your birthday a secret | Money | The Guardian
description: Using a fake DOB or leaving the field blank when making an online account can offer protection from identity theft
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Using a fake DOB or leaving the field blank when making an online account can offer protection from identity theft
Content: Giving your date of birth can reveal an important piece in the jigsaw for scammers hoping to steal your identity.Photograph: kmt_rf/AlamyView image in fullscreenGiving your date of birth can reveal an important piece in the jigsaw for scammers hoping to steal your identity.Photograph: kmt_rf/AlamyScam watchMoneyA gift to scammers: why you should probably keep your birthday a secretUsing a fake DOB or leaving the field blank when making an online account can offer protection from identity theftShane HickeySun 1 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 02.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou get a call from your bank saying there has been suspicious activity on your account. They read out your name, address and date of birth so you are happy it is a legitimate caller.But you are talking to criminals who have used your date of birth as part of a web of verifying information to convince you they are someone else.People’s DOBs are often held in online accounts after being entered as part of a sign-up process for a retailer, loyalty scheme, newsletter or online competition. In arecent hack of the online retailer Asoscustomers’ dates of birth were among the details taken by scammers.Now cybersecurity professionals have warned people to resist entering a date of birth, or to put in a fake one, to limit the amount of personal data that is online, frustrating criminals’ attempts to “jigsaw” together personal profiles.‘They call every week’: the phishing attacks targeting past victimsRead moreJake Moore, an adviser for the cybersecurity company ESET, says information gathered during hacks can be sold on and used by scammers, either to trick people into trusting them, or to impersonate them.“A date of birth alone is not particularly valuable to criminals, but combined with other information, such as names and phone numbers, it can help criminals … commit identity fraud,” he says.Alexandre François, who investigates scams for the intelligence company WhoisXML API, found that eight out of 14 retailers he surveyed recently asked for a date of birth on sign-up. “Retailers may also have little incentive to remove this field, as the full date gives them the customer’s age, which is useful for marketing and targeting,” he says.What it looks likeView image in fullscreenA woman delivering a package from Asos.Photograph: True Images/AlamyYou may hear about a hack either in the news, or in an email from an organisation telling you that your data has been compromised. How the scam manifests itself will depend on what happens to the information that has been stolen.If a retailer is hacked, and the details end up on the dark web, they can be used to make phishing emails look more authentic, says Serpil Hall, a security expert from Datos Insights. Hackers can also use them to try to convince company help desks that they are talking to the victim. But it may not all happen straight after a security breach.“The process typically runs like this: a retail breach provides a name, date of birth, email and address,” she says. “Other leaked data adds credentials, phone numbers and identifiers. Public information such as social profiles, employment details and relatives adds more context. The result is an enriched identity profile with more identifiers and greater confidence when matching records.”What to doBe wary of anyone who contacts you out of the blue, even if they seem to have a lot of information.“Using a different birthday on low-risk websites can reduce exposure, but it is even better to not enter any personal fields that aren’t mandatory,” says Moore. “It is even worth using a separate email address for shopping online, too, so you can bin the email if it gets caught up in a breach and you can start again.”François says shops only need your payment card details and a delivery address. (You will, however, need to verify your age in some cases if you are buying age-restricted items, such as knives.)François says: “Strictly speaking, you only need to give your real date of birth, and your real name, where they are checked against official records and used to prove who you are: your bank or any lender, the tax office, the driving licence and passport agencies, right-to-work checks, a police notice. In those systems the date of birth works as a key. A shop is not one of them.”Leaving a birthday field blank is best, he says. “If this is not an option, use the same date across all retailers, possibly the first day of your birth month, so that you do not forget it.”Explore more on these topicsMoneyScam watchIdentity fraudScamsConsumer affairsCybercrimeHackingOnline shoppingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the US midterms and election interference: Trump’s attempted heist is already under way | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Voters are turning against the Republicans. But the clearest possible message is needed to safeguard democracy
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Voters are turning against the Republicans. But the clearest possible message is needed to safeguard democracy
Content: ‘The January 6 insurrection showed how acute the peril to American democracy had become. It is more so now.’Photograph: Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘The January 6 insurrection showed how acute the peril to American democracy had become. It is more so now.’Photograph: Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionUS politicsThe Guardian view on the US midterms and election interference: Trump’s attempted heist is already under wayEditorialVoters are turning against the Republicans. But the clearest possible message is needed to safeguard democracySun 1 Nov 2026 12.30 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 14.56 ESTShareThe psychologist Jennifer Freyd identified a pattern often used by perpetrators: deny, accuse, and reverse victim and offender. More than one observer has noted that Donald Trump employs that pattern politically. With polls suggesting Republicans are likely to lose the House and perhaps the Senate too in the midterms, the man who refused to accept Americans’ democratic verdict in 2020is hawking a narrative of cheating Democratswho will steal seats via illegitimate votes.The January 6 insurrection showed how acute the peril to American democracy had become. It is more so now. This time, Republican efforts to undermine the results began well in advance. In 2020, Mr Trump’s vice-president, Mike Pence, the attorney general, William Barr, and others refused his most outrageous demands; now the justice department is supine. And the supreme court’sgutting of the Voting Rights Act, which safeguarded against the worst kinds of racial discrimination, means that states no longer require pre-approval for decisions that could well tilt a race. Districts have already been redrawn.Courts have so far blocked executive orders unconstitutionally claiming election powers that clearly lie with states. But the blizzard of efforts ensures that Republicans do not need to succeed every time. A few thousand or even hundred votes in key places could have a profound effect on the outcome. The all‑out push also intimidates potential voters. Whatever happens to the federal criminal investigation intoalleged non‑citizen voting in California, and whether or not Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers are actually stationed near polling placesas mooted, legitimate voters may fear drawing attention to undocumented relatives. Finally, all these threats and initiatives establish the false story of a stolen election, to be taken up more powerfully after votes are cast.Mr Trump repeated his call for the prosecution of Mary Peltola, the Democratic senate candidate in Alaska, after the New York Times reported that her campaign had sought to confuse voters by recruiting another candidate with the same name as her Republican opponent, despite its denials. The state’s Republican governorhas not committed to certifying the resultif she wins. Putting up similarly named candidates is an old trick, as well as a dirty one. Though not inherently illegal, it is unethical and could potentially lead to criminal charges. It isnot grounds for contesting the result of this race. But it is a gift to Republicans claiming that Democrats are pursuing election fixes – when the clear evidence is that the threat to US democracy comes from Mr Trump and his enablers.There are two key checks to their wide-ranging and concerted efforts. The first is that, despite facing horrific abuse and death threats, election officials – including Republicans – have beenassiduously preparing to resist anti-democratic efforts. That is tempered, however, by the determined Republican push to control election boards, with a growing number ofelection deniersin place.The second is that asurge in early votingsuggests that the obvious threat to democracy is motivating citizens to participate, and to ensure that their ballots count. Recent elections elsewhere – notably Brazil, where Mr Trump’s favoured far‑right candidate was rejected – show that a decisive message from voters is harder to challenge than a marginal one. The best defence of democracy is to show that people care about it. And the clearer the verdict, the better the prospects of upholding it.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionDonald TrumpUS economyRepublicansHouse of RepresentativesUS SenateeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The US founders made a grave error in granting presidents pardon power | James Rosen | The Guardian
description: Trump’s utter abuse of the power proves it. As the midterms approach, voters have not forgotten January 6
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trump’s utter abuse of the power proves it. As the midterms approach, voters have not forgotten January 6
Content: ‘It started on the first day of his second term, when he pardoned more than 1,500 insurrectionists who had stormed the US Capitol.’Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It started on the first day of his second term, when he pardoned more than 1,500 insurrectionists who had stormed the US Capitol.’Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpThe US founders made a grave error in granting presidents pardon powerJames RosenTrump’s utter abuse of the power proves it. As the midterms approach, voters have not forgotten January 6Sun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 15.41 ESTShareFrombetraying Ukraineanddispatching masked agentswhokilled Americansto deporting US citizens andpulling out of accordscontrolling climate change andIranian nuclear weapons, the list of Donald Trump’s abuses is long and growing still longer, seemingly by the day.Looking back decades from now, historians will see that at the top of this shameful list is Trump’s utter abuse of his pardon power. It started on the first day of his second term, when he pardoned more than 1,500 insurrectionists who, on 6 January 2021, had stormed the US Capitol.More recently, as documented inastonishing accountsby the New York Times, Wall Street Journal and 60 Minutes, Trump has overseen a robustpardons marketin which friends or relatives of criminalsoffer to pay millionsfor presidential clemency.Centuries before this unprecedented malfeasance, George Mason tried to warn us.At the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, Mason cautioned the new country’s most powerful men – among them George Washington, James Madison, Benjamin Franklin and Alexander Hamilton – against the dangers of giving future American presidents too much power.Trump’s pardons are harming violent crime survivors | Johnny OlszewskiRead moreThe risk was greatest, he told other delegates, in the absolute pardon power then being enshrined in our supreme law. Mason spoke out strongly against granting a president “power of pardoning because he may frequently pardon crimes which were advised by himself”.The convention had dragged on for nearly four months in the oppressive summer heat of Philadelphia, the Constitution Hall windows closed against eavesdroppers, the delegates sweltering in their elaborate attire. Fifty-five men came to the gathering, but 16 had left, driven home to their manors by the heat and humidity.Washington, who would become the newborn nation’s first president in 19 months, presided as Mason addressed his peers. It was as if he had a crystal ball displaying Trump’s cynical visage.“It may happen, at some future day, that he will establish a monarchy and destroy the republic.”Mason spoke on 15 September 1787, two days before the convention concluded. Perhaps they were too hot and exhausted to focus, but the delegates voted against limiting presidents’ pardon power. Even when Mason begged them at least to put treason beyond the pardon realm, they deferred.Two years later, Mason delivered another forceful rebuke, this time at the Virginia Ratifying Convention.“The president of the United States has the unrestrained power of granting pardons for treason, which may be sometimes exercised to screen from punishment those whom he had secretly instigated to commit the crime, and thereby prevent a discovery of his own guilt,” Mason said.Mason’s effort, though, was doomed: James Madison, already known as “the father of the constitution” because of his contributions to it, told fellow Virginia delegates that even treason could be within the reach of clemency because presidents who protected it would face impeachment and possible removal from office.As brilliant as Madison was, not quite 236 years later Trump has proven the fallacy of his logic. Despite being impeached twice, he was elected to a second term.Mason would go down in history as one of only three delegates who refused to sign the Constitution. So strong was his opposition, he declared that “he would sooner chop off his right hand than put it to the Constitution as it now stands.”The supreme court needs to put limits on Trump’s use of the pardoning power | Steven GreenhouseRead moreAlexander Hamilton, who among the founders favored the strongest federal government, led the drive to quash limits on presidential pardon power. He and his allies cited a centuries-old British tradition called the “royal prerogative of mercy”, under which English kings and queens pardoned criminals.This rationale, of course, was contradictory bordering on irrational – given that the delegates were fashioning a governing document to cement American independence from Britain and its monarchical government. And in subsequent centuries, British monarchs have pardoned far fewer criminals than US presidents.While inflation and the war in Iran are the top issues voters cite in the forthcoming midterm elections, they have not forgotten January 6. Almost six years later, a large majority of Americanstell pollstersthat Trump’s pardoning of violent insurrectionists was wrong.There have been plenty of other bad presidential pardons, from Jimmy Carter protecting his wayward brother Billy to Joe Biden pardoning his son Hunter. Bill Clinton pardoned 140 people and commuted the sentences of 36 others on his last day in office, 20 January 2001, among them his brother and several large campaign donors. Gerald Ford’s pardon of Richard Nixon following his resignation over the Watergate scandal was widely criticized at the time, though historians have assessed it more kindly since then.Trump’s pardon of the insurrectionists, however, stands alone because of his motivation: they used violence in a failed attempt to keep him in office after he had lost his re-election bid. No previous president had abused his pardon power to reward the subversion of US democracy.James Rosen is a former political reporter and Pentagon correspondent for McClatchy who has received awards from the National Press Club, Military Reporters and Editors, and the Society of Professional Journalists, which in 2021 named him top opinion columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS Capitol attackUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US elections | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: From the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculous
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: From the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculous
Content: ‘I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionUS midterm elections 2026A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US electionsDave SchillingFrom the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculousSun 1 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 15.41 ESTShareChances are, as you’re reading this, your bunker is fully stocked, your doors are locked, and you’re peeking at your computer screen through gaps between your fingers.After all, it’s election day on Tuesday. Once again, democracy will be tested – like Beavis & Butthead taking the SATs. I’m not looking forward to it, and I’m sure you aren’t either.I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.Now, it feels like anything can and will happen this week – from delayed results and slow counts to Donald Trump sending in theDC Comics Suicide Squadto your local polling place. That’s all we need,John Cenachecking your ID before you vote.It’s enough to make you crawl up into a ball and beg for mommy. But fear is a passive emotion, one that leaves a person paralyzed and incapable of action.My preference is for the fully formed anger of the middle-aged curmudgeon. A shaken fist and a choice expletive is healthier than babbling for hours in your panic room. So, in lieu of a voter guide telling you how to fill out your ballot, here’s a list of all the most irritating, confounding and downright stupid things to scream about on Tuesday.The Cheesecake Factory discourseDuring a recent campaign stop, the former president Barack Obama compared the aesthetics of the recentTrump-led White House renovations with a Cheesecake Factory. Not only am I annoyed that this is even a talking point during a crucial campaign, I also resent the comparison being made. I’d rather eat at a Cheesecake Factory than the White House, any day of the week. I have to assume Bill Maheragrees with me.The continued importance of Spencer PrattHere in California, the race everyone is talking about is a contest for Los Angeles mayor, a famous stepping stone to jobs as prestigious as “Ambassador to Country Chosen by Random Lottery Draw” or “Special Adviser to Herbalife”. It’s neck-and-neck between incumbent Karen Bass and the city councilperson Nithya Raman. The unfortunate twist in this daytime soap opera is that the reality show star they combined to defeat in the first round of voting this summer, Spencer Pratt, isstill popular enoughthat his supporters could tip the scales toward one candidate or the other. The only thing I can think of that’s worse than Spencer Pratt as mayor of LA is Spencer Pratt deciding the next mayor of LA.The curious case of the two Dan SullivansAccording to the New York Times, some Democrats figured out that the best way to unseat the senator Dan Sullivan was to force him to run against himself. Retired teacher Dan Sullivan was allegedly recruited to run for US Senate by the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola, in the hopes of unseating … Dan Sullivan. (The Peltola campaign has denied any involvement in his candidacy.)Mary Peltola made a mistake. But her Republican opponent would be a disaster for Alaska | Kim HeacoxRead moreThe Sullivan v Sullivan smackdown has the Republican party so worried that the justice department issuing to invalidatethe results of the election if Sullivan (the senator) narrowly loses to Sullivan (the not-senator) or Peltola (the not-Sullivan).I’m no fan of Dan Sullivan, but I’m not sure how I feel about Dan Sullivan either! This is the kind of goofy dirty trick that makes people hate politics. Who are you really fooling here? Old people? People who are too busy to read the fine print about which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent Alaskan senator? People with an acute case of Sullivantitis (a crippling disease that causes blindness to the name “Dan Sullivan”)? Can’t this country ever be normal?Please don’t message me. I realize the answer is no. I just hope this election is more entertaining than The Undertaker v The Undertaker at WWF SummerSlam 1994. Unlike that match, this face-off of doppelgangerswon’t involve Leslie Nielsen.The continued push to close polling placesIn an attempt to depress turnout amongst Democratic-leaning voters, red state election boards in states such as North Carolina areshutting polling placesin blue areas. In North Carolina in particular, voting sites were shut on numerous college campuses, but that didn’t stop a group of predominantly students from organizing marches in excess of two hours so that they could maintain the franchise.When I was a young man, the main tool crooked politicians had to keep people from voting was good, old-fashioned apathy. We should have changed the motto on the quarter from “E pluribus unum” to “They’re all bums, anyway.” In 2026, politicians have infuriated people to such a degree that they’ll walk miles just to vote.It’s inspiring to see young people exercising their rights in the face of an actively hostile state government, but I find the notion of our nation’s leaders blatantly making it more onerous for citizens to vote absolutely abhorrent. I mean, the peer pressure is bad enough.‘I voted’ stickers and selfiesI get why the stickers exist. An elaborate campaign of shame and embarrassment for those that didn’t bother to vote. I can’t think of two more powerful forces in my life than shame and embarrassment. They’re really the only two reasons I get out of bed these days, but I don’t have to like it.Like a lollipop at the end of a haircut, the “I voted” sticker is the little treat at the end of a long period of interminable waiting. The only difference is, I don’t need to take a picture with myroot beer-flavored Dum Dum. And I hate to be cynical here, but anyone who hasn’t planned on or even considered voting will not be swayed by a sticker.As much as I despise people shirking their responsibility to democracy, I hate internet trends even more. Instead of wearing an “I voted” sticker on Tuesday, just slap it on your laptop. That way, anyone in your general vicinity will have to stop and double-check that there isn’t an election that day.Donald Trump’s Mr America beauty pageantThis is Donald Trump’s last campaign of his risible political career. He has been a cancerous influence on our discourse since 2011, breaking traditions, norms, rules, and some priceless artifacts along the way.I’m sure he’s getting nostalgic for the rush of election fervor – the ups and downs, the thrill of victory and the agony of not admitting defeat. These are some of the last campaign rallies he’ll ever lead, some of the final moments of political combat he’ll engage in in his lifetime.Most of us would get wistful, maybe a tad somber. These days will never come again. Instead, the president is pondering the strength and power that emanates fromvarious Republican buttocks.Nothing, and I mean nothing, makes me bang my head against a wall this election cycle than my social media feed being littered with clips of Donald Trump sexualizing his colleagues.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS politicsDonald TrumpDemocratsRepublicansUS SenatecommentShareReuse this content

title: Life is full of suffering – but leaning into moments of pleasure can allow the nervous system to rest | Nadine Levy | The Guardian
description: The simplicity of breathing; the sweetness of laughter; the privilege of lying on a bed. Buddhism teaches us how to enjoy the small pleasures
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The simplicity of breathing; the sweetness of laughter; the privilege of lying on a bed. Buddhism teaches us how to enjoy the small pleasures
Content: ‘The point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure but to lean into it when it naturally arises.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure but to lean into it when it naturally arises.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesMaking sense of itBuddhismLife is full of suffering – but leaning into moments of pleasure can allow the nervous system to restNadine LevyThe simplicity of breathing; the sweetness of laughter; the privilege of lying on a bed. Buddhism teaches us how to enjoy the small pleasuresMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.17 ESTShareThere is a particularBuddhist storythat reassured me I had found the right path.The story goes that Prince Siddhartha Gautama was deep in spiritual practice – arduous, unforgiving practice. He had tried everything from breath-holding to extreme fasting. But none of it brought the freedom from suffering he sought.As is sometimes the case in those moments, he was graced with a memory. He remembered being a child, sitting under the shade of a rose apple tree while his father worked nearby. As he sat there, free from preoccupation, his mind settled and his experience became infused with a deep sense of pleasure and ease.This memory gestured at what later became a fundamental Buddhist idea: put simply, extreme self-denial is not the path to freedom. More radically, could it be that a certain kind of pleasure – a more refined pleasure – might help point the way?Surviving desire: what Buddhist thought teaches us about our war on want | Making sense of itRead moreI’ve always been intrigued by pleasure, its limits but also its invitation. The pleasure Siddhartha remembered was not wily or sneaky, waiting to trick him into attachment, but rather carried him towards freedom of heart.Admittedly, the Buddha distinguished this kind of pleasure from sensual pleasures, which can become tangled with craving, acquisition and a mistaken belief that happiness lies in getting more.But the point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure but to lean into it when it naturally arises.As humans, we are strangely adept at trying to elicit and extract pleasure, to plan for it and prolong it, but not so good at receiving it when it is right in front of us.Stress candiminishour sensitivity to pleasure. Psychologists use the term “anhedonia” to describe the diminished capacity to anticipate or experience pleasure, a phenomenon associated with a range of mental health conditions.As a teenager, I had a free-spirited friend who wholeheartedly called out, “I love bed!” before she went to sleep. We could hear her down the corridor.I loved bed too; we all did. But would we admit it?She noticed the sheets, the relief of placing a tired body down, the privilege of a pillow. Boy, she knew how to receive pleasure when it was being offered.The Buddha observed that all experience is associated with a tonal quality – pleasant, painful or neutral. In Buddhism, we call thisvedanā,or feeling tone. And then there is all the manhandling we do with feeling: judging it, willing it to stay, tweaking it.When working with mindfulness students who are having a hard time, I often do a pleasure check.I ask, sometimes provocatively, “What are you doing in your free time?” Then: “Are you able to read a good novel? Could you go for a massage or a meandering walk in the sun?” What I am really asking is: can you be with pleasure intentionally, even amid suffering?These conversations also make it plain that access to pleasure is not enjoyed equally. The time, safety and space necessary to notice and receive pleasure are affected by our social and material circumstances. But when pleasure does arise amid turbulence, allowing it to register can offer the nervous system a chance to rest, even for a moment.We feel this viscerally: a slower breath, a softening, a release. And if we are quiet, we might notice our minds relishing it – “How terrific, I love this.” Or as the US novelistKurt Vonnegutput it: “If this isn’t nice, I don’t know what is.”Can we let pleasure simply hold our attention without trying to prolong it?Pleasure arrives with different inflections. Some forms leave us aching for more. Others are more sublime, spiritual even – the kind the Buddha spoke of: the mind that gathers and settles. The simplicity of the breathing body. The sweetness of simply existing.I once had a teacher who started meditation sessions with: “It feels good to be in the body.” It was a low bar for pleasure but somehow I felt it.Then there is the pleasure of living a life of non-harm, of treating ourselves and others with dignity, love and respect. Subtler still is the pleasure of laying down the burden, even for a moment, of having to be and do.It’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdom | Muhammad AbdulsaterRead moreI remember marvelling that in my mother’s final weeks, days in the hospital could still brim with pleasure. Among the many unpleasant experiences, there was the sweetness of laughter, a leg massage, a feeling of togetherness, and a daughter’s recognition of the comfort and familiarity of being with her mum.Each evening, I would think how strange it was that there was so much pleasure in despair.And here receptivity was key. I suspect without it, I might have seen only what was painful and missed the pleasure braided through.Every time I sit to meditate, I consciously luxuriate in the pleasure of breathing.Of course, pleasure dissipates, and unpleasant and neutral sensations arrive too. Yet in Buddhist practice, these too are met with the samereceptive attention: “Oh, this is unpleasant, and it will change.” Sometimes there is even a kind of pleasure in this honesty.And, for the record, I still love bed.Dr Nadine Levy is a senior lecturer at theNan Tien Institute. She coordinates its health and social wellbeing program and the graduate certificate in applied mindfulnessExplore more on these topicsBuddhismMaking sense of itReligionMeditationPhilosophyHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The UK’s legal cannabis market is booming – so why can’t this talented artist get any to treat his epilepsy? | Kojo Koram | The Guardian
description: Companies have rushed to supply the drug as a wellness treatment, but patients with serious illnesses aren’t able to get NHS prescriptions, says author and academic Kojo Koram
Author: Kojo Koram
Headline: Companies have rushed to supply the drug as a wellness treatment, but patients with serious illnesses aren’t able to get NHS prescriptions, says author and academic Kojo Koram
Content: Artist Louis Petit, who has epilepsy and needs medicinal cannabis, with his mother, Emma Matthews, at his  studio in Haggerston, London.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArtist Louis Petit, who has epilepsy and needs medicinal cannabis, with his mother, Emma Matthews, at his  studio in Haggerston, London.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The GuardianOpinionCannabisThe UK’s legal cannabis market is booming – so why can’t this talented artist get any to treat his epilepsy?Kojo KoramCompanies have rushed to supply the drug as a wellness treatment, but patients with serious illnesses aren’t able to get NHS prescriptionsSun 1 Nov 2026 07.33 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 11.52 ESTShareIn 2022, a prodigiously talented young artist named Louis Petit was preparing to return to the UK, having been effectively exiled in the Netherlands as a teenager so he could access the medical cannabis he needed to control his epilepsy. Six years earlier, Louis, then 12, had been diagnosed with a rare form of the neurological disease when medical cannabis was still illegal in the UK.But in Rotterdam, where it was legal, doctors helped him discover that a medical cannabis oil called Bedrolite, in combination with the right mix of anti-epileptic treatment, could slow and eventually stop his seizures. This was something his neurologists in the UK had previously considered impossible.By the time Louis won a place at City and Guilds of London Art School in 2022, the UK government had legalised medicinal cannabis, pressed by parents needing the drug to treat their epileptic children –most notably Charlotte Caldwell and Hannah Deacon.Louis assumed his troubles were behind him. “It seems naive now, but I think both me and my mum thought Britain would welcome me back, saying, ‘Thank God you’re better’,” Louis told me. But Louis has never been able to get a prescription for medical cannabis through the NHS. Instead, like almost everyone who needs the drug in this country, his only access has come through the expensive private sector. And now the producer of Bedrolite, a Dutch company, Bedrocan, hasdeclared bankruptcy.This means there is a high chance that, in the near future, the drug that keeps Louis well will stop being available privately, in a huge blow to all patients who rely on it. If this was people with diabetes facing a shortage of insulin, or people with high blood pressure running out of beta blockers, politicians would be falling over themselves to be seen trying to secure the long-term supply. But because this is epilepsy and cannabis – a medicine that has been stigmatised by a 50-year “war on drugs” – successive governments have avoided the issue, allowing this current crisis to develop, despite patients warning for years that they can’t be just abandoned to the private market.View image in fullscreenLouis Petit in Great Ormond Street hospital in 2018.Photograph: Family HandoutWhen the then home secretary, Sajid Javid,legalised medicinal cannabis in 2018, he stood up in parliament and promised patients who needed cannabis medication that their arduous fight was finally coming to an end. “Having been moved by heartbreaking cases involving sick children,” Javid said, “it was important to me that we took swift action to help those who can benefit from medicinal cannabis.”But these benefits reached a fraction of those who needed help. Since the first few patients received their prescriptions on the NHS, the vast majority of others – including Louis – have been met with a wall of refusal fromthe healthcare system, with doctors’ requests for public funding to prescribe cannabis medication rarely granted in practice.Until 2025, there werefewer than five prescriptionsfor unlicensed cannabis-based products such as Bedrolite given out across the entire NHS. In the absence of an accessible NHS route, the private market has become the only option for treatment for most patients,costing them anything up to £4,000 a monthfor their medicine.The result of medicinal cannabis being handed over wholesale to the private sector is that cannabis has quietly become one of the new growth sectors in Britain, with many cannabis companies getting rich from the boom.Remote online prescriptions,48-hour door-to-door deliveryandtargeted advertisementson social media have all helped grow the private customer base.But while private suppliers offer customer-friendly products such as cannabis vape pens and gummies on prescription, Bedrolite is a cannabis oil that was modified specially for children with drug-resistant epilepsy, and can’t be replaced with general cannabis. There is a much larger market for presenting cannabis as the new must-have wellness treatment for the on-the-go millennial suffering from anxiety, sleep issues or chronic pain medicine than there is for trying to treat acute but rare ailments such as complex epilepsy or multiple sclerosis.And there is little commercial incentive for private companies to spend huge amounts of money on the expensive, large-scale, clinical, randomised control trials that are needed to get more cannabis medication licensed and mainstreamed on the NHS. Successive governments washed their hands of this issue once legalisation eased the immediate pressure from families with sick loved ones who were campaigning against an outright ban.This dynamic leaves us in the paradoxical position whereby medical cannabis has become one of Britain’s new growth industries at exactly the same time that the most vulnerable patients, who desperately need the medication, cannot access it.“It’s been one shock after another since we came home,” said Louis’s mother, Emma. “If his neurologists’ funding request to NHS England had been approved last year, his Bedrolite supply would be guaranteed. There is enough stock in the Netherlands to last into 2028. But it’s not available to those without NHS prescriptions.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInitially, it was feared that the drug would stop being on sale in the UK before Christmas, but last week one UK drug manufacturer, Target Healthcare,told familiesit will secure a six-month stockpile of Bedrolite, offering temporary relief. However, what happens in six months’ time is anyone’s guess.The possible consequences of epileptic patients such as Louis suffering a forced withdrawal from the medication they use to control their seizures could be severe. The UK government needs to intervene and negotiate with Bedrolite’s manufacturer to secure the supply for all patients who need it in Britain.But beyond this emergency, the UK government needs to stop ignoring the medical cannabis industry and put in place the necessary investment and regulatory frameworks for it to become an accepted prescription on the NHS.Even before the recent bankruptcy of Bedrocan,families and campaignershave been insisting that patients shouldn’t be forced to live at the mercy of the volatile private market, all because politicians are too scared of the negative headlines that might come from mainstreaming a still-stigmatised drug such as cannabis on the NHS.“Health shouldn’t be an issue of whether you are wealthy enough to afford it or even be able to access it,” Louis said to me as we parted. We will see over the next couple of months if the politicians in charge of this country agree.Dr Kojo Koram is professor of law and political economy at Loughborough University and the author of The Next Fix: The Winners and Losers in the Future of DrugsDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
