title: TV tonight: oceanic wonder with David Attenborough in Blue Planet III | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Take the plunge with shrimps, starfish and tawny nurse sharks. Plus, a mysterious, gambling-themed “quiz event” with Bradley Walsh. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Take the plunge with shrimps, starfish and tawny nurse sharks. Plus, a mysterious, gambling-themed “quiz event” with Bradley Walsh. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Arm wrestle … Two shrimps and a starfish prepare for battle on Blue Planet III.Photograph: BBC Studios/Mike VeitchView image in fullscreenArm wrestle … Two shrimps and a starfish prepare for battle on Blue Planet III.Photograph: BBC Studios/Mike VeitchTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: oceanic wonder with David Attenborough in Blue Planet IIITake the plunge with shrimps, starfish and tawny nurse sharks. Plus, a mysterious, gambling-themed “quiz event” with Bradley Walsh. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Jack SealeandHollie RichardsonSun 1 Nov 2026 01.15 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 06.46 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlue Planet III8pm, BBC OneLife is every bit as strange and beautiful at the bottom of the ocean as it is on land – and it is even more profuse. In his 101st year,David Attenboroughis still finding amazing things to show us. The quality of footage the BBC Natural History Unit now records is truly startling. The return of this beloved series begins in tropical seas where constant sunlight stimulates an extraordinary range of life. Look out for the remarkable team-hunting strategies of the tawny nurse sharks, as well as an incredible tussle between a pair of shrimps and a starfish that culminates in the shrimp stealing and eating the starfish’s arm (don’t worry, it grows back). Consistently amazing.Phil HarrisonBBC Young Musician: The Final7pm, BBC TwoViolinist Sofia Demetriades, saxophonist Kezia Colton and recorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni are the three contenders as Petroc Trelawny hosts the climax of the search for the next Nicola Benedetti or Sheku Kanneh-Mason. In the auditorium at Bristol Beacon, the remaining trio must decide: push for that little bit of extra magic in their performance or focus on technical perfection?Jack SealeThis City Is Ours9pm, BBC OneHow far is Michael willing to go to protect Diana? As the third episode of this tense crime drama begins, Michael faces an ultimatum with terrifying ramifications. Elsewhere, the problems are mounting for the Phelans as they search for Banksey. It’s gripping stuff, underpinned by a lead performance of restrained menace by James Nelson-Joyce.PHMortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing9pm, BBC TwoLiving the bream: we’re now in season nine but Bob and Paul’s elegiac riverbank escapades still charm and amuse. This time, there’s a touching Ted tribute which is undermined somewhat by Bob wondering if the deceased dog will “go up or down”. Then, to some fishing: but will Norfolk’s rivers surrender their bounty?PHAdultery9pm, ITV1View image in fullscreenRomola Garai and Andrew Knott in Adultery.Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITVAn illicit weekend away in the Lakes is never going to end well, is it? But that’s the stage Beth (Romola Garai) and Tom (Dominic Cooper) are at with their affair. At home, their kids – who are also dating each other – are also hitting some hurdles. What a mess.Hollie RichardsonBradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot9pm, Channel 4A Bradley Walsh gameshow seems an odd choice for Sunday primetime. In fact, based on the track record of the production company and the lack of information, speculation is mounting that trickery is afoot. For the record, we’re promised a “quiz event” with a million bucks on the line. We might get something else entirely so it’s surely worth tuning in to find out?PHLive sportWomen’s Super League Football: Charlton v Chelsea, 2.15pm, BBC TwoAt The Valley.Premier League Football: Liverpool v Arsenal, 3pm, Sky Sports Main EventNewcastle v Everton is on Mon at 6.30pm.The caption of the Adultery image was amended on 1 November 2026; it shows Andrew Knott, rather than Dominic Cooper as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightDavid AttenboroughfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It’s snow time: the best winter activity holidays in Europe for non-skiers | Winter sports holidays | The Guardian
description: From husky sledding and chasing the northern lights in Lapland to bear-spotting in Transylvania, here’s our pick of wild and magical snowy breaks in Europe
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From husky sledding and chasing the northern lights in Lapland to bear-spotting in Transylvania, here’s our pick of wild and magical snowy breaks in Europe
Content: E-fatbiking through the snowy forests of Ruka in Finland.View image in fullscreenE-fatbiking through the snowy forests of Ruka in Finland.Winter sports holidaysIt’s snow time: the best winter activity holidays in Europe for non-skiersFrom husky sledding and chasing the northern lights in Lapland to bear-spotting in Transylvania, here’s our pick of wild and magical snowy breaks in EuropeFiona KerrSun 1 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArctic thrills and survival skills inFinnish LaplandAt Ruka, the first skiers of the year slalomed down the slopes on 2 October. Just inside the Arctic Circle, Ruka’s long snow-sure season and cosy village atmosphere make it a popular ski resort with Finnish families. The long polar nights mean there are only a few hours of dim twilight each day, but the slopes here are floodlit, so that never stops play.The Narnia-like setting offers just as much action off the runs as on them, and in December the resort launchesRuka Guides, guided adventures from a dedicated activity centre. Spend the morning e-fatbiking through snowy forests (from €90) or cutting a hole in a frozen lake to catch fish (from €89), before learning Arctic survival skills (from €85) or snowshoeing in the evening darkness on the hunt for the northern lights (from €89).Other, more offbeat diversions include floating in a thermal suit down the freezing Kiveskoski river in meditative silence (from €135), whizzing down an alpine coaster at up to 25mph (from €11.88) and practising your sun salutation in the forest surrounded by grazing reindeer (from €45).Dasher and Dancer are a clue to the other reason Ruka is such a hit with children: the main merry man himself. Father Christmas, Mrs Claus and the elves live atSanta’s Cottage, about 30 minutes’ drive from Ruka, where they test how good little helpers are at gingerbread baking and Christmas card making, before those wannabe elves sing Santa’s favourite carol to him in Finnish, post cards at the post office and sledge down the hillside outside (from €105).All activitiesatruka.fi.Rukariutta Superior apartments sleep up to six from €362 a night (rukapalvelu.fi).Lumo Lakeside Lodges sleep up to two adults and two children from €215(rukasafaris.fi)Stargazing in the CairngormsView image in fullscreenThe Tomintoul and Glenlivet area of the Cairngorms is a designated International Dark Sky Park.Photograph: Cairngorms Astronomy GroupIn the depths of winter, the sun sets just a shade after 3.30pm in the Cairngorms national park and doesn’t rise again until about 8.50 the following morning. Those long hours of darkness combined with low levels of light pollution (the area around Tomintoul and Glenlivet is an International Dark Sky Park) makes it the perfect place for stargazing.While it’s easy to be dazzled by the Milky Way without even reaching for a telescope, the Discovery Centre in the village of Tomintoul lends out stargazing kits (pre-booking required) to help visitors delve deeper into the cosmos at one of their recommended viewing sites, such as the nearby Tomintoul Field of Hope, with its purpose-built Skyhide pavilion.The centre is also the meeting point for astronomy events (there is a close-up look at the moon on 18 November and an evening of meteor spotting when the Geminids shower is at its peak around mid-December (suggested donation £7,cairngormsdarkskypark.org).A short drive away, just north of Aviemore, storyteller Sarah Hobbs leads monthlyStargazing Storywalks. The 1½-mile after-dark amble weaves in Gaelic and Pictish tales of the night sky from thousands of years ago, from warrior queens to one-eyed giants, and ends with a cup of foraged wild tea (£20pp, Oct-March). For something a little more strenuous,Hillgoersorganises regular three-mile night walks with certified star rangers, spotting glowing planets and nocturnal wildlife (£40pp, maximum of eight in a group).The Lazy Duckcontinues the dark-sky theme with a clutch of off-grid huts among the pines of the Abernethy Forest with stargazing windows above the beds (from £187 a night in December).There are plenty of winter activities in daylight hours too, from driving theSnowRoads route, which winds along the highest public roads in Britain, to meeting the country’s only free-roaming reindeer herd (guided hill trips run Feb-Dec from £29.40pp,cairngormreindeer.co.uk).Toboggansand glaciers in ChamonixView image in fullscreenThe Grotte de Glace, carved into the Mer de Glace glacier above Chamonix-Mont-Blanc.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyAt the foot of Mont Blanc, Chamonix is famous among skiers for its gnarly off-piste terrain and intense black runs. But that dramatic landscape makes it prime territory for action off the slopes too. One of Responsible Travel’s new trips this season is a four-night self-guided snowshoeing holiday in the Chamonix valley.Using the traditional mountain spa town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains as its base, the itinerary ventures deep into the snow-covered Vallorcine valley, hiking through larch meadows and pine forests, heading up the Flégère gondola to walk along a balcony trail facing Mont Blanc, and taking in the views from the summit of Mont d’Arbois at 1,833 metres.The Mont Blanc massif is one of the most densely glaciated areas in the Alps, and while the ice is receding due to the climate crisis, taking the dinky redMontenverscog train up to the Mer de Glace is still an impressive experience. This huge river of ice winds some 5 miles between the mountains, and at the top a cable car followed by around 200 steps descends into the Grotte de Glace, a blue tunnel carved into the glacier (€49.70 for the train, gondola and ice cave visit).A more intrepid ice-spotting option is Les Contamines-Montjoie circular snowshoeing route, which climbs through pine forests to the Plateau du Truc, with its views of the d’Armancette, Miage and Covagnet glaciers.Back in Chamonix, theMont-Blanc Museumopened in July, tracing the valley’s history and Alpine exploits from the ice age to today, showcasing objects that include memorabilia from the first Winter Olympic Games (held in Chamonix in 1924) and the walking stick of Jacques Balmat, half of the two-man team that made the first ascent of Mont Blanc in 1786. That climb is only for serious mountaineers, but the cable car from Chamonix town centre is a shortcut toAiguille du Midi’s almost-as-impressive 3,842-metre peak (€43 round trip) – leaving plenty of energy to hit the nearby La Luge toboggan run (€23 for the pedestrian lift pass and one descent;ski-saintgervais.com).A four-night self-guided snowshoeing trip in Chamonix from £790pp withResponsible Travel, includingB&B accommodation, route maps, smartphone navigation app, GPS trackers and 24/7 phone supportSnowshoeing and bearspotting in TransylvaniaView image in fullscreenA Eurasian brown bear in Transylvania, Romania.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyHiking along narrow trails in thePiatra raiului national park, you’re more likely to come across bear or wolf tracks than other walkers’ footprints. The Carpathian mountains are one of Europe’s last bastions for large predators – there are thought to be more than 10,000 brown bears and around 2,500 grey wolves in Romania alone.A week-long guided trip with Exodus makes tracks into Transylvania’s dramatic karst landscape, and is an atmospheric introduction to snowshoes and crampons. Base camp is the family-run Villa Hermani guesthouse, over 1,000 metres above sea level in the village of Magura, where there’s always a warming glass of homemadepălincă(fruit brandy) waiting.Hikes climb up to the high ridge of Dealul Măgurice or to the plateau between the Piatra Craiului and Bucegi mountains, where the only thing that might break the silence is the howling of a wolf. One of the most spectacular walks heads along the Zărnești Gorge, its vertical limestone walls rising 200 metres above the icy canyon floor.When not snowshoeing through Christmas-card scenes, take in medieval churches, the cobbled old town of Brașov and the Libearty bear sanctuary, which has rescued over 120 brown bears from the cruelty of captivity. And while Bram Stoker never set foot in Romania, let alone Bran Castle (often said to be the inspiration for Dracula’s lair), you can. With its frosty turrets and towers set against the Carpathians, it looks more gothic than ever, and even better without the bloodthirsty summer crowds.Exodus’s seven-night Transylvania winter walkand snowshoetrip from£1,459pp, including all accommodation, meals, transport and activities, tour guide, snowshoes and polesIgloos and Christmas markets in InnsbruckView image in fullscreenA luxury igloo at Iglu-Dorf, near Innsbruck.Innsbruck is ringed by the Austrian Alps, meaning wherever you wander in the city – among the medieval alleys of the Altstadt or past the colourful houses along the River Inn – snow-covered mountains are the constant backdrop. Those jagged peaks are home to 12 ski areas within 15 to 75 minutes of the city by public transport, and some are worth the trip for the snow-plough-averse too.Zaha Hadid’s swooping, modernist Bergisel ski jump is a dominant sight above the town and the vertiginous view is even better from its observation deck. The architect also designed four of the Nordpark Cable Railway stations that feature fluid glass canopies mimicking natural ice formations and glaciers. They take skiers and non-skiers up to the Nordkette mountains for a bird’s eye view of the Tirolean capital.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere’s plenty more to get pulses racing without clipping on a pair of skis, from bobsleighing down the 1,399-metreOlympic trackat Igls at speeds of up to 115km/h (from €45 for bobrafting, €119 for piloted race bobsleighing) to night sledding atRangger Köpfl(€25). For more icy fun, there are igloos to spend the night in atIglu-Dorfin Kühtai, Austria’s highest ski resort (from €537 for up to three people, including cheese fondue, community sauna and breakfast).Back down in Innsbruck, Christmas market season kicks off in November, and there are seven dotted around the streets and squares, from the historic old town market to the lofty Hungerburg – be sure to trykiachl,a doughnut-like pastry served either savoury with hot sauerkraut, or sweet topped with wild cranberry jam.New skating experienceIce Magicalso launches this winter, with illuminated ice paths connecting different parts of the city, alongside light installations and projections, ice disco nights and DJs (from €8).Nordic ice-skating in SwedenView image in fullscreenIceskating in the Stockholm archipelago.Photograph: Henrik Trygg/Getty ImagesWhile Scandinavians started using animal bones to make primitive ice skates thousands of years ago, wild, or Nordic, skating as we know it (long-distance skating outdoors on natural ice for sport rather than utility) evolved in Sweden in the 1900s. Stockholm’s Skridskoseglarklubb (“Skate Sailing Club”) was formed in 1901 and today has more than 10,000 members, who share the latest ice information online to find the ideal skating locations.Nordic skates have long blades attached only at the front of the boot, used to make long, rhythmic glides; other specialist safety kit includes long, pointy poles to assess ice thickness and a backpack that doubles as a flotation device.Wild is the operative word here, and it is prudent as a beginner to skate with a pro. Stockholm-basedIce Guideruns a number of trips, from one-day introductions to multi-day tours, which head out on to Lake Mälaren or the Baltic Sea in the Stockholm archipelago (from £143 including all gear, transport and lunch).Hellasgården, less than half an hour outside Stockholm, is another popular skate spot with ploughed tracks on Lake Källtorpssjön, and there are holes cut in the ice for the bravest swimmers (and a sauna for after).While in the city centre, get your frozen kicks at the ice rink atKungsträdgården(skate rental about £7.50 an hour) or by joining the boisterous crowd at a Djurgården IF ice hockey match at the Hovet stadium.Ruby Fridaopened this summer and has doubles from £70 room-onlyA foodiewalkin the Dolomites, northern ItalyView image in fullscreenHiking through the Drei Zinnen nature park in the Dolomites.Hearty Tirolean food is made for winter:Knödeldumplings smothered in melted butter and parmesan, the ricotta- and spinach-filled pasta pockets ofSchlutzkrapfen, the cast-iron skillet hash ofBauerngröstl. Hiking through the slopes and valleys of the Dolomites’ Drei Zinnen (Three Peaks) nature park on a week-long trip with self-guided walking holiday specialists Inntravel is a good way to work up an appetite.From the charmingly traditional Hotel Drei Zinnen in the village of Sesto near the Austrian border, a network of 100km of well-groomed, partially cleared paths (meaning no snowshoes required) branches out through the Fischleintal valley and beyond into the nature park.Mountain huts (rifugios) are dotted along routes for a warming lunch: Talschlusshütte serves mountain pine and porcini mushroom risotto and classic comfortingGerstensuppe(barley soup) along the Fischleintal valley walk; while the 100-year-old Dreischusterhütte among the fir trees in the nearby Innerfeldtel valley is much loved for itsKaiserschmarrn(shredded pancake) and homemadeApfelkiachl(fried apple rings).Other routes start with a cable car ride and cut across the snowglobe landscapes of the Kreuzbergpass (stopping for a drink on the terrace at the Klammbach hut, of course) or loop around the banks of the frozen Lake Toblach.Hotel Drei Zinnen has welcomed a fair few winter explorers through its doors since it opened in 1930. One regular guest – the mountaineer and author of Seven Years in Tibet Heinrich Harrer – inspired the hotel’s original owner Hans Watschinger to transform the establishment and the village of Sesto (Sexten in German) into a winter destination. It’s still run by the Watschinger family, and today there’s daily afternoon cake and a Finnish sauna to ease walk-weary muscles, and four-course nightly feasts of Italian favourites and local South Tirolean specialities to fuel up for another day in the mountains.A seven-night Italian Dolomites Winter Walking trip from £1,076, including half-board accommodation, local bus pass and transfers (inntravel.co.uk)Husky sledding, reindeerand thenorthernlightsin NorwayView image in fullscreenFeeding reindeer in Tromsø.For as long as the lights of the aurora borealis have danced across the sky, the people living beneath them have told stories explaining the mysterious, spectral glow – are they omens or gods, communication from spirits or threat of war? For some Sámi communities in northern Scandinavia, they were the souls of the dead, souls that were not to be disturbed by looking, talking, waving or pointing at them, in case the ghostly veil snatched you into the sky or cut off your head.At 217 miles (350km) above the Arctic Circle, Tromsø is the ideal destination for northern lights chasers and learning about the indigenous Sámi people – many of whom still herd reindeer across the vast wilderness.The Oskal family have lived a way of life shaped by reindeer for generations, and their herd spends winter around the camp near Tromsø and summer roaming free in the mountains. The family now share that traditional way of life throughTromsø Arctic Reindeer, opening up their camp to visitors to sled ride, feed the herd and join the family around the fire in thelavvu(tent), forjoik(traditional Sámi song) and perhaps glimpses of the aurora overhead (experiences start at 990 kroner/£75 for reindeer feeding).At the gateway to Norway’s frozen far north, Tromsø is the launchpad for numerous activities – ice fishing and fjord cruising, husky sledding and snowmobile safaris – and the lively university town is interesting in itself. It was once the departure point for expeditions to the north pole – a history captured at thePolar Museumon the harbour front – and today also draws cultural travellers for concerts in the angular Arctic Cathedral and the international film festival in January.Three-night trip to Tromsø from £767pp, including B&B and an aurora-chasing trip, withDiscover the WorldExplore more on these topicsWinter sports holidaysAdventure travelArctic holidaysEurope holidaysWalking holidaysWinter walksMeteorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The kindness of strangers: In 1989 I lost a wallet with $1,000 in it. A couple went to incredible lengths to return it | Backpacking holidays | The Guardian
description: Cash was king in those days, and that money was enough to last me for a month as I slowly travelled from Australia back to the UK
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: Cash was king in those days, and that money was enough to last me for a month as I slowly travelled from Australia back to the UK
Content: ‘It wasn’t until the next morning that I realised the incredible lengths they had gone to in order to return my wallet.’Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It wasn’t until the next morning that I realised the incredible lengths they had gone to in order to return my wallet.’Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty ImagesKindness of strangersBackpacking holidaysThe kindness of strangers: In 1989 I lost a wallet with $1,000 in it. A couple went to incredible lengths to return itCash was king in those days, and that money was enough to last me for a month as I slowly travelled from Australia back to the UKRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesSimon Kelsey as told toKatie CunninghamSun 1 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 17.06 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a hot night in 1989 when my wallet – stuffed with $1,000 cash – fell out of my pocket.After university, I left the UK and went travelling in Australia for a year. I saw the delights of the east coast – mostly from various building sites, as I worked my way around doing long hours in the blistering sun. But I loved every minute of it. After 10 months, I had saved enough to make my way slowly back home.I was enjoying one last night out in Darwin with a gang of traveller friends with whom I was flying to Timor the next day. The intention was to island hop all the way to Singapore.The kindness of strangers: After a tearful breakup dinner, another patron paid our billRead moreCash was king in those days, and the $1,000 I had in my wallet was enough to last me a month on the road. The beers went down easy and I was completely unaware when, at some point in the evening, I lost my wallet. I was still none the wiser when I went to bed to get some sleep before the flight the next morning.At 1.30am, I awoke to a loud knocking on my door. I stumbled out of bed, bleary-eyed, and opened the door to the hostel manager and an elderly couple – who were holding my wallet.That couple had spent hours trawling every backpacker place in Darwin (they’d been to four!) before eventually finding me, care of my student ID card. Every dollar was still there.Still half asleep, and worse for wear after the evening’s drinks, I didn’t fully appreciate the extent of their kindness in the moment. I thanked them and went back to bed, but it wasn’t until the next morning that I realised the incredible lengths they had gone to in order to return my wallet. Without them, my trip would have been ruined.I’ve always wished I could thank them properly, but in lieu of that I made a pledge to myself – and in a way, to them – that I would always go that extra mile to help people when I have the chance.When I do get the opportunity to lend someone a hand, I always tell them to pay it forward. So I like to think that kind couple in Darwin have actually helped countless others, too.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: How to make the perfect venison casserole – recipe | Stew | The Guardian
description: Venison casserole is as autumnal as fallen leaves, a glass of red and a fire in the grate. But who makes the best version?
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Venison casserole is as autumnal as fallen leaves, a glass of red and a fire in the grate. But who makes the best version?
Content: Felicity Cloake's venison casserole 05aPhotograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake's venison casserole 05aPhotograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.How to cook the perfect ...StewHow to make the perfect venison casserole – recipeVenison casserole is as autumnal as fallen leaves, a glass of red and a fire in the grate. But who makes the best version?Felicity CloakeSun 1 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 08.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBecause I don’t eat it very often, I always forget how much I like venison. Or, rather, how much I like it in certain contexts: the natural leanness of a wild animal doesn’t naturally lend itself to soloing in juicy burgers or sausages, but, when slow-cooked, it’s fabulous – rich in flavour, and soft enough to eat with a spoon, should you so desire. It also tends to be good value both in season and frozen for the rest of the year, and, as red meat goes, a pretty climate-friendly option (though not straightforwardly so,as this piece explains) that pairs beautifully with seasonal spuds and kales, and is even better when made ahead of time and reheated. In fact, it’s the perfect autumn and winter entertaining option, even if the only people you’re entertaining are yourselves, the dog and the cast of Celebrity Traitors.The meatFew recipes specify the cut, perhaps because venison is so often sold in chunks, so the assumption is that it’s going to be used for just this purpose, and rarely do the vendors elucidate further than saying the meat is for “stewing” or simply “diced”.Caroline Conran, whose recipe in her 1978 British Cookingis attributed to nameless “ghillies” (Scottish hunting guides), suggests using leg or haunch, whileGary Rhodes is firm in his beliefthat “venison for stewing should come from the haunch, or you can use neck”. Meanwhile,David Eyrecalls for a whole shoulder inThe Eagle Cookbook, which, like the haunch, feels like a great extravagance, even though, in truth, it is my favourite – the shoulder is better marbled than either the haunch or the diced venison I buy, which, once slow-cooked, makes for a richer, stickier result. That said, you can counteract the meat’s leanness by adding other fats, of which more later, so the only cut you should steer clear of, simply because it’s too tender for such treatment, is the saddle.View image in fullscreenJohn William, AKA “the deer man” of Raasay, soaks the meat overnight in “gutsy red wine”. All thumbnail images by Felicity Cloake.John William, “the deer man” of Raasay, whose recipe is includedin Sue Lawrence’s A Taste of the Scottish Islands, soaks the meat overnight in “gutsy red wine”. I cannot speak for Raasay venison, and I imagine William knows what he’s talking about, but my testers and I don’t detect much difference with the wild Devon meat I use. Indeed, chemist Hervé Thisconcludedthat one would have to marinade meat for several days for the alcohol to have a noticeably tenderising effect, while the flavour penetration of any marinade is mere millimetres. By all means, marinate if you like, then, but I think you’re better off trusting in the mingling of flavours that takes place in the pot.Rhodes tells readers of his book More Rhodes Around Britain that, “I like to cut the meat into large pieces rather than dice. It takes a little longer to cook, but the texture and taste are better.” Sceptical though I am that it will cook through, after trialling it I find myself inclined to agree; two-bite chunks remain juicier in the middle.The vegetablesEveryone starts their stew with onions (though you could use shallots instead, not least because their sweetness would be welcome here), but after that is where the recipes start to diverge. Rhodes and Eyre go for a classic triumvirate with carrot and celery, and the latter, like William, also includes leek. Clarissa Dickson Wright champions beetroot,writing in the Game Cookbookshe co-authored with Johnny Scott that “the brilliant food writer Claire Macdonald discovered there is an enzyme in [it] that breaks down the fibres in venison. When I was staying at Kinloch Lodge, the blissful hotel on Skye, she told me it would tenderise even the toughest old stag.” Again, wild animals are particularly hard to generalise about, especially one that might be anything from a 9kg muntjac to an 190kg red deer, but, on this evidence, I wouldn’t be rushing to add chunks of beetroot for anything other than flavour – its sweet earthiness is delicious with the meat.View image in fullscreenClarissa Dickson-Wright’s venison casserole features lots of beetroot, because it helps break down enzymes and ‘would tenderise even the toughest old stag’.Indeed, I’m going to focus on sweetness: even more than beetroot, we love the fruitiness of boththe prunes in the Claire Macdonald Game Cookbook, and Clarissa Dickson Wright’s redcurrant jelly (in truth, most fruity jellies would work, should you have something similar hanging out in the cupboard). And if you’re a fan of sweet-and-sour combinations, may I encourage you to consider popping in some of Macdonald’s pickled walnuts as well – as one of my testers put it, along with the prunes, they “completely blended into the gravy and gave it a lovely richness and depth of flavour – neither too sweet nor too salty”.I like to include as many vegetables in a casserole as possible, hence the onions, carrots and leek here, all of which will echo the sweetness of the prunes and preserve. If rich, sweet and savoury doesn’t appeal, bear William’s recipe in mind; with its chopped red pepper and tomatoes, it has a lighter, more southern feel, though if you do go down that road, maybe add some of Eyre’s garlic, too (I’d be tempted to include a glug of red wine to beef it out a bit as well, but then I don’t know the meaning of the world light).The seasoningThough bacon might seem to belong in the “meat” paragraph above, it’s purely here for its delicious, savoury fat, fat that the free-roaming deer hasn’t had the chance to build up on its wild perambulations. If you don’t care for pork, an extra slug of oil, plus a dash of William’s Worcestershire sauce, should prove a satisfactory replacement.Rhodes adds bay, Dickson Wright and Eyre thyme, Eyre parsley stalks and Conran juniper berries, a classic seasoning for venison and one that I love. But seeing as we already have the jelly, I’ve stuck with thyme here, because I think its austere, savoury aromatic quality works with fruit and meat.The liquidDickson Wright, who probably couldn’t move for deer carcasses and pheasant skeletons while writing her Game Cookbook, instructs me to make a game stock, which drives the dog wild for the hour it takes in the pressure cooker (expert guidance viaCatherine Phipps’ excellent Modern Pressure Cooking). Should you also have bones going to waste, it’s worth your while doing the same, though both the beef stock in Conran’s recipe and the vegetable version in Macdonald’s won’t do any harm, and we don’t find we miss anything in Eyre’s version, which tops up red wine with water.View image in fullscreenClaire Macdonald’s twice-cooked version features prunes and pickled walnuts.Wine, in fact, features in almost every recipe, and with good reason: its fruit, acidity and tannins combine with the browned meat and bacon to produce a richly savoury sauce. If you’d prefer to leave it out, use the same amount of beef stock and add either a glass of port, as Conran does, or an extra spoonful of redcurrant jelly and a squeeze of lemon. You’ll notice I’ve been generous with the quantity, because a couple of the recipes I try don’t have enough gravy for my testers’ liking – and what’s the point of a casserole without gravy, as one tartly (and ungratefully) observes.The cookingEveryone except Conran bakes their casseroles – you can, of course, use the hob for the recipe below, but I find it much easier to keep things at a constant low simmer in the oven. To my surprise, the venison doesn’t need as long as I’d imagined either: two hours at 160C proves quite sufficient for both Eyre and Dickson Wright’s offerings, and though you can stick it in a very low oven overnight, as William recommends (no doubt particularly useful if you have an AGA or similar), there’s really no need. In the interests of making the most of the fuel, I’d strongly urge you to consider baking some potatoes at the same time.View image in fullscreenDavid Eyre’s venison and pancetta casserole calls for a whole shoulder of venison, ‘which feels like a great extravagance’.A final piece of advice: should you have the luxury of time, Macdonald’s tip that “twice cooking is almost obligatory for casseroles; the flavours are vastly better than if the casserole is made and eaten straight away”, is a good one. Take it out of the oven after 90 minutes, then, when you’re ready to eat it the next day or the day afterwards, put it back in there at the same temperature for half an hour. It also freezes well.Prep20 minCook2½ hrServes4100g streaky bacon800g venison, preferably boned shoulder, if available2 tbsp neutral oil, or lard or dripping2 tbsp plain flourSalt and black pepper1 large onion, peeled and chopped1 leek, trimmed, washed and chunkily sliced1 carrot, coarsely diced2 sprigsfresh thyme, or ½ tsp dried thymefr300ml red wine8 stoned soft prunes, halved1 tbsp redcurrant jelly, or other fruit jellyHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Chop the bacon into wide pieces. Drain any liquid from the venison and, if it isn’t already diced, cut it into large, two-bite chunks.View image in fullscreenHeat the oil in an ovenproof casserole dish for which you have a lid on a medium-high flame.Fry the bacon in the hot fat until it releases its fat and begins to turn golden.View image in fullscreenMeanwhile, toss the venison with the flour and a good pinch of salt and pepper.View image in fullscreenScoop out the bacon with a slotted spoon and put in a large bowl, then add a few pieces of the venison and brown on all sides – don’t overcrowd the pan or you won’t achieve that deep, brown colour that brings with it such flavour. Scoop each batch out as soon as it’s done and add to the bacon bowl.View image in fullscreenWhen all the venison is browned, turn down the heat to medium-low and add the onion, leek, carrot and a pinch of salt. Fry, stirring regularly, until the veg have softened and are starting to colour; stir in the thyme towards the end.View image in fullscreenScoop the vegetables into the meat bowl, then add a splash of wine to the pan, and stir to dislodge and dissolve any bits from the base.View image in fullscreenStir in the prunes and fruit jelly, then return the meat and vegetables to the pan, and add the rest of the wine and just enough water mostly to cover the meat – a few bits will stick out of the top like icebergs, but, without knowing the diameter of your pan, it’s impossible to give a precise amount of water.View image in fullscreenBring to a simmer, then cover and put in the oven for 90 minutes if making ahead of time, or two hours if serving immediately. If reheating later, return the stew to the oven and cook at the same temperature for 30 minutes. Check the seasoning, stir in a little extra water if it’s too dry for your liking, then serve with mashed potato and greens.Venison – love it, hate it, or somewhere in between? Is it theethical red meat, or is thispure greenwashing and speciesism, as Peta claims? Why don’t we eat more of it in this country (Bambi?) and, if you love it, what’s your favourite way to prepare it?Explore more on these topicsStewHow to cook the perfect ...GameFoodMeatWinter food and drinkAutumn food and drinkClarissa Dickson WrightrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Moods, Leeds LS2: ‘Puzzling, if not quite a car crash’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: The crumpet has the texture of a damp Always Ultra
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The crumpet has the texture of a damp Always Ultra
Content: Moods, Leeds: ‘An all-day restaurant and bar with a tattoo parlour and hair salon attached.’Photograph: Shaw & Shaw/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMoods, Leeds: ‘An all-day restaurant and bar with a tattoo parlour and hair salon attached.’Photograph: Shaw & Shaw/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewMoods, Leeds LS2: ‘Puzzling, if not quite a car crash’ – restaurant reviewThe crumpet has the texture of a damp Always UltraGrace DentSun 1 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 07.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve done some fairly rash things in my time, but I’ve never popped into anywhere for king scallops with ’nduja and come out with a swallow tattoo on my neck, though what is this life without adventure? Which is whereMoodscomes in: the space is an all-day restaurant, bar, tattoo parlour and hair salon in Leeds, offering violetta potato with ox cheek, a short back and sides, and the chance to tattoo “Mum” on your lower left arm, all in one Grade II-listed building.It occupies the former First White Cloth Hall on Kirkgate, built in 1711 for the trade of white undyed cloth. This cavernous ark, with roof timbers dating back to the 1470s, lurked on Historic England’sHeritage at Risk registerfor more than 20 years, during which time it was under almost constant threat from the bulldozers. It tookthe National Lottery Heritage Fund,Leeds Civic TrustandRushbond, a Leeds-based developer with a penchant for rescuing buildings, to drag it out of danger. Then Will and Hayley Moody arrived, slotting in theirBuzz Club Tattoo Studioand ahair and beauty salon called Self, and now, on the ground floor, there’s Moods, a kitchen reportedly run by Craig Rogan. Laugh at the tattoo/hair/dinner triumvirate, if you want (I know I did), but it’s a grim joke that we treat our old buildings like this, and that hospitality is in a state so wild thatthisseems to be the solution. Bring on the bright new future of ye olde small plates, buzzcuts and half-sleeve emporiums, all under 400-year-old timbers.View image in fullscreen‘If there are traces of the advertised yuzu and dill in here, they are destroyed by the sheer volume of cream’: Moods’ oak-smoked salmon with rye bread.Moods is incredibly cool, which I know immediately because of the gorgeous amounts of disdain with which I’m treated by the receptionist when I pop by at 2.30pm to try the all-day menu. She looks at me bamboozled, as many Gen Z-ers do, as if I have announced myself as an intergalactic equerry from Zarg requesting the keys to a plutonium source. Eventually, I’m tucked away by a wooden dresser that’s used as a base for cleaning supplies and cutlery. Only 42 other better tables are lying empty.The all-day menu looks rather fabulous, though. There is a wild mushroomcrumpetwith Old Winchester and black truffle honey at £14. There is mead-glazed pancetta with potato rösti and mushroom ketchup, as well as fried chicken brioche with elderflower and pickled cucumber. And all of it cooked by Rogan,Simon Rogan’s son, trained by his father atL’Enclumeand atFera at Claridge’s. He’s channelling this greatness via osmosis; I can smell it in the air. Well, that and Jangro spray sanitiser.View image in fullscreenMoods’ post-noon brunch menu looks ‘rather fabulous’ and includes the likes of salt-baked beetroot salad.Doubtless Moods is a fabulous place to drink cocktails at the long open bar in the centre of the room, where the signature peach melba comes with caramelised peach vodka and ice-cream foam. But the food proper turns out to be more of an uphill struggle. I order that crumpet, envisioning ceps, girolles, perhaps a random morel, on a home-baked sourdough crumpet with good butter. What arrives resembles nothing so much a Warburtons Giant Crumpet topped with chopped chestnut mushrooms fried in butter and a few herbs, and a big handful of cress. The buttery mushroom liquor has soaked into the crumpet while it waited, and it now has the texture of a damp Always Ultra. And where is the Old Winchester?Next up, oak-smoked salmon with rye bread for £16: two tiny triangles of fish are draped over a shedload of creme fraiche– at least seven tablespoons of the stuff –a bit of roughly chopped kohlrabi, long pieces of chopped apple and yet more cress. If there are traces of the advertised yuzu and dill in here, they are destroyed by the sheer volume of cream. It is puzzling, if not quite a car crash. Then again, I was in an actual car crash once, and I definitely enjoyed theSugar Puffsthey gave me with my 10am discharge papers a lot more.View image in fullscreen‘Channelling Simon Rogan’s greatness via osmosis’: Moods’ lemon raspberry muffin.Writing all this off as a bad start, I return the next morning for breakfast, hoping to make more sense of the place. From the outset, things do not look good. Breakfast, a staff member mutters, doesn’t start until 10am, even though the doors open at eight, the music is on, the coffee machine is on and the cakes are being unloaded. There are also at least 11 staff bumbling about. How about just a coffee then, I ask. A white americano, please? God, I’m needy. By this point, I’m reducing myself to a small speck of a woman the size of a postage stamp, and I’m upsetting nobody. A black americano arrives, and then someone takes pity and allows me to order porridge, which turns up half cooked with a ramekin of what they call bramble preserve (AKA blackberry jam). I ask brightly if I might meet the famous chef, mainly out of mischief, but he’s not here. I might go back when the place is in a better mood.Moods98 Kirkgate, Leeds LS2, 0113-390 4552. Open all week, brunch 8am-4pm, bar small plates noon-9pm. Brunch from about £15 a head; bar small plates from about £8 each, all plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content
